boundaries.barrio_km2.plain: The area of the barrio polygon in square kilometers. It is measured by the observatory on the shoreline-clipped shape, not taken from the Census Bureau.
boundaries.barrio_km2.plain_es: El área del polígono del barrio en kilómetros cuadrados. La mide el observatorio sobre la forma recortada en la línea de costa; no viene del Negociado del Censo.
boundaries.barrio_km2.definition: Area of the unsimplified shoreline-clipped polygon, in km², rounded to 2 decimals: polygon area in square degrees x (111.32 x cos(latitude of the centroid)) x 110.57.
boundaries.barrio_km2.method: build_barrios in landuse.py computes it from the polygon before simplification. It is a local approximation that ignores the curve of the Earth; it is good enough to compare barrios.
boundaries.barrio_km2.how_to_read: Use it as the denominator for places per km². It can include a little inland water. With boundaries as of January 1, 2023, the 901 values add up to 8,916 km² and run from 0.09 km² (the barrio Toa Alta, in Toa Alta) to 64.08 km² (Lapa, in Salinas).
caveats: It is not the Census Bureau's land area. The shoreline polygons keep some inland water, so a municipality's barrio areas can add up to more or less than its Census land area (with 2023 boundaries: Carolina +5.1%, Salinas -1.1%, Mayagüez -1.0%).
The area is an approximation, not a survey measurement.

boundaries.barrio_geoid.plain: A ten-digit Census code that identifies the barrio: 72 for Puerto Rico, three digits for the municipality and five digits for the barrio. It is unique, so use it to join data.
boundaries.barrio_geoid.plain_es: Un código censal de diez dígitos que identifica el barrio: 72 para Puerto Rico, tres dígitos para el municipio y cinco para el barrio. Es único, así que úselo para unir datos.
boundaries.barrio_geoid.definition: The geoid of the Census county subdivision: state code 72 (2 digits), municipality code (3 digits) and county subdivision code (5 digits). All 901 values are different and all start with the GEOID of the municipality.
boundaries.barrio_geoid.how_to_read: Use it to join to Census Bureau tables for county subdivisions. The field is spelled geoid in lower case here and GEOID in the municipality file.
caveats: Keep it as text, as the Census Bureau does. If one table holds the code as text and the other as a number, a join will not match.
Codes follow the Census boundaries as of January 1, 2023; a later release may change a code or split a barrio.
boundaries.barrio_geoid.source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD layer 7, field GEOID

boundaries.barrio_name.plain: The name of the barrio without the word barrio. Names repeat: the same name appears in several municipalities, and a town-center barrio-pueblo can share its name with the barrio around it. Use the code to tell them apart.
boundaries.barrio_name.plain_es: El nombre del barrio sin la palabra barrio. Los nombres se repiten: el mismo nombre aparece en varios municipios, y un barrio-pueblo (el centro del pueblo) puede llamarse igual que el barrio que lo rodea. Use el código para distinguirlos.
boundaries.barrio_name.definition: BASENAME from the Census Bureau's county subdivision layer. With boundaries as of January 1, 2023, the 901 barrios have 694 different names. Six municipalities (Lajas, Hatillo, Orocovis, Canóvanas, Lares, Hormigueros) have two barrios with the same name; in Lajas they are Lajas barrio and Lajas barrio-pueblo.
boundaries.barrio_name.method: Copied from the Census layer. The full Census name (with barrio or barrio-pueblo) is not kept in the published file.
boundaries.barrio_name.how_to_read: Pair the name with the municipality, or better, use the geoid.
caveats: Names alone are not unique, even inside one municipality.

With boundaries as of January 1, 2023, 79 of the 901 barrios, in 73 municipalities, have the same name as their municipality (for example Cabo Rojo, Luquillo, Dorado). In 73 of them this is the barrio-pueblo that holds the town. In six municipalities (Hatillo, Orocovis, Lares, Canóvanas, Lajas, Hormigueros) it is also the name of the ordinary barrio next to the barrio-pueblo. The barrio type comes from the Census layer; the published file does not carry it.
boundaries.barrio_name.source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD layer 7, field BASENAME

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Barrios (click inside a barrio)

boundaries.barrios.plain: The 901 barrios of Puerto Rico, the sub-municipal districts the Census Bureau calls county subdivisions, with counts of tourism places inside each one. The map draws them as dashed outlines you can click.
boundaries.barrios.plain_es: Los 901 barrios de Puerto Rico, las divisiones dentro de cada municipio que el Negociado del Censo llama subdivisiones de condado (county subdivisions), con la cantidad de lugares turísticos en cada uno. El mapa los dibuja con contornos de línea discontinua en los que se puede hacer clic.
boundaries.barrios.definition: The file barrios.geojson holds 901 shapes in the 78 municipalities. Each is a county subdivision from the US Census Bureau's generalized layer (a version with simplified edges, made for maps at a scale of 1:500,000), with boundaries as of January 1, 2023, cut at the shoreline. In the Census layer 827 are barrios and 74 are barrios-pueblo, the barrio that holds a town center. The file itself does not mark which is which. The observatory adds eleven attributes: name, municipality, Census code, area, six counts of tourism places and one density.
boundaries.barrios.method: build_barrios in landuse.py pages TIGERweb layer 7 (county subdivisions) for state code 72, keeps each polygon's name and code, counts the tourism places inside each polygon, simplifies the polygon for display (tolerance 0.0003 degrees, about 33 m) and rounds coordinates to 5 decimals. Area is measured on the unsimplified polygon. See boundaries.barrio_selection and boundaries.barrio_stats.
boundaries.barrios.how_to_read: Click a barrio on the map for its area, tourism places, places per km², places in a flood hazard area, places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable (and of a frequent stop) and places within 400 m of any mapped stop. The lodging count is in barrios.geojson only. Compare barrios by places per km², not by raw counts: with boundaries as of January 1, 2023, areas run from 0.09 to 64 km².
caveats: A barrio is a Census statistical unit. It is not a neighborhood, a community (comunidad) or an electoral unit, and its edges do not follow the street grid.
Barrio names repeat. Use the code (geoid) to tell barrios apart; see boundaries.barrio_name.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 325 of the 24,209 counted tourism places (1.3%) have a pin outside every barrio polygon, so barrio counts add up to less than the municipality counts. Almost all are pins at or just off the coast. Measured on the original (unsimplified) shapes, 323 of the 325 lie outside the shoreline polygons of the municipalities. Measured on the published shapes, about 290 are within 100 m of a barrio polygon.
The outlines are the Census Bureau's Generalized ACS 2023 version, with boundaries as of January 1, 2023. They are not 2020 Census boundaries; cite them as 2023.
The file calls the place count assets. It counts listed tourism places, not financial or physical assets, and not other kinds of business.
Counts describe listings in Overture Maps, not visitors, sales or capacity.
boundaries.barrios.geography: 901 barrios in 78 municipalities, from 1 barrio in Florida to 31 in Ponce. 892 shapes are one polygon; 9 have several parts (Cabezas, Machos, Arecibo, Flamenco, Playa, San Isidro, Fraile, Sabanetas, Palo Seco).
boundaries.barrios.source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD MapServer layer 7 (County Subdivisions 500K, https://tigerweb.geo.census.gov/arcgis/rest/services/Generalized_ACS2023/Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD/MapServer/7). The count of 827 barrios and 74 barrios-pueblo comes from the layer's LSADC field (legal/statistical area description code, read on 2026-10-03); barrios.geojson does not carry that field.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Barrios (click inside a barrio)

boundaries.barrio_municipality.plain: The municipality the barrio belongs to, spelled the way the observatory spells it.
boundaries.barrio_municipality.plain_es: El municipio al que pertenece el barrio, escrito como lo escribe el observatorio.
boundaries.barrio_municipality.definition: The first five digits of the barrio's geoid identify its municipality. The build converts that code to the observatory's municipality name using the 2020 Census county layer. Every barrio has a municipality; all 78 municipalities have at least one barrio.
boundaries.barrio_municipality.method: build_barrios in landuse.py looks the code up in a table from municipality code to name made in build.py (fips_to_muni).
boundaries.barrio_municipality.how_to_read: Use it to group barrios by municipality. It is set by the Census code, not by where tourism places sit.
caveats: A barrio sits wholly in one municipality. Tourism places near a municipality line can be listed under the neighboring municipality in places.json.
boundaries.barrio_municipality.source_detail: Census Bureau code (GEOID, first five digits) matched to the municipality list

boundaries.barrio_stats.plain: Barrio counts add up tourism places. They use the same place list and filters as the municipality statistics: places from Overture Maps (an open map database) with a confidence score of 0.50 or higher, without places of worship. A place counts in the barrio whose polygon contains its map pin.
boundaries.barrio_stats.plain_es: Los conteos por barrio suman lugares turísticos. Usan la misma lista de lugares y los mismos filtros que las estadísticas por municipio: lugares de Overture Maps (una base de datos abierta de mapas) con una puntuación de confianza de 0.50 o más, sin lugares de culto. Un lugar cuenta en el barrio cuyo polígono contiene su marcador.
boundaries.barrio_stats.definition: Place basis: listings in places.json with confidence of 0.50 or more and a type other than Places of Worship. A pin is the latitude and longitude of the listing in the source. A place counts in the barrio whose polygon contains its pin; a place whose pin lies inside no barrio polygon is not counted in any barrio. For each counted place the barrio gets six tallies. assets: one for every place. sfha: one if the place lies in a Special Flood Hazard Area of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). transit: one if the nearest mapped stop of any kind (stop, bus station, rail station or ferry terminal) is 400 m or less away in a straight line. lodging: one if the place is in the ACCOMMODATIONS category. acc_cur400: one if the nearest stop with a current timetable is 400 m or less away. acc_freq400: one if that is so and the busiest stop with a current timetable within 400 m has 20 or more weekday calls. km2 is the polygon area. assets_per_km2 is assets divided by km2.
boundaries.barrio_stats.method: build_barrios in landuse.py tests each place against the unsimplified barrio polygons with a within test and uses the first polygon found. The place's barrio name is also written to places.json:barrio. km2 = polygon area in square degrees x (111.32 x cos(latitude of the centroid)) x 110.57, which treats the polygon as flat and scales it for its latitude (see boundaries.barrio_km2). assets_per_km2 uses the unrounded area and is rounded to 2 decimals.
boundaries.barrio_stats.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the basis is 24,209 places island-wide. Of these, 23,884 have a pin inside a barrio polygon and are counted, and 325 (1.3%) have a pin inside none. Barrio totals are close to, but not equal to, municipality totals. In municipalities.json, 41 municipalities have more places than their barrios add up to, one has one fewer, and 36 match. San Juan differs most (3,424 places against 3,373 in its barrios).
caveats: A barrio's municipality comes from its Census code; a place's municipality in places.json comes from the municipality polygon. A place near a boundary can therefore be in one municipality and in a barrio of the next. In the 2026-10 snapshot, this is why Caguas shows one more place in its barrios (840) than in its municipality total (839): one place filed under San Lorenzo falls in a Caguas barrio.

The file calls the place count assets. It counts listed places, not financial or physical assets. Only listings the observatory classes as gastronomy, attractions, accommodations or visitor services are counted; other businesses are not.
The count of places with a mapped transit stop (transit) includes stops from expired timetables and volunteer-mapped stops. The counts acc_cur400 and acc_freq400 leave them out.
These are counts of listed places. They do not measure visitors, spending, building area or flood damage.

The barrio counts keep the values of the last full build. The nightly refresh updates places.json and municipalities.json but not barrios.geojson, so between full builds the barrio transit counts can lag them. In the 2026-10 snapshot the three transit counts equal the counts of the places of each barrio in places.json and place_access.json.
boundaries.barrio_stats.source_detail: Overture Maps places; FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer (SFHA_TF = T); transit stops from the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and municipal timetable feeds (General Transit Feed Specification, GTFS) and from OpenStreetMap; Census TIGERweb county subdivisions

boundaries.barrio_selection.plain: The observatory uses the Census Bureau's county subdivisions as barrios. They are a US Government work with no US copyright, and each has a unique 10-digit Census code. The observatory does not use data from the Centro de Recaudación de Ingresos Municipales (CRIM, the Municipal Revenue Collection Center), because the license text on its services restricts redistribution.
boundaries.barrio_selection.plain_es: El observatorio usa como barrios las subdivisiones de condado del Negociado del Censo. Son una obra del Gobierno de Estados Unidos sin derechos de autor en ese país, y cada una tiene un código censal único de 10 dígitos. El observatorio no usa datos del Centro de Recaudación de Ingresos Municipales (CRIM), porque el texto de la licencia de sus servicios limita la redistribución.
boundaries.barrio_selection.definition: Barrios are the county subdivisions of Puerto Rico in the Census Bureau's generalized layer (TIGERweb Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD, layer 7), selected with the filter STATE = 72. For boundaries as of January 1, 2023, the query returns 901 features of two types: barrio and barrio-pueblo. The Census Bureau also defines finer units (subbarrios) in a separate layer; the observatory does not use them.
boundaries.barrio_selection.method: fetch_barrios in landuse.py requests the layer in pages of 500 features with the fields GEOID and BASENAME and keeps the result for later builds, which download it again only when run with the refresh option.
boundaries.barrio_selection.how_to_read: Treat the 901 barrios as Census units. If you need the barrio list that a municipal or planning office uses, check that office's own list; it may differ.
caveats: CRIM's administrative boundaries layer lists 902 barrios (read on 2026-10-01); the Census layer has 901.
Of the 74 barrios-pueblo (town centers), 73 are named like their municipality. In six municipalities the barrio around the town has the same name as the barrio-pueblo, for example Lajas.
boundaries.barrio_selection.source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD MapServer layer 7 (https://tigerweb.geo.census.gov/arcgis/rest/services/Generalized_ACS2023/Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD/MapServer/7). The split into 827 barrios and 74 barrios-pueblo comes from the Census LSADC field (legal/statistical area description code), read from the layer on 2026-10-03; barrios.geojson does not carry that field. The CRIM license text was read on 2026-10-01 in the license information of its Catastro Digital service items.

boundaries.shoreline_clipped.plain: The observatory draws municipalities and barrios up to the shoreline, not out to sea. The Census Bureau's legal 2020 boundaries run into the ocean, so using them would put offshore points inside a municipality and count sea as part of its area.
boundaries.shoreline_clipped.plain_es: El observatorio dibuja los municipios y los barrios hasta la línea de costa, no mar adentro. Los límites legales de 2020 del Negociado del Censo se extienden al océano, así que usarlos pondría puntos en el mar dentro de un municipio y contaría el mar como parte de su área.
boundaries.shoreline_clipped.definition: The 2020 Census county layer holds legal boundaries. They extend into coastal water, typically about 3 nautical miles (5.6 km) offshore. Across the 78 municipalities the layer's own fields report about 8,870 km² of land and 4,920 km² of water, and its polygons enclose about 13,800 km². The generalized 500k layer used for display, for municipality lookup and for barrios is cut at the shoreline; its polygons enclose about 8,900 km².
boundaries.shoreline_clipped.method: Shoreline-clipped polygons (Generalized_ACS2023 layers) are used for the map, for placing every tourism place in a municipality, and for the barrio layer. The 2020 county layer (legal boundaries) is read only for its attributes: POP100, HU100 and, in municipalities.json, land_km2. A place whose pin lies outside every shoreline polygon is given the municipality whose polygon is nearest (muni_locate.py, called by make_muni_locator in build.py). Until the 2026-11 fix it was given the municipality with the nearest center point in municipalities.py. In the barrio layer such a place is not counted.
boundaries.shoreline_clipped.how_to_read: Municipality land areas (AREALAND, land_km2) count land only. Barrio areas (km2) are polygon areas that stop at the shoreline and can include some inland water. If you need a boundary that includes coastal waters, use the Census Bureau's full-resolution 2020 boundaries, not this file.
caveats: The shoreline polygons still hold some inland water such as rivers and lagoons, and the barrio area is a local approximation. With the 2023 boundaries, the 901 barrio areas add up to 8,916 km², 0.5% above the Census land area (8,869 km²). By municipality, the barrio areas add up to between 1.1% below the Census land area (Salinas) and 5.1% above it (Carolina: 123.5 km² of barrio area against 117.5 km² of land).

Pins just off the coast, such as on piers, can fall outside every polygon. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 324 of the 24,209 counted places (1.3%) fall outside every municipality polygon and took the municipality with the nearest center point (the next full build gives them the nearest polygon instead), and 325 fall outside every barrio polygon and are left out of the barrio counts; 323 places are in both groups.
The Census Bureau's own land area (AREALAND) is a separate figure from polygon area; see boundaries.municipio_land_area.
boundaries.shoreline_clipped.source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 and Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD layer 7 (shoreline-clipped); tigerWMS_Census2020 layer 82 (legal boundaries). Areas in the text are sums over the 78 municipalities.

boundaries.display_copies.plain: The shapes published for the maps are simplified copies. They are fine for drawing, not for measuring. The build does its place counts and barrio areas on the original shapes, and takes land-use areas from the Plan's own area attribute.
boundaries.display_copies.plain_es: Las formas que se publican para los mapas son copias simplificadas. Sirven para dibujar, no para medir. La compilación de los datos hace los conteos de lugares y las áreas de los barrios con las formas originales, y toma las áreas de uso de terrenos del atributo de área del propio Plan.
boundaries.display_copies.definition: Each layer is simplified before it is published, with a tolerance in degrees (1 degree of latitude is about 111 km) and rounded coordinates. Municipalities: tolerance 0.0002 degrees (about 22 m), up to 6 decimals. Barrios: 0.0003 degrees (about 33 m), 5 decimals. Land use (Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015): 0.001 degrees (about 110 m), 4 decimals. Simplification removes detail and keeps each shape valid (it does not cross itself).
boundaries.display_copies.method: build.py (simplify_fc) and landuse.py (build_barrios, build_landuse) call the Shapely simplify function with preserve_topology=True, which keeps each shape valid but does not keep it aligned with its neighbors. Tests of whether a place's pin lies inside a shape use the full-detail shapes. Land-use area shares use the Plan layer's Shape_Area attribute, not the polygons. Barrio km² is measured on the full-detail barrio polygon. The 2D map leaves water and road polygons out of its drawing; the file keeps them.
boundaries.display_copies.how_to_read: If you measure an area or a distance on the published polygons, expect errors of the size of the tolerance. For the land-use layer that is about 110 m, which is large for small parcels.
caveats: Small islands, narrow strips and thin barrios lose detail.
Each shape is simplified on its own, so neighboring shapes can show thin gaps or overlaps along shared edges.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, a recount on the published barrio shapes does not match the observatory's counts. Of the 24,209 places, it puts 365 in no barrio (the observatory's count is 325), 17 in two barrios and 96 in a different barrio. Use the published counts, not a recount.
Numbers in the dictionary that come from the Plan layer's own area attribute will not match an area measured on the published polygons.
boundaries.display_copies.source_detail: Code: build.py simplify_fc; landuse.py build_barrios, build_landuse

geo.blockgroups_layer.plain: The outlines of the census block groups, the Census Bureau's smallest areas for survey estimates, about 1,200 residents each, drawn in a simplified form. No page draws them yet.
geo.blockgroups_layer.plain_es: Los contornos de los grupos de bloques, las áreas más pequeñas del Negociado del Censo con estimados de encuesta, de unas 1,200 personas residentes cada una, dibujados de forma simplificada. Ninguna página los dibuja todavía.
geo.blockgroups_layer.definition: The file geo/blockgroups.geojson holds 2,513 shapes, one for each of the 2,555 block groups of the 2020 Census that has land. The other 42 are all water, with no land, residents or housing units, and have no outline. Each shape has one property, GEOID, the block group's 12-digit id; names, counts and areas are in the crosswalk. The shapes are the Census Bureau's cartographic boundary file at 1:500,000, clipped to a simplified outline of the coast.
geo.blockgroups_layer.method: geo.py reads cb_2020_72_bg_500k.zip, keeps the GEOID and rounds coordinates to 5 decimals (about 1 m). The shapes come in NAD83 longitude and latitude, which the observatory treats as WGS 84.
geo.blockgroups_layer.how_to_read: Join to the crosswalk by GEOID to name a block group and give its counts. Draw the outlines; do not measure them.
caveats: For drawing only. The Census Bureau says these files 'should not be used for: geographic analysis including area or perimeter calculation'. Use the crosswalk's land area.
Survey estimates for block groups are rough: see methods.small_area_estimates.
A block group is a statistical area of the Census, not a neighborhood.
geo.blockgroups_layer.geography: 2,513 of the 2,555 block groups of Puerto Rico

geo.tracts_layer.plain: The outlines of the census tracts, the Census Bureau's small areas of about 3,300 residents each, drawn in a simplified form. No page draws them yet.
geo.tracts_layer.plain_es: Los contornos de los sectores censales, las áreas pequeñas del Negociado del Censo de unas 3,300 personas residentes cada una, dibujados de forma simplificada. Ninguna página los dibuja todavía.
geo.tracts_layer.definition: The file geo/tracts.geojson holds 939 shapes, one for each of the 981 census tracts of the 2020 Census that has land. The other 42 tracts are all water, with no land, residents or housing units, and have no outline. Each shape has one property, GEOID, the tract's 11-digit id; names, counts and areas are in the crosswalk. The shapes are the Census Bureau's cartographic boundary file at 1:500,000, clipped to a simplified outline of the coast.
geo.tracts_layer.method: geo.py reads cb_2020_72_tract_500k.zip, keeps the GEOID and rounds coordinates to 5 decimals (about 1 m). The shapes come in NAD83 longitude and latitude, which the observatory treats as WGS 84 (they differ by about a meter).
geo.tracts_layer.how_to_read: Join to the crosswalk by GEOID to name a tract and give its counts. Draw the outlines; do not measure them.
caveats: For drawing only. The Census Bureau says these files 'should not be used for: geographic analysis including area or perimeter calculation'. Use the crosswalk's land area.
The coast is simplified, so an outline can differ from the coast on the base map by tens of meters, and offshore areas are missing.
A tract is a statistical area of the Census, not a neighborhood.
geo.tracts_layer.geography: 939 of the 981 census tracts of Puerto Rico

geo.weights_barrio_tract.plain: For each barrio, how many residents and housing units lie in each census tract it touches. It lets a count known for tracts be spread over barrios, or the reverse, because the two do not fit one inside the other.
geo.weights_barrio_tract.plain_es: Para cada barrio, cuántas personas residentes y unidades de vivienda quedan en cada sector censal que toca. Permite repartir entre los barrios un conteo conocido por sectores censales, o al revés, porque unos no caben exactamente dentro de los otros.
geo.weights_barrio_tract.definition: weights.barrio_tract in geo/crosswalk.json: one row for each pair of a barrio and a tract that share at least one census block with residents or housing units, with five values: barrio id, tract id, residents, housing units and number of blocks. The 2,057 rows cover 896 barrios; the 5 barrios with no residents and no housing units have none. 407 barrios lie in one tract; 489 lie in two or more tracts (up to 35), and they hold 81% of the island's residents.
geo.weights_barrio_tract.method: geo.py puts each census block in the barrio that holds its internal point and in the tract named by the first 11 digits of its id, then adds residents, housing units and blocks for each pair. Housing units are the preferred weight because the Census Bureau does not add noise to them at block level.
geo.weights_barrio_tract.how_to_read: To spread a count from tracts over barrios, split each tract's count among its barrios in proportion to their housing units in that tract (the row's housing units over the tract's housing units), then add up for each barrio. To go from barrios to tracts, do the same with the roles swapped. Label the result 'estimated from tracts using 2020 housing units' and show no margin of error for it. When a survey table has the Census Bureau's own barrio rows, use those.
caveats: It assumes a count is spread over a tract like its housing units. Incomes, rents and poverty often differ inside a tract, so the result is rough.
Percentages, medians and averages are not split this way. Weighting them gives only a rough figure.
The weights are 2020 counts.
geo.weights_barrio_tract.geography: 896 barrios and the 981 tracts they touch

geo.block_table.plain: The list of every 2020 census block of Puerto Rico with its 15-digit id, residents, housing units, land area and an internal point. The build keeps it and does not publish it. The crosswalk's numbers and weights are counted from it.
geo.block_table.plain_es: La lista de todos los bloques censales de 2020 de Puerto Rico, con su identificador de 15 dígitos, residentes, unidades de vivienda, superficie terrestre y un punto interno. La compilación de los datos la conserva, pero no la publica. Los números y los pesos de la tabla de equivalencias se calculan a partir de ella.
geo.block_table.definition: 41,987 blocks, 36,570 of them with residents: 3,285,874 residents and 1,598,159 housing units. Six columns: geoid, pop, hu, land_m2, lon and lat. Two programs read it: network.py (the transit coverage, which uses the blocks with residents) and geo.py (the crosswalk). population_blocks.json is a published extract: the 36,570 blocks with residents as longitude, latitude, residents and meters to the nearest scheduled stop, in the same order but without the id (adding the ids would add 141 KB compressed to a file the Transit tab loads).
geo.block_table.method: network.load_block_table pages TIGERweb layer 10 (2020 Census Blocks) for state code 72 and keeps GEOID, POP100, HU100, AREALAND, INTPTLAT and INTPTLON. It saves the table once (cache/network/census_blocks_ids.json) and reads it again until the build is run with its refresh option. network.load_blocks returns the blocks with residents from the same table, unchanged from before the table existed.
geo.block_table.how_to_read: Not for display. To count something inside an area (residents near a stop, in a flood zone, in a barrio), give each block to the area that holds its internal point, then add residents or housing units.
caveats: Residents are noise-injected for privacy; housing units are not at block level.
A block is counted wholly in or out of an area by its one internal point, even if the area cuts the block.
41 blocks have housing units and no residents, and 53 have 6,503 residents and no housing units (people in group quarters are not counted in housing units).

geo.crosswalk.plain: The list of every area the observatory can join data to: the island, 7 tourism regions, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups. For each it gives a code, its parent, its names, its land area, its 2020 residents and housing units, and a point inside it.
geo.crosswalk.plain_es: La lista de todas las áreas a las que el observatorio puede unir datos: la isla, 7 regiones turísticas, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 sectores censales y 2,555 grupos de bloques. Para cada una da un código, el área a la que pertenece, sus nombres, su superficie terrestre, sus residentes y unidades de vivienda de 2020, y un punto dentro de ella.
geo.crosswalk.definition: The file geo/crosswalk.json has one row for each unit in six levels (island 1, tourism region 7, municipio 78, barrio 901, census tract 981, block group 2,555). A row has ten values: id, parent, name_es, name_en, norm, km2, pop, hu, lat and lng, and each has its own entry. The file also holds the weights that carry numbers between barrios and tracts, which do not fit one inside the other (geo.weights_barrio_tract), and the totals: 3,285,874 residents, 1,598,159 housing units and 41,987 census blocks, 36,570 of them with residents. Census blocks are not units: they are used only to count the weights.
geo.crosswalk.method: geo.py reads the block table (geo.block_table) and the Census Bureau's attribute tables for municipios, tracts, block groups and county subdivisions, puts each block in its barrio by the block's internal point, and adds the blocks up to every unit. It stops, and writes nothing, unless the blocks add up exactly to the Census Bureau's own residents and housing units for all 78 municipios, 981 tracts, 2,555 block groups and 939 county subdivisions. python geo.py --check repeats the checks on the published file: ids are unique, every parent exists, and the residents, housing units and land areas of the children add up to their parent.
geo.crosswalk.how_to_read: Join a dataset to the crosswalk by id, never by name. A file whose rows carry the id of a unit can be shown at that level, added up to the parent when it counts people or things, or moved to a level that does not fit inside it with the weights. Rules and examples: docs/geography.md.
caveats: The regions are the Puerto Rico Tourism Company's tourism regions, the only region scheme the observatory holds. They are not planning regions.
Barrios and census tracts do not fit one inside the other: 489 of the 896 barrios that have residents or housing units (55%), holding 81% of residents, lie in two or more tracts.
Counts are 2020 Census counts. They do not show change since 2020; use the survey and population-estimate series for later years.
The 38 county subdivisions called 'Municipio subdivision not defined' are offshore water with no land, no residents and no housing units. They are not units.
geo.crosswalk.geography: the island, 7 tourism regions, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups (4,523 units)
geo.crosswalk.source_detail: TIGERweb 2020 layers 82 (counties), 6 (tracts), 8 (block groups), 10 (blocks) and 20 (county subdivisions); the tourism region of each municipio from municipios.geojson

geo.unit_hu2020.plain: The number of homes, occupied or empty, the 2020 Census counted in an area.
geo.unit_hu2020.plain_es: La cantidad de viviendas, ocupadas o desocupadas, que el Censo de 2020 contó en un área.
geo.unit_hu2020.definition: The housing units (occupied and vacant) counted by the 2020 Census in the unit: the sum of its census blocks. A housing unit is a house, an apartment, a mobile home or a room meant as separate living quarters. The island has 1,598,159. The Census Bureau does not add noise to housing-unit counts at block level, so they are the better weight for moving numbers between areas.
geo.unit_hu2020.method: Census block housing units (HU100 of TIGERweb layer 10) added up to each unit as for residents.
geo.unit_hu2020.how_to_read: Use it for the base of a housing count or a share of homes, and as the weight in geo.weights_barrio_tract.
caveats: A 2020 count: homes built or lost since 2020 are not in it.
Group quarters are not housing units: 41 blocks have housing units and no residents, and 53 have residents and no housing units.
geo.unit_hu2020.geography: the island, 7 tourism regions, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups (4,523 units)

geo.unit_point.plain: A point that lies inside the area, for placing a label or a marker. It is not the center.
geo.unit_point.plain_es: Un punto que queda dentro del área, para colocar una etiqueta o un marcador. No es el centro.
geo.unit_point.definition: lat and lng are a latitude and longitude in degrees (WGS 84), rounded to 5 decimals. For a municipio, barrio, tract or block group they are the Census Bureau's internal point (INTPTLAT, INTPTLON), which always lies inside the unit. For the island and the tourism regions they are a point inside the union of the municipio outlines.
geo.unit_point.method: Copied from the Census Bureau's internal points; for the island and regions, shapely's representative point of the union of the municipio outlines.
geo.unit_point.how_to_read: Use it to put a label on a unit or to fly the map to it. It is not the center of the unit and not where most people live.
geo.unit_point.geography: the island, 7 tourism regions, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups (4,523 units)

geo.unit_km2.plain: How much land an area covers, in square kilometers, water left out. It is the base for figures per square kilometer.
geo.unit_km2.plain_es: Cuánto terreno abarca un área, en kilómetros cuadrados, sin contar el agua. Es la base de las cifras por kilómetro cuadrado.
geo.unit_km2.definition: The Census Bureau's land area (AREALAND) in square kilometers to four decimals. Water is left out. For the island it is the sum of the census blocks, and for a tourism region the sum of its municipios.
geo.unit_km2.method: Copied from the Census Bureau's tables for each unit and added up for the island and the regions. The land areas of the children add up to their parent within rounding: each area is rounded to 0.0001 km².
geo.unit_km2.how_to_read: Use it as the base of a density (residents, housing units or places per km²). It is measured on the Census Bureau's own boundaries, not on the simplified outlines the maps draw.
caveats: It can differ from the km2 in barrios.geojson, which was measured on a generalized outline cut at the shoreline (for the barrio Guayabal in Juana Díaz: 15.31 here and 15.68 there).
geo.unit_km2.geography: the island, 7 tourism regions, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups (4,523 units)

geo.unit_names.plain: The name of an area in Spanish and in English, and a plain form of it for matching what a person types.
geo.unit_names.plain_es: El nombre de un área en español y en inglés, y una forma simplificada del nombre para compararlo con lo que una persona escribe.
geo.unit_names.definition: name_es and name_en are the display names. A tourism region, municipio or barrio has the same name in both languages. A tract is 'Sector censal 9564' in Spanish and 'Census tract 9564' in English; a block group is 'Grupo de bloques 2, sector censal 9563' and 'Block group 2, census tract 9563'. norm is the Spanish name in lower case without accents. It is for matching what a person types, in the search box or the chat; a dataset joins by id.
geo.unit_names.method: Region names are the Tourism Company's; municipio and barrio names are the Census Bureau's (the same as in municipios.geojson and barrios.geojson, which geo.py checks); tract and block group names are built from the Census Bureau's tract and block group numbers.
geo.unit_names.how_to_read: Show the municipio with a barrio name, because names repeat.
caveats: Barrio names repeat: 694 different names for 901 barrios (Collores and Quebrada Arenas each name six barrios).
geo.unit_names.geography: the island, 7 tourism regions, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups (4,523 units)

geo.unit_parent.plain: The area a unit belongs to: a region belongs to the island, a municipio to a region, a barrio or a census tract to a municipio, and a block group to a tract.
geo.unit_parent.plain_es: El área a la que pertenece una unidad: una región pertenece a la isla, un municipio a una región, un barrio o un sector censal a un municipio, y un grupo de bloques a un sector censal.
geo.unit_parent.definition: The parent value of each row is the id of the next larger unit: tourism region to island, municipio to region, barrio to municipio, tract to municipio, block group to tract. The island has none (null). Barrios and tracts both belong to a municipio, but neither fits inside the other.
geo.unit_parent.method: Barrio, tract and block group parents come from the first digits of the Census id; a municipio's region comes from municipios.geojson.
geo.unit_parent.how_to_read: Add the children to get the parent for counts of people, housing units or places. Do not add percentages, medians or averages: work them out again from their parts.
caveats: To move a number between barrios and tracts, use geo.weights_barrio_tract, not the parent.
geo.unit_parent.geography: the island, 7 tourism regions, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups (4,523 units)

geo.regions.plain: The regions the observatory offers: the 15 municipios of the Eastern Region of FPR's Eastern Region Strategic Vision and the seven tourism regions. A region's figures are always added up from its municipios.
geo.regions.plain_es: Las regiones que ofrece el observatorio: los 15 municipios de la Región Este de la Visión Estratégica de la Región Este de FPR y las siete regiones turísticas. Las cifras de una región siempre se suman a partir de sus municipios.
geo.regions.definition: The file geo/regions.json lists 8 regions. Each has an id (ersv, or the crosswalk's reg- code), a kind (planning or tourism), a name in Spanish and English, its source, and the codes and names of its municipios. Figures are not stored: counts are added from the municipios, shares whose parts are published are pooled (the sum of the parts over the sum of the base), and any other rate, median or level is shown as the range of its municipios (map) or as the average of its municipios weighted by residents, marked as an estimate (regional profile).
geo.regions.method: regions.py reads the tourism region of each municipio from the crosswalk (geo.crosswalk) and the Eastern Region's list from the program, checks that each Eastern Region code has the name the crosswalk gives it, and writes the file. python regions.py --check compares a rebuild with the published file. The seven tourism regions cover the 78 municipios once each (tests/profile_region.test.js).
geo.regions.how_to_read: Choose a region in the map's Region tab, or open profile.html?region=ersv. The Eastern Region (ERSV) is Canóvanas, Ceiba, Culebra, Fajardo, Humacao, Juncos, Las Piedras, Loíza, Luquillo, Maunabo, Naguabo, Río Grande, San Lorenzo, Vieques and Yabucoa: 409,525 residents in the 2020 Census.
caveats: A region's rate that is not pooled from published parts is an estimate (the residents-weighted average of its municipios), and a median of medians is not the region's median.
The Eastern Region is the ERSV's definition; other FPR programs may group the east differently.
geo.regions.geography: 8 regions: 1 FPR planning region and 7 tourism regions, each a set of whole municipios
geo.regions.source_detail: FPR, Eastern Region Economic Development Council, Human Capital Demographic Profile (2025): the list of the 15 municipios; the crosswalk for the tourism regions

view.label: Map, Region tab
Regional area profile: Eastern Region

geo.unit_pop2020.plain: The number of people the 2020 Census counted in an area.
geo.unit_pop2020.plain_es: La cantidad de personas que el Censo de 2020 contó en un área.
geo.unit_pop2020.definition: The residents counted by the 2020 Census in the unit: the sum of its census blocks. For every municipio, barrio, tract and block group it equals the Census Bureau's own figure for that unit, which geo.py checks when it builds the file. The island has 3,285,874.
geo.unit_pop2020.method: Census block residents (POP100 of TIGERweb layer 10) added up to each unit through the block's id (tract, block group, municipio) or its internal point (barrio).
geo.unit_pop2020.how_to_read: A 2020 count, not a figure for today. Do not compare it with a survey estimate of the same area as if both measured the same thing: the survey is a sample with a margin of error.
caveats: The Census Bureau adds statistical noise to block counts to protect privacy, so counts of small units are approximate.
People in group quarters, such as a dormitory or a nursing home, are counted: 53 blocks hold 6,503 residents and no housing units.
geo.unit_pop2020.geography: the island, 7 tourism regions, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups (4,523 units)

geo.unit_id.plain: The code that names an area and ties data to it. A municipio has 5 digits, a barrio 10, a census tract 11 and a block group 12, and each code starts with the code of the area it sits in.
geo.unit_id.plain_es: El código que nombra un área y le vincula datos. Un municipio tiene 5 dígitos, un barrio 10, un sector censal 11 y un grupo de bloques 12, y cada código empieza con el código del área donde está.
geo.unit_id.definition: The id value of each row. Island: 72, the Census code of Puerto Rico. Tourism region: reg- and a short name (reg-capital, reg-atlantico, reg-mar, reg-caribe, reg-cordillera, reg-sol-norte, reg-sol-sur). Municipio: 5 digits (72 and a 3-digit municipio code). Barrio: 10 digits (the municipio code and a 5-digit county subdivision code). Census tract: 11 digits (the municipio code and a 6-digit tract code). Block group: 12 digits (the tract code and 1 digit). These are the Census Bureau's GEOIDs, so any Census table joins to them. A census block has 15 digits (its block group and 3 digits); blocks are not units.
geo.unit_id.method: Copied from the Census Bureau's GEOID. The region ids are made by geo.py from the Tourism Company's region names.
geo.unit_id.how_to_read: Keep ids as text. They start with 72, and a tract id has 11 digits, more than a spreadsheet keeps as a number. The first 5 digits of a barrio, tract or block group id are its municipio; the first 11 digits of a block group id are its tract.
caveats: Barrio names repeat (694 different names for 901 barrios), so join by id.
Five-year survey windows that end in 2020 or earlier use the 2010 Census geography, whose tract and block group codes differ from these.
geo.unit_id.geography: the island, 7 tourism regions, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups (4,523 units)

municipalities.land_km2.plain: How much dry land the municipality covers, in square kilometers, from the 2020 Census. Water is not included.
municipalities.land_km2.plain_es: Cuánta tierra firme cubre el municipio, en kilómetros cuadrados, según el Censo de 2020. No incluye el agua.
municipalities.land_km2.definition: The Census Bureau's 2020 land area of the municipality (field AREALAND, in square meters) divided by 1,000,000 and rounded to one decimal. Land area leaves out water. The 78 values add up to 8,868.5 km² for Puerto Rico.
municipalities.land_km2.method: Read from the Census Bureau's TIGERweb (its online map and data service) 2020 counties layer (layer 82). The legal boundaries in that layer run out to sea, about 3 nautical miles, but the land-area field counts land only, so offshore water does not enter the figure. build.py divides by 1,000,000 and rounds to one decimal.
municipalities.land_km2.how_to_read: In the 2020 Census data, Arecibo is the largest municipality by land (326.4 km²) and Cataño the smallest (12.5 km²). Land area is the denominator of places per km²; the Analysis tab also uses it for its per-km² option. The Municipality tab shows it rounded to whole km².
caveats: It is land only. It leaves out inland water and the sea inside the legal boundary.

Mayagüez's 200.9 km² includes Isla de Mona and Monito. In the 2026-10 snapshot, only 3 of Mayagüez's 589 counted tourism places sit there, so its places per km² is lower than it would be for its main-island part alone.

The boundary file municipios.geojson carries its own AREALAND from a different Census layer, cut at the shoreline. In the 2026-10 snapshot files, rounded to one decimal, it differs from this value in 37 municipalities, by up to 1.1 km² (Manatí). Use land_km2 from municipalities.json for density.
municipalities.land_km2.source_detail: Census TIGERweb 2020 counties layer 82, STATE = '72', field AREALAND; downloaded 2026-10-01.

view.label: Map, Municipality tab: header line (whole km²)
Map, Rankings tab: download the municipality table (CSV) for the one-decimal value

municipalities.municipality.plain: The name of one of Puerto Rico's 78 municipalities. It ties every statistic, and every tourism place, to a municipality.
municipalities.municipality.plain_es: El nombre de uno de los 78 municipios de Puerto Rico. Conecta cada estadística, y cada lugar turístico, con un municipio.
municipalities.municipality.definition: The municipality name as Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) spells it in its municipality list (municipalities.py), with accents and without the word 'Municipio', for example Bayamón, Río Grande or San Juan. It is also the key of each record in municipalities.json. The 78 names are all different and match the 78 municipality boundaries of the 2020 Census.
municipalities.municipality.method: FPR keeps a list of the 78 names, with a center point for each. The build matches each name to the Census municipality boundary after removing accents, capital letters and the word 'Municipio'. Each tourism place is then given a municipality from where its pin (the point where Overture places the listing) sits (see 'How a tourism place is assigned to a municipality').
municipalities.municipality.how_to_read: Use the name to link this table to places.json, which spells its municipality field the same way. Names keep their accents, so 'Mayagüez' does not match 'Mayaguez' unless you remove the accents from both.
caveats: A municipio is the Census Bureau's county equivalent. Its boundary covers the whole municipality, not only the town center.
Isla de Mona and Monito belong to Mayagüez in these data (barrio 'Isla de Mona e Islote Monito'). Culebra and Vieques are municipalities of their own.
The map draws a simplified boundary cut at the shoreline. The Census Bureau's legal 2020 boundaries run out to sea, about 3 nautical miles, so they include coastal water.
municipalities.municipality.source_detail: Names and center points: FPR list in municipalities.py. Boundaries: Census TIGERweb 2020 counties layer 82 (legal boundaries, used for names and counts) and TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11 (500k boundaries clipped to the shoreline, the boundaries drawn on the map and used to place each tourism place).

view.label: Map: click a municipality, or search for one, to open its profile (Municipality tab)

municipalities.region.plain: The tourism region the Puerto Rico Tourism Company places the municipality in, such as Porta Capital or Porta del Mar. There are seven regions.
municipalities.region.plain_es: La región turística en la que la Compañía de Turismo de Puerto Rico ubica el municipio, como Porta Capital o Porta del Mar. Hay siete regiones.
municipalities.region.definition: The Puerto Rico Tourism Company (PRTC) tourism region of the municipality. Each of the 78 municipalities is in exactly one of seven regions: Porta Atlántico, Porta Capital, Porta Caribe, Porta Cordillera, Porta del Mar, Porta del Sol Norte and Porta del Sol Sur. Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) copied the assignment from the PRTC regions page into municipalities.py. It is a fixed list, not calculated from any data.
municipalities.region.method: Looked up from the municipality name in municipalities.py (REGION_BY_MUNI in build.py). places.json has no region field: the map shows a place's region through its municipality. FPR compared the seven lists below with the PRTC regions page on 3 October 2026, and all 78 municipalities matched.
municipalities.region.how_to_read: The regions follow the PRTC's grouping. The observatory's tourism counts are Overture listings, not PRTC statistics, so do not compare them with PRTC's own inventories or reports. The observatory stores no regional totals: add up the municipality rows if you need them.
caveats: The regions are tourism-promotion regions, not statistical or planning regions, and they do not follow compass areas: Cayey is in Porta Capital and Maunabo is in Porta del Mar.
The assignment is a fixed copy, checked on 3 October 2026. If the PRTC changes its regions, the observatory keeps the old grouping until FPR updates its list.
Regions hold 9 to 15 municipalities each, so region totals are not comparable without adjusting for size.
