boundaries.municipio_hu2020.plain: The number of homes in the municipality in the 2020 Census, whether lived in or empty. A home can be a house, an apartment, a mobile home or a room.
boundaries.municipio_hu2020.plain_es: La cantidad de viviendas del municipio en el Censo de 2020, ocupadas o desocupadas. Una vivienda puede ser una casa, un apartamento, una casa móvil o un cuarto.
boundaries.municipio_hu2020.definition: HU100 is the number of housing units in the municipality in the 2020 Census, as published in the Census Bureau's TIGERweb county layer for 2020. A housing unit is a house, apartment, mobile home or room meant as separate living quarters. Occupied, vacant and seasonal units are all included.
boundaries.municipio_hu2020.method: Read from the 2020 Census county layer (not the generalized layer) and joined to the shoreline-clipped shapes by GEOID.
boundaries.municipio_hu2020.how_to_read: Use it for how many dwellings exist, not how many are lived in. Occupied units equal households. In the 2020 Census the 78 values add up to 1,598,159. The smallest is Culebra (1,563) and the largest is San Juan (193,244).
caveats: It counts dwellings, not households, and not tourism lodging.
Vacant units are included. A high count in a coastal municipality can include many seasonal or second homes.

In 2020 the Census Bureau held the total number of housing units exact (its privacy method adds no noise to this total), so this is a census count, not a sample estimate. The method does add small random changes to the split between occupied and vacant homes. That split is not in this field (see housing.census_vacant_units).
boundaries.municipio_hu2020.source_detail: TIGERweb tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 82, field HU100

boundaries.municipios.plain: The outline of each of Puerto Rico's 78 municipalities, cut at the shoreline, with its 2020 Census population and housing units. The maps use it to draw and shade municipalities and to tell which municipality a click or a place falls in.
boundaries.municipios.plain_es: El contorno de cada uno de los 78 municipios de Puerto Rico, recortado en la línea de costa, con su población y sus unidades de vivienda del Censo de 2020. Los mapas lo usan para dibujar y colorear los municipios y para saber en qué municipio cae un clic o un lugar.
boundaries.municipios.definition: The file municipios.geojson holds 78 shapes, one per municipality. The shapes come from the US Census Bureau's generalized county layer (a version with simplified edges, made for maps at a scale of 1:500,000), with boundaries as of January 1, 2023. The Census Bureau treats Puerto Rico's municipalities as counties. The observatory keeps the Census name, code and land area, adds the 2020 Census population and housing units, and adds its own municipality name and the tourism region.
boundaries.municipios.method: build.py (step_census_shoreline) pages the Census Bureau's TIGERweb layer Counties 500K for state code 72. It simplifies each shape for display (tolerance 0.0002 degrees, about 22 m) and joins population and housing units from the 2020 Census county layer by GEOID (all 78 codes match). The build uses the unsimplified shapes to place each tourism place in a municipality (a test of whether the pin lies inside the shape). A pin outside every shape is given the municipality whose shape is nearest (muni_locate.py).
boundaries.municipios.how_to_read: Use it to see where a municipality starts and ends on land. Do not use it to measure area or to decide whether a particular lot lies inside a municipality.
caveats: The Census Bureau generalizes these shapes (1:500,000) and the observatory simplifies them again by about 22 m, so edges can differ from larger-scale maps by more than 22 m.
Shapes stop at the shoreline. The Census Bureau's legal 2020 boundaries reach into the sea; see boundaries.shoreline_clipped.

The population and housing units are 2020 counts attached by code to shapes with boundaries as of January 1, 2023. The shapes themselves are not the 2020 polygons. Cite the shapes as 2023 and the counts as 2020.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, 324 of the 24,209 counted tourism places (1.3%) have a pin outside every municipality shape, and so do 348 of the 32,541 listings in the places file. That build gave each the municipality with the nearest center point, which can be the wrong municipality near a boundary. From the next full build each takes the municipality whose shape is nearest, which moves 60 of the drawn listings (59 of them counted).
boundaries.municipios.geography: 78 municipalities, including Culebra and Vieques. 72 shapes are one polygon; 6 have several parts (Fajardo, Culebra, Mayagüez, Ceiba, Ponce, Toa Baja). Mayagüez includes Isla de Mona.
boundaries.municipios.source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County MapServer layer 11 (Counties 500K, https://tigerweb.geo.census.gov/arcgis/rest/services/Generalized_ACS2023/State_County/MapServer/11): shapes, NAME, GEOID, AREALAND. TIGERweb tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 82 (Counties, 2020 Census): POP100, HU100.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Boundaries

boundaries.municipio_geoid.plain: A five-digit Census code that identifies the municipality: 72 for Puerto Rico followed by three digits for the municipality. Barrio codes start with it.
boundaries.municipio_geoid.plain_es: Un código censal de cinco dígitos que identifica el municipio: 72 para Puerto Rico, seguido de tres dígitos para el municipio. Los códigos de los barrios empiezan con él.
boundaries.municipio_geoid.definition: GEOID is the Census Bureau's geographic identifier. For a municipality it is the 2-digit state code 72 plus the 3-digit county code. Codes run from 72001 to 72153. Each barrio's geoid begins with the GEOID of its municipality.
boundaries.municipio_geoid.method: Copied from the Census layer. The build matches it to the 2020 Census layer to attach population and housing units, and uses its first five digits to find a barrio's municipality.
boundaries.municipio_geoid.how_to_read: Use the code to join Census Bureau tables or other federal data. It stays the same when a name is spelled differently.
caveats: Keep it as text, as the Census Bureau does. If one table holds the code as text and the other as a number, a join will not match.
boundaries.municipio_geoid.source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11, field GEOID

boundaries.municipio_land_area.plain: The land area of the municipality in square meters, as the Census Bureau reports it, without water. Divide by 1,000,000 for square kilometers.
boundaries.municipio_land_area.plain_es: El área de tierra del municipio en metros cuadrados, según la informa el Negociado del Censo, sin contar el agua. Divida entre 1,000,000 para obtener kilómetros cuadrados.
boundaries.municipio_land_area.definition: AREALAND from the Census Bureau's generalized county layer (a version with simplified edges, made for maps at a scale of 1:500,000), with boundaries as of January 1, 2023: the land area inside the municipality, in square meters, not counting water.
boundaries.municipio_land_area.method: Copied from the Census layer without change.
boundaries.municipio_land_area.how_to_read: Use it as the denominator for density when you work with this file. 1 km² equals 1,000,000 m². With boundaries as of January 1, 2023, the 78 values add up to 8,869 km². The smallest is Cataño (12.5 km²) and the largest is Arecibo (326.2 km²).
caveats: municipalities.json holds a second land area (land_km2) taken from the 2020 Census layer. The raw values differ for all 78 municipalities, by at most 0.26 km² in 77 of them and by 1.07 km² in Manatí. After rounding to one decimal, 37 municipalities still differ. Places per km² in municipalities.json uses the 2020 value.
This is the Census Bureau's land area, not the area of the drawn polygon.
boundaries.municipio_land_area.source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11, field AREALAND

boundaries.municipio_census_name.plain: The municipality's name as the Census Bureau writes it. It always ends in the word Municipio.
boundaries.municipio_census_name.plain_es: El nombre del municipio como lo escribe el Negociado del Censo. Siempre termina con la palabra Municipio.
boundaries.municipio_census_name.definition: The NAME field of the Census Bureau's county layer. All 78 values end in the word Municipio.
boundaries.municipio_census_name.method: Copied from the Census layer. The build keeps the field so that readers can match the file to Census Bureau tables.
boundaries.municipio_census_name.how_to_read: Use it to match Census Bureau tables. For joins inside the observatory, use the observatory spelling (municipality) or the code (GEOID).
caveats: Names are a weaker match than codes: spellings, accents and the word Municipio can differ between sources. To match Census Bureau tables, use the code (see boundaries.municipio_geoid).
boundaries.municipio_census_name.source_detail: TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 State_County layer 11, field NAME

boundaries.municipio_name.plain: The municipality's name as the observatory spells it, with accents (for example Mayagüez). Files that list places and municipalities use it to match their rows; the yearly series files use the 5-digit Census code (GEOID) instead.
boundaries.municipio_name.plain_es: El nombre del municipio como lo escribe el observatorio, con acentos (por ejemplo, Mayagüez). Los archivos que listan lugares y municipios lo usan para emparejar sus filas; los archivos de series anuales usan en su lugar el código censal de 5 dígitos (GEOID).
boundaries.municipio_name.definition: The Census name with the word Municipio removed, matched without regard to accents or capitals to the observatory's list of 78 municipalities (municipalities.py). The list's spelling is stored. municipalities.json, places.json and barrios.geojson use the same spelling. The yearly series files (economy_series.json, housing_series.json) use the 5-digit GEOID instead.
boundaries.municipio_name.method: build.py (MUNI_BY_NORM) lower-cases the Census name, strips accents and looks it up in the observatory's list.
boundaries.municipio_name.how_to_read: Use this field to match rows between the place and municipality files. The land-use file uses the same spelling for 78 of its 79 municipality values; one water polygon carries the variant Guayanabo (see land.municipio).
caveats: Names are text with accents. Joins that strip accents on one side only will fail.
boundaries.municipio_name.source_detail: Census Bureau name (NAME) matched to the observatory's own list of municipalities

boundaries.municipio_pop2020.plain: The number of people the 2020 Census counted in the municipality on Census Day, April 1, 2020. The same count is stored in municipalities.json (see municipalities.population_2020).
boundaries.municipio_pop2020.plain_es: La cantidad de personas que el Censo de 2020 contó en el municipio el Día del Censo, 1 de abril de 2020. El mismo conteo está en municipalities.json (vea municipalities.population_2020).
boundaries.municipio_pop2020.definition: POP100 is the total resident population of the municipality in the 2020 Census, as published in the Census Bureau's TIGERweb county layer for 2020.
boundaries.municipio_pop2020.method: Read from the 2020 Census county layer (not the generalized layer) and joined to the shoreline-clipped shapes by GEOID.
boundaries.municipio_pop2020.how_to_read: It describes April 2020, not today. In the 2020 Census the 78 values add up to 3,285,874, the Census count for Puerto Rico. The smallest is Culebra (1,792) and the largest is San Juan (342,259). For yearly estimates, see the resident population series.
caveats: The Census Bureau applied disclosure avoidance (a method that protects privacy) to 2020 counts. See its 2020 disclosure avoidance documentation for how this affects small areas.

The Housing page's 2020 population is not this count. It is the Census Bureau's updated April 2020 base for its estimates, which includes post-census count corrections. In the 2026-10 snapshot it differs from this count by 1 to 31 people in 68 of the 78 municipalities; the island total is the same, 3,285,874. See housing.population and methods.population_vintage_break.
People are counted where they usually live, including people in group quarters such as nursing homes.
Estimates after 2020 come from a different Census program and can differ from this count.
boundaries.municipio_pop2020.source_detail: TIGERweb tigerWMS_Census2020 MapServer layer 82, field POP100

boundaries.municipio_region.plain: The tourism region the municipality belongs to, one of the seven Porta regions of the Puerto Rico Tourism Company. A tourism region is not a Census, planning or political unit.
boundaries.municipio_region.plain_es: La región turística a la que pertenece el municipio, una de las siete regiones Porta de la Compañía de Turismo de Puerto Rico. Una región turística no es una unidad censal, de planificación ni política.
boundaries.municipio_region.definition: The tourism region of each municipality, the same assignment as municipalities.region (see there for the seven regions and their members). Here it is the field region of municipios.geojson.
boundaries.municipio_region.method: Looked up by municipality name in municipalities.py and written to municipios.geojson and municipalities.json.
boundaries.municipio_region.how_to_read: Use it to group municipalities the way the Tourism Company does. The observatory stores no regional totals: add up the municipality rows if you need them. The observatory's counts are Overture listings, not Tourism Company statistics.
caveats: Regions are tourism groupings, not compact areas: Porta del Mar runs from Loíza to Maunabo and Yabucoa and includes Culebra and Vieques, and Porta Capital runs from San Juan and Bayamón to Cayey.
boundaries.municipio_region.source_detail: Region assignment: Puerto Rico Tourism Company, https://tourism.pr.gov/regions/ (as coded in municipalities.py). The Census layer supplies only the list of 78 municipalities; the Census Bureau is not the source of the grouping.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: Boundaries

data.build_barrios.plain: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the build published 901 barrio polygons.
data.build_barrios.plain_es: En el corte de datos de 2026-10, la compilación publicó 901 polígonos de barrios.
data.build_barrios.definition: barrios.barrios is the number of barrio (county subdivision) polygons written to the barrios file, from the Census Bureau's county subdivisions (TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023, layer 7).
data.build_barrios.method: landuse.py (build_barrios) counts the polygons it writes.
data.build_barrios.how_to_read: Barrios are divisions of a municipality. The count is the number of polygons, not of neighborhoods.
caveats: Barrio boundaries are the Census Bureau's. Some barrios are named the same in different municipalities.
data.build_barrios.source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb Generalized_ACS2023 Places_CouSub_ConCity_SubMCD MapServer layer 7 (County Subdivisions 500K); landuse.py (BARRIOS_URL, build_barrios)

data.build_generated_at.plain: When the full build wrote the data, as a date and time in UTC. In the 2026-10 snapshot it is 2026-10-02 02:31 UTC, which is 2026-10-01 at 10:31 pm in Puerto Rico.
data.build_generated_at.plain_es: Cuándo la compilación completa escribió los datos, como fecha y hora en UTC. En el corte de datos de 2026-10 es 2026-10-02 02:31 UTC, que en Puerto Rico es 2026-10-01 a las 10:31 p. m.
data.build_generated_at.definition: The moment the full build finished collecting data and wrote meta.json, in ISO 8601 form with a +00:00 offset, which means UTC, Coordinated Universal Time. Puerto Rico is 4 hours behind UTC all year.
data.build_generated_at.method: build.py writes the current UTC time as a text with second precision.
data.build_generated_at.how_to_read: The 2026-10 snapshot's value is 2026-10-02T02:31:31+00:00. The map shows only the first ten characters, the UTC date: as hover text on the snapshot label and in the About tab. That date can be one day later than the date in Puerto Rico.
caveats: The value is the time of the last full build. The nightly transit refresh does not change it; the 'network' part has its own date.
Source data can be older than this time, because the build can reuse source files downloaded earlier. Overture places and OpenStreetMap roads have their own extract dates, shown in their entries.
data.build_generated_at.source_detail: build.py (meta['generated_at']); written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source

data.build_info.plain: A small file that says when the data snapshot was built, which area it covers, how many records each step kept, and which sources were used. Cite its snapshot label and date.
data.build_info.plain_es: Un archivo pequeño que dice cuándo se generó el corte de datos, qué área cubre, cuántos registros conservó cada paso y qué fuentes se usaron. Cite su etiqueta de corte y su fecha.
data.build_info.definition: meta.json has 13 parts: label, generated_at, bbox, counts, sources, housing, landuse, barrios, transport, network, time, taxonomy_dropped_top and access. The full build (build.py) writes all of them. The nightly transit refresh (refresh_network.py) rewrites the 'network' part on nights when it finds a changed feed. Through access.py it also rewrites the 'access' part, and the count places_near_transit inside 'transport', when a value changes.
data.build_info.method: build.py collects the sources, classifies and filters the data, writes every data file and then writes meta.json with the label, the time, the settings and the counts of what each step kept.
data.build_info.how_to_read: Use the label and the build date to say which snapshot a figure comes from. The counts describe what the build kept; the data entries describe each dataset.
caveats: Parts of the file can be from different dates. 'network' is rewritten by the nightly transit refresh when it finds a changed feed, and 'access' (with the count places_near_transit in 'transport') when an access value changes; every other part keeps the values of the last full build.
Some counts (for example time.trips) were not refreshed with 'network', so they can differ from the matching count in 'network'.
The license field of each source is named 'license' in this file; the source records of this dictionary name it 'license'.

values.label: Name of the snapshot, for example 'Snapshot 2026-10'.
values.generated_at: Date and time of the full build, in UTC.
values.bbox: Map box [west, south, east, north] in decimal degrees.
values.counts: Eleven values: ten counts of what the build read or kept (Overture place records, tourism places with and without the confidence cut-off, listings, duplicates folded, places of worship, flood polygons, protected-area records, municipalities and residents) and the confidence cut-off, 0.5.
values.sources: In the file of 2026-10-02, credit records for 30 sources: name, link and license for each, and a credit line for 25 of them. The keys are older source ids.
values.housing: Settings of the housing step: the two American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year vintages, the number of municipalities covered and the affordability method.
values.landuse: Land-use plan facts: number of polygons, plan version, land-class groups, zoning-layer status and places on protected land.
values.transport: Counts of transit features, kinds, walking distance, places near any mapped stop and the ride-hailing listing. The nightly refresh keeps the count places_near_transit in step with places.json.
values.network: Transit network facts: operators, status counts, routes, scheduled stops, weekday trips and residents near a stop. Rewritten by the nightly refresh on nights when a transit feed changed.
values.time: Facts for the time views: weekday trips and storms near Puerto Rico.
values.taxonomy_dropped_top: The 25 most common Overture categories that the build dropped as not tourism-related, with counts.
values.access: The island-wide access figures: shares of tourism places near a stop with a current timetable, near a frequent stop and near any mapped stop, the stop counts by timetable state, and the number of current and expired feeds, as of one date. Rewritten by the nightly refresh when a value changes.

data.build_info.source_detail: build.py (main) and the SOURCES, meta and counts of transport.py, network.py, housing.py, landuse.py and timeseries.py

view.label: Map header: the snapshot label (hover for the build date)

data.build_housing.plain: In the 2026-10 snapshot, meta.json records four housing settings: the latest survey window (2020-2024), the earlier window used for change (2008-2012), the number of municipalities with data (78) and the name of the affordability method.
data.build_housing.plain_es: En el corte de datos de 2026-10, meta.json guarda cuatro ajustes de vivienda: el periodo de encuesta más reciente (2020-2024), el periodo anterior que se usa para medir el cambio (2008-2012), el número de municipios con datos (78) y el nombre del método de asequibilidad.
data.build_housing.definition: acs_latest is the last year of the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates used for the latest figures. acs_base is the last year of the earlier 5-year estimates, used for change over time. municipalities_with_acs counts the municipalities with ACS data in the latest vintage. method is the build's text naming the affordability method of the State of Housing study (2023) by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR).
data.build_housing.method: housing.py sets the two vintages (LATEST and BASE), counts the municipalities for which the latest ACS tables returned data, and records the method text.
data.build_housing.how_to_read: ACS 5-year figures are averages over five years of survey responses, not a single year.
caveats: The 2020-2024 estimates have margins of error, which are larger for small municipalities.
The method text is a build setting. The housing entries explain each measure.
The method text in the file calls the affordability table Table 6, the number this dictionary and the Housing page use. The study PDF prints that table as Table 8.

The 5% rate is the one the study states in its endnotes for the maximum mortgage. The study's printed maximum loans work out at a rate of 4.994%, so using exactly 5% leaves the observatory's figures $19 to $65 below them. It is a modeling assumption, not a mortgage rate in force in any year, and the result is an indicator, not a loan limit and not advice on buying a home.

values.acs_latest: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2024, the ACS 2020-2024 5-year estimates.
values.acs_base: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2012, the ACS 2008-2012 5-year estimates, used as the earlier point for change.
values.municipalities_with_acs: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 78 municipalities with ACS data in the latest vintage.
values.method: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 'FPR State of Housing 2023, Table 6 affordability method (30% of income, 78% to principal and interest, 30-year loan at 5%)'.

data.build_housing.source_detail: housing.py (LATEST, BASE, build_housing); ACS is the US Census Bureau American Community Survey

data.build_landuse.plain: Facts about the land-use layer: how many polygons it has, which plan it comes from, and its land classes. It also records whether the zoning service answered (it did not in the 2026-10 snapshot) and how many listings sit on protected rural land.
data.build_landuse.plain_es: Datos sobre la capa de uso de terrenos: cuántos polígonos tiene, de qué plan viene y sus clases de terreno. También dice si el servicio de calificación respondió (no respondió en el corte de datos de 2026-10) y cuántos listados están en suelo rústico protegido.
data.build_landuse.definition: put_polygons counts the polygons of the published land-use file. put_version names the plan version. groups maps 12 land-class codes to their Spanish names. The plan uses 17 class codes; the build file names 12 of them. The five less common subtypes of specially protected rural land (SREP-AE, SREP-EA, SREP-AP, SREP-EP, SREP-P) are not in this list. calificacion records whether the zoning (Calificación de suelos) service answered at build time. places_on_protected_land counts listings whose point lies in a protected rural land class.
data.build_landuse.method: landuse.py reads the Junta de Planificación land-use plan, simplifies the polygons for display, tests whether each listing falls inside a polygon, and tries to reach the zoning service.
data.build_landuse.how_to_read: The plan describes how land is meant to be used under the 2015 plan, not what is built there today.
caveats: places_on_protected_land counts all listings, including places of worship and listings below the 0.5 confidence cut-off, not only the tourism places in the statistics.

'Protected land' here means the Junta's SREP land classes (specially protected rural land). It is not the same as the USGS protected areas (PAD-US). In the places file of the 2026-10 snapshot, 2,151 listings are in SREP classes and 1,013 listings carry a PAD-US area; do not compare the two counts.
In the 2026-10 snapshot the zoning layer was not reachable at build time (calificacion.available is false, reason HTTPError), so the observatory has no zoning layer.
The published polygons are simplified by about 110 m (0.001 degree) for display. Counts of listings use the full-detail polygons.
The Junta states no data license (its site footer reads 'Todos los derechos reservados'). See the source record before reusing the polygons.

values.put_polygons: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 996 polygons in the published land-use file (display copy).
values.put_version: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 'PUT-2014, 30-NOV-2015', the Plan de Uso de Terrenos version used.
values.groups: SU Suelo Urbano (urban land); SURP Suelo Urbanizable Programado (programmed developable land); SURNP Suelo Urbanizable No Programado (non-programmed developable land); SRC Suelo Rústico Común (common rural land); SREP Suelo Rústico Especialmente Protegido (specially protected rural land); SREP-E ecological; SREP-A agricultural; SREP-H water resources (hídrico); SREP-EH ecological and water; SREP-AH agricultural and water; AGUA water; VIAL road.
values.calificacion: In the 2026-10 snapshot: {available: false, reason: 'HTTPError'}; the zoning service did not answer at build time.
values.places_on_protected_land: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2,151 listings in the SREP classes.

data.build_landuse.source_detail: landuse.py (build_landuse, try_fetch_calificacion); Junta de Planificación Plan de Uso de Terrenos (PUT), version of 30 November 2015

data.build_bbox.plain: The rectangle the build asked Overture and OpenStreetMap about: west -67.97, south 17.85, east -65.2, north 18.57. It covers Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra and Mona.
data.build_bbox.plain_es: El rectángulo por el que la compilación les preguntó a Overture y a OpenStreetMap: oeste -67.97, sur 17.85, este -65.2, norte 18.57. Cubre Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra y Mona.
data.build_bbox.definition: Four numbers [west, south, east, north] in decimal degrees: -67.97, 17.85, -65.2, 18.57. The build requests Overture Maps places and OpenStreetMap transit stops, stations and terminals inside this box.
data.build_bbox.method: Set by hand in build.py (and repeated in transport.py) as a rectangle around the island group. It is not computed from the data.
data.build_bbox.how_to_read: Places and stops outside the rectangle are not requested. A rectangle also takes in open sea, so it is larger than the land.
caveats: The box limits only the Overture and the OpenStreetMap transit-stop requests. Flood zones, protected areas and Census boundaries are requested by Puerto Rico's own codes. Roads and place names come from the Puerto Rico extract of OpenStreetMap.
data.build_bbox.geography: The map box: west -67.97, south 17.85, east -65.2, north 18.57 (Puerto Rico, Vieques, Culebra, Mona and the sea around them)

data.build_taxonomy_dropped.plain: The 25 most common Overture categories the build left out as not tourism-related, with record counts. Beauty salons, grocery stores and doctors' offices are examples.
data.build_taxonomy_dropped.plain_es: Las 25 categorías de Overture más comunes que la compilación dejó fuera por no estar relacionadas con el turismo, con su número de registros. Algunos ejemplos son los salones de belleza, los supermercados y las oficinas médicas.
data.build_taxonomy_dropped.definition: A list of 25 pairs [category, count], largest first. The count is the number of Overture place records with that primary category that the observatory's rules did not place in a tourism category. The pair '(none)' counts records with no category.
data.build_taxonomy_dropped.method: build.py counts the primary Overture category of every record that classify() could not assign, before duplicate folding, and keeps the 25 largest groups.
data.build_taxonomy_dropped.how_to_read: Use it to check what the observatory treats as outside tourism, for example whether a category you care about was dropped. In the 2026-10 snapshot, '(none)' is 3,388, and the 25 pairs add up to 28,986 of the 63,117 dropped records.
caveats: Dropped means not classified as tourism by the observatory's rules. It does not mean the places are unimportant.
Only the top 25 are stored. In the 2026-10 snapshot, about 34,100 dropped records are in smaller categories.
data.build_taxonomy_dropped.geography: Puerto Rico (the map box, see the entry on the map box)
data.build_taxonomy_dropped.source_detail: build.py (parse_places, classify); Overture Maps Places, release 2026-09-23.1

data.build_label.plain: The name of the data snapshot, for example 'Snapshot 2026-10'. Cite it so readers know which build you used.
data.build_label.plain_es: El nombre del corte de datos, por ejemplo "Corte 2026-10". Cítelo para que se sepa qué versión de los datos se usó.
data.build_label.definition: Text set at build time. It is the --label option when one is given. Otherwise it is the word 'Snapshot' followed by the year and month of the build, in UTC.
data.build_label.method: build.py writes args.label or 'Snapshot' plus the build date formatted as year-month.
data.build_label.how_to_read: The label names the full build. It appears next to the check mark in the header of the map, 3D, housing and dictionary pages. It does not change when the nightly transit refresh runs.
caveats: The label dates the build, not the data in it. Each dataset keeps its own reference date, for example April 2020 for census counts and 2015 for the land-use plan.
A month label does not say the day. The build date is in the build date and time entry.
The label is not a version number. Two builds in one month can have the same label.
data.build_label.source_detail: build.py (meta['label']); written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source

data.build_sources.plain: A list in meta.json with a record for each of 30 source keys (file of 2026-10-02): name, link and license, and for 25 of them the credit line to print. The Sources section of this dictionary gives the same facts with canonical ids.
data.build_sources.plain_es: Una lista en meta.json con un registro para cada una de 30 claves de fuente (archivo del 2026-10-02): nombre, enlace y licencia, y para 25 de ellas la línea de crédito que se debe imprimir. La sección "Fuentes" de este diccionario da los mismos datos con los identificadores oficiales.
data.build_sources.definition: An object whose keys are source ids (older ones, such as 'census' or 'osm_roads') and whose values have the text fields name, url and license. Most values also have credit; fpr_housing_2023 adds home and program. Each module adds its own sources when it builds.
data.build_sources.method: build.py merges the SOURCES dictionaries of build.py, transport.py, network.py, timeseries.py, housing.py, housing_series.py, economy_series.py and landuse.py.
data.build_sources.how_to_read: Use the 'credit' text when you print a map or a chart. For a record with no credit text, use the credit line in the Sources section. For license terms, follow the link and read the source's own terms. In the file of 2026-10-02, 25 of the 30 values have credit; housing_pep, housing_census, housing_acs, housing_fema and housing_derived have none.
caveats: The same source can appear under several keys (for example 'osm', 'osm_transport', 'osm_routes' and 'osm_roads' are all OpenStreetMap).

The meta.json written on 2026-10-02 has no records for the economy series (economy_qcew, economy_laus, economy_acs, economy_usaspending, economy_openfema, economy_pep, economy_cpi and economy_overture). Their credit lines are in economy_series.json (sources) and in the Sources section of this dictionary.
License text is what the source states. It is not legal advice. Check the source's terms before reuse.

The license text in meta.json is the build's short summary. The Sources section of this dictionary is the maintained list. Where they differ (for example for the Junta de Planificación land-use plan and zoning service, and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) sea level rise layers), use the Sources section.
Not every source is open data. Each source record states its license or says that none is stated.
data.build_sources.source_detail: meta.json 'sources': keys overture, fema, padus, census, census_shore, noaa_slr, osm, ati_gtfs, osm_transport, faa_airports, uber, muni_gtfs, ntd, osm_routes, census_blocks, hurdat2, census2010, acs_latest, acs_2012, fpr_housing_2023, nalcab, census_barrios, put2015, calificacion, osm_roads, housing_pep, housing_census, housing_acs, housing_fema, housing_derived

data.build_time.plain: Facts for the time views: the number of weekday trips, which weekday the timetable stands for, and how many Atlantic storms passed near Puerto Rico (from 1851 through 2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
data.build_time.plain_es: Datos para las vistas de tiempo: el número de viajes de lunes a viernes, qué día de la semana representa el horario y cuántas tormentas del Atlántico pasaron cerca de Puerto Rico (desde 1851 hasta 2025 en el corte de datos de 2026-10).
data.build_time.definition: trips is the weekday trip count at the last full build. trips_day is the label of the timetable day used. The weekday timetable uses each feed's Wednesday service or, if a feed has none, the first of Tuesday, Thursday, Monday or Friday that it serves. storms_near_pr counts Atlantic tropical cyclones whose track came within 250 km of a point at the center of the island (18.22, -66.45). major_hurricanes_near_pr counts those whose strongest wind near Puerto Rico was category 3 or higher on the Saffir-Simpson scale. storm_years gives the first and last year in the list.
data.build_time.method: build.py counts the weekday trips it writes. timeseries.py reads the HURDAT2 best-track database of NOAA (the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration), keeps storms within 250 km of the island's center and assigns a category from the peak wind (in knots) within that distance: 64 or more category 1, 83 category 2, 96 category 3, 113 category 4, 137 category 5.
data.build_time.how_to_read: The storm counts are storms that came near the island, not storms that struck it.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, trips (3,312) is the weekday trip count written by the last full build. It includes 15 trips on five routes whose stop order is unreliable. A later nightly refresh leaves those routes out, which gives 3,297, the count in the network part of meta.json and in trips.json. Use 3,297 for the timetable replay.
The category is from the wind near Puerto Rico, not the storm's peak anywhere on its track.

Distance and category come from the recorded track points (about every six hours), not from the line between them. A storm whose recorded points were all farther than 250 km is left out even if its path crossed the circle.
250 km is measured from one point at the center of the island, so a storm can pass nearer the east or west end than the center and still be left out.

Observation methods changed a great deal between 1851 and 2025. Older tracks and winds are less certain, and the National Hurricane Center (NHC) revises past seasons from time to time, so do not read the counts as a trend by decade.

values.trips: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 3,312 weekday trips at the last full build, including 15 trips on five routes whose stop order is unreliable. The timetable file has 3,297.
values.trips_day: 'weekday (typical Wednesday service)': the label of the timetable used for Monday to Friday. It uses each feed's Wednesday service or, if a feed has none, the first of Tuesday, Thursday, Monday or Friday that it serves.
values.storms_near_pr: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 157 Atlantic storms within 250 km of (18.22, -66.45), 1851 to 2025.
values.major_hurricanes_near_pr: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 29 of those storms were category 3 or higher near Puerto Rico.
values.storm_years: In the 2026-10 snapshot: [1851, 2025], the first and last year in the list of storms.

data.build_time.geography: Puerto Rico and its surrounding waters
data.build_time.source_detail: build.py (meta['time']); timeseries.py (load_hurricanes); HURDAT2 is the National Hurricane Center's Atlantic hurricane database

data.build_access.plain: The island-wide access figures: the share of tourism places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable, of a frequent stop and of any mapped stop, the stop counts by timetable state and the feeds that are current or expired, as of one date.
data.build_access.plain_es: Las cifras de acceso de toda la isla: la proporción de lugares turísticos a 400 m o menos de una parada con horario vigente, de una parada frecuente y de cualquier parada mapeada; el número de paradas según el estado de su horario, y las fuentes de horarios vigentes o vencidas, a una fecha dada.
data.build_access.definition: as_of is the date against which the observatory judged whether each timetable had ended. basis says which places are counted and places counts them. near_m, far_m and frequent_calls are the two distances and the number of weekday calls that the figures use. The shares are percentages of the counted places: any400_pct (any mapped stop within 400 m), cur400_pct and cur800_pct (a stop with a current timetable within 400 m or 800 m), freq400_pct (with 20 or more weekday calls), sat400_pct and sun400_pct (with Saturday or Sunday service), hub400_pct (a rail station or ferry terminal within 400 m, any source) and paper_pct (within 400 m of a mapped stop but of no stop with a current timetable). stops counts the stops, stations and terminals by timetable state: current, expired and osm. feeds counts the operators whose timetable feed has an end date, as current (not ended on the as-of date) or expired.
data.build_access.method: access.py (island_summary) computes the figures from places.json, transport.json and operators.json, with the same rules as the municipal fields (see methods.access_profile). build.py writes the block into meta.json and refresh_network.py rewrites it through access.py.
data.build_access.how_to_read: Use these as the island totals behind the municipal fields. Each share is the number of places divided by all the places counted, not an average of municipal shares. In the 2026-10 snapshot, as of 2026-10-06: 47.5% of the 24,209 counted places are within 400 m of any mapped stop, 32.2% of a stop with a current timetable, 21.3% of a frequent stop, 22.4% of a stop with Saturday service and 6.4% with Sunday service; 15.4% are near only an expired or unscheduled stop.
caveats: The figures describe timetables on the as-of date. They change on the day a feed ends: 9 of the 18 current feeds end between 2026-10-31 and 2027-01-31 (see methods.access_profile).
The nightly refresh rewrites this part only when a value changes, so as_of can be older than the last run.
The limits of the municipal fields apply: straight-line distance, schedule-based figures with no real-time data, and públicos, taxis, ride-hailing and rental cars in no timetable.

values.as_of: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 2026-10-06. The date against which each timetable was judged. A feed counts as current when its end date is on or after it.
values.basis: Text: 'confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship left out'. The places counted.
values.places: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 24,209 tourism places counted.

values.far_m: 800: the distance, in meters, of the longer test (cur800_pct and the 'Stop 400–800 m away' class).

data.build_access.source_detail: access.py (island_summary, run by build.py and refresh_network.py); the places, stops and feed dates it reads are those of places.json, transport.json and operators.json

data.build_network.plain: The latest facts about the transit network: operators and the state of their data, routes, stops, weekday trips, and residents within 400 m of a stop. It is rewritten when a nightly check finds a changed feed.
data.build_network.plain_es: Los datos más recientes sobre la red de transporte colectivo: los operadores y el estado de sus datos, las rutas, las paradas, los viajes de lunes a viernes y los residentes a 400 m o menos de una parada. Se vuelve a escribir cuando una revisión nocturna encuentra un cambio en una fuente de horarios.
data.build_network.definition: built is the date of the last full build or nightly refresh that wrote changes. operators counts the operators listed. by_status counts them by the state of their schedule data. routes counts the routes on the map. scheduled_stops counts stops in timetable feeds. weekday_trips counts trips in the typical-weekday timetable. residents is the 2020 population in census blocks. residents_within_400m counts residents in blocks whose nearest scheduled stop is 400 m or less away.
data.build_network.method: network.py reads every operator's timetable feed and the 2020 Census block counts and measures the distance from each block to its nearest scheduled stop; refresh_network.py rewrites this part of meta.json when it finds a changed feed.
data.build_network.how_to_read: The Transit tab shows these figures. In the file written on 2026-10-02, 925,788 of 3,285,874 residents (28.2%) live within 400 m of a scheduled stop.
caveats: In the file written on 2026-10-02, routes (165) includes 16 volunteer-mapped routes in OpenStreetMap; the other 149 come from timetable feeds.

scheduled_stops includes stops of operators whose timetables have expired, so residents_within_400m is higher than the count that uses only unexpired timetables (729,507 in the file written on 2026-10-02).
by_status is as of the build or refresh date. The browser works out each status again from the feed end date when the page opens.

values.built: 2026-10-02: date of the last full build or nightly refresh that wrote changes to this part.
values.operators: In the file written on 2026-10-02: 44 operators listed. They are Puerto Rico agencies in the federal National Transit Database (municipal systems, the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses (AMA, the Metropolitan Bus Authority), the Puerto Rico Highway and Transportation Authority (públicos) and the Puerto Rico Maritime Transport Authority (ferries)), the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) itself, and one group for routes that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap.
values.by_status: In the file written on 2026-10-02: community 1, current 17, expired 7, expiring 1, in_ati 2, none 16. The feed status codes are explained in the entry on operators by status.
values.routes: In the file written on 2026-10-02: 165 routes drawn on the map.
values.scheduled_stops: In the file written on 2026-10-02: 3,847 stops in timetable feeds.
values.weekday_trips: In the file written on 2026-10-02: 3,297 trips in the typical-weekday timetable.
values.residents: In the file written on 2026-10-02: 3,285,874 residents in the 36,570 census blocks that have residents (2020 Census).
values.residents_within_400m: In the file written on 2026-10-02: 925,788 residents whose census block has a scheduled stop within 400 m.

data.build_network.source_detail: network.py (build_network, coverage); refresh_network.py; the operator checklist is from the National Transit Database of the Federal Transit Administration (FTA)

data.build_transport.plain: Counts of transit features, the 400 m walking distance, and how many tourism places are near any mapped stop. It also records the date of the ride-hailing listing check.
data.build_transport.plain_es: Conteos de elementos del transporte colectivo, la distancia a pie de 400 m y cuántos lugares turísticos están cerca de alguna parada mapeada. También guarda la fecha en que se revisaron los listados de servicios de transporte por aplicación.
data.build_transport.definition: gtfs counts operators with a feed, routes and scheduled stops. osm_features and faa_airports count the other features. features is the total number of rows in the transit features file. kinds counts the rows by kind. walk_access_m is the walking distance used for access to a stop: 400 m. places_near_transit counts tourism places within that distance of any mapped stop, station or terminal, including stops whose timetable has ended and stops that volunteers mapped. uber_listed_municipalities and uber_checked record the ride-hailing listing. sources holds the credit records of the four sources.
data.build_transport.method: transport.py counts the features it assembles from the timetable feeds, OpenStreetMap and the FAA airport list, and the tourism places within 400 m of the nearest stop, station or terminal of any mode (not taxi, EV charging or airport).
data.build_transport.how_to_read: The numbers describe the last full build, except places_near_transit, which the nightly refresh recomputes through access.py. The nightly refresh also updates scheduled stops in the transit file, but not the other counts. The counts in the table of codes are from the 2026-10 snapshot. For the places near a stop with a current timetable, see the access part of this file.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot, gtfs.routes (165) counts every route on the map, including 16 routes mapped by volunteers in OpenStreetMap that have no timetable. The routes with a timetable feed number 149.

places_near_transit counts the nearest stop, station or terminal of any of those kinds, including the 459 OpenStreetMap bus stops that have no timetable (2026-10 snapshot). It is not on the same basis as the 'scheduled stop' figures in the Transit tab.

places_near_transit counts straight-line distance to the nearest stop; the places file stores the distance as a whole number of meters, cut and not rounded, so in the 2026-10 snapshot 14 listings just over 400 m (11 of them counted tourism places; 3 are places of worship) show a value of 400 there.
The ride-hailing figure is a listing on Uber's public cities page (57 municipalities, checked 45-10-01). It is not measured coverage.
'Not listed' on Uber's page does not mean Uber does not operate there.

values.gtfs: In the 2026-10 snapshot: {operators_with_feed 25, routes 165, stops 3,847}: operators whose feed status is current, expiring or expired at build time; all routes on the map; scheduled stops.
values.osm_features: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 544 OpenStreetMap features kept (bus stops, stations, terminals, airports, taxi stands, EV charging points) after folding those that repeat an official stop, station or airport.
values.faa_airports: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 14 airports from the FAA list.
values.features: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 4,405 rows in the transit features file (3,847 scheduled stops + 544 OpenStreetMap features + 14 airports).
values.kinds: In the 2026-10 snapshot: transit_stop 3,781; bus_station 91; rail_station 16; ferry_terminal 13; airport 25; bus_stop 459; taxi 9; ev_charging (electric vehicle charging) 11.
values.walk_access_m: 400: the walking distance, in meters, used for access to a stop.

values.uber_listed_municipalities: In the 2026-10 snapshot: 57 municipalities on Uber's Puerto Rico cities page.
values.sources: Credit records for the timetable feeds, OpenStreetMap, FAA airports and the Uber listing.

data.build_transport.source_detail: transport.py (build_transport, meta); GTFS means General Transit Feed Specification, the standard format of public timetable feeds; FAA is the Federal Aviation Administration

measures.bivariate_map.plain: When two shaded layers are visible, the map colors each municipality by both at once: three classes for each dataset, nine colors in all. It shows where two things are high together, low together, or differ.
measures.bivariate_map.plain_es: Cuando hay dos capas sombreadas visibles, el mapa colorea cada municipio por ambas a la vez: tres clases por cada conjunto de datos, nueve colores en total. Muestra dónde dos cosas son altas a la vez, bajas a la vez o no coinciden.
measures.bivariate_map.definition: The first shaded layer runs left to right (→) and the second runs upward (↑). Each is cut into three classes (low, middle, high), and a municipality's color is the pair of its two classes. Each layer's three classes follow its own class method. With quantiles (the default) the cut-offs are terciles. The legend title says 'terciles of each' only when both layers use quantile classes; if either layer uses equal intervals or natural breaks, it says 'three classes of each'. With the default 'Same classes in every year', the terciles are thirds of all municipality values from every year pooled, not thirds of the 78 municipalities in the year shown, so one year can have far more places in one class. Untick 'Same classes in every year' on a layer to cut the year on screen into thirds. A municipality with no value in either layer is gray. A map can shade at most two datasets; further datasets must be shown as symbols.
measures.bivariate_map.method: Function ecRenderMap in site/js/economy.js calls ecBreaks with three classes for each layer and picks a color from a 3 × 3 palette. Each layer keeps its own year, rescaling and 'Same classes in every year' setting. The legend title names the kind of classes and the legend gives the cut-offs of each axis.
measures.bivariate_map.how_to_read: Shade poverty first and median household income second. Each municipality's color then shows its poverty class along the horizontal axis (→) and its income class along the vertical axis (↑). Read the two axes of the legend, and their cut-offs, before the colors. In the 2026-10 snapshot, with all years pooled, the poverty axis reads 'up to 45.0%' for low and 'above 51.8%' for high.
caveats: 'High' and 'low' are relative, not absolute. With the default settings they compare a municipality with the values of all years pooled, not only with the other municipalities in the year shown. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 poverty classes (low, middle, high) hold 44, 21 and 13 municipalities. Median household income, in the dollars of each year, holds 1, 13 and 64.

The legend title says 'terciles of each' only when both layers use quantile classes. Otherwise it says 'three classes of each', and each layer's classes follow its own method (equal intervals or natural breaks). With the default settings, terciles are terciles of all years pooled (see the definition), not thirds of the year on screen.
The two layers can be for different years. Check the year shown beside each layer in the legend.
A bivariate map shows two patterns together. It does not show that one causes the other.
measures.bivariate_map.source_detail: Any two shaded datasets in the Analysis tab.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty and median household income together

measures.class_breaks.plain: A shaded map sorts the municipalities into five color classes. The Analysis tab sets the class limits one of four ways: the same number of municipalities in each class (quantiles), classes of equal width (equal intervals), limits at gaps in the data (natural breaks), or four limits that the user types.
measures.class_breaks.plain_es: Un mapa sombreado reparte los municipios en cinco clases de color. La pestaña Análisis fija los límites de las clases de una de cuatro maneras: la misma cantidad de municipios en cada clase (cuantiles), clases del mismo ancho (intervalos iguales), límites donde hay saltos en los datos (cortes naturales) o cuatro límites que escribe quien usa el mapa.
measures.class_breaks.definition: Class limits for a shaded layer whose values have no natural center. The values of the 78 municipalities are pooled (all years together when 'Same classes in every year' is on) and sorted. Quantiles: the limits are the values one fifth, two fifths, three fifths and four fifths of the way along the sorted list, so each class holds about the same number of values. Equal intervals: the range from the lowest to the highest value is cut into five equal widths. Natural breaks (Jenks): the limits are chosen so that values inside a class are as alike as possible and classes are as different as possible. A value equal to a limit goes in the lower class. My own limits: four numbers in rising order typed in the layer's Settings, which start from the classes the layer has at that moment; text that is not four rising numbers is ignored (the classes stay quantiles until it is fixed). Typed limits apply to a layer shaded alone: two shaded layers together use three classes each, and a scale around a center (index, difference, change, location quotient) keeps its own cut-offs. A municipality with no value is gray and listed as 'No data'.
measures.class_breaks.method: The functions make, classOf, jenks and parseBreaks of Core.classify (site/js/core/classify.js), with pool and breaks of the layer engine (site/js/core/engine.js). Quantile limits take pool[floor(n × i ÷ 5)] for i = 1 to 4. Natural breaks use the Fisher-Jenks dynamic program; when the pool has more than 1,500 values the code runs it on every nth value to keep the page fast. The Puerto Rico row is not in the pool. Bivariate maps use three classes instead of five (see the bivariate entry). The Map layers tab's municipality shading uses quintiles only (see the quintile entry).
measures.class_breaks.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the same poverty data give three different sets of limits (percent, all years pooled): quantiles 41.3, 46.4, 50.5 and 54.9; equal intervals 30.1, 39.3, 48.6 and 57.8; natural breaks 33.5, 41.3, 48.2 and 55.0. All three describe the same data. The legend lists each range and how many municipalities fall in it.
caveats: A color class is not a verdict. Dark does not mean good or bad, only higher than the limit.
With quantiles, two municipalities with almost the same value can sit in different classes, and with equal intervals a class can have no municipality.

With 'Same classes in every year' on, the five classes are not equal-sized in any single year. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 2024 poverty map has 28, 21, 15, 9 and 5 municipalities in its five classes.
Values for years that are not on screen shape the limits when classes are fixed across years.
Typed limits are kept in the shareable link, so a link that holds them opens the same classes.

values.Quantiles (equal counts): Each class holds about the same number of municipalities. This is the default.
values.Equal intervals: Each class covers the same width of values. A class can be empty if a few values are extreme.
values.Natural breaks: Limits are chosen so that values inside a class are as alike as possible, which tends to put limits where the data have gaps. The limits are not round numbers.
values.My own limits: Four limits typed by the user, in rising order. Use them to hold the classes to round numbers or to a policy threshold.

measures.class_breaks.source_detail: Any shaded dataset in the Analysis tab. The class methods are a display choice by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate, quantiles
Same data, equal intervals
Same data, natural breaks
Same data, limits typed by the user (20, 30, 40, 50)

measures.diverging_scale.plain: When a value has a natural center, the map shades distance from that center instead of equal-count classes. Red means below the center, blue means above, and pale gray means near it.
measures.diverging_scale.plain_es: Cuando un valor tiene un centro natural, el mapa sombrea la distancia a ese centro en lugar de usar clases con la misma cantidad de municipios. El rojo indica que está por debajo del centro, el azul que está por encima y el gris claro que está cerca.
measures.diverging_scale.definition: Used for 'Index' (center 100), 'Difference from Puerto Rico' (center 0), 'Location quotient' (center 1) and 'Change since the base year' (center 0). The span is the largest distance from the center among all values in the pool. Five classes follow from t = (value − center) ÷ span: t below −0.5 (strongly below), −0.5 up to −0.1 (below), −0.1 to +0.1 (near the center), +0.1 up to +0.5 (above), above +0.5 (strongly above). The classes are not equal-count and not chosen by the quantile, equal-interval or natural-breaks setting.
measures.diverging_scale.method: Function ecBreaks (branch for a diverging output with five classes) and ecClass in site/js/economy.js. The colors run dark red, light red, pale gray, light blue, dark blue. In a bivariate map a diverging layer is cut into three classes by the layer's class method instead. The Housing page uses the same rule around 0 for its change maps.
measures.diverging_scale.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, for poverty as an index (Puerto Rico = 100) the largest distance from 100 among the pooled values is 57.2, so the limits sit at 71.4, 94.3, 105.7 and 128.6. A municipality at 100 is the same as the island; one at 130 is in the highest class.
caveats: One extreme value stretches the span and pushes most municipalities into the pale middle class.
Red and blue show direction from the center, not good and bad.
The legend lists only classes that hold at least one municipality.
measures.diverging_scale.source_detail: Rescaled Analysis tab layers (index, difference, location quotient, change).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate as an index (diverging colors)

measures.fixed_classes.plain: By default the color limits are set from all years of a dataset together, so a color means the same range in every year. When you move the year slider you see real change, not a map that re-sorts itself.
measures.fixed_classes.plain_es: De forma predeterminada, los límites de color se fijan con todos los años de un conjunto de datos a la vez, para que un color signifique el mismo rango en cada año. Al mover la barra de años se ve el cambio real, no un mapa que se reordena solo.
measures.fixed_classes.definition: The checkbox 'Same classes in every year' in a layer's Settings. On (the default): class limits, the diverging scale's span and the size of the largest symbol are calculated from the values of all municipalities in every year the dataset has, with the layer's own settings (rescaling, inflation adjustment, base year). Off: they are calculated from the year on screen only, so every year uses all five colors but colors are not comparable between years. The box is not shown for one-time snapshot datasets, which have a single year.
measures.fixed_classes.method: Function ecPool in site/js/economy.js builds the pool: every year of the dataset when the layer is fixed, otherwise the current year only. The limits are cached by dataset, rescaling, inflation setting, base year, class method and year. The Housing page always pools every year and states it in its legend note.
measures.fixed_classes.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the poverty rate has 78 municipalities × 15 windows = 1,170 values, and they set the limits. With the box on, a map for 2014 and a map for 2024 use the same limits, so a change of color between the two maps reflects a change in the data. With the box off, the inner limits for 2024 alone would be 37.2, 42.2, 46.1 and 50.3, against 41.3, 46.4, 50.5 and 54.9 when pooled.
caveats: A rate that moves across the whole period can leave most municipalities in the lowest or highest classes in the first or last years.
The legend counts show how many municipalities fall in each class in the year on screen. They are not equal.
The setting is saved in a shared link as the 'fixed' flag of each layer.
The pool holds every year the dataset has, including years before 2010 that the year bar does not offer (federal awards from 2008 and the FEMA series from 2001).
measures.fixed_classes.source_detail: Any shaded or symbol dataset with more than one year.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate, classes fixed across years
Same map, classes from one year only

measures.proportional_symbols.plain: A sized-symbol layer draws one circle per municipality whose area is proportional to the value. Counts, such as jobs, are better shown this way than as shaded color.
measures.proportional_symbols.plain_es: Una capa de símbolos de tamaño variable dibuja un círculo por municipio, con un área proporcional al valor. Los conteos, como los empleos, se muestran mejor así que con color sombreado.
measures.proportional_symbols.definition: A circle is drawn at the area-weighted center of each municipality's largest polygon, so islands and detached parts do not pull it into the sea. The radius is 30 px × √(|value| ÷ largest |value|) (20 px on a phone), with a minimum of 2.5 px. Because area grows with the square of the radius, the circle's area is proportional to the value. The largest |value| comes from all years when classes are fixed. Circles are drawn from the largest to the smallest so small ones stay visible. When the layer has negative values, as change layers do, blue circles mark increases and red circles mark decreases, and size follows the absolute value.
measures.proportional_symbols.method: Function ecRenderMap (symbols) and ecCentroid in site/js/economy.js. The legend shows three circles: the largest value, half of it and a tenth of it.
measures.proportional_symbols.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's jobs in 2025 (253,816) draw a circle of 29.9 px against 30 px for the largest value in any year (255,426). A municipality with 50,000 jobs would draw 13.3 px.
caveats: Below the minimum size the circle is larger than proportional. A value under about 0.7% of the largest is drawn at 2.5 px (about 1,800 jobs when the largest value is 255,426, as in the 2026-10 snapshot).
The eye reads area poorly. Check the numbers in the inspector.
Circles sit at the center of the municipality's largest polygon, not at the places where the activity happens, and large circles overlap in the San Juan area.
Symbols can be added for any dataset, but they suit counts and dollar totals. The page advises shading rates.
measures.proportional_symbols.source_detail: Any dataset in the Analysis tab; circles are drawn with Leaflet.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: jobs as sized symbols

data.catalog.plain: The small file the map reads first, and the three it reads on first use. catalog.json holds the fields (domains) of the registry, a headline figure and trend for each, and the size of every published file; catalog_index.json holds an index of everything the dictionary documents, catalog_es.json the words of the Spanish summaries, for searching in Spanish, and catalog_views.json the ready-made views of each topic.
data.catalog.plain_es: El archivo pequeño que el mapa lee primero y los tres que lee al usarlos. catalog.json tiene los temas del registro, una cifra principal y una tendencia para cada uno, y el tamaño de cada archivo publicado; catalog_index.json tiene un índice de todo lo que documenta el diccionario, catalog_es.json las palabras de los resúmenes en español, para buscar en español, y catalog_views.json las vistas listas de cada tema.
data.catalog.definition: catalog.json holds: version; built (the build time of the data, equal to meta.generated_at); snapshot (the label); domains (every domain of the registry with its Spanish and English names and descriptions, icon, accent, status, example questions, the number of dictionary entries, the number of wanted datasets by status and, for the fields that have one, a headline figure with its value, year, unit, period, trend and the way it goes on the map); and weights (the raw and the compressed size of every published file, an estimate). catalog_index.json holds the version and the build time, and: index (one row for each dictionary entry, as a list of column names and a list of rows: id, name, domain, domains, kind, geography levels, years covered, timeline, sources, the strictest license class among the sources, how the entry goes on the map and the words people use to ask for it); and sources (the data sources behind the index, with their license class). catalog_es.json holds the version and the build time, and words_es (for each entry that has a Spanish summary, the words of that summary as the page searches them: without accents, in lower case, each once, without words of one or two letters or common little words). catalog_views.json holds the version and the build time, and presets (for each topic that has them, its ready-made views: id, name and note in Spanish and English, the datasets with how each is drawn, the layers switched on, and the ids of the data sources).
data.catalog.method: catalog.py builds the four files from dictionary_src/domains.json, site/data/dictionary.json, the series files (housing_series.json and economy_series.json), municipalities.json, wanted.json, meta.json and the sizes of the files in site/data. python catalog.py --check says whether the files on disk are current; it ignores the build time and the sizes. Compressed sizes are an estimate (gzip, level 6) of what a web server sends. The index is a file of its own so the map's first load stays small (docs/performance.md).
data.catalog.how_to_read: Read a headline figure as the number for the whole island over the period it names. The index lets a page find data without loading the whole dictionary (about 2.4 MB). The weights tell a visitor what a module costs before it loads.
caveats: A headline figure is not a score and the fields are not comparable with one another. See methods.headline_figures for how each is worked out and what it counts.

The license class in the index is the strictest class among an entry's sources. It describes the sources as recorded in the sources list, not a legal review, and it can be strict for an entry that only cites a study (for example, an entry that cites a study with no stated license is marked 'license not stated').

How an entry goes on the map is read from where the entry says its data live (a yearly series file, a field of municipalities.json) or, for a layer, from the list in dictionary_src/map_layers.json. Entries with neither have no 'Add to map' button.
The sizes are estimates, and they can lag the files until catalog.py runs again (for example after the nightly transit refresh).

values.domains: One object for each domain of the registry, system domains included (they are left out of the overview).
values.index: In catalog_index.json. {fields: [...], rows: [[...], ...]}. One row for each dictionary entry; the column 'map' is how it goes on the map: ['econ', dataset key] or ['econ', dataset key, scale], ['layers', layer keys] or none.
values.sources: In catalog_index.json. The data sources behind the index, with their license class. Base maps, libraries and tools are left out.
values.weights: {file name: {raw, gz}} in bytes for every published file except the four catalog files.
values.presets: In catalog_views.json. {topic id: [ready-made views]}; each view {id, name, note, show: [[dataset key, 'fill' or 'symbol', {norm: its scale, ramp: its colors}]], on: [layer keys], sources: [source ids]}. A view replaces what is on the map.
values.words_es: In catalog_es.json. {entry id: the words of its Spanish summary, separated by spaces}, for the entries that have a Spanish summary.

data.catalog.geography: Whole observatory (not geographic); the headline figures are for Puerto Rico as a whole
data.catalog.source_detail: catalog.py (build, headline, island_value, build_index, map_action, weights); the sources are those of the figures named in methods.headline_figures

Map, Catalog tab

data.compliance_review.plain: Whether a published file still needs a review before it can be relied on, and why: a review of personal data, of a license or of federal grant content that is still open, one that was cleared and when, a license the sources do not state, or nothing to review.
data.compliance_review.plain_es: Si un archivo publicado todavía necesita una revisión antes de que se pueda confiar en él, y por qué: una revisión de datos personales, de una licencia o de contenido de fondos federales que sigue pendiente, una que se aprobó y cuándo, una licencia que las fuentes no declaran, o nada que revisar.
data.compliance_review.definition: review.status is open when a review of the file in the data contract (dictionary_src/datasets.json) is open, cleared when every review was cleared, unstated when the file has no review and its license class is unstated, that is, at least one of its sources states no license (a file takes the most restrictive license class of its sources, and review.licence_from names the sources that set it), and none otherwise. review.open lists each open review with its type (pii, license or compliance) and a short reason in Spanish and English; review.cleared is the latest date a review was cleared. review.flags lists federal-grant (the file holds or describes federal grant money or a grant-funded program), counts-only (sensitive items are counted but not drawn or named), license-unstated and licensed-not-open.
data.compliance_review.method: registry.py reads the reviews, flags and license class of the file's record in datasets.json. contract.py checks them: a review needs a type, a status and a note; an open review should have a summary and a cleared one a date; a file flagged federal-grant must have a compliance review.
data.compliance_review.how_to_read: On 2026-10-19, 7 reviews are open in 6 files: the names of drawn places (places.json), two license reviews (municipalities.json and housing.json, withdrawn on 2026-11-23 with the figures they covered), federal grant content (housing.json, housing_series.json and economy_series.json) and the terms of HRSA's files (health_series.json). 24 files have a source that states no license, most often the municipal GTFS feeds (15 files); barrios.geojson, for example, takes the class from those feeds alone, while its other sources state a license.
caveats: The status says what the data contract records; it is not a legal opinion.
Federal grant content needs Finance and Compliance review before external communication.

values.open: Pendiente / Open, with the reason of each open review.
values.cleared: Aprobada / Cleared, with the date of the latest clearance.
values.unstated: Licencia sin declarar / License not stated: no review is open, and at least one source states no license; the cell names it (review.licence_from).
values.federal-grant: Flag: federal grant money or a grant-funded program.
values.counts-only: Flag: sensitive items counted but not drawn or named.
values.licence-unstated: Flag: at least one source states no license (a file takes the most restrictive license class of its sources); the flag names it.
values.licensed-not-open: Flag: a source licensed to FPR whose data need written permission to republish; the flag names it.

data.compliance_review.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source

view.label: Data management: published data files
Data management: definitions

data.registry.plain: A list of the data files the observatory publishes. For each file it gives the title, the size, the records, fields and values, the dates it was first published and last updated, the dictionary items that document it and the state of its compliance review; for the whole folder, the totals, their history and the counts of what is not published. It does not list registry.json itself. The Data management page, the data dictionary and the Ask the observatory chat read it.
data.registry.plain_es: Una lista de los archivos de datos que publica el observatorio. Para cada archivo da el título, el tamaño, los registros, campos y valores, las fechas de su primera publicación y de su última actualización, los elementos del diccionario que lo documentan y el estado de su revisión de cumplimiento; para toda la carpeta, los totales, su historial y los conteos de lo que no se publica. No incluye el propio registry.json. La leen la página de Gestión de datos, el diccionario de datos y el chat "Preguntar al observatorio".
data.registry.definition: registry.json holds built (the date its content last changed), snapshot (the label of the build), total_bytes, limits, used_fraction, needs_planning, growth_note, totals (the counts of the whole folder), history (the totals on each date they changed), domain_names (the names of the domains in Spanish and English), withheld (the counts of what is not published) and files, one row for each published file except registry.json itself.
data.registry.method: registry.py calls ledger.py for every published file: ledger.py reads the file, counts its records, fields, values and vertices with the adapter of the file's family (docs/data-management.md) and computes its content hash. registry.py then updates the ledger (dictionary_src/data_ledger.json: the first-published and last-updated dates, the versions and the history of the totals), adds the titles, domains, license classes, reviews and flags of the data contract (dictionary_src/datasets.json) and the number of dictionary entries that name each file, and writes registry.json only when something other than the date changed. python registry.py --check fails when the ledger or registry.json does not describe the files as they are; it never compares a date with today.
data.registry.how_to_read: Use it to see what the observatory holds, how big each file is and when it changed. The Data management page shows it as a table with totals, a growth chart and the counts of what is not published; the data dictionary summarizes it. In the map's Ask the observatory chat, ask 'how big is the database?' to see it summarized.
caveats: A file added after the last registry run is not listed until registry.py runs again; the tests (python registry.py --check) fail until it does.

In a full build the registry is written last, after the dictionary and the catalog, so their sizes are current. catalog.json is written before it, so the weight it gives registry.json is one build behind.
Sizes are the bytes of the files as published, with line ends counted as one byte; a copy checked out on Windows can be larger on disk.
The list shows what is published, not what is planned. Planned data is in the wanted-data list.

values.built: Date the content of the registry last changed (2026-10-19 in the current file).
values.snapshot: The label of the build, from meta.json: Snapshot 2026-10.
values.total_bytes: Total size of the listed files: about 81.1 million bytes (77.3 MB of 1,048,576 bytes) on 2026-10-19.
values.used_fraction: 0.077 on 2026-10-19: the total divided by the site limit, rounded to 3 decimals.
values.needs_planning: false on 2026-10-19: true when the total or any file passes 60% of its limit.
values.growth_note: A planning note that says the data folder only grows and that very large files may later move to separate storage.
values.totals: files, bytes, records, fields, values and vertices (the last four over the data files only), items (the entries of the data dictionary), counted_files, documenting_items (the entries that name at least one file), first_published and last_updated. On 2026-10-19: 77 files, 409,574 records, 1,381 fields and 3,520,446 values in 60 data files.
values.history: One row for each date on which a total changed. See the entry on the growth of the published data.
values.domain_names: The name of each domain in Spanish and English, from dictionary_src/domains.json.
values.withheld: Counts of what is not published. See the entry on what is not published.
values.files: One row for each published file except registry.json. See the entry on the file rows.

data.registry.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source
