Data dictionary: published data files (a summary)

data.registry_files.plain: One row for each published data file: its name, title, size, domains, license class, size tier, geography level and time type; its kind and, for a data file, its records, fields, values and vertices; the dates it was first published and last updated; how many dictionary items document it; and the state of its compliance review.
data.registry_files.plain_es: Una fila por cada archivo de datos publicado: su nombre, título, tamaño, temas, clase de licencia, rango de tamaño, nivel geográfico y tipo de tiempo; su clase y, en un archivo de datos, sus registros, campos, valores y vértices; las fechas de su primera publicación y de su última actualización; cuántos elementos del diccionario lo documentan; y el estado de su revisión de cumplimiento.
data.registry_files.definition: Each row has the fields file, title, bytes, gzip_bytes, loaded_by, kind, records, fields, values, vertices, first_published, last_updated, versions, documented_by and review. A file that has a record in the data contract (dictionary_src/datasets.json) also has title_es, domains, licence_class, tier, geography and time. Rows for JSON files that hold series or lists also have datasets, years, built or items.
data.registry_files.method: registry.py sets file to the file name; title, title_es, domains, licence_class, tier, geography and time to the values of the file's record in dictionary_src/datasets.json (the title is the file name when there is no record); bytes to the size of the file with line ends counted as one byte and gzip_bytes to its size compressed at gzip level 6; loaded_by to the pages that fetch it without a click (dictionary_src/routes.json); kind, records, fields, values and vertices to what ledger.py counts; first_published, last_updated and versions to the ledger's; documented_by to the number of dictionary entries whose where.files name the file; and review to the state of its reviews. For a JSON file smaller than 41,943,040 bytes (40 x 1,048,576) it also sets datasets to the number of rows in a 'vars' list, years to the first and last of a 'years' list, built to a 'built' date and items to the number of rows in an 'items' or 'entries' list.
data.registry_files.how_to_read: Add the bytes of rows to see their combined size; add records or values only within the data files. The title names the content of the file and, in brackets, its main source when the registry gives one.
caveats: datasets counts all rows in the file's variable list. In the file of 2026-10-19, economy_series.json has 74 rows, of which 13 carry a definition but no yearly values (their values are in the housing series).
years is the range in the file's own list of years, not a guarantee that every variable has every year.
records, fields and values are null for documentation and index files, which are listed and sized but not counted.

values.file: File name in site/data/, for example landuse.geojson.
values.title: Plain title, for example 'Land use plan (Junta de Planificación, 2015)'.
values.domains: Domain ids from the domain registry, primary first, for example ["environment.land"]. Defined in dictionary_src/domains.json.
values.licence_class: One of open, open-with-conditions, own, unstated, licensed-not-open. See dictionary_src/README.md.
values.tier: Size budget of the file: small (up to 1 MB), medium (up to 8 MB) or large (up to 50 MB).
values.geography: Geography level of the file: island, region, municipio, barrio, tract, block-group, block, point, line, polygon, raster, network or none.
values.time: Time type of the file: point, period, window, vintage, snapshot, event or static.
values.bytes: Size in bytes, line ends counted as one byte. On 2026-10-19 the largest file is landuse.geojson (17,741,073 bytes).
values.datasets: Number of rows in the file's variable list. In the file of 2026-10-05: economy_series.json 70, housing_series.json 46.
values.years: [first, last] of the file's years. In the file of 2026-10-05: economy_series.json [2001, 2025], housing_series.json [2003, 2025].
values.built: Date stored in the file. In the file of 2026-10-05: dictionary.json 2026-10-05, economy_series.json 2026-10-04, housing_series.json 2026-10-03, operators.json 2026-10-02.
values.items: Number of rows in the file's item or entry list. On 2026-10-19: gazetteer.json 48,450, wanted.json 164 (2026-11-14).
values.gzip_bytes: Size compressed with gzip at level 6, about what a browser downloads (docs/performance.md).
values.loaded_by: The pages that fetch the file without a click, as [{route, when}] with when 'first' or 'later'; an empty list when the file loads only on use.
values.kind: data (counted), documentation (the files whose primary domain is system.docs: the dictionary, the catalog, meta.json, wanted.json) or index (gazetteer.json).
values.records: Observation units counted by ledger.py; null for documentation and index files. See the entry on records, fields and values.
values.fields: Variables with at least one value; null for documentation and index files.
values.values: Non-null observations (data points); null for documentation and index files.
values.vertices: Positions of the file's geometry; null for a file without geometry.
values.first_published: Date the file first reached the published site (YYYY-MM-DD, Puerto Rico). See the entry on the dates.
values.versions: Number of content versions published, for example 8 for places.json on 2026-10-19.
values.documented_by: Number of dictionary entries whose where.files name the file, for example 38 for acs_barrio.json.
values.review: The state of the file's reviews: {status, flags, open, cleared, cleared_types}. See the entry on the compliance review.

data.registry_files.source_detail: registry.py (records, build) and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source

data.registry_limits.plain: The total size of the published data and its share of the hosting limit the build plans for. On 2026-10-06 the data use about 7% (about 71 million bytes) of a 1 GB site limit.
data.registry_limits.plain_es: El tamaño total de los datos publicados y la parte que ocupa del límite de hospedaje previsto. El 2026-10-06 los datos usan cerca del 7% (unos 71 millones de bytes) de un límite de 1 GB para el sitio.
data.registry_limits.definition: total_bytes is the sum of the sizes of the listed files. limits holds the site limit (1,048,576,000 bytes), the single-file limit (104,857,600 bytes) and the planning fraction (0.6). used_fraction is total_bytes divided by the site limit, rounded to three decimals. needs_planning is true when the total is at least 60% of the site limit or any single file is at least 60% of the file limit.
data.registry_limits.method: registry.py adds the file sizes, divides by PAGES_SITE_LIMIT, and compares with WARN_AT (0.6).
data.registry_limits.how_to_read: 0.062 means the data folder uses 6.2% of the site limit (file of 2026-10-04). The planning line is at 60%, about 629 million bytes. In the file of 2026-10-04 the total is about 65 million bytes, needs_planning is false, and the largest file, landuse.geojson (17,741,073 bytes), is 16.9% of the single-file limit.
caveats: The sum covers site/data/ only. The pages, scripts, fonts and images add less than 1 MB.

The limits are the planning values set in registry.py for GitHub Pages ('about 1 GB' for a site and 100 MB for a file, as its comments say). They are not a statement of GitHub's current rules; check GitHub's documentation.

Sizes on the Data management page, the data dictionary page and in the Ask the observatory chat use 1 MB = 1,048,576 bytes, so 100,000,000 bytes shows as 95.4 MB. Entries that give a size in MB use 1 MB = 1 million bytes.

values.total_bytes: About 71 million in the file of 2026-10-06: sum of the sizes of the listed files.
values.limits.site_bytes: 1,048,576,000: planning limit for the whole site (1,000 x 1,024 x 1,024 bytes).
values.limits.file_bytes: 104,857,600: limit for one file (100 x 1,024 x 1,024 bytes).
values.limits.plan_at_fraction: 0.6: the share of a limit (60%) at which needs_planning turns true.
values.used_fraction: 0.068 in the file of 2026-10-06: total_bytes / site_bytes, rounded to 3 decimals.
values.needs_planning: false in the file of 2026-10-06: neither the total nor any file has reached 60% of its limit.
values.built: 2026-10-06: date the registry was written (current file).
values.growth_note: Text: a planning note that says the data folder only grows and that very large files may later move to separate storage.

data.registry_limits.source_detail: registry.py (PAGES_SITE_LIMIT, PAGES_FILE_LIMIT, WARN_AT); written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source

data.file_dates.plain: When a data file first appeared on the published site, and when its content last changed. A rebuild that writes the same data on another day changes neither date, so the dates show when new information was added.
data.file_dates.plain_es: Cuándo apareció un archivo de datos por primera vez en el sitio publicado y cuándo cambió su contenido por última vez. Una compilación que escribe los mismos datos otro día no cambia ninguna de las dos fechas, así que las fechas muestran cuándo se agregó información nueva.
data.file_dates.definition: first_published is the date the file first reached the published site; it never moves. last_updated is the last date its content hash changed, and versions the number of content versions published. The content hash is the SHA-256 (its first 16 hexadecimal digits) of the file's JSON in canonical form (keys sorted, no spaces) without the build stamps built, generated_at and snapshot_built outside its records; a file that is not JSON is hashed as bytes. Dates are Puerto Rico dates (UTC-4).
data.file_dates.method: The ledger (dictionary_src/data_ledger.json) keeps each file's dates, versions, hash, size and counts. Up to 2026-10-19 it was rebuilt from git (python ledger.py --backfill): each commit of the first-parent history of main is a publication on its Puerto Rico date; a file's first_published is the date of the first such commit that holds it, and last_updated the date of the last one that changed its content hash. From then on, registry.py compares the hashes at every build: a changed hash sets last_updated to the build date and adds a version; a new file gets both dates; first_published never moves; a rebuild with the same content changes nothing. The nightly transit refresh runs the same step and commits the ledger with the data.
data.file_dates.how_to_read: On 2026-10-19, flood.geojson was first published on 2026-10-01 and never changed (one version); places.json was first published on 2026-10-01 and last updated on 2026-10-18 (eight versions).
caveats: Before 2026-10-19 a date is the day the change was merged into main, which publishes the site; from then on it is the day of the build that changed the file, which can be a few days before the merge.
Only content counts: a new build date written inside a file is not an update.
catalog.json and the dictionary files change whenever the dictionary or the size of any file changes, so they are updated often.

versions counts each build that changed the content. A branch built several times with different content counts each build; python ledger.py --backfill origin/main followed by python registry.py counts it again from the history of main.
data.file_dates.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source

view.label: Data management: published data files

data.registry_history.plain: The totals of the published data on each date they changed: files, size, records, fields, values and dictionary items. It shows when new information was added.
data.registry_history.plain_es: Los totales de los datos publicados en cada fecha en que cambiaron: archivos, tamaño, registros, campos, valores y elementos del diccionario. Muestra cuándo se agregó información nueva.
data.registry_history.definition: history is a list of rows {date, files, bytes, records, fields, values, items}: the totals at the end of each Puerto Rico date on which one of them changed. records, fields and values add the data files; bytes adds every listed file; items is the number of entries in the data dictionary (null before it existed).
data.registry_history.method: Rebuilt from git up to 2026-10-19 (python ledger.py --backfill: the totals after each commit of the first-parent history of main, keeping the last state of each date), then extended by registry.py at every build: a row is added when the totals differ from the last row, and a second build on the same day replaces that day's row.
data.registry_history.how_to_read: From 2026-10-01 to 2026-10-19 the published values went from 728,325 in 13 files to 3,520,446 in 77 files.
caveats: The counts of old versions use today's adapters.
A date with no row is a date on which no total changed.
data.registry_history.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source

view.label: Data management: growth

data.records_fields_values.plain: How much data a published file holds: its records (the observation units, such as a municipio in a year or a place), its fields (the variables they carry) and its values (the data points: each field of each record that holds a value). Vertices count the positions of its geometry apart. The Data management page shows them for every file, with totals.
data.records_fields_values.plain_es: Cuántos datos contiene un archivo publicado: sus registros (las unidades de observación, como un municipio en un año o un lugar), sus campos (las variables que llevan) y sus valores (los datos: cada campo de cada registro que tiene un valor). Los vértices cuentan aparte las posiciones de su geometría. La página de Gestión de datos los muestra para cada archivo, con totales.
data.records_fields_values.definition: A record is an observation unit: a feature of a GeoJSON file; a row of a table (a place, a stop, a trip, a road edge, a census block); in a series file, an area in a period that holds at least one value (a municipio in a year, a barrio in a five-year window). A field is a variable the records carry (a GeoJSON property, a series variable, a margin of error, a column); a cell that holds a list is one field, and in a file with several tables the fields of each table are counted. A value (data point) is a non-null scalar in a field of a record; a list cell counts its non-null elements; null, absent and the empty string are missing. Metadata (titles, labels, notes, sources, build dates, methods, checks), geometry coordinates, the keys a file stores once as a lookup (geo.ids, years) and lookup tables (a legend, the CPI deflator, the gazetteer) are not values. A vertex is a position of a geometry: a GeoJSON coordinate pair, a point's latitude and longitude, a path point, a road node or shape point.
data.records_fields_values.method: ledger.py reads each published file and applies the adapter of its family: GeoJSON (features and their properties; the positions of the geometry), series (every area and period of geo.ids and the years of each variable and margin of error, with the per-area and island tables of economy_series.json and housing_series.json), columnar files (one list per field, one position per record: the exposure files, place_access.json, wcrp_rvi_inputs.json, wcrp_social.json), lists of records (places.json, transport.json, hurricanes.json, population_blocks.json), and one adapter each for the tables of transit_supply.json, the trips files, operators.json, geo/crosswalk.json, housing.json and landuse_summary.json. roads.bin is read from its header: one record per road edge with three fields (length, road class, one-way), and its nodes and shape points as vertices. Documentation (system.docs) and the place-name index (system.tools) are listed and sized but not counted. The counts of municipalities.json, barrios.geojson, places.json and acs_barrio.json were checked by an independent script (docs/data-management.md).
data.records_fields_values.how_to_read: In the file of 2026-10-19 the 60 data files hold 409,574 records, 1,381 fields and 3,520,446 values; roads.bin holds 679,263 of the values (226,421 road edges). A value that two files repeat counts in each, so the total measures what is published, not distinct facts.
caveats: A record is not the same unit in every file: a municipio in a year, a barrio in a window, a place, a trip. Compare records within a family of files.
Coded values such as 99,999 meters (beyond the search limit) count as values; only null, absent and empty text are missing.
The counts of the versions published before 2026-10-19 (the growth history) use today's adapters on the old files.
data.records_fields_values.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source

Data management: definitions

data.wanted.plain: A list of datasets that could be added to the observatory, with the source, the license as understood so far, and what still has to be confirmed for each. The Ask the observatory chat reads it to answer 'What data is missing?'.
data.wanted.plain_es: Una lista de conjuntos de datos que se podrían agregar al observatorio, con la fuente, la licencia según se entiende hasta ahora y lo que falta confirmar de cada uno. El chat "Preguntar al observatorio" la lee para contestar "¿Qué datos faltan?".
data.wanted.definition: wanted.json holds the date of its last edit, a note, a note about the older 'theme' field, the list of five statuses and one row (item) for each dataset that could be added or that was found unavailable. A row says what has been checked and what has not.
data.wanted.method: Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) writes and updates the list by hand. Status moves from candidate to checked, building, live or blocked. The chat reads the file in the browser.
data.wanted.how_to_read: Read a row as an idea with a list of things still to confirm, not as a promise. A row in 'candidate' status has not been checked for license or coverage. In the file of 2026-11-14 the last edit is dated 2026-11-14 and there are 137 rows.
caveats: Licenses are not settled. In the file of 2026-11-04, 55 of the 118 rows begin 'US Government work'; the others say 'Not stated', 'To confirm', 'ODbL 1.0', 'No license', that the source's terms bar automated access, or something similar. Check each source's terms before any use.
The list is edited by hand, so a status can lag behind what the observatory already publishes. For what the observatory publishes now, see the table of published data files in this dictionary.
A row's 'size' and 'cadence' are as understood before any data are collected and may change.

Some candidates are published at record level by their source: PPP loans (geography 'Business address'; the row says borrower names are public but only aggregates are needed) and fatal traffic crashes (geography 'Crash point'). Records like these can relate to identifiable people or businesses. The PPP row says only aggregates are needed.

values.updated: Date of the last edit: 2026-10-06 in the current file.
values.note: Text saying that source, license, coverage and terms are confirmed before a dataset is added, that every row has a domain from the domain registry, and that status moves from candidate to checked, building, live or blocked.
values.domain_note: Text saying that 'theme' is the older grouping that the chat still reads and that it will be replaced by 'domain'.
values.statuses: The five status codes: candidate, checked, building, live, blocked.
values.items: One row for each dataset: 164 rows in the file of 2026-11-14.

data.wanted_item.plain: Each row of the wanted-data list says what the dataset is and why it would help. It gives the publisher, license, geography, update rate, size, status and what to check first.
data.wanted_item.plain_es: Cada fila de la lista de datos deseados dice qué es el conjunto de datos y por qué ayudaría. Da quién lo publica, la licencia, la geografía, cada cuánto se actualiza, el tamaño, el estado y qué revisar primero.
data.wanted_item.definition: A row has the fields id, theme, domain, domains, title, why, source, url, license, geography, cadence, size, status and check. Rows that were tested by request also have checked_on, and rows for blocked data may have who_to_ask. All are text, except domains (a list), url (a link or empty) and checked_on (a date).
data.wanted_item.method: Written by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR). The fields describe a candidate dataset before any data are collected.
data.wanted_item.how_to_read: 'why' says how the dataset would be used in the observatory. 'check' says what has to be confirmed before it could be added, such as coverage of Puerto Rico or reuse terms.
caveats: In the file of 2026-10-03, url is empty in 3 rows: gtfs-rt, recovery and municipal-finance.
license 'To confirm' means the license has not been confirmed. It is not a statement that the data are open.
size is a rough label. In the file of 2026-10-03, 20 rows are 'small', 6 are 'medium' and 4 start with 'large'.

values.id: Short identifier, for example cbp or gtfs-rt.
values.theme: Older grouping of the dataset, still read by the chat. In the file of 2026-10-05 there are 10 themes: Infrastructure and services 17, Health and education 17, Economy 10, Hazards and resilience 10, Governance and recovery 8, Population and households 7, Land and buildings 6, Tourism 5, Mobility and safety 3, Housing 1.
values.domain: Primary domain id from the domain registry (dictionary_src/domains.json), for example hazards.
values.domains: All domain ids, primary first, then secondary ones.
values.title: Name of the dataset.
values.why: What the observatory would gain from it.
values.url: Link to the publisher's page; empty when the row gives none.
values.licence: The license or terms as understood so far, for example 'US Government work, public domain' or 'To confirm'.
values.geography: Finest geography the source offers, for example Municipio, Station or Raster.
values.cadence: How often the source updates, for example Annual or Live.
values.size: Expected size: small, medium or large, sometimes with a note.
values.status: One of candidate, checked, building, live, blocked. See the entry on statuses.
values.check: What was found when the source was tested by request, and what still has to be confirmed before the dataset could be added.
values.checked_on: Date the source was tested by request (2026-10-05 for rows tested in the audit of that date).
values.who_to_ask: For blocked data: the organization to ask in writing. The observatory contacts nobody by itself.

data.wanted_item.source_detail: wanted.json items; written by FPR, not taken from an external source

data.wanted_status.plain: Every candidate dataset has a status. On 2026-11-24, 23 rows are 'candidate', 47 'checked', 31 'blocked', 63 'live' and 0 'building'.
data.wanted_status.plain_es: Cada conjunto de datos candidato tiene un estado. El 2026-11-24, 23 filas están en "Candidato", 47 en "Verificado", 31 en "Bloqueado", 63 en "En vivo" y 0 en "En construcción".
data.wanted_status.definition: The status says how far a candidate has moved from an idea to published data: candidate (not yet checked), checked (source, license, coverage and terms confirmed), building (Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) is collecting the data), live (published in the observatory) or blocked (could not be collected).
data.wanted_status.method: FPR sets the status by hand. The chat shows it next to each title.
data.wanted_status.how_to_read: Count of rows per status in the file of 2026-11-24: candidate 23, checked 47, building 0, live 63, blocked 31.
caveats: The list is edited by hand, so a status can lag behind what the observatory already publishes. A 'live' status means the dataset is already in the observatory. In the file of 2026-10-06, four rows have that status.
Blocked rows (broadband, gtfs-rt) say in their 'check' field why they could not be collected.

values.candidate: In the file of 2026-11-24: 23 rows. An idea. Source, license, coverage and terms still have to be confirmed.
values.checked: In the file of 2026-11-19: 47 rows. The source was tested by request on 2026-10-05 or later (the row's 'checked_on'); the 'check' field gives what was found and what still needs confirming. Collection has not started.

The dataset is published in the observatory.
values.blocked: In the file of 2026-11-16: 31 rows, for example hurricane shelters (no license stated), open dumps (no license stated), the locations of the water systems outside PRASA (not public), SAMHSA's live treatment locator (no license stated), the newest HUD CHAS window (HUD User refuses scripts), real-time bus and train positions and the police incident feed. The dataset could not be collected when the file was last edited (2026-10-06); the 'check' field gives the reason and 'who_to_ask' names the organization to ask in writing.

data.wanted_status.source_detail: wanted.json 'statuses' and 'items.status'; written by FPR, not taken from an external source

data.registry_withheld.plain: Counts of what the observatory holds back to protect homes, privacy and sensitive services: tourism places counted but not drawn, listings that are not tourism, health center sites, shelters, private homes on the National Register, public housing at an approximate location, treatment facilities and tax-exempt organizations. Counts only: no names and no locations.
data.registry_withheld.plain_es: Conteos de lo que el observatorio no publica para proteger los hogares, la privacidad y los servicios sensibles: lugares turísticos contados pero no dibujados, listados que no son turismo, sitios de centros de salud, albergues, casas privadas del Registro Nacional, residenciales públicos con ubicación aproximada, centros de tratamiento y organizaciones exentas de impuestos. Solo conteos: sin nombres y sin ubicaciones.
data.registry_withheld.definition: withheld lists rows {id, count, of, parts, file, doc}: count is the number held back, of the number it belongs to, parts a breakdown, file the published file the count is read from and doc the dictionary entry that gives the rule. The ids: places_not_drawn (the rows of places.json with withheld), not_tourism (meta.json counts.not_tourism_dropped), hrsa_sites (health_series.json notes.sites.service_sites), shelters (0: none is published; with the status of the wanted.json row shelters), nrhp_private_homes (community_series.json notes.historic_places.counted_not_drawn_residences), public_housing_approximate (facility_series.json notes.public_housing.not_drawn_approximate_location), treatment_facilities (community_series.json notes.treatment_facilities.facilities) and nonprofits (nonprofit_series.json notes.organizations).
data.registry_withheld.method: registry.py reads each count from the published file at every build, so the page follows the data.
data.registry_withheld.how_to_read: On 2026-10-19: 1,005 of 32,541 places counted but not drawn (971 holiday rentals, 34 named by a street address), 2,577 listings that are not tourism left out, 160 health center sites, no shelters, 73 of 342 National Register listings, 132 of 304 public housing developments, 87 treatment facilities and 2,572 organizations.
caveats: These are counts of what is held back, not a list of it: no name or location is published.
data.registry_withheld.source_detail: registry.py and ledger.py; written by the observatory's own build step, not an external source

measures.inflation_adjustment.plain: Ticking 'Inflation-adjusted' restates dollars of different years in the dollars of the latest year, using the US Consumer Price Index. It lets you compare money across years. The observatory does not use a Puerto Rico price index, so the result is an approximation.
measures.inflation_adjustment.plain_es: Al marcar "Ajustado por inflación", los dólares de distintos años se expresan en dólares del año más reciente, con el Índice de Precios al Consumidor de EE. UU. Así se puede comparar el dinero entre años. El observatorio no usa un índice de precios de Puerto Rico, así que el resultado es una aproximación.
measures.inflation_adjustment.definition: Adjusted value = value × (CPI of the reference year ÷ CPI of the data year). The CPI is the Bureau of Labor Statistics Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), US city average, all items, not seasonally adjusted (series CUUR0000SA0), annual average, 1982-84 = 100. The reference year is the latest year in the CPI table. The table runs from 2000 to the latest full calendar year at the time of the build, so it holds a factor for every year of every dollar dataset (the earliest is 2001, for FEMA Public Assistance). A year outside the table would take the nearest end of the table. The option appears on datasets whose unit is dollars (dollar levels and dollar totals) and does not change counts or percentages.
measures.inflation_adjustment.method: Function cpiFactor in site/js/economy.js, applied in ecCalc before any rescaling, so per-resident and per-km² dollars are also in reference-year dollars. In a change layer the base value is restated with its own year's factor. Margins of error are multiplied by the same factor. The CPI values are stored in economy_series.json (deflator.cpi) and come from economy_series.py, which reads the annual averages from the public Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data API (Application Programming Interface).
measures.inflation_adjustment.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot the reference year is 2025, and $1,000 in 2014 equals $1,360 in 2025 dollars (CPI 321.943 ÷ 236.736). Puerto Rico's median gross rent rose 25.1% between the 2010-2014 and 2020-2024 windows in nominal dollars but fell 5.6% in 2025 dollars.
caveats: The observatory uses the US city average and no Puerto Rico price index. Prices in Puerto Rico can move differently from the US average, so adjusted values are an approximation.

The CPI table starts in 2000, so every year of every dollar dataset has its own factor, including the years 2001 to 2009 of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) series that the Trend chart shows.

American Community Survey (ACS) dollar figures are labeled by the last year of a five-year window, and the factor uses that last year. The Census Bureau's documentation of the 2013-2017 Puerto Rico Community Survey 5-year estimates says monetary values are adjusted to the dollars of the final year of the period with the national CPI. The observatory applies no adjustment of its own to ACS dollars, so they are the figures the Bureau published. The Analysis tab describes them as dollars of each window's last year, and the Housing page describes them as 'not adjusted for inflation' (the observatory itself adds no adjustment). Check the Bureau's documentation for the window you cite.
Federal fiscal-year awards (October to September) use the CPI of the calendar year with the same number. Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) wages are for the calendar year.
The adjustment is one national index applied to every municipality and every kind of spending.
measures.inflation_adjustment.source_detail: Bureau of Labor Statistics CPI-U US city average, series CUUR0000SA0. Dollar datasets: ACS medians and incomes, QCEW wages and pay, USAspending awards, OpenFEMA dollars, FEMA National Risk Index expected annual loss.

exposure.method.plain: The observatory counts how many residents and homes are inside a hazard or protected land, or near transit, by giving each census block to the layer that holds its one internal point. The results are computed from open layers, not measured.
exposure.method.plain_es: El observatorio cuenta cuántas personas residentes y viviendas están dentro de una zona de riesgo o de un terreno protegido, o cerca del transporte colectivo, asignando cada bloque censal a la capa que contiene su único punto interno. Los resultados se calculan a partir de capas abiertas; no son mediciones.
exposure.method.definition: A census block is the smallest area of the 2020 Census (41,987 in Puerto Rico, 36,570 with residents). Its internal point is a point the Census Bureau guarantees lies inside the block. A block is in a layer if its point is inside a polygon of the layer, or within 400 m of a stop, and then all of its 2020 residents and housing units are counted as exposed. Counts are added up to the municipio, the barrio and the census tract that hold the block, so they add up exactly between levels. Residents are the 2020 Census count; the Census Bureau adds noise to small counts to protect privacy, and does not for housing units at block level.
exposure.method.method: Checks made when the files are built: every area's total equals the geography crosswalk's; every set lies inside its superset for every block (sea level steps, flood areas, protected areas, the transit classes); the three files add up to the same municipio and island figures. Checks made once, on the data: counting from the simplified flood outlines instead of FEMA's full-resolution ones changes the island count of residents in the 1% flood area by 0.3% (316,309 against 317,290); NOAA's polygons read the fast way give the same blocks as GDAL's default on three layers (inundation at 3 ft and at 10 ft, low-lying areas at 3 ft); the six transit fields match the Transit tab (stop_cur to the decimal in all 78 municipios; stop_sched within 0.5% of a municipio's residents and 0.02% on the island). Whole-block counting was also compared with spreading each block's residents evenly over its outline, on the blocks with no water (98.9% of residents; docs/analysis/exposure-2026-10). For the island the two differ by 1.1 points of the island's residents or less in every layer tested: the 1% flood area 9.5% by internal point against 10.5% by area; sea level rise at 3 ft 0.7% against 0.8%; protected areas 1.7% against 1.5%. For a municipio the middle difference is 1.1 points or less and the largest 11.2 points. The counts that assume nothing about where people live inside a block (only the blocks wholly inside a layer, and every block the layer touches) are far apart: for the 1% flood area 5.1% to 24.1% of the island's residents, against 9.6% counted.
exposure.method.how_to_read: Read each figure as 'residents (or homes) in blocks whose internal point is inside the layer', a close estimate of how many are in the layer. Treat small differences between areas as noise.
caveats: A block cut by a boundary is counted whole in or out, so a count near an edge can be too high or too low. Large areas average this out; a single barrio or tract does not: one barrio or tract in ten differs from an area-weighted count by more than 6 points of its residents in the 1% flood area, 4 points for sea level rise at 10 ft and 3 points for protected areas, and the largest difference is 74 points. Read small-area counts as rough and look at the total beside them.
Computed, not measured: no one counted the people inside the polygons.

Not included yet: storm surge (NHC SLOSH), and distance to schools, hospitals and shelters. They need data that the observatory has not harvested yet (listed in wanted.json); the method adds a layer without changing the files above.
exposure.method.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files
exposure.method.source_detail: See each exposure entry. Method note and results: docs/exposure.md.

exposure.share.plain: Out of every 100 residents (or homes) in an area, how many are exposed. It is the count divided by the area's total, times 100.
exposure.share.plain_es: De cada 100 residentes (o viviendas) de un área, cuántos están expuestos. Es el conteo dividido entre el total del área, multiplicado por 100.
exposure.share.definition: share = 100 x exposure count / total of the same measure (residents or housing units) for the same area. For a group of areas, add the counts and add the totals, then divide. The files hold counts and totals, not shares, so any group of areas gets an exact share.
exposure.share.method: Worked out wherever it is shown, from the counts and totals of the exposure files (never stored, never averaged across areas).
exposure.share.how_to_read: A share is for comparing areas of different size. A share of 100% means every resident (or home) counted in the area is exposed; an area with a total of zero has no share.
caveats: A small area has a share that swings with one block: look at the count as well.
Shares of different layers overlap: a resident can be in a flood area and in a protected area at once, so they cannot be added.
exposure.share.geography: 78 municipios, 901 barrios and 981 census tracts, in three files

methods.hexagon_counts.plain: The Map layers tab can draw the tourism places that pass its filters as hexagons instead of pins. Every hexagon covers the same area, so the number in it also says how crowded the place is. Three more shading choices count the places that pass the filters in each municipality.
methods.hexagon_counts.plain_es: La pestaña Capas del mapa puede dibujar como hexágonos, en lugar de marcadores, los lugares turísticos que pasan sus filtros. Cada hexágono cubre la misma área, así que el número que contiene también indica qué tan concentrados están los lugares. Otras tres opciones de sombreado cuentan los lugares que pasan los filtros en cada municipio.
methods.hexagon_counts.definition: Hexagons: the map points of the places are projected with a Lambert azimuthal equal-area projection centered on Puerto Rico and counted in a grid of regular hexagons of 2, 10 or 50 square kilometers, as the user chooses. In that projection equal areas on the plane are equal areas on the ground, so every hexagon covers the same ground area (to about 0.3% on the real earth). The legend gives five classes of the counts, with the number of hexagons in each, and states the method. Municipalities: the same places counted in each municipality, as a total, per 1,000 residents (2020 Census) and per square kilometer of land. Both follow the filters of the Map layers tab (categories, minimum confidence, places of worship) and change when a filter changes; the fixed counts in the shading menu (tourism places, per 1,000 residents, per km²) stay as they were built.
methods.hexagon_counts.method: Core.hexbin (site/js/core/hexbin.js) projects each place and assigns it to the hexagon that holds it, using axial coordinates; site/js/app.js draws the hexagons (drawHexes) and counts the municipalities (countShown) from the places that pass the filters. The view is kept in the link as pv=hex2, pv=hex10 or pv=hex50, and the municipal shading as s=shown, s=shown_per_1000_residents or s=shown_per_km2. The tourism places file (about 3 MB compressed) is downloaded the first time the view is used.
methods.hexagon_counts.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot with the default filters (confidence 0.50 or higher, places of worship left out), the 23,467 places with a pin (the 24,209 counted places less the 742 holiday rentals and numbered units, which are counted but not drawn) fall in 950 hexagons of 10 square kilometers: the busiest holds 447 and half hold 8 or fewer. In hexagons of 2 km² they fall in 2,833 (busiest 309) and in hexagons of 50 km² in 231 (busiest 1,988). By municipality, San Juan has 3,424 counted places, Vieques 237 and Culebra 136.
caveats: A hexagon is a counting unit, not a place: it ignores municipal and barrio borders, and a busy hexagon can straddle two municipalities.
Counts depend on the size of the hexagon. Compare hexagons of the same size only; the legend names the size.
Equal area is exact on a sphere of the earth's mean radius; on the real earth, which is slightly flattened, areas are right to about 0.3%.
The places are listings, not businesses, and the filters decide which listings count (see methods.municipality_assignment).
Hexagons over the sea are not drawn: only hexagons that hold a place appear.
methods.hexagon_counts.geography: hexagons of 2, 10 or 50 km² and 78 municipalities
methods.hexagon_counts.source_detail: The places are the Overture Maps listings that the observatory classifies (places.json). Residents and land area are the municipal fields of municipalities.json.

view.label: Map, Map layers tab: tourism places as hexagons of 10 km²
Map, Map layers tab: places that pass the filters, per km² in each municipality

measures.chat_trend.plain: When asked how something has changed, the Ask the observatory chat gives the island's change and the three municipalities that rose most and fell most. It ignores very small starting values so that tiny bases do not produce huge percentages.
measures.chat_trend.plain_es: Cuando se le pregunta cómo ha cambiado algo, el chat "Preguntar al observatorio" da el cambio de la isla y los tres municipios que más subieron y más bajaron. No toma en cuenta los valores iniciales muy pequeños, para que una base diminuta no produzca porcentajes enormes.
measures.chat_trend.definition: The change runs from a start year to an end year. With no year in the question, the start is the dataset's first year from 2003 on and the end is its latest year. Two years in the question set the start and the end. One year after 'since' (or 'desde') sets the start. A named year that the dataset does not have is ignored. For rates and ratios the change is the difference in points. For counts and dollars it is the percent change. For counts it uses only municipalities whose starting value is at least 50, for dollar totals at least $100,000, and for dollar levels (such as medians and average pay) a starting value above zero. The answer lists the three largest rises and the three largest falls, and puts 'Change since the base year' on the map with the starting year as the base.
measures.chat_trend.method: Function Tools.trend in site/js/chat.js; the base values and the thresholds are in the minBase constant of that function. The chat's map step calls the Analysis tab with norm 'change' and the starting year as the base. For dollar datasets it also turns on 'Inflation-adjusted' on the layer it opens.
measures.chat_trend.how_to_read: Ask 'How has poverty changed since 2014?' The reply gives Puerto Rico's poverty rate in 2014 and now, the three municipalities where it rose most (or fell least) and the three where it fell most. If no municipality fell, the second list is headed 'Rose least'.
caveats: Municipalities below the minimum starting value are left out of the rises and falls, though they appear on the map.

For dollar datasets the figures in the reply are in the dollars of each year, but the map the chat opens is already inflation-adjusted (its legend title ends '2025 dollars'), so the two can differ. Untick 'Inflation-adjusted' on the layer to see the map in the dollars of each year.
For FEMA series the change compares the first declaration year from 2003 on with the latest one, which means one set of disasters against another. It is not a trend in yearly spending.
Survey windows can overlap and the population series changes base in 2020, so read changes with the entries on both.
It names patterns, not causes.
measures.chat_trend.source_detail: Any dataset with more than one year in the Analysis tab.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate, change since 2014 (then ask the chat: How has poverty changed since 2014?)

measures.municipal_median.plain: The Housing page shows the middle value of the 78 municipalities, the lowest, the highest and the Puerto Rico figure above each chart. The middle value is not the island figure.
measures.municipal_median.plain_es: Sobre cada gráfica, la página de Vivienda muestra el valor central de los 78 municipios, el más bajo, el más alto y la cifra de Puerto Rico. El valor central no es la cifra de la isla.
measures.municipal_median.definition: The median of the municipal values that have a value in the year on screen: sort them and take the middle one, or the average of the two middle ones when the count is even. Each municipality counts once, whatever its population. Lowest and highest are the smallest and largest of the same values. The Puerto Rico figure is the dataset's own island value, not a calculation from the municipalities.
measures.municipal_median.method: Function updateViz and the median helper in site/js/housing.js. They run on the values of the 78 municipalities in the year the dataset resolves to (see the nearest-year rule). The line above each chart reads 'Median of the 78 municipalities, lowest, highest, Puerto Rico'. The words 'the 78 municipalities' are fixed text, so the label still says 78 when fewer municipalities have a value.
measures.municipal_median.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, for median household income in the 2020-2024 window, the middle of the 78 municipal values is $24,070, the lowest is $16,314 (Las Marías), the highest is $46,731 (Guaynabo) and Puerto Rico as a whole is $26,297. The middle municipal value ($24,070) is not the island median ($26,297). The island figure covers all households. The middle value counts each municipality once.
caveats: Each municipality counts once, so the middle value is not weighted by population and is not the island median.
The label always says 78, even when fewer municipalities have a value in the year shown. Check the ranked chart for the count.
For survey series the middle value uses the estimates alone. Margins of error are not used.
measures.municipal_median.source_detail: Housing page series: American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates, Population Estimates and census counts, and OpenFEMA housing assistance.

view.label: Housing page: the line above each chart

measures.rank.plain: A municipality's position when the 78 municipalities are sorted from the highest value to the lowest. Rank 1 is the highest value, not the best result.
measures.rank.plain_es: La posición de un municipio cuando los 78 municipios se ordenan del valor más alto al más bajo. La posición 1 es el valor más alto, no el mejor resultado.
measures.rank.definition: 1 + the number of municipalities with a higher value, among the municipalities that have a value. It is written '#19 of 78'. The Puerto Rico row has no rank. On the Analysis tab and the Housing page, municipalities with the same value share the better rank: if three tie for fifth, all show #5 and the next shows #8. The 2D map's Municipality tab note and Rankings tab work differently (see the cautions).
measures.rank.method: Function ecRank in site/js/economy.js (Analysis tab inspector and popup) and rankOf in site/js/housing.js (Housing page). Both count the municipalities with a higher value. The rank follows the layer's settings: year, rescaling, inflation adjustment and base year. The Ask the observatory chat's municipality profile also lists a position for each indicator, under the note 'Rank 1 = the highest value among the 78 municipalities'.
measures.rank.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Ponce has rank #19 of 78 for poverty rate in the 2020-2024 window: 18 municipalities have a higher rate. For poverty, rank 1 is the highest rate; for income, rank 1 is the highest income.
caveats: Rank 1 is the highest value. Whether that is good or bad depends on the dataset.

On the 2D map, the Municipality tab note ('Rank #n of 78 by tourism places') and the Rankings tab give the position in the sorted list, so tied municipalities get consecutive ranks, not one shared rank. The Ask the observatory chat's municipality profile does the same.
The 'of n' shrinks when some municipalities have no value, so ranks from different datasets are out of different totals.
Ranks use the unrounded values. Two municipalities that show the same rounded number can have different ranks.
A rank hides the size of the gap between neighbors. Use the value, and its margin of error for survey series.
measures.rank.source_detail: Any dataset in the Analysis tab, the Housing page series and the tourism place counts.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: click a municipality to see its rank

measures.correlation.plain: The correlation r is a number from −1 to +1 that shows how closely two datasets move together across the municipalities. It shows a pattern across places, not a cause.
measures.correlation.plain_es: La correlación r es un número de −1 a +1 que muestra qué tan de cerca se mueven juntos dos conjuntos de datos entre los municipios. Muestra un patrón entre lugares, no una causa.
measures.correlation.definition: Pearson's correlation coefficient r between two layers across the municipalities that have a value in both, with n the number of such municipalities. Near +1 the points lie close to a rising straight line, near −1 to a falling line, near 0 there is no straight-line pattern. The scatter plot also draws the least-squares line of the second layer on the first. Each municipality counts once, whatever its population. On log scales only municipalities with both values above zero are used and no line is drawn. The workbench's Correlations tab gives r for every pair of visible layers, and also Spearman's rank correlation (Pearson on the ranks).
measures.correlation.method: Scatter tab of the workbench: ecBenchScatter in site/js/economy.js, using the visible layers with their current year, rescaling and settings. The chat: chPearson in site/js/chat.js, which needs at least 8 municipalities with both values and compares each dataset in its default view (counts per 1,000 residents, dollar totals per resident, everything else as published) at its latest year unless a year is named. The chat says 'rise together' when r > 0, 'move in opposite directions' when r < 0 and 'show little relationship' when |r| < 0.3.
measures.correlation.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, across the 78 municipalities, poverty and median household income (2020-2024 window) have r = −0.89: where poverty is higher, income tends to be lower. Unemployment (2025) and poverty (2024) have r = 0.67. Tourism-related jobs as a share of jobs and median household income have r = −0.02 with n = 39: no pattern, and only 39 municipalities have both values.
caveats: A pattern across municipalities is not proof that one thing causes the other, and it does not say what is true for the people or households inside them.
The two layers can be for different years (each shows its latest year at or before the one chosen). Check the year shown beside each layer in the legend.
A few large municipalities, a few extreme values or noisy survey figures for small municipalities can move r a lot. r only measures straight-line patterns.

With 'Log scales' ticked, r is still calculated on the original values of the municipalities with both values above zero. It is not the correlation of the logarithms and does not describe the curve drawn.
No significance test or confidence interval is calculated. Check n: a low n (withheld or missing values) makes r less reliable.
The result depends on the settings: the same pair can have a different r per 1,000 residents than as a raw count.
measures.correlation.source_detail: Any two datasets in the Analysis tab; scatter plots are drawn with Chart.js.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty and median household income (open the Workbench, Scatter tab)

measures.model_output.plain: Figures that an outside model produced and that a person loaded in the workbench. They are model results, not observed data, and the observatory checks only their format.
measures.model_output.plain_es: Cifras que produjo un modelo externo y que una persona cargó en la mesa de trabajo. Son resultados de un modelo, no datos observados, y el observatorio solo verifica su formato.
measures.model_output.definition: A CSV file with a header of lines starting with '#' (model_name, model_version, run_id, date, assumptions_url, license, contact_label) and the columns geography_key, geography_level, period, variable, value, unit and, optionally, lower and upper; or a GeoJSON FeatureCollection with a 'model' member holding the header and the same fields in each feature's properties. geography_level is 'municipio' (the five-digit code; 72 is Puerto Rico as a whole); period is a year. Each variable becomes a dataset of the Analysis tab labeled 'Model output (not observed data)', with the header in its definition. lower and upper must bracket the value; the map shows the value.
measures.model_output.method: Core.scenario.parseModel (site/js/core/scenario.js) checks the header, every row and the size (5 MB and 20,000 rows at most) and refuses the whole file on any error, listing up to 50; js/scenarios.js adds each variable to the engine. The format is in docs/scenarios.md; site/samples/model_output_sample.csv is a sample with made-up values.
measures.model_output.how_to_read: Read it as what a model says under its assumptions (the header's assumptions_url), not as a measurement.
caveats: Not observed data: the observatory checks the format, not the numbers.
The header names a team or organization as the contact; e-mail addresses and telephone numbers are refused.
measures.model_output.source_detail: The file a person loads; the observatory publishes no model results.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Scenarios)

measures.outliers.plain: When you use the Ask the observatory chat to compare two datasets, it names the municipalities that sit farthest from the usual pattern. Each gets a score: the bigger the score, positive or negative, the bigger the exception.
measures.outliers.plain_es: Cuando se usa el chat "Preguntar al observatorio" para comparar dos conjuntos de datos, este nombra los municipios que más se alejan del patrón usual. Cada uno recibe una puntuación: mientras mayor sea, positiva o negativa, mayor es la excepción.
measures.outliers.definition: For two datasets A (first) and B (second), the observatory fits the straight line B = intercept + slope × A across the municipalities by least squares. A municipality's residual e is its actual B minus the B the line predicts from its A. The standard deviation of the residuals is s = √(Σe² ÷ (n − 2)). The standardized residual is z = e ÷ s, in standard deviations. The municipalities with the largest |z| are the 'biggest exceptions': three in a comparison (listed only when |r| is at least 0.3) and two in each pattern. A positive z means B is higher than the line predicts.
measures.outliers.method: Function chPearson in site/js/chat.js returns the outliers sorted by |z|; the compare answer and the patterns answer list them as 'Biggest exceptions'. The residuals use all municipalities with both values, including the municipality being scored.
measures.outliers.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, for poverty (first) against median household income (second), 2020-2024 window: Guaynabo has z = +3.95, Gurabo +3.30 and Culebra −2.38. Guaynabo's and Gurabo's incomes are much higher than their poverty rates predict, and Culebra's is lower.
caveats: The score is not a test and not an error flag. It only says how far a municipality is from a straight-line pattern. A high |z| can be a real difference, noisy survey data or a different year.
The score changes if you swap the datasets, because the line is fitted to the second one.
It is not a leave-one-out score. A municipality that pulls the line toward itself looks less extreme.
It is meaningful only where a straight-line pattern is a fair description.
measures.outliers.source_detail: Any two datasets in the Analysis tab, compared in the chat.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty and median household income (then ask the chat: Do poverty and income move together?)

measures.peer_municipios.plain: For each municipio, the five municipios most like it in population and in residents per square kilometer.
measures.peer_municipios.plain_es: Para cada municipio, los cinco municipios más parecidos en población y en residentes por kilómetro cuadrado.
measures.peer_municipios.definition: The latest population of each municipio (Census Bureau estimates) and its residents per km² of land are each put on a log scale and then on z-scores across the 78 municipios. The five municipios at the shortest straight-line distance on those two numbers are the peers, nearest first.
measures.peer_municipios.method: Core.stats.peers and Core.stats.zscores (site/js/core/stats.js), called by profile.js (peersOf).
measures.peer_municipios.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot the peers of San Juan are Bayamón, Carolina, Guaynabo, Caguas and Toa Baja.
caveats: Similar in size and density only, not in income, economy or anything else.
measures.peer_municipios.source_detail: Population: the Analysis tab's population series; land area: Census TIGER (municipalities.json).

view.label: Area profile of San Juan

measures.patterns_ranking.plain: When asked for the most interesting patterns, the Ask the observatory chat compares many pairs of datasets from different areas of life, ranks them by how closely they move together and shows up to five. It starts with a note on where jobs concentrate.
measures.patterns_ranking.plain_es: Cuando se le piden los patrones más interesantes, el chat "Preguntar al observatorio" compara muchos pares de conjuntos de datos de distintas áreas de la vida, los ordena según qué tan de cerca se mueven juntos y muestra hasta cinco. Comienza con una nota sobre dónde se concentran los empleos.
measures.patterns_ranking.definition: Step 1: 26 datasets (listed in INSIGHT_KEYS in site/js/chat.js) are taken in their default view at their latest year: counts per 1,000 residents, dollar totals per resident, tourism jobs as a share of jobs, everything else as published. Step 2: the chat compares every pair of datasets except two kinds. It skips pairs in the same area, because Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) puts each dataset in one area: welfare, housing, work, mobility, tourism, money or people. It also skips pairs that are linked by definition, such as the employment rate and the unemployment rate (the code lists eight such pairs; seven involve datasets in this list). Step 3: it keeps pairs with at least 60 municipalities and |r| of at least 0.4, and sorts them by |r|. Step 4: it picks the strongest pairs, with no dataset used twice and no pair of areas used twice, until five are chosen. The answer starts with the municipality that has the most jobs: its share of the island's jobs, its share of residents and the share held by the five biggest job centers. It then adds a fixed sentence that many people cross municipal lines to work. That sentence is not calculated. It is an inference from jobs counted at the workplace and people counted at home, not a measured commuting flow.
measures.patterns_ranking.method: Function chInsights in site/js/chat.js, which calls chPearson (see the correlation entry). The result is computed once per page load. Nothing is sent anywhere.
measures.patterns_ranking.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 262 pairs from different areas were compared and 40 passed the cut-offs. San Juan holds 27% of the island's jobs and 10% of its residents, and San Juan, Guaynabo, Bayamón, Carolina and Ponce together hold 49% of the jobs. The five pairs shown: median household income and median gross rent (r = 0.80); working from home and driving alone to work (−0.70); federal awards per resident and jobs per 1,000 residents (0.66); government share of jobs and adults with a bachelor's degree (−0.64); residents aged 65 and over and the employment rate (−0.51).
caveats: Strongest is not most important. The list is an automatic scan of many pairs, and no significance test is applied.
The areas are FPR's own grouping. Pairs inside one area, such as poverty and income, are skipped, so some expected links do not appear.

In the 2026-10 snapshot, the federal awards and jobs pair is sensitive to San Juan: r is 0.66 with it and 0.52 without it (n = 77). San Juan has the most jobs, and statewide awards are often filed there.
Each dataset is at its own latest year (2024 or 2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot), so a pair can mix years.
A pattern across municipalities is not a cause, and the list changes when the data are updated.
measures.patterns_ranking.source_detail: The 26 datasets in INSIGHT_KEYS: survey series from the American Community Survey (ACS), unemployment from Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), jobs, pay and work sites from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), federal awards from USAspending, Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance from OpenFEMA, and the population denominators.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab (then open the chat and ask: What are the most interesting patterns?)

measures.composite_index.plain: A score you build yourself in the workbench from several datasets, with your own directions and weights. It is your own index, not an official one.
measures.composite_index.plain_es: Una puntuación que usted construye en la mesa de trabajo con varios conjuntos de datos, con sus propias direcciones y pesos. Es su propio índice, no uno oficial.
measures.composite_index.definition: Choose two to twelve datasets, say for each whether a higher value is better or worse, and give each a weight. Each input is read as a shaded map shows it (counts per 1,000 residents, dollar totals per resident, rates and shares as published) at the year the year control picks, and put on one scale across the 78 municipalities: z-scores (standard deviations from the average municipality), 0 to 100 between the lowest and the highest, or the percentile rank (0 to 100). An input where lower is better is turned round. The score is the weighted mean of the inputs a municipality has; a municipality with less than 80% of the weight present is left blank. Puerto Rico as a whole gets no score. The table gives each municipality's score, the share of the weight it has and what each input adds (the additions sum to the score).
measures.composite_index.method: Core.composite (site/js/core/composite.js: scale, compute) and economy.js (ecIxInputs, ecIxApply, ecBenchComposite). The inputs, directions, weights and scale are kept in the map's link (#ix=), so a shared link rebuilds the same composite.
measures.composite_index.how_to_read: A higher score means more of what you marked as better, relative to the other municipalities. Read the contributions to see which inputs drive a place's score.
caveats: User-built composite, not an official index: the result depends entirely on the inputs, directions and weights chosen.
Standardizing across municipalities compares places with each other, not with a target.
Inputs from different years and from surveys with margins of error are combined without carrying the margins.
measures.composite_index.source_detail: Any datasets of the Analysis tab.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab (press Workbench, then Composite)

measures.change_since_base_year.plain: How much a value has changed between a base year you choose and the year on the map. Counts and dollars show percent change. Rates show the change in percentage points.
measures.change_since_base_year.plain_es: Cuánto ha cambiado un valor entre el año base que se elija y el año del mapa. Los conteos y los dólares muestran el cambio porcentual. Las tasas muestran el cambio en puntos porcentuales.
measures.change_since_base_year.definition: For counts, dollar totals and dollar levels: (value now − value at the base) ÷ value at the base × 100, in percent. For rates and ratios: value now − value at the base, in the dataset's own unit (percentage points for percent rates, years for median age, index points for the Gini index). On the Analysis tab the base value is the dataset's latest value at or before the chosen base year; the Housing page needs a value in the base year itself. If the year on the map is not later than that base data year, or there is no base value, the municipality is blank. A base value of zero gives a blank for percent change.
measures.change_since_base_year.method: Case change of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js. The default base year is 2014 on the Analysis tab and 2012 on the Housing page. 'Change measured from' lists every year from 2010 to the year before the latest one (on the Analysis tab, the latest year on the year bar; on the Housing page, the latest survey window), so any of them can be chosen. With 'Inflation-adjusted' ticked, both ends are first restated to the same Consumer Price Index (CPI) dollars. The legend title shows the span, for example '(2014 → 2024)'. Colors use the diverging scale centered on 0.
measures.change_since_base_year.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Puerto Rico's poverty rate fell 4.72 percentage points between the 2010-2014 window (2014) and the 2020-2024 window (2024); San Juan's fell 2.10 points. In the same snapshot, median gross rent for Puerto Rico rose 25.1% in nominal dollars over the same span. The 'Change measured from' list ends in 2024 on the Analysis tab and in 2023 on the Housing page.
caveats: Survey windows that share years overlap. Windows labeled 2022 and 2024 share three survey years, so their difference understates real change. The Census Bureau advises comparing windows that do not overlap.
A base year before 2020 and a year after it cross the population estimate break, which can move per-1,000 values and population change.
Percent change from a small base is large. The Ask the observatory chat leaves out municipalities whose starting value is below a minimum for this reason.
Percent change is not meaningful when the base is near zero or negative, as it can be for federal loans (an estimated cost).
No margin of error is calculated for a change. Both ends are estimates.
Dollar changes are in the dollars of each year unless 'Inflation-adjusted' is ticked. The Housing page's change fields are never adjusted for inflation.
Median age is a 'rate' in the Analysis tab, so its change is labeled 'pts' although it is in years.
measures.change_since_base_year.source_detail: Any dataset with more than one year in the Analysis tab, or a Housing page series.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate, change since 2014
Housing page: change maps with a base year

measures.difference_from_pr.plain: The municipality's value minus the Puerto Rico value, in the same unit. It shows how far above or below the island a place sits.
measures.difference_from_pr.plain_es: El valor del municipio menos el valor de Puerto Rico, en la misma unidad. Muestra cuánto más arriba o más abajo que la isla está un lugar.
measures.difference_from_pr.definition: Value − Puerto Rico value, in the dataset's own unit: dollars for dollar levels, percentage points for percent rates, the dataset's unit otherwise. The option is offered for rates, dollar levels and ratios.
measures.difference_from_pr.method: Case diff of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x − a[Puerto Rico]. A percent rate is labeled 'pts'. Dollars are shown with no decimals, and negative values carry a minus sign. Colors use the diverging scale centered on 0.
measures.difference_from_pr.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's median household income in the 2020-2024 window is $1,695 above Puerto Rico's: $27,992 against $26,297.
caveats: No margin of error is calculated for a difference. For survey series, check the margins of both numbers before reading a small difference.
The island figure is the dataset's own island value, not the average of the municipalities.
A difference in percentage points is not a percent difference. Use the index for the relative gap.
measures.difference_from_pr.source_detail: Any rate, level or ratio dataset in the Analysis tab.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: median household income, difference from Puerto Rico

measures.per_resident.plain: A dollar total divided by the municipality's residents. It lets a large and a small municipality be compared on wages, federal awards or disaster aid.
measures.per_resident.plain_es: Un total en dólares dividido entre las personas residentes del municipio. Permite comparar un municipio grande con uno pequeño en salarios, fondos federales o ayuda por desastres.
measures.per_resident.definition: Dollar total ÷ resident population. The unit is dollars per resident, in the dollars of the data year, or in the dollars of the latest Consumer Price Index (CPI) year when 'Inflation-adjusted' is ticked. The option is offered for dollar totals only: total wages paid, federal awards (all types, contracts, grants, direct payments, loans, other), Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance obligated and FEMA Individual Assistance approved. Federal awards are obligations (legal commitments to pay) in a federal fiscal year. They are not payments, money spent or a measure of need. Federal loans count at their estimated cost to the government (the subsidy cost), not the amount lent, and can be negative. FEMA dollars are grouped by the year of the disaster declaration, not the year the money was obligated, paid or spent, and Individual Assistance is the amount approved.
measures.per_resident.method: Case perCapita of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ popAt(year)[i], shown with no decimals and a dollar sign. The Puerto Rico row divides the island total by the island population. A new shaded dollar-total layer starts in this view.
measures.per_resident.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, federal awards recorded for San Juan in fiscal year 2025 come to about $42,076 per resident, against $12,068 for Puerto Rico. Part of the gap reflects where awards are recorded: awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to the capital (see the caution on statewide awards below). The data do not show how large that part is. The figure is not what each resident received.
caveats: Per resident does not mean that each resident received the amount. Money goes to governments, firms, programs and households.

Federal awards are filed by place of performance as the awarding agency reports it. Awards to the Commonwealth government for statewide programs are often attributed to the capital, so San Juan's figure can include money that serves other places and other municipalities' figures can be low. The data cannot say how much.

A large part of FEMA Public Assistance cannot be placed in a municipality and is recorded as statewide: in the 2026-10 snapshot, 14% of the 2024 total and up to 88% in some years. The Puerto Rico row includes it, so Puerto Rico's per-resident figure can be higher than the sum of its municipalities would give.

The Puerto Rico row for federal awards is USAspending's total for the territory. It also counts awards that name no municipality (21.6% of the fiscal year 2025 total in the 2026-10 snapshot), so it is higher than the sum of the 78 municipalities.
Federal fiscal years run from October to September, and the dollars of a fiscal year are matched to the CPI of the calendar year with the same number.
The population series starts in 2010. In the Trend chart, FEMA Public Assistance values for 2001 to 2009 shown per resident are divided by the 2010 population.

For total wages, the dollars are paid by employers located in the municipality, wherever the workers live. Wages per resident is not residents' income; use American Community Survey income figures for that.
measures.per_resident.source_detail: Numerators: USAspending awards by place of performance, OpenFEMA Public Assistance and Housing Assistance, Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) total wages, FEMA National Risk Index expected annual loss. Denominator: Census Bureau population series.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: federal awards per resident

measures.index_pr_100.plain: The municipality's value as a percent of the Puerto Rico value, so that the island equals 100. Above 100 means higher than the island; below 100 means lower.
measures.index_pr_100.plain_es: El valor del municipio como porcentaje del valor de Puerto Rico, de modo que la isla equivale a 100. Más de 100 significa más alto que la isla; menos de 100, más bajo.
measures.index_pr_100.definition: Value ÷ Puerto Rico value × 100. It has no unit. The option is offered for rates, dollar levels (such as medians and average pay) and ratios. It is a relative comparison: 120 means 20% higher than the island figure, not 20 percentage points higher.
measures.index_pr_100.method: Case index of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ a[Puerto Rico] × 100, shown with no decimals. The layer title reads 'index (puerto rico = 100)'. Colors use the diverging scale centered on 100. The Puerto Rico value is the dataset's own island figure (for survey series, the Census Bureau's island estimate), not the average of the 78 municipalities.
measures.index_pr_100.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's poverty rate in the 2020-2024 window (shown as 2024) has an index of 96 (95.8 before rounding): about 4% below the island's rate. To see the gap in percentage points, use 'Difference from Puerto Rico'.
caveats: A relative comparison. A rate that is small on the island can swing the index widely for small changes.
The island figure is not the mean of the municipalities. For medians the island median is not the median of the municipal medians.
No margin of error is calculated for an index. Survey figures for small municipalities can be noisy.
measures.index_pr_100.source_detail: Any rate, level or ratio dataset in the Analysis tab.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate as an index

measures.location_quotient.plain: A location quotient compares a sector's share of local jobs with its share of jobs on the whole island. A value of 1 means the same concentration as Puerto Rico; 2 means twice as concentrated.
measures.location_quotient.plain_es: El cociente de localización compara la proporción de empleos locales de un sector con su proporción de empleos en toda la isla. Un valor de 1 significa la misma concentración que en Puerto Rico; 2 significa el doble de concentración.
measures.location_quotient.definition: (Sector jobs in the municipality ÷ all jobs in the municipality) ÷ (sector jobs in Puerto Rico ÷ all jobs in Puerto Rico). It has no unit. The jobs are annual averages from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), in the same year. The numerator is private-sector jobs in the sector, except for the datasets 'Jobs (all employers)', 'Private-sector jobs' and 'Government jobs', which count what their names say. Both denominators count all jobs, government included. The option is offered for the jobs family (25 datasets in the 2026-10 snapshot).
measures.location_quotient.method: Case lq of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: (x ÷ jobs[i]) ÷ (pr ÷ jobs[Puerto Rico]), shown with two decimals. The result is blank when a denominator is missing or zero. Jobs data start in 2014; an earlier chosen year shows 2014. Colors use the diverging scale centered on 1.
measures.location_quotient.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, accommodation jobs in San Juan have a location quotient of 1.26 in 2025: the share of San Juan's jobs in hotels, inns and other places to stay is 26% higher than the island's share. Below 1 the sector is less concentrated than on the island.
caveats: A high quotient means concentration, not size. A municipality with few jobs can have a high quotient from a handful of employers.
Blank where the sector is withheld or the municipality has no such employers; blank is not zero.
Both denominators include government jobs. For the 19 sector datasets and the tourism datasets, the numerators count private-sector jobs only.
For 'Jobs (all employers)' every municipality shows 1.00 (and 100% as a share of jobs), so the option tells nothing there.
Jobs are counted at the work site, not where workers live.
measures.location_quotient.source_detail: Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: accommodation jobs, location quotient

measures.per_1000_housing_units.plain: A count divided by the number of homes in the municipality and multiplied by 1,000. It shows how common something is compared with the housing stock, so a municipality does not look high only because it has more homes.
measures.per_1000_housing_units.plain_es: Un conteo dividido entre la cantidad de viviendas del municipio y multiplicado por 1,000. Muestra qué tan común es algo en relación con las viviendas que hay, para que un municipio no parezca alto solo porque tiene más viviendas.
measures.per_1000_housing_units.definition: Value ÷ housing units × 1,000. The housing units are the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimate for the latest window that ends at or before the year shown (the first window when the year chosen is earlier). It is calculated to three decimals and shown with one. It is offered for counts of things that sit on housing (tourism places, transit stops, vacant or seasonal homes, households, people), not for jobs, not for exposure counts (which have a share of their own area) and not for housing units themselves. The result is blank when the value or the housing units are missing or zero; the Puerto Rico row uses the island's housing units.
measures.per_1000_housing_units.method: Case perHU of compute in Core.normalize (site/js/core/normalize.js): x ÷ housing units × 1000, with the housing units of the series housing_units (the engine's housing-unit denominator, E.hu). A new layer does not start in this view: shaded counts start per 1,000 residents.
measures.per_1000_housing_units.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan has 3,424 tourism places and 201,026 housing units (2020-2024), which is 17.0 places per 1,000 housing units (10.4 per 1,000 residents). Culebra has 136 places and 1,539 housing units: 88.4 per 1,000 housing units. Read it as how many of these there are for every 1,000 homes.
caveats: Housing units are a survey estimate with a margin of error; the margin is not carried into the rate.
Seasonal and vacant homes count as housing units, so a municipality with many second homes has a larger denominator than its residents suggest.
The housing units are those of the survey window that ends at or before the year shown, not of the year itself (see methods.acs_windows).
A small municipality can swing widely when a few units change.
measures.per_1000_housing_units.source_detail: Denominator: ACS 5-year table B25001 (Housing Units), as in housing.housing_units. Numerator: any count the Analysis tab offers; the example uses the tourism places counted from Overture Maps.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: tourism places per 1,000 housing units

measures.per_1000_residents.plain: A count divided by the municipality's residents and multiplied by 1,000. It puts a small and a large municipality on the same footing.
measures.per_1000_residents.plain_es: Un conteo dividido entre las personas residentes del municipio y multiplicado por 1,000. Pone a un municipio pequeño y a uno grande en igualdad de condiciones.
measures.per_1000_residents.definition: Value ÷ resident population × 1,000. The unit is the dataset's unit per 1,000 residents, for example jobs per 1,000 residents or tourism places per 1,000 residents. The option is offered for counts only. The population is the resident population of the same year as the data (a Census count or a July 1 estimate). When the population has no value for that year, the latest earlier year is used, or the first year if none is earlier.
measures.per_1000_residents.method: Case per1000 of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ popAt(year)[i] × 1000, calculated to three decimals and shown with one. The result is blank when the value or the population is missing or zero. The Puerto Rico row uses the island population.
