The population is the housing series 'population' (see the entry for resident population).
measures.per_1000_residents.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 data show 770 jobs located in San Juan for every 1,000 San Juan residents, against 298 for Puerto Rico as a whole. The jobs are counted where people work, so the figure says how many jobs sit in San Juan, not how many San Juan residents hold one. See 'Workplace basis and residence basis'.
caveats: The population series steps up in 2020 because of a change of estimate base, so a per-1,000 value for 2019 and one for 2020 are not on the same basis.
The denominator counts residents only. Visitors, commuters and people who live in a municipality part of the year are in the numerator (jobs, places, households) but not in the denominator.
For survey series labeled by the last year of a five-year window, the denominator is that one year's population, not an average over the window.

For the five tourism-place datasets the Analysis tab divides by the latest population estimate (2025 in the 2026-10 snapshot), while municipalities.json:assets_per_1000_residents divides by the 2020 census count. In the 2026-10 snapshot San Juan shows 10.4 places per 1,000 residents in one and 10.0 in the other.
A small municipality can swing widely when a few units change.
measures.per_1000_residents.source_detail: Numerators: any count in the Analysis tab. Denominator: Census Bureau census counts (2010, 2020) and Population Estimates (other years).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: jobs per 1,000 residents

measures.per_km2.plain: A count or a dollar total divided by the municipality's land area in square kilometers. It shows how tightly something is packed on the land.
measures.per_km2.plain_es: Un conteo o un total en dólares dividido entre el área de terreno del municipio en kilómetros cuadrados. Muestra qué tan concentrado está algo en el terreno.
measures.per_km2.definition: Value ÷ land area in km². The unit is the dataset's unit per km² of land (jobs per km², dollars per km²). The option is offered for counts and for dollar totals. The land area is the Census Bureau's 2020 land area, the same for every year.
measures.per_km2.method: Case perkm2 of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ land_km2, taken from municipalities.json. Counts are shown with one decimal and dollar totals with none. The Puerto Rico row divides by the sum of the 78 land areas.
measures.per_km2.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 data show about 2,045 jobs per km² of land in San Juan, against 107 for Puerto Rico, whose land area is the sum of the 78 municipalities (8,868.5 km²). A high value marks a dense job center.
caveats: Land area only, from the 2020 Census. Water is not in the denominator, and the area does not change from year to year.
An average over the whole municipality. Jobs and places cluster in town centers, so a municipality with large rural or protected areas looks sparse even where its center is dense.
The areas are rounded to 0.1 km² in municipalities.json, which matters little except for very small areas.
measures.per_km2.source_detail: Denominator: land area (AREALAND) from the Census Bureau's 2020 boundary layer. Numerators: any count or dollar total in the Analysis tab.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: jobs per km²

measures.percentile.plain: The municipality's position in the list of the 78 municipalities, from 0 (lowest value) to 100 (highest value). It says how a place compares with the others, not by how much.
measures.percentile.plain_es: La posición del municipio en la lista de los 78 municipios, de 0 (el valor más bajo) a 100 (el valor más alto). Indica cómo se compara un lugar con los demás, no por cuánto.
measures.percentile.definition: Position of the value in the sorted list of municipal values, as a percent of the way from the lowest (0) to the highest (100): (number of lower values) ÷ (number of municipalities with a value − 1) × 100. With 78 municipalities each step is 1.3 points. Municipalities with the same value share the lower percentile. The Puerto Rico row is blank. Municipalities without a value are left out and the list gets shorter.
measures.percentile.method: Case pctile of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: the index of the value in the ascending sorted list (first match for ties) ÷ max(1, n − 1) × 100, shown with no decimals. It uses the layer's own settings for year, inflation adjustment and base year.
measures.percentile.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Guaynabo has the lowest poverty rate of the 78 municipalities in the 2020-2024 window (percentile 0) and Guánica the highest (percentile 100). A percentile of 50 is the middle of the list.
caveats: A percentile ignores distances. Two municipalities one percentile apart can be far apart in value, or almost equal.
Each municipality counts once, whatever its population. It is not a percentile of people.
Municipalities with a blank value (for example withheld sectors) are left out, so the steps are larger than 1.3 points when fewer than 78 have a value.
measures.percentile.source_detail: Any dataset in the Analysis tab.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate as a percentile

measures.share_of_jobs.plain: A sector's jobs as a percent of all jobs located in the municipality. It shows how much of a local economy rests on one sector, such as tourism.
measures.share_of_jobs.plain_es: Los empleos de un sector como porcentaje de todos los empleos ubicados en el municipio. Muestra cuánto depende una economía local de un solo sector, como el turismo.
measures.share_of_jobs.definition: Jobs in the dataset ÷ all jobs located in the same municipality × 100, in percent. The denominator is the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) total for all employers (private and government) in the same year, or in the latest earlier year if the data year has none. The option is offered for the jobs family (25 datasets in the 2026-10 snapshot).
measures.share_of_jobs.method: Case shareJobs of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ jobsAt(year)[i] × 100, shown with one decimal. Jobs data start in 2014. If you choose an earlier year, the layer shows 2014 (the year shown beside the layer reads 'first data 2014') and divides by the 2014 total.
measures.share_of_jobs.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, tourism-related jobs were 10.0% of San Juan's jobs in 2025 and 10.5% of Puerto Rico's. The Analysis tab's 'Tourism economy' view shades this measure.
caveats: For the 19 sector datasets and the tourism datasets, the numerator counts private-sector jobs while the denominator counts all jobs, government included. Sector shares therefore do not add up to 100%. For 'Jobs (all employers)' the share is 100% wherever it has a value.

Where the Bureau of Labor Statistics withholds a sector in a municipality, the share is blank, not zero. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 34 of the 78 municipalities have no 2024 figure for accommodation and food services, and 39 have none for 2025.
Where arts, entertainment and recreation is withheld, tourism-related jobs count accommodation and food services alone, so the share is slightly low there.

Tourism-related jobs is a grouping of industries (accommodation, food services, arts, entertainment and recreation). It includes jobs that serve residents and does not count every job that serves visitors.
Jobs are counted at the employer's work site, not where workers live.
measures.share_of_jobs.source_detail: US Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages: sector jobs and total jobs.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: tourism-related jobs as a share of local jobs

measures.share_of_pr_total.plain: The municipality's value as a percent of the Puerto Rico value. It shows how much of the island's jobs, dollars or places sit in one municipality.
measures.share_of_pr_total.plain_es: El valor del municipio como porcentaje del valor de Puerto Rico. Muestra qué parte de los empleos, los dólares o los lugares de la isla está en un solo municipio.
measures.share_of_pr_total.definition: Value ÷ Puerto Rico value × 100, in percent. The option is offered for counts and for dollar totals, except federal loans (an estimated cost that can be near zero or negative). The Puerto Rico value is the island figure published for that dataset in the same year.
measures.share_of_pr_total.method: Case sharePR of ecCalc in site/js/economy.js: x ÷ a[Puerto Rico] × 100, shown with two decimals. The result is blank when the island value is missing or zero. A shaded count layer is better shown per 1,000 residents when the aim is to compare municipalities of different size.
measures.share_of_pr_total.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 2025 data show San Juan with 26.79% of Puerto Rico's jobs and 10.4% of its residents. A share well above the municipality's share of residents marks a place that concentrates the activity.
caveats: The island value is not always the sum of the 78 municipalities, so shares may not add up to 100%. In the 2026-10 snapshot: Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) jobs in 2025, the municipalities add to 943,002 and the island figure is 947,557 (the municipalities hold 99.5%); Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance in 2024, the municipalities hold 86% of the island figure and 14% is recorded as statewide; federal awards in fiscal year 2025, the municipalities hold 78.4% and 21.6% names no municipality.
Where a sector figure is withheld for a municipality, that municipality is blank, not zero, and the shares shown do not add up to 100%.
A share says how big a municipality's part is, not how well it is doing.
measures.share_of_pr_total.source_detail: Numerators and island values come from the same Analysis tab dataset.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: share of Puerto Rico's jobs

measures.show_as.plain: Each layer on the Analysis tab can show a dataset as published or rescaled. Rescaled views include per resident, per square kilometer, share of the island, comparison with Puerto Rico, change since a base year and percentile. The options offered depend on the kind of number.
measures.show_as.plain_es: Cada capa de la pestaña Análisis puede mostrar un conjunto de datos tal como se publicó o en otra escala. Las otras escalas incluyen por residente, por kilómetro cuadrado, proporción de la isla, comparación con Puerto Rico, cambio desde un año base y percentil. Las opciones que aparecen dependen del tipo de número.
measures.show_as.definition: The 'Show as' list in each layer's Settings. The kind of dataset decides the options. Counts (people, jobs, places, households, work sites): As published, Per 1,000 residents, Per 1,000 housing units (not for jobs, for exposure counts or for housing units themselves), Per km², % of the Puerto Rico total. Exposure counts (residents or housing units inside a hazard, a protected area or near transit) also get % of the area's own residents or housing units, which is how they start. Counts of jobs (25 datasets in the 2026-10 snapshot: total, private-sector and government jobs; tourism-related jobs; accommodation jobs; food service jobs; and the 19 sector jobs) also get % of the municipality's jobs and Location quotient. Dollar totals (total wages, federal awards by type, Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) dollars): As published, $ per resident, $ per km² and % of the Puerto Rico total (not offered for federal loans). All other datasets (rates, dollar levels such as medians and average pay, and ratios): As published, Index (Puerto Rico = 100), Difference from Puerto Rico. Every dataset that is not a one-time snapshot also gets Change since the base year, and every dataset gets Percentile among municipalities.
measures.show_as.method: The functions options, compute and describe of Core.normalize (site/js/core/normalize.js) build the list, do the arithmetic and set the unit and the number of decimals shown. The calculation runs in your browser from the published series each time the map draws. A new shaded count layer starts as 'Per 1,000 residents', a new shaded dollar total starts as '$ per resident', and everything else starts as 'As published', including every symbol layer.
measures.show_as.how_to_read: Shade rates and rescaled counts; show raw counts as sized symbols. A shaded map of raw counts mostly shows which municipalities are big. The legend title names the option in use, for example 'Jobs (all employers) · per 1,000 residents'.
caveats: An option changes the question, not the data. A municipality can rank high in jobs per 1,000 residents and low in total jobs.

For share, index, difference and location quotient, 'Puerto Rico' is the island figure published for that dataset. It is not always the sum or the average of the 78 municipalities. Each option's entry says what applies.

'% of the Puerto Rico total' is not offered for federal loans. That series is the estimated cost of loans to the government, which can be near zero or negative in a year, so a share of the island figure would not mean much.

Margins of error are shown only when a layer is shown 'As published'. A value whose margin is wide, or a rate built on very few counted, is marked less reliable in every view (hatching and italics: see measures.less_reliable_values).

values.As published: The dataset's own number in its own unit.
values.Per km²: Count (or dollars) ÷ land area in square kilometers.
values.% of the Puerto Rico total: Value ÷ Puerto Rico value × 100. Not offered for federal loans.
values.% of the municipality's jobs: Jobs in a sector ÷ all jobs in the municipality × 100.
values.Location quotient (Puerto Rico = 1): The sector's share of local jobs ÷ its share of island jobs.
values.$ per km²: Dollar total ÷ land area in square kilometers.
values.Change since the base year: Percent change for counts and dollars; difference for rates and ratios.
values.Percentile among municipalities: Position among the 78 municipalities: 0 is the lowest, 100 the highest.

measures.show_as.source_detail: Inputs are the Analysis tab datasets: jobs and wages from the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW), unemployment from Local Area Unemployment Statistics (LAUS), survey series from the American Community Survey (ACS), population from the Population Estimates, federal awards from USAspending, FEMA dollars from OpenFEMA and tourism places from Overture. The menu is a design choice by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR).

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: add a layer, open Settings, choose 'Show as'

methods.small_area_estimates.plain: Survey figures for barrios, census tracts and block groups are rough. Look at the margin of error every time, read an empty value as 'not known', and never add or average margins, medians or percentages.
methods.small_area_estimates.plain_es: Las cifras de encuesta para barrios, sectores censales y grupos de bloques son aproximadas. Revise siempre el margen de error, lea un valor vacío como "no se sabe" y nunca sume ni promedie márgenes, medianas o porcentajes.
methods.small_area_estimates.definition: small_area.py builds four files from the American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year tables that acs_small.py reads: population_series.json (the Population domain's 8 variables for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico), acs_barrio.json (901 barrios, 34 variables), acs_tract.json (981 census tracts, 34 variables) and acs_blockgroup.json (2,555 block groups, 13 variables). Each holds the estimate and the margin of error of every area for the four windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024. Every variable of the level files also exists for the 78 municipalities under the same key, so the layer engine reads a tract as one more level of the same dataset.
methods.small_area_estimates.method: The Census Bureau publishes each table for the whole country in one large file, sorted by area code, and its server accepts requests for part of a file. The observatory asks only for the rows it needs: 0.5 to 1.5 MB per table for all five levels. It checked the result against the municipality rows that the Housing page series read from the same files (395 values, none different), and the pieces add up: block groups to tracts, tracts and barrios to municipalities, municipalities to the island. The 38 offshore county subdivisions that are not units of the crosswalk are dropped and counted. Each variable is then worked out for every area with the functions that make the municipal series, so a value has the same definition at every level. Block groups have 13 variables: the 10 of the plan's first wave (population, housing units, households, tenure, vacancy and other vacant units, household size, crowding, home value and income per person), median age, and the shares under 18 and 65 and over. Barrios and census tracts have those and 21 more, 34 in all: the 16 variables of the plan's first and second waves (internet counts as two columns) and 17 more from tables that the build already reads (household income, rent, year built, housing types, poverty, work, education, vehicles, internet, inequality, sex, household types, veterans and disability). The Census Bureau does not publish poverty, the Gini index, income by tenure or disability for block groups, so they are not in that file. The tests check, without the cache of Census rows, that the counts of population, housing units and households of the block groups, tracts and barrios of each municipality add up exactly to the municipality; that every published value is plausible (shares between 0 and 100, no median of 0, no margin without an estimate); and that the areas with no margin for their population are the controlled totals and no other. They also read the cell numbers behind the Population variables against the Census Bureau's own labels in every vintage: the labels of the five tables are committed in tests/fixtures/acs_labels, and the build stops if one differs. With the cache, the municipal values equal the ones the Housing page series publishes (1,716 values in 2020-2024, none different) and the cached Census rows give the published files again. The code is small_area.py, with acs_small.py, in the project's repository.
methods.small_area_estimates.how_to_read: Compare areas only when their margins are small next to the difference. Typical margin of error as a share of the estimate in 2020-2024 (the median over the areas that have both): median home value: 5% for a municipality, 17% for a barrio, 12% for a census tract and 19% for a block group; median household income: 9% for a municipality, 30% for a barrio and 25% for a census tract (not published for block groups); median gross rent: 9% for a municipality, 23% for a barrio and 24% for a census tract; people under 18: 7% for a municipality, 40% for a barrio, 32% for a census tract and 57% for a block group; vacancy rate: 12% for a municipality, 42% for a barrio, 34% for a census tract and 58% for a block group; unemployment rate: 28% for a municipality, 82% for a barrio and 72% for a census tract. The CSV by area marks a value whose margin of error is above 30% of the estimate as less reliable (no map or table draws the areas below the municipality yet); docs/small-area.md gives the share of areas flagged for every variable and level. Median gross rent has no estimate for 41% of barrios and 13% of tracts (45% of block groups in the Census Bureau's table, which the observatory does not publish). For the share of renter households paying 30% or more of income, which is not published below the municipality, the typical margin is about plus or minus 18 points for a municipality, 36 for a tract and 55 for a block group among the units with 20 or more renter households.
caveats: Every margin is at 90% confidence. Do not add or average margins, and do not sum medians or rates: only counts add up from a finer level to a coarser one.
An empty value means the Census Bureau gives none (it writes negative codes such as -666666666): it is not zero.

Two things the Census Bureau prints are not estimates, and the observatory leaves them empty too. One is a median at the edge of an open-ended interval: it prints the boundary and marks the margin ***, such as 51 for 'rent is 50% or more of income', 2,499 for 'under $2,500' and 1938 for 'built before 1939'. The other is a median of 0, the same edge in the oldest window (it prints 0 where later windows print the boundary 1938 or a real median). In 2020-2024 that is rent as a share of income in 74 census tracts, rent as a share of income in 47 barrios, median household income in 4 census tracts, median household income in 1 barrio, median year built in 2 census tracts, median home value in 1 barrio.

A share of exactly 100% is published without a margin: the proportion formula would give a margin of zero, which would read as exact. In 2020-2024 that is the owner-occupied share in 45 barrios, the share of detached homes in 59 barrios, the share with an internet subscription in 39 barrios, the share of family households in 22 barrios; in census tracts it is at most 4 areas for any variable, and in block groups the owner-occupied share in 50 areas. A margin that works out to zero for another reason (three published values) is dropped too. A share of 0% keeps the margin the formula gives, and the CSV by area marks it less reliable.

For a total that the Census Bureau controls to its own population or housing estimate it prints no margin (marked *****: no sampling error). The observatory gives such a total a margin of zero, as the Bureau says may be done, so a share of it keeps the margin of its numerator. The total population of the island and of 76 of the 78 municipalities is one. The number of women is controlled in 52 of the municipalities: the zero is given to a total, not to a number of women, so the share of women has no margin there.

Five-year windows that share years are not independent of each other: the change from one window to the next is not a trend. The four windows use the 2020 geography (981 tracts, 2,555 block groups, 939 county subdivisions), so no crosswalk is needed between them.
Barrios do not fit inside tracts, so a barrio value is the Census Bureau's own barrio row, never made from tracts.
Survey estimates are not the 2020 Census counts of the crosswalk: they come from a sample, are for a five-year window and have margins of error.

Some variables are almost always flagged below the municipality: in 2020-2024 the margin is above 30% of the estimate for at least 80% of the census tracts that have a value for overcrowded homes (100%), veterans (100%), mobile homes (more than 99%), the unemployment rate (more than 99%), seasonal or occasional-use units (97%), households with no vehicle (96%), other vacant units (89%), households with no internet access (89%), units in buildings of 5 or more (84%).

For six of those nine the municipal value is rough too (municipalities flagged out of 78: mobile homes 77 of 78, overcrowded homes 72 of 78, veterans 48 of 78, seasonal or occasional-use units 39 of 78, units in buildings of 5 or more 38 of 78, the unemployment rate 35 of 78): compare broad groups, not neighboring places. A margin above 100 points is not an interval: read it as 'not known'.

Very small areas: in 2020-2024, 30 of the 901 barrios have fewer than 50 estimated residents and 60 census tracts have none. 14 of those barrios show both a share of people with a disability and a share of veterans; one with 8 estimated residents reads 100% with a disability, plus or minus 580 points. Do not quote such a value: its margin says it is not known.
The margin of a sum is the Census Bureau's approximation (the square root of the sum of the squares of the margins of the cells): it can overstate the margin.

Not published below the municipality: cost burden (the share of renters or owners paying 30% or more of income), because its margin is about 36 points for a tract and 55 for a block group; the affordability measures of the 2023 study (maximum affordable loan, affordability ratio), which are calculations with assumptions and not survey figures; and the rental and homeowner vacancy rates, whose denominators are a handful of homes.

The municipal series made before item 7 leave a share's margin blank when its denominator has none: the bachelor's share (housing.bachelors_pct) has a margin for only 5 of the 78 municipalities in 2020-2024 because the Census Bureau controls the adult total of the other 73, while its barrio and tract values have one. The Population series follows the Census Bureau's rule instead.

The map shows municipalities. The areas below are in the files, in the CSV by area (the information button of a dataset on the Analysis tab; it marks the less reliable values and says where a margin is missing) and in the layer engine, as the levels barrio, tract and block-group.
methods.small_area_estimates.geography: island, 78 municipios, 901 barrios, 981 tracts, 2,555 block groups
methods.small_area_estimates.source_detail: ACS 5-year table-based summary files, https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/{vintage}/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/. Measurements for every variable and level: docs/small-area.md (2020-2024 window); the study that preceded the files: docs/analysis/small-area-2026-10.

data.count_duplicates_folded.plain: How many listings were merged into another listing because they looked like the same place. The observatory keeps the best record of each group.
data.count_duplicates_folded.plain_es: Cuántos listados se unieron a otro porque parecían ser el mismo lugar. El observatorio se queda con el mejor registro de cada grupo.
data.count_duplicates_folded.definition: The number of listings removed by duplicate folding: for each group of listings judged to be the same place, the group size minus one.
data.count_duplicates_folded.method: Listings are compared only when they have the same category and the same address town (the municipality named in the address, or the nearest municipality center when the address names none). Two such listings are treated as one place when they are close (within 600 m; within 1,000 m for beaches, parks, nature reserves, scenic areas, historic sites and tourist attractions) and their names are very similar (a match score of at least 0.95, or at least 0.8 when within 150 m or, for those types, 600 m). Listings that share a phone number, have somewhat similar names (at least 0.5) and are within 500 m are also merged. The kept record has the highest confidence, then the most contact details, then the most social links.
data.count_duplicates_folded.how_to_read: A listing's 'duplicates' value in the places file says how many records it absorbed. In the 2026-10 snapshot, these add up to 1,005.
caveats: The rules can merge two real places with similar names that stand close together, and can miss duplicates with different names.
Folding is done on listings, not on what is physically on the ground.
data.count_duplicates_folded.geography: Puerto Rico (the map box, see the entry on the map box)
data.count_duplicates_folded.source_detail: build.py (dedup, similarity). The separate phone, email and social-media fields are used only while matching duplicates and are not published.

data.count_flood_polygons.plain: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the observatory held 4,894 flood-zone polygons for Puerto Rico from FEMA. Of these, 2,517 are in high-risk zones.
data.count_flood_polygons.plain_es: En el corte de datos de 2026-10, el observatorio tenía 4,894 polígonos de zonas inundables de Puerto Rico de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias). De ellos, 2,517 están en zonas de alto riesgo.
data.count_flood_polygons.definition: The number of polygon records in the National Flood Hazard Layer of FEMA (the Federal Emergency Management Agency) for Puerto Rico (map codes starting with 72), counted before they are simplified for display. The published flood file has the same number. Polygons in zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99 and VE are Special Flood Hazard Areas (a 1% chance of flooding in any year).
data.count_flood_polygons.method: build.py requests every record of layer 28 of FEMA's public service where DFIRM_ID begins with 72, and counts them.
data.count_flood_polygons.how_to_read: It counts polygon records, not square kilometers and not flooded places. Zone X includes areas of moderate and minimal hazard. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the polygons by zone were X 2,368, AE 1,760, VE 539, A 191, AO 25, D 9, AH 1 and A99 1. The 2,517 in zones A, AE, AH, AO, A99 and VE are Special Flood Hazard Areas.
caveats: A flood map shows hazard at a point, not what the building or road is built to withstand.
FEMA can revise the layer. The observatory shows it as downloaded on the build date.
data.count_flood_polygons.source_detail: FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer, layer 28, DFIRM_ID LIKE '72%'

data.count_listings_total.plain: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the observatory's places file holds 32,541 unique listings, after duplicates are folded and the 2,577 listings that are not tourism are left out. The count includes places of worship and listings below the confidence filter.
data.count_listings_total.plain_es: En el corte de datos de 2026-10, el archivo de lugares del observatorio tiene 32,541 listados únicos, después de unir los duplicados y dejar fuera los 2,577 listados que no son turismo. El conteo incluye los lugares de culto y los listados por debajo del filtro de confianza.
data.count_listings_total.definition: Number of listings kept after classification and duplicate folding: tourism places at any confidence plus places of worship.
data.count_listings_total.method: build.py counts the records left after classify() and dedup().
data.count_listings_total.how_to_read: This is the size of the places file, not a tourism count. Use 'Tourism places counted in the statistics' for statistics. In the 2026-10 snapshot, tourism places at any confidence (27,509) plus places of worship (5,032) make 32,541.
caveats: Includes places of worship (5,032 in the 2026-10 snapshot), which the tourism statistics leave out.
Includes listings with confidence below 0.5.
data.count_listings_total.geography: Puerto Rico (the map box, see the entry on the map box)
data.count_listings_total.source_detail: Overture Maps Places, release 2026-09-23.1, classified and de-duplicated by build.py

data.count_min_confidence.plain: The cut-off the observatory uses on Overture's confidence score: 0.5. Listings below it are hidden on the map by default and left out of the tourism statistics.
data.count_min_confidence.plain_es: El límite que el observatorio usa en la puntuación de confianza de Overture: 0.5. Los listados por debajo se esconden en el mapa de forma predeterminada y quedan fuera de las estadísticas de turismo.
data.count_min_confidence.definition: A number between 0 and 1. Overture gives each place record a confidence score. The observatory keeps a listing in its tourism statistics only when the score is at least this value.
data.count_min_confidence.method: Set by hand in build.py (MIN_CONF). The map's confidence filter starts at the same value.
data.count_min_confidence.how_to_read: A higher cut-off keeps fewer listings, those that Overture scores as more confident. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 0.5 cut-off keeps 24,209 tourism places; with no cut-off it would keep 27,509.
caveats: The score is Overture's estimate, not a check by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR).
The cut-off is a choice. A different one gives different counts.

Some fields do not use the cut-off. The municipality counts assets_all_confidence and listings_all, and the three land-use place fields (places_on_protected_land, places_on_protected_land_pct and places_urban_pct), include listings of any confidence.

data.count_municipalities.plain: The build covers 78 municipalities. That is every municipio of Puerto Rico.
data.count_municipalities.plain_es: La compilación cubre 78 municipios. Son todos los municipios de Puerto Rico.
data.count_municipalities.definition: The number of municipalities for which the build computed statistics. It is the number of municipalities in the build's list (municipalities.py).
data.count_municipalities.method: build.py counts the municipalities in its statistics table.
data.count_municipalities.how_to_read: Every municipality-level figure in the observatory has one value for each of these 78.
caveats: Culebra and Vieques are municipalities of their own and are included.
data.count_municipalities.source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb, 2020 Census county equivalents (municipios) of Puerto Rico

data.count_overture_places.plain: In the 2026-10 snapshot, Overture Maps held 99,323 place records inside the observatory's map box, in every category. The observatory keeps only the tourism-related ones.
data.count_overture_places.plain_es: En el corte de datos de 2026-10, Overture Maps tenía 99,323 registros de lugares dentro del recuadro del mapa del observatorio, de todas las categorías. El observatorio se queda solo con los relacionados con el turismo.
data.count_overture_places.definition: Number of place records in the Overture Maps Places theme, in the release the snapshot uses, with a point inside the map box. Every category is counted: shops, offices and clinics as well as tourism places.
data.count_overture_places.method: build.py downloads the records with the overturemaps command and counts them. It then classifies each record into the observatory's tourism taxonomy, drops the records with no tourism category and folds duplicates.
data.count_overture_places.how_to_read: This is the raw size of the source, not the number of tourism places. For tourism places use the entry 'Tourism places counted in the statistics'. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 63,117 records were dropped as not tourism-related (3,388 of them have no category at all) and 1,088 more were folded as duplicates, which leaves 35,118 listings; 2,577 of them are not tourism (homes, housing and care services) and are left out, which leaves 32,541 (since 2026-10-18).
caveats: Listings are third-party records that the observatory has not checked on the ground, so a listing can be of a business that has closed or moved. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the observatory folded 1,088 duplicates that it found.
In the 2026-10 snapshot, the 63,117 dropped records are the difference between this count and the 36,206 classified records; meta.json does not store that number.
data.count_overture_places.geography: Puerto Rico (the map box, see the entry on the map box)
data.count_overture_places.source_detail: Overture Maps Foundation, Places theme, release 2026-09-23.1, downloaded 2026-10-01. meta.json does not store the release name.

data.count_worship_places.plain: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 5,032 listings are places of worship, such as churches. The places file keeps them and the map hides them by default. The tourism statistics leave them out. Only the all-listings count and the three land-use place fields count them.
data.count_worship_places.plain_es: En el corte de datos de 2026-10, 5,032 listados son lugares de culto, como iglesias. El archivo de lugares los conserva y el mapa los esconde de forma predeterminada. Las estadísticas de turismo los dejan fuera. Solo los cuentan el conteo de todos los listados y los tres campos de lugares del uso de terrenos.
data.count_worship_places.definition: Listings whose observatory type is 'Places of Worship' (religious categories in Overture, matched by build.py), after duplicate folding.
data.count_worship_places.method: build.py assigns the type 'Places of Worship' to categories that match place of worship, church, cathedral, chapel, synagogue, mosque, temple or religious, then counts them.
data.count_worship_places.how_to_read: They are left out of tourism statistics, the route planner's tourism count and the transit-access shares. The all-listings count of each municipality (listings_all) and the three land-use place fields (places_on_protected_land, places_on_protected_land_pct and places_urban_pct) are the exceptions: they count them.
caveats: This count includes worship places at any confidence.
data.count_worship_places.geography: Puerto Rico (the map box, see the entry on the map box)
data.count_worship_places.source_detail: Overture Maps Places, release 2026-09-23.1, classified by build.py (RULES)

data.count_protected_units.plain: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the observatory held 665 protected-area records for Puerto Rico from the USGS Protected Areas Database. They carry 640 different area names.
data.count_protected_units.plain_es: En el corte de datos de 2026-10, el observatorio tenía 665 registros de áreas protegidas de Puerto Rico de la base de datos de áreas protegidas del USGS (Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos). Tienen 640 nombres de área distintos.
data.count_protected_units.definition: The number of polygon records of the Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US 4.1), kept by the USGS (United States Geological Survey), with state PR. The count is of records, not of areas: several records can carry one unit name. Records with designation PROC are proclamation boundaries.
data.count_protected_units.method: build.py requests every record of the PAD-US service where State_Nm is PR, and counts them.
data.count_protected_units.how_to_read: A protected area is not always a closed area. Protected status describes how land is managed. The Pub_Access field of the published file says whether the public may enter. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 665 records carry 640 different unit names. Seven records are proclamation boundaries (designation PROC): five National Wildlife Refuges (Cabo Rojo, Culebra, Desecheo, Laguna Cartagena and Vieques), El Yunque National Forest and San Juan National Historic Site.
caveats: The tourism places statistics do not count the proclamation boundaries (seven in the 2026-10 snapshot) as 'in a protected area'. The route planner's protected-area share does.
Several records can belong to one unit.
data.count_protected_units.source_detail: USGS PAD-US 4.1, Protection Mechanism Category service, State_Nm = 'PR'

data.count_population_2020.plain: The 2020 Census counted 3,285,874 residents in Puerto Rico's 78 municipalities.
data.count_population_2020.plain_es: El Censo de 2020 contó 3,285,874 residentes en los 78 municipios de Puerto Rico.
data.count_population_2020.definition: The sum of the 2020 Census resident counts (field POP100) of the 78 municipios, as given by the Census Bureau's TIGERweb service. Residents on Census Day, 1 April 2020.
data.count_population_2020.method: build.py adds the POP100 values of the 78 municipio records.
data.count_population_2020.how_to_read: It is the 2020 count, not the present population. Later estimates are in the population series.
caveats: The count is a point in time (April 2020) and has not been updated for later years.
The Census Bureau's resident count (POP100) includes people in group quarters such as dormitories and care homes, as the Census Bureau defines it. The observatory does not separate them.
data.count_population_2020.source_detail: US Census Bureau TIGERweb, 2020 Census, layer 82, field POP100

data.count_tourism_places_all_confidence.plain: Tourism places before the confidence filter: 27,509 in the 2026-10 snapshot. It counts every listing except places of worship, even those Overture scores below 0.5.
data.count_tourism_places_all_confidence.plain_es: Los lugares turísticos antes del filtro de confianza: 27,509 en el corte de datos de 2026-10. Cuenta todos los listados menos los lugares de culto, incluso los que Overture califica por debajo de 0.5.
data.count_tourism_places_all_confidence.definition: Listings after duplicate folding that are not places of worship, whatever their Overture confidence. It is the tourism places counted in the statistics plus the listings with confidence below 0.5.
data.count_tourism_places_all_confidence.method: build.py counts listings whose type is not 'Places of Worship', without the confidence test.
data.count_tourism_places_all_confidence.how_to_read: Switch the confidence filter on the map to 0 to see this larger set. The default statistics do not use it. In the 2026-10 snapshot, 27,509 minus 24,209 leaves 3,300 listings below 0.5.
caveats: Overture gives these listings a confidence score below 0.5. The score is Overture's own estimate and the observatory has not checked the listings.
The separate phone, email and social-media fields are not published; name, address and website are copied as the source wrote them (see the entry on fields the observatory does not publish).
data.count_tourism_places_all_confidence.source_detail: Overture Maps Places, release 2026-09-23.1, classified by build.py (RULES)

data.count_tourism_places.plain: In the 2026-10 snapshot, the map and the tourism statistics count 24,209 tourism places in four groups: Attractions, Gastronomy (restaurants, bars and cafes), Accommodations and Visitor services. Places of worship and low-confidence listings are left out.
data.count_tourism_places.plain_es: En el corte de datos de 2026-10, el mapa y las estadísticas de turismo cuentan 24,209 lugares turísticos en cuatro grupos: "Atracciones", "Gastronomía" (restaurantes, bares y cafés), "Alojamientos" y "Servicios para visitantes". Quedan fuera los lugares de culto y los listados de baja confianza.
data.count_tourism_places.definition: Listings after duplicate folding that are tourism supply (not homes, housing or care services), are not places of worship and have an Overture confidence of at least 0.5. The map's default filter and the tourism statistics use this basis. It equals the sum of the municipality counts of tourism places.
data.count_tourism_places.method: build.py counts listings whose type is not 'Places of Worship' and whose confidence is at least 0.5 (MIN_CONF), after leaving out the listings that are not tourism (places_privacy.not_tourism).
data.count_tourism_places.how_to_read: Use it as 'listings in the observatory's tourism data', not as the number of businesses open today.
caveats: The categories are the observatory's own rules (build.py), not Overture's categories.
A count of listings, not of businesses. Listings can be closed, moved or missing.
The separate phone, email and social-media fields are not published; name, address and website are copied as the source wrote them (see the entry on fields the observatory does not publish).

What the count includes changed on 2026-10-18 (HANDOFF decision 47). Meta users file homes, condominiums, public housing estates, subdivisions and care homes under tourism categories, mostly lodging and historic site. Those listings are not tourism supply, so they are no longer counted: 2,370 of the 26,579 places counted before were left out, which gives 24,209. Holiday rentals stay counted (they are tourism supply), although the map does not draw them. Every published figure built on this count was rebuilt the same day.
data.count_tourism_places.source_detail: Overture Maps Places, release 2026-09-23.1, classified by build.py (RULES)

municipalities.acs_table_map.plain: Use this list to find the Census Bureau table and cell behind each housing and household field. It helps you cite the original numbers. The 'Code' column lists field names in municipalities.json, not coded values.
municipalities.acs_table_map.plain_es: Use esta lista para encontrar la tabla y la celda del Negociado del Censo detrás de cada campo de vivienda y hogares. Sirve para citar los números originales. La columna "Código" presenta nombres de campos de municipalities.json, no valores codificados.
municipalities.acs_table_map.definition: For each field, the American Community Survey (ACS) table number, the cell numbers used and the calculation. Table numbers are the Census Bureau's own (for example B25077). 'Cell 001' is the first line of the table. In the 2026-10 snapshot the latest window is 2020-2024. The baseline window for the change fields is 2008-2012. In the table-based files the estimate for cell 001 is the column B25077_E001 and its margin of error is B25077_M001.
municipalities.acs_table_map.method: Latest window (2020-2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot): the Census Bureau's table-based summary files, one file per table (acsdt5y2024-<table>.dat), filtered to the rows for Puerto Rico's municipalities (the Census Bureau calls them municipios; geographic codes starting 0500000US72). Baseline window: the 2012 ACS 5-year Puerto Rico sequence files (PuertoRico_All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups.zip), with cells located through the Census Bureau's sequence-and-table lookup file. Tables read for the latest window: B25077, B25064, B19013, B25002, B25004, B25003, B15003, B25070, B25091, B01003, B17001, B01002, B23025. Tables read for the baseline: B25077, B25064, B19013, B15002, B01003.
municipalities.acs_table_map.how_to_read: To cite a number, give the table, the window and the geography, for example 'US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B25077, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico'. For a change field cite both windows ('2020-2024 compared with 2008-2012') and both tables. For a calculated field cite the input tables and say who calculated it. If you took the number from the observatory's files rather than from the Census Bureau, cite the observatory as well (Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory).
caveats: The keys of the list are field names in municipalities.json, not codes found in the data.
The observatory reads the Census Bureau's summary files directly and needs no data API key.
Census codes for values that are not available (-666666666 and below) become empty fields. In the 2026-10 snapshot, no estimate in the 2020-2024 files used for the 78 municipalities is negative.

values.acs_year: Not an ACS cell. The last year of the latest window, set when the observatory is rebuilt (2024 in the 2026-10 snapshot).
values.median_home_value: B25077 cell 001 (median value, owner-occupied housing units). Baseline: same cell, 2008-2012.
values.median_gross_rent: B25064 cell 001 (median gross rent, renter-occupied units paying cash rent). Baseline: same cell, 2008-2012.
values.median_hh_income: B19013 cell 001 (median household income in the past 12 months, households). Baseline: same cell, 2008-2012.
values.seasonal_units: B25004 cell 006 (vacant: for seasonal, recreational, or occasional use).
values.seasonal_pct: B25004 cell 006 divided by B25002 cell 001.
values.owner_occupied_pct: B25003 cell 002 (owner occupied) divided by cell 001 (occupied housing units).
values.renter_cost_burden_pct: B25070 cells 007 to 010 (30.0 percent or more) divided by cell 001 minus cell 011 (not computed).
values.owner_cost_burden_pct: B25091 cells 008 to 011 (30.0 percent or more, with a mortgage) divided by cell 002 minus cell 012 (not computed).
values.poverty_pct: B17001 cell 002 (below the poverty level) divided by cell 001 (population for whom poverty status is determined).
values.employment_rate_pct: B23025 cell 004 (employed civilians) divided by cell 001 (population 16 and over).
values.bachelors_pct: B15003 cells 022 to 025 (bachelor's, master's, professional, doctorate) divided by cell 001 (population 25 and over). Baseline for the change: B15002 cells 015-018 and 032-035 over cell 001.
values.max_affordable_loan: Calculated from B19013 cell 001 with the Table 6 method (see methods.affordability_method).
values.affordability_ratio: Calculated: B25077 cell 001 divided by max_affordable_loan.
values.bachelors_change_pts: Share from B15003 (latest window) minus share from B15002 (2008-2012).
values.population_change_2012_pct: B01003 cell 001 (total population), latest window against 2008-2012.
values.residents_per_unit: Not ACS. 2020 census population (POP100) divided by 2020 census housing units (HU100), Census Bureau TIGERweb.

municipalities.acs_table_map.source_detail: US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year summary files. Latest window: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2024/table-based-SF/data/5YRData/acsdt5y2024-<table>.dat, one file per table (for example acsdt5y2024-b25077.dat). 2008-2012 baseline: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2012/data/5_year_by_state/PuertoRico_All_Geographies_Not_Tracts_Block_Groups.zip, with cells located through https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/2012/documentation/5_year/user_tools/Sequence_Number_and_Table_Number_Lookup.txt

economy.acs_work_income_tables.plain: Use this list to find the Census Bureau table and cells behind each income, worker, commuting, vehicle and internet figure on the Analysis tab. It helps you cite the original numbers. The 'Code' column lists variable ids, not coded values.
economy.acs_work_income_tables.plain_es: Use esta lista para encontrar la tabla y las celdas del Negociado del Censo que hay detrás de cada cifra de ingreso, personas trabajadoras, viaje al trabajo, vehículos e internet de la pestaña Análisis. Ayuda a citar los números originales. La columna "Código" enumera identificadores de variables, no valores codificados.
economy.acs_work_income_tables.definition: In Puerto Rico the American Community Survey (ACS) is called the Puerto Rico Community Survey (PRCS). The Codes list gives, for each variable on the Analysis tab, the ACS table, who is counted and the cells used. 'Cell 1' is the first line of the table, and table numbers and titles are the Census Bureau's own.
economy.acs_work_income_tables.method: The observatory lists the tables and the number of cells each must have (B19083: 1, B19001: 17, B08301: 21, B08303: 13, B25044: 15, B28002: 13, B24080: 21). Before it publishes, the observatory checks that each table has the expected number of cells, and a mismatch stops the update. The one exception is table B28002 (internet): a vintage that lacks it or lays it out differently is left out without stopping the update. The observatory reads the Census Bureau's per-sequence summary files for windows ending 2010 to 2020 and its table-based summary files for windows ending 2021 and later, for the 78 municipio rows and the Puerto Rico row. Table B28002 is not in the Puerto Rico summary files for windows ending 2010 to 2016, so the internet figures start with 2013-2017. Shares are calculated by the observatory; their margins of error follow the Census Bureau's formulas (margins of summed cells are combined as the square root of the sum of their squares; a share whose numerator is part of its denominator uses the proportion formula).
economy.acs_work_income_tables.how_to_read: To cite a number from the Census Bureau, give the table, the window and the geography, for example 'US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates 2020-2024, table B25044, Ponce Municipio, Puerto Rico'. The percentage shares are not printed in the Census Bureau's tables: the observatory calculates them, so cite the observatory for a share and the cells for the Census Bureau's own counts. On the Analysis tab, the info (i) button beside a dataset opens its definition and sources, links to its entry in this dictionary and offers a CSV of every year, with the margins of error. In the downloaded CSV, the column headed 2024 is the 2020-2024 window and the column '2024 margin of error' holds its margin. In economy_series.json, find the variable under 'vars' by its key; 'years' and 'moe' hold one list per window, in the order of 'geo.names' (Puerto Rico is last). The trend line and the trend chart plot one point per window, labeled by its last year. Under each trend line in the inspector, the caption gives the length of the trend and the first and last label; for these survey series it counts windows, not separate years of data (in the 2026-10 snapshot, '15 yrs · 2010–24'). Neighboring points share four of their five survey years, so they are not independent yearly values.
caveats: Income bands in B19001 are in the dollars of the window's last year: the Census Bureau states the table in inflation-adjusted dollars of that year. The observatory does not convert one window's dollars to another's.

The means-of-transportation shares use all workers as the base, including those who worked from home. The travel-time share uses workers who did not work from home. Neither base is the same count as the civilian employed residents in the class-of-worker table.
Margins of error are published at the 90% confidence level and cover sampling error only.

Windows that include 2017 or 2020 carry survey disruption. The Census Bureau says it halted Puerto Rico Community Survey data collection from October to December 2017 after Hurricane María (https://www.census.gov/library/stories/2020/08/estimating-puerto-rico-population-after-hurricane-maria.html). It also says margins of error for 5-year estimates that include 2020 data rose because fewer interviews were completed in 2020 (https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/technical-documentation/user-notes/2022-04.html). The windows ending 2017 to 2021 include 2017 and the windows ending 2020 to 2024 include 2020. The observatory makes no adjustment.
Neighboring windows share four of their five years of survey responses, so the change from one window to the next mostly reflects one year of new responses.

values.gini: Table B19083, Gini Index of Income Inequality. Households. Cell 1.
values.hh_income_under_25k_pct: Table B19001, Household Income in the Past 12 Months (in inflation-adjusted dollars of the window's last year). Households. Cells 2 to 5 divided by cell 1.
values.hh_income_75k_plus_pct: Table B19001, Household Income in the Past 12 Months (in inflation-adjusted dollars of the window's last year). Households. Cells 13 to 17 divided by cell 1.
values.workers_16plus: Table B24080, Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over. Civilian employed residents 16 and over. Cell 1.
values.gov_worker_pct: Table B24080, Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over. Civilian employed residents 16 and over. Cells 7, 8, 9, 17, 18 and 19 divided by cell 1.
values.self_employed_pct: Table B24080, Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over. Civilian employed residents 16 and over. Cells 5, 10, 15 and 20 divided by cell 1.
values.nonprofit_worker_pct: Table B24080, Sex by Class of Worker for the Civilian Employed Population 16 Years and Over. Civilian employed residents 16 and over. Cells 6 and 16 divided by cell 1.
values.commute_drive_alone_pct: Table B08301, Means of Transportation to Work. Workers 16 and over, including those who worked from home. Cell 3 divided by cell 1.
values.commute_transit_pct: Table B08301, Means of Transportation to Work. Workers 16 and over, including those who worked from home. Cell 10 divided by cell 1.
values.commute_walk_pct: Table B08301, Means of Transportation to Work. Workers 16 and over, including those who worked from home. Cell 19 divided by cell 1.
values.work_from_home_pct: Table B08301, Means of Transportation to Work. Workers 16 and over, including those who worked from home. Cell 21 divided by cell 1.
values.commute_45plus_pct: Table B08303, Travel Time to Work. Workers 16 and over who did not work from home. Cells 11 to 13 divided by cell 1.
values.no_vehicle_hh_pct: Table B25044, Tenure by Vehicles Available. Occupied housing units (households). Cells 3 and 10 divided by cell 1.
values.internet_subscription_pct: Table B28002, Presence and Types of Internet Subscriptions in Household. Households. Cell 2 divided by cell 1. First window: 2013-2017.
values.no_internet_pct: Table B28002, Presence and Types of Internet Subscriptions in Household. Households. Cell 13 divided by cell 1. First window: 2013-2017.

economy.acs_work_income_tables.source_detail: US Census Bureau, ACS 5-year summary files: https://www2.census.gov/programs-surveys/acs/summary_file/. To find a table by its number: https://data.census.gov/

municipalities.acs_reliability.plain: Survey figures are estimates with a margin of error. The municipality file does not show the margins. Take extra care in small municipalities and with small differences.
municipalities.acs_reliability.plain_es: Las cifras de encuesta son estimados con un margen de error. El archivo de municipios no muestra los márgenes. Tenga cuidado especial con los municipios pequeños y con las diferencias pequeñas.
municipalities.acs_reliability.definition: The American Community Survey (ACS) interviews a sample of households, so every estimate has a margin of error. The Census Bureau publishes it at the 90% confidence level: it is 90% confident that the true value lies within the estimate plus or minus the margin. The municipality file carries estimates only. Margins for most fields are in the Housing page series (housing_series.json, 'moe' values, by window).
municipalities.acs_reliability.method: Margins are read from the Census Bureau's own margin columns. For shares and sums the observatory computes margins with the Census Bureau's formulas.
municipalities.acs_reliability.how_to_read: Check the margin before ranking or comparing. Add and subtract the margin to get a range for each municipality. If the two ranges overlap, the survey may not be able to tell the municipalities apart. For a formal test, use the Census Bureau's formula for the margin of a difference. In the 2026-10 snapshot, margins are widest in the smallest municipalities, such as Culebra, Vieques, Florida and Maricao.
caveats: In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window), margins of error in the Housing page series run across the 78 municipalities as follows: median home value ±$1,926 (Carolina) to ±$44,042 (Vieques); median gross rent ±$16 (San Juan) to ±$240 (Culebra); median household income ±$805 (Mayagüez) to ±$7,604 (Culebra); people below poverty ±1.1 points (San Juan) to ±9.5 points (Culebra); employment rate ±0.7 points (San Juan) to ±5.9 points (Culebra and Vieques); cost-burdened renters ±0.7 points (Gurabo) to ±67.9 points (Florida).
The maximum affordable loan, the affordability ratio and the change fields have no margin of error. Their inputs do.

For total population and for the adult population aged 25 and over the Census Bureau sets the survey totals to its own estimates and often publishes no margin. In the 2026-10 snapshot (2020-2024 window) that holds for total population in 76 of 78 municipalities and for the adult population in 73 of 78. The observatory does not calculate a share's margin when the Census Bureau publishes none for the total the share is built on, so shares built on those totals show no margin in the Housing page series (for example 'Adults 25+ with a bachelor's degree or higher (%)'). The Population series and the files below the municipality give such a total a margin of zero instead, so their shares keep the margin of the numerator (methods.small_area_estimates). A missing margin does not mean the figure is exact.
Windows that end one year apart share four of five survey years. A difference between neighboring windows mostly reflects one year of new responses. The 2008-2012 and 2020-2024 windows share none.
A margin covers sampling error only. It does not cover mistakes in answers, such as owners' estimates of home value.
municipalities.acs_reliability.source_detail: US Census Bureau ACS 5-year margins of error; Housing page series (housing_series.json)

methods.acs_windows.plain: Survey figures come from five years of responses pooled together. The observatory labels each window by its last year, so '2024' means the 2020-2024 window. They are averages over a window, not figures for one year.
methods.acs_windows.plain_es: Las cifras de la encuesta combinan cinco años de respuestas. El observatorio identifica cada ventana por su último año, así que "2024" significa la ventana 2020-2024. Son promedios de una ventana, no cifras de un solo año.
methods.acs_windows.definition: The American Community Survey (ACS) 5-year estimates pool the responses collected over 60 months. In Puerto Rico the Census Bureau runs the survey as the Puerto Rico Community Survey (PRCS); its 5-year estimates are published with the ACS tables that the observatory reads. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the observatory reads every window from 2006-2010 to 2020-2024 (15 windows) and labels each one by its last year: 2010 is 2006-2010 and 2024 is 2020-2024. Windows one year apart share four of their five years. The Census Bureau's documentation of the 2013-2017 PRCS 5-year estimates says money values are adjusted to the dollars of the final year of the period, using the national Consumer Price Index. Check the Bureau's documentation for the window you cite before you compare dollar figures across windows. A window is a reading of a typical year in that period, not of its last year.
methods.acs_windows.method: housing_series.py reads the per-sequence summary files for the windows labeled 2010-2020 and the table-based files for 2021 onward, and finds the next window by itself. economy_series.py reads further tables from the same windows. The Housing page spells out the window ('ACS 2020-2024'), and so does the Analysis tab's year chip ('2020–2024'): a series made only from ACS tables is a window in Core.adapters and Core.time, and a series that mixes a yearly count into a survey (jobs per employed resident) is not. A table the survey did not yet have is skipped for early windows: the internet questions start with the 2013-2017 window, labeled 2017.
methods.acs_windows.how_to_read: Read a figure labeled 2024 as 'the typical value over 2020-2024'. To judge real change, compare windows that do not overlap, for example 2014, 2019 and 2024.
caveats: Because windows overlap, a change between neighboring labels mostly reflects one year of new responses and understates real change.
A window pools years before and after an event, so it smooths sudden changes. The 2020-2024 window mixes the pandemic years with later years.

Windows that include 2017 or 2020 carry survey disruption. The Census Bureau halted Puerto Rico Community Survey data collection from October to December 2017 after Hurricane María. It also says margins of error for 5-year estimates that include 2020 data rose because fewer interviews were completed in 2020. The windows ending 2017 to 2021 include 2017, and the windows ending 2020 to 2024 include 2020. The observatory makes no adjustment. See 'Census tables behind the income, worker, commuting and internet figures' (economy.acs_work_income_tables) for the Census sources.
Small municipalities have small samples, so figures are noisy. Margins of error are published (90% confidence) and shown where they exist.
For rescaling by population, the observatory uses the population of the last year of the window, not an average.
methods.acs_windows.source_detail: US Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates, summary files 2006-2010 through 2020-2024; US Census Bureau, Puerto Rico Community Survey, Multiyear Accuracy of the Data (5-year 2013-2017), for the dollar adjustment.

measures.nearest_year_rule.plain: One year control sets every layer. A layer that has no value for that year shows its latest earlier year, and a small note beside the layer (the year chip) says which year it used.
measures.nearest_year_rule.plain_es: Un solo control de año rige todas las capas. Una capa que no tiene valor para ese año muestra su año anterior más reciente, y una nota pequeña junto a la capa (la etiqueta del año) indica qué año usó.
measures.nearest_year_rule.definition: For the year chosen on the year bar, each layer shows its own data year: the latest year in its series that is not later than the chosen year. If every year in the series is later, it shows its first year and the year chip says 'first data'. A one-time snapshot layer always shows its snapshot year. With 'Latest' chosen, each layer shows its own last year. The same rule picks the denominators for per-1,000, per-resident, share-of-jobs and location-quotient views.
measures.nearest_year_rule.method: The function resolve of Core.time (site/js/core/time.js), used by the layer engine (the Analysis tab) and by the Housing page. The year chip comes from E.chip: '2019 (latest at or before 2020)', 'first data 2014', 'snapshot 2026' or, for a survey window, '2016–2020'. The year bar lists the years from 2010 on. Population, jobs and housing units for rescaling come from E.pop, E.jobs and E.hu, which apply the same rule.
measures.nearest_year_rule.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot: choose 2020, and unemployment from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) shows 2019, because the observatory's unemployment series has no 2020 value, while poverty shows the survey window that ends in 2020. Choose 2012, and jobs show 2014 as 'first data 2014', because the jobs series starts in 2014. Choose 2015, and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance shows 2011, the latest declaration year in the data before 2015. Choose 2025, and survey series show the 2020-2024 window.
caveats: A layer can be older than the year you chose. Read the year chip beside each layer in the legend.

FEMA series have values only for years with a disaster declaration. A year with none shows the last earlier declaration year, not zero, and the dollars are those of that earlier disaster. In the 2026-10 snapshot, choosing 2019 shows 2017 for Public Assistance.
Two layers can describe different years. The table, the scatter plot and the correlation use each layer's own data year.
In the Analysis tab the year chip for a survey series names the whole five-year window, for example 2020–2024, while the year bar counts it by its last year (2024).
The year bar in a shared link stores your choice. Without it the link opens at 'Latest'.
measures.nearest_year_rule.source_detail: Every dataset in the Analysis tab.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: unemployment rate with the year set to 2020

methods.snapshot_labelling.plain: The observatory's data are rebuilt as a snapshot with a label such as 'Snapshot 2026-10'. The label names the full build, not every file. Transit files refresh nightly and some series files carry their own build dates.
methods.snapshot_labelling.plain_es: Los datos del observatorio se reconstruyen como un corte de datos con una etiqueta como "Corte 2026-10". La etiqueta nombra la construcción completa, no cada archivo. Los archivos de transporte colectivo se actualizan cada noche y algunos archivos de series tienen sus propias fechas de construcción.
methods.snapshot_labelling.definition: A full build (python build.py) downloads or reuses every source, writes every data file and then meta.json, whose 'label' is the --label text or, by default, 'Snapshot' plus the year and month of the build in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC). meta.json also holds 'generated_at'. The time-series builders write their own 'built' dates, and a nightly job refreshes only the transit data: the transit files and the transit and access fields of places.json, municipalities.json and meta.json. The label is shown on the map pages, appears in the file name of the municipality table download (for example pr_digital_twin_municipalities_Snapshot_2026-10.csv) and in every citation the data dictionary offers.
methods.snapshot_labelling.method: build.py (label, generated_at); refresh_network.py (nightly, writes only when a feed or an access value changed, leaves the label as it is); housing_series.build and economy_series.build (their own 'built' dates); registry.main and dictionary.build run at the end of a full build. Downloads are kept between builds, so a rebuild reuses them unless a refresh is requested.
methods.snapshot_labelling.how_to_read: Quote the snapshot label, the year or window of the figure and the date you retrieved it (the Cite button adds the retrieval date). As of 2026-10-04, the full build of the 2026-10 snapshot is dated 2026-10-02 (UTC), the transit files 2026-10-02, the housing series 2026-10-03 and the economy series 2026-10-04. The access fields of the tourism places (place_access.json and the acc_ fields) are as of 2026-10-06. The build date is on the map page: hover over the snapshot label at the top or open the About section. The dictionary entry for each dataset says how old its source data are.
caveats: A month label does not give the day, and two builds in one month can share a label.
Parts of one snapshot can have different dates: the label names the full build only.
Source data can be older than the build, because the build reuses cached downloads. Each source's own release date applies.
Rebuilding can change numbers: new releases, revised estimates and changed source records all flow in.
methods.snapshot_labelling.source_detail: Sources captured at the snapshot: Overture places, Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) flood zones, Protected Areas Database of the United States (PAD-US), Census boundaries; transit feeds refreshed nightly.

methods.population_vintage_break.plain: Population estimates for 2011-2019 were built on the 2010 census and never revised after the 2020 census. The series therefore steps up in 2020. Do not read that step as one year of growth.
methods.population_vintage_break.plain_es: Los estimados de población de 2011-2019 se basaron en el Censo de 2010 y nunca se revisaron después del Censo de 2020. Por eso la serie da un salto hacia arriba en 2020. Ese salto no debe leerse como un año de crecimiento.
methods.population_vintage_break.definition: A vintage is one annual release of Census Bureau population estimates. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the observatory uses Vintage 2020 for 2011-2019 (built on the 2010 census) and Vintage 2025 for 2020-2025 (built on the 2020 census). The 2010 and 2020 values are April 1 values; the other years are July 1 estimates.
methods.population_vintage_break.method: In the 2026-10 snapshot, population() in housing_series.py reads PRM-EST2020.csv (2010 and 2011-2019) and the cc-est2025-agesex-72 file (2020 and 2021-2025) and records each year's basis in the series ('basis'). The notes of housing_series.json say: 'Estimates for 2011-2019 were made before the 2020 census and were not revised to match it; 2020 and later are on the 2020 census base.' The 2020 value is the April 2020 base of the latest estimates. It includes the Census Bureau's post-census count corrections, so a few municipalities differ from the census count in municipalities.json:population_2020.
methods.population_vintage_break.how_to_read: Compare years inside one base (2011-2019, or 2020-2025), or compare the two census counts (2010 and 2020). Do not compare 2019 with 2020 as if both rested on the same count. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the island-wide July 2019 estimate is 3,193,553 and the 2020 value is 3,285,874, a rise of 2.9%; the 2021 estimate is 3,262,731, a fall of 0.7%.
caveats: Everything divided by population is affected: per-1,000 and per-resident values step in 2020 as well.
'Population change since 2010' compares each year with the 2010 census count. The 2011-2019 values rest on the 2010 base and the 2020-2025 values on the 2020 base, so that series also steps at 2020.
These are estimates, not head counts, and the Census Bureau publishes no margin of error for them.
The American Community Survey also estimates population. The observatory's population series does not use it, so the two can differ.

The series labels the 2020 value '2020 census count', but it is the April 2020 base of the latest estimates, which includes the Census Bureau's post-census count corrections. In the 2026-10 snapshot it matches the census count for the island (3,285,874) but differs from municipalities.json:population_2020 in 68 of 78 municipalities, by 1 to 31 people.
methods.population_vintage_break.source_detail: US Census Bureau Population Estimates, municipios of Puerto Rico (Vintage 2020 and Vintage 2025); 2010 and 2020 census counts.

measures.trend_line.plain: The small line beside each value in the workbench's Inspector, and the Trend view of the workbench, show how a layer's value moved across the years. A caption under each small line says how many years it covers. The Housing page profile has similar lines.
measures.trend_line.plain_es: La línea pequeña junto a cada valor en el Inspector de la mesa de trabajo, y la vista Tendencia de la mesa de trabajo, muestran cómo cambió el valor de una capa a lo largo de los años. Una leyenda debajo de cada línea pequeña indica cuántos años abarca. El perfil de la página de Vivienda tiene líneas parecidas.
measures.trend_line.definition: The Trend column of the workbench's Inspector view shows the layer's calculated values (with the same rescaling, inflation and base-year settings) for each data year from 2010 on, as one small line per layer for the place you selected. The column header reads 'Trend' with 'years shown; dot = chosen year' under it. Under each line a caption gives the number of years from the first to the last (counting years with no data), then the span, in the form 'N yrs · 2014–25'. When some years have no value it adds the number of values, in the form 'N yrs, M values · 2010–25'. A dot marks the data year on the map. The line needs at least two values and is not drawn for one-time snapshots. The Housing page profile has lines of the same kind, drawn from every year the series has, with a caption of the number of years only ('N yrs'). The Trend view charts the places you click or add, with the layer's settings. It uses years from 2010 on, and from the first year for the three Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) datasets. It draws at most eight lines.
measures.trend_line.method: Functions ecSpark and ecBenchTrend in site/js/economy.js and spark in site/js/housing.js. Each line in the Trend column (and on the Housing page profile) is scaled between that place's own lowest and highest value. The chart joins points across years with no value (spanGaps).
measures.trend_line.how_to_read: Use the line for direction and timing, then read the numbers in the table. The caption tells you whether the line covers a full run of years or has gaps. In the 2026-10 snapshot, Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) jobs read '12 yrs · 2014–25'. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) unemployment rate reads '16 yrs, 15 values · 2010–25' because it has no 2020 value. On the Housing page the resident population reads '16 yrs'.
caveats: Each small line is scaled to its own minimum and maximum, so the steepness of two lines cannot be compared between rows or between municipalities.

Where years have no value the chart draws a straight line across the gap, which suggests steady change. FEMA series have values only for years with a disaster declaration. The observatory's unemployment series has no 2020 value.
For survey series each year on the line is a five-year window, so '15 yrs' means 15 overlapping windows, not 15 separate years of responses.
The population series changes base in 2020 and survey windows overlap, which can bend or smooth a line (see the entries on both).
For a 'Change since the base year' layer the line starts after the base year.

The Trend view draws at most eight lines. Puerto Rico always comes first when it is chosen, then the municipalities in list order, so with more than seven municipalities chosen the last ones in the list are left out and Puerto Rico stays.
measures.trend_line.source_detail: Any dataset with more than one year in the Analysis tab; the Trend tab chart is drawn with Chart.js.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: poverty rate (click a municipality, choose 'Open in the workbench', then read the Trend column)
Housing page: the small lines beside each value in a municipality profile

methods.latest_year.plain: 'Latest' means the newest year each dataset has, and datasets do not all end in the same year. The build looks for the newest release itself, so 'latest' moves when the data are rebuilt.
methods.latest_year.plain_es: "Último" significa el año más reciente que tiene cada conjunto de datos, y no todos terminan en el mismo año. La compilación busca por sí mismo la publicación más reciente, así que "Último" cambia cuando se reconstruyen los datos.
methods.latest_year.definition: On the year bar, 'Latest' makes every layer show its own last year. The table of codes below gives those years for the 2026-10 snapshot.
methods.latest_year.method: Each series script finds its last year when it runs. housing_series.py asks the Census Bureau's server whether the next American Community Survey (ACS) window and the next population vintage exist, starting from 2024 and 2025. economy_series.py asks the BLS server whether the next QCEW year exists, starting from 2024, reads unemployment and CPI through the last full calendar year, and reads federal awards through the last fiscal year, counted as final from 15 November. The page then shows 'Latest' by taking the last year of each series (ecResolve in site/js/economy.js, resolve in site/js/housing.js).
methods.latest_year.how_to_read: Check the year chip beside each layer before comparing two layers on 'Latest': they may describe different years. For a fixed comparison, choose a year on the year bar.
caveats: The newest year of some sources can be revised. The Analysis tab's description of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) unemployment series calls its latest year preliminary. USAspending.gov says new or updated data appear the day after an agency submits them, so a recent fiscal year can change. Check the QCEW release notes for its newest year.
The newest values can be thinner than earlier ones: fewer sector figures are published, and small municipalities swing more.
A shared link opens at 'Latest' unless it stores a year, so the same link can show later data after a rebuild.

The observatory has no 2020 value for its four unemployment series (rate, labor force, employed and unemployed). The annual average for 2020 is empty in the BLS data the observatory downloaded, so the series skip 2020.

values.Jobs, work sites and pay (Quarterly Cens: 2025. Mining jobs (industry code 21 in the North American Industry Classification System, NAICS) and jobs per employed resident end in 2024.
values.Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEM: 2024, the latest declaration year with funded projects in the OpenFEMA file at build time
values.FEMA Individual Assistance (OpenFEMA): 2022, the latest declaration year with approved housing assistance in the OpenFEMA file at build time
values.Consumer Price Index: 2025, the reference year for inflation adjustment

methods.latest_year.source_detail: The release calendars of each source decide the last year available at build time.

measures.less_reliable_values.plain: A value is marked less reliable when it is a survey estimate whose margin of error is large next to the estimate, or a rate or share built on fewer than ten counted. On a shaded map the municipality is hatched, a symbol gets a dashed outline, and the value in a pop-up or table is in italics. The mark says how much to trust a number, not whether it is right.
measures.less_reliable_values.plain_es: Un valor se marca como menos confiable cuando es un estimado de encuesta con un margen de error grande en comparación con el estimado, o una tasa o proporción basada en menos de diez casos contados. En un mapa sombreado el municipio aparece rayado, un símbolo lleva un contorno de línea discontinua y el valor en una ventana emergente o una tabla aparece en cursiva. La marca indica cuánto confiar en una cifra, no si es correcta.
measures.less_reliable_values.definition: Two rules, applied to the values a layer shows. (1) Margin of error: the published margin of error (90% confidence) is more than 30% of the estimate; an estimate of zero with any margin counts, because the margin cannot be small next to nothing. For a change since a base year, either of the two years counts.
