(2) Few counted: a rate or share of a count (per 1,000 residents, per 1,000 housing units, % of the municipality's jobs, % of the area's residents or housing units, location quotient; or a share whose dataset names the count it rests on) where the count is above zero and below 10. A figure that the source withholds is not flagged: the municipality has no value and the legend says why (see methods.qcew_suppression). A municipality with no published margin is never flagged by rule 1.
measures.less_reliable_values.method: Core.reliability (site/js/core/reliability.js). isUnreliable(value, moe) is true when moe is above zero and either the value is zero or moe ÷ |value| is above 0.3. assess() applies it to the published estimates of the year shown and the small-count rule to the layer's counts, and the layer engine keeps the result (E.reliability). The 2D map draws the hatch as a pattern over the municipality (a dark line beside a white one, so it shows on pale and dark colors and in print), the legend lists each flag in words with the number of municipalities, and the pop-up, the workbench table and the hover card set the value in italics with a sentence below. The Housing page uses the same rule and the same sentence.
measures.less_reliable_values.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, 74 of the 78 municipalities are hatched for workers who walk to work (2020-2024) and 66 for nonprofit workers, because few residents in a small municipality give such an answer; none is hatched for median household income. For rule 2, 10 municipalities have fewer than 10 housing units inside the area flooded by 3 feet of sea level rise, so their share of housing units is hatched.
caveats: A flag is a caution, not a verdict: a flagged value can be close to the truth, and an unflagged one can be off.
The thresholds are conventions. 30% is the rule the Housing page has always used; fewer than 10 is a common point below which a count is treated as small.

Margins of error are not carried through a rescaling (per 1,000 residents, index, difference, change, percentile). The flag describes the published estimate, and the legend says so when a view other than 'As published' is flagged.
A value with no margin published (for example a figure that is not from a survey) is never flagged by the margin rule.
Housing page tables set zero estimates that carry a margin in italics, as the Analysis tab does; before 2026-10 they were left as ordinary figures.
measures.less_reliable_values.source_detail: Margins of error: American Community Survey 5-year estimates, published by the Census Bureau or computed by Foundation for Puerto Rico with the Bureau's formulas (see measures.margin_of_error). The thresholds, 30% and 10 counted, are display conventions chosen by FPR, not statistical tests.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: workers who walk to work (74 of 78 municipalities hatched)
Housing page: full data for seasonal units, with margins and italic values

measures.margin_of_error.plain: Figures from the American Community Survey are estimates from a sample, so they carry a margin of error. A figure of 38.8% ± 1.1 percentage points means the Census Bureau is 90% confident that the true value lies between 37.7% and 39.9%.
measures.margin_of_error.plain_es: Las cifras de la Encuesta sobre la Comunidad (ACS) son estimados basados en una muestra, así que tienen un margen de error. Una cifra de 38.8% ± 1.1 puntos porcentuales significa que el Negociado del Censo tiene un 90% de confianza de que el valor real está entre 37.7% y 39.9%.
measures.margin_of_error.definition: The margin of error (written ±) is the Census Bureau's published margin at the 90% confidence level: the Bureau is 90% confident that the true value lies within the estimate plus or minus the margin. The observatory carries the Bureau's margins for single cells such as medians. For sums and shares it computes the margin with the Bureau's formulas: the margin of a sum is the square root of the sum of the squared margins, and shares use the Bureau's proportion formula. If that formula would take the square root of a negative number, it uses the ratio formula. Margins are in the same unit as the estimate: percentage points for percent figures, dollars for dollar figures. On the Analysis tab the margin of a rate prints in percentage points with one decimal (for example '±1.1 pts').
measures.margin_of_error.method: Functions derive, pct and Cells in housing_series.py, derive_econ in economy_series.py and derive_pop in small_area.py compute and store the margins (the 'moe' values of housing_series.json, economy_series.json, population_series.json and, for the levels below the municipality, acs_barrio.json, acs_tract.json and acs_blockgroup.json; see methods.small_area_estimates). The Analysis tab shows '±' in the inspector and the popup when a layer is shown as published (a rate in percentage points, for example '±1.1 pts', and a dollar figure in dollars); with 'Inflation-adjusted' ticked the margin is multiplied by the same factor. The Housing page shows ± in its readouts and profile. Downloads of a series (comma-separated values, CSV, files) add a margin column per year. A value whose margin is above 30% of the estimate is marked less reliable (hatching, a dashed outline, italics) by Core.reliability; see measures.less_reliable_values.
measures.margin_of_error.how_to_read: In the 2026-10 snapshot, San Juan's poverty rate in the 2020-2024 window is 38.84% ± 1.08 points. Culebra's is 25.74% ± 9.48 points and Maricao's 52.89% ± 7.73 points. San Juan's median household income is $27,992 ± $1,036. In that snapshot 94 of the 562 Analysis tab datasets have margins of error. Census Bureau guidance: a difference between two estimates is statistically significant at the same confidence level when it is larger than the square root of the sum of the two squared margins. Use this rule for two estimates from different places in the same window. It does not apply to two overlapping windows. A municipality compared with Puerto Rico is not an independent comparison, because the island figure includes the municipality, so treat that result as approximate.
caveats: Margins are wide for small municipalities and narrow for large ones.

Rescaled views (per 1,000, index, difference, change, percentile) hide the margin. No margin is calculated for a difference, an index, a change or the affordability figures. A value whose published margin is wide is still marked less reliable in those views (see measures.less_reliable_values).
On the Analysis tab the margin of median age prints as '± … pts' although median age is in years.
A margin covers sampling error only. It does not cover mistakes in answers, such as an owner's estimate of home value.

Datasets from sources that are not surveys have no margin: Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW) jobs, the Population Estimates, USAspending and OpenFEMA. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) unemployment series is a model estimate and has none in the observatory.

A share shows no margin when the observatory cannot calculate one from the margins published for its cells. In the 2026-10 snapshot, for adults with a bachelor's degree, 68 to 73 of the 78 municipalities have no margin in the 2021 to 2024 windows, while all 78 have one in 2010 to 2020. The Population series and the files below the municipality give such a total a margin of zero instead (the Census Bureau says it may be treated as zero), so their shares keep the margin of the numerator; see methods.small_area_estimates.
measures.margin_of_error.geography: 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico; for the variables of the Census small-area files also 901 barrios, 981 census tracts and 2,555 block groups
measures.margin_of_error.source_detail: American Community Survey 5-year estimates; margins as published by the Census Bureau or computed by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) with the Bureau's formulas.

view.label: Map, Analysis tab: click a municipality to see the ± beside the poverty rate
Data dictionary: entries that have margins of error

methods.shared_links.plain: A link from the map or the housing page stores your view settings in the web address: where the map is looking, which layers are on and the year. It holds no table of data and no name or account. If you plan a route, the link also holds the route's map coordinates, so check it before you share it.
methods.shared_links.plain_es: Un enlace del mapa o de la página de Vivienda guarda la configuración de la vista en la dirección web: hacia dónde mira el mapa, qué capas están activas y el año. No contiene tablas de datos, nombres ni cuentas. Si se planifica una ruta, el enlace también guarda las coordenadas de la ruta en el mapa, así que revíselo antes de compartirlo.
methods.shared_links.definition: The 2D map writes #Municipality&c=lat,lng,zoom&l=layers&s=shading&r=route&e=economy layers&ey=year&eb=base year&slr=feet into the address as you work. The 'e' part lists each Economy layer as ten values joined by dots: dataset key, mode (shaded or symbols), rescaling, color ramp, class method, visible, same classes in every year, inflation-adjusted, opacity and symbol color. 'ey' is written only when you choose a year ('Latest' has none) and 'eb' only when the base year is not 2014. The 3D view writes #c=lat,lng,zoom and r. The housing page writes ?m=municipality, then y=year only when you choose a year ('Latest' has none) and c=base year only when it is not 2012 (and ?d=dataset for an open dataset). The dictionary writes #entry and its filters as ?q=, domain, source, kind, time, file and moe.
methods.shared_links.method: Functions writeHash, parseHash and applyHash in site/js/app.js, ecEncode and ecRestore in site/js/economy.js, writeUrl in site/js/housing.js and the 3D page's address writer. The page updates the address in the browser (history.replaceState); nothing is sent to a server. A dataset key that no longer exists is skipped when a link is opened, and a rescaling that does not suit the dataset falls back to 'As published'.
methods.shared_links.how_to_read: A shared link shares a view, not a table of numbers. If the data were rebuilt after you made the link, the same view can show different numbers. To fix numbers in a report, cite the snapshot label and the date and keep the downloaded data file.
caveats: Route points are saved as coordinates with four decimals (about 11 meters). A route that starts at a home would put that location in the link. The link also holds the map center (four decimals) and the municipality you selected. Check a link before sharing it.
A link without a year opens at 'Latest', which moves when the data are rebuilt.
Not everything is stored: an open workbench tab, the Ask the observatory chat and the selected municipality in the Analysis tab are not in the link.
methods.shared_links.source_detail: Map position and zoom come from the Leaflet (2D) and MapLibre (3D) maps.

methods.headline_figures.plain: Each field on the Topics tab shows one figure for the whole of Puerto Rico. It is either the Puerto Rico value of a yearly series, for example the median rent, or a total or share worked out from the 78 municipal values by a rule written next to the field in the registry. It is a figure to start from, not a score.
methods.headline_figures.plain_es: Cada campo de la pestaña Temas muestra una cifra para todo Puerto Rico. Es el valor de Puerto Rico de una serie anual, por ejemplo la mediana del alquiler, o un total o una proporción que se calcula con los 78 valores municipales según una regla escrita junto al campo en el registro. Es una cifra de partida, no una puntuación.
methods.headline_figures.definition: The registry (dictionary_src/domains.json) names one dictionary entry as the headline of a field, with a short label in Spanish and English. For a yearly series (the housing and economy series files) the figure is the Puerto Rico value of the latest year and the trend is the Puerto Rico value of every year. For a measure held for each municipality (a field of municipalities.json) the registry also gives an 'island' rule: a sum of one field, a ratio of the sums of two fields times a scale, or an average of one field weighted by another. The result is rounded to the decimals the registry gives. The period on the card says what the figure covers: a five-year estimate, a calendar year, a year of declaration, or the snapshot.
methods.headline_figures.method: catalog.py headline() reads the last element of each year's array in the series file (the Puerto Rico row) and keeps the years that have a value. island_value() applies the registry's rule to the municipal values. In the 2026-10 snapshot the rules are: tourism places listed is the sum of the municipal counts; tourism places in a flood hazard area is the sum of places in a flood hazard area divided by the sum of places, times 100; tourism places inside protected areas is the sum of the municipal counts; residents within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable is the average of the municipal shares weighted by the 2020 residents, which equals the island share apart from rounding.
methods.headline_figures.how_to_read: Read each figure with its period and its name: they say what it counts. A headline is chosen to start a conversation about a field. It does not say which field matters most, and a different headline for the same field would tell a different story.
caveats: Several headlines count tourism places (Overture Maps listings), not businesses, visitors or hazards in general. That is what the data hold today; fuller hazard and land figures for residents and homes are planned.
A five-year estimate (the American Community Survey) has a margin of error that the card does not show. The Housing page and the dictionary entry do.
A series of events (FEMA Public Assistance) shows the latest year that has a value, which can be small next to the years of large disasters. Read it with its trend line.
The share of residents near a stop with a current timetable depends on the date: it is computed as of the build date, and a feed that ends changes it (see methods.access_profile).
Where a field has no headline yet, or no data, the card says so instead of leaving the field out.

view.label: Map, Topics tab

methods.citation.plain: Cite the original source for the data and the observatory for how the data were put together. The Cite button on each dictionary entry gives a ready credit line and APA, Chicago and BibTeX versions.
methods.citation.plain_es: Cite la fuente original por los datos y el observatorio por la forma en que se reunieron los datos. El botón "Citar" de cada entrada del diccionario da una línea de crédito lista y versiones en APA, Chicago y BibTeX.
methods.citation.definition: Each dictionary entry has a Cite button with four formats. The credit line joins the credit lines of the entry's sources and adds 'Processed by Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory (snapshot label)'. APA 7 and BibTeX give Foundation for Puerto Rico as author and the entry name and its years as the title. Chicago gives the entry name only. All three add the snapshot label, the address of the entry, the original sources and the date you retrieved it. The year is the year of the snapshot build. The dictionary page also has a citation for the whole site. It uses the address of the page you are on, or https://observatory.foundationpr.org/ when the page runs on a local address.
methods.citation.method: Functions citeTexts and citePanel in site/js/dictionary.js. The credit line of each source is stored in the dictionary's source list. When the page runs on a local address, the public address is used in the citation.
methods.citation.how_to_read: Say what the figure is, the year or window, the snapshot label and the retrieval date. For survey figures, add the window ('2020-2024 American Community Survey 5-year estimates'). For figures the observatory calculates, such as rates per 1,000 residents or the affordability ratio, say that Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) calculated them from the named sources. Example, calculated figure: 'In 2025 there were about 770 jobs located in San Juan for every 1,000 residents (FPR calculation from US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, 2025 annual average, and US Census Bureau Population Estimates, Vintage 2025; PR Data Observatory, Snapshot 2026-10, retrieved [date]).' Example, survey figure: 'San Juan's poverty rate was 38.8% ± 1.1 percentage points (90% confidence), 2020-2024 American Community Survey 5-year estimates (PR Data Observatory, Snapshot 2026-10, retrieved [date]).' Measure and method entries are not data sets. In the APA citation of one of them, delete '[Data set]'. In the APA and BibTeX citations, delete a title ending '(Not tied to a year)'. Every dataset dialog on the Analysis tab and the Housing page links to its dictionary entry, where the Cite button is.
caveats: The observatory's citation does not replace the source's own terms. Check the license or terms of the source, which are in the Sources section, before reuse.

Terms differ by source. Examples: OpenStreetMap data need credit and share-alike under the Open Database License (ODbL); municipal transit feeds state no license; Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) data are provided as is; OpenFEMA asks for a statement that the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) does not endorse the product. Check each source's terms in the Sources section. This is not legal advice.
Credit lines are recorded in the source list. Check each source's own terms for the wording it requires; the observatory does not give legal advice.
Numbers can change when the data are rebuilt, so always give the snapshot label.
methods.citation.source_detail: Not a data entry. The sources listed are examples of those that figures from the observatory credit. When you cite this entry, credit the observatory only.

methods.rounding_display.plain: The observatory keeps more decimals than it shows. Maps, legends and tables round numbers for reading. Downloads and data files keep the stored precision. Cite the stored value with its unit and year.
methods.rounding_display.plain_es: El observatorio guarda más decimales de los que muestra. Los mapas, las leyendas y las tablas redondean los números para facilitar la lectura. Las descargas y los archivos de datos mantienen la precisión guardada. Cite el valor guardado con su unidad y su año.
methods.rounding_display.definition: Display: numbers use US format (commas for thousands, points for decimals). A missing value shows as a dash on the page, 'No data' in gray on the map, and an empty cell in downloads. Legend and axis labels, negative dollar amounts, the Ask the observatory chat's changes and the Housing page's signed changes use a true minus sign (−). Other negative figures, such as those in the Analysis tab inspector and table, use a plain hyphen (-). The Analysis tab gives each dataset its own number of decimals (counts none, most percentages one, the Gini index three). A rescaling overrides it: per 1,000 one decimal; per km² one decimal (none for dollars); dollars per resident none; difference from Puerto Rico the dataset's own decimals (none for dollars); share of Puerto Rico two; share of jobs one; location quotient two; index none; percentile none; change one (two for ratios). Margins of error (±) print with one decimal for rates, in percentage points. Legend and axis labels are shortened (255K, 1.5K, 12M). Median year built shows as a whole year. The Housing page shows dollars to the whole dollar. Stored precision: place coordinates six decimals, confidence three, tourism places per 1,000 residents and per km² two, flood share one, land area one, survey shares two, Gini three.
methods.rounding_display.method: Functions ecFmt, ecCompact and ecOut in site/js/economy.js; fmt in site/js/common.js; the rounding in build.py, housing_series.py and economy_series.py. Downloads are comma-separated values (CSV) files. The table download from the Analysis tab writes the calculated values (per-1,000 values already rounded to three decimals), a series download writes the stored values, and the municipality download on the Rankings tab writes municipalities.json as stored.
methods.rounding_display.how_to_read: Round only in your own text, and say the year and the unit. If two numbers look equal on screen, check the stored values in a download.
caveats: Rounded shares may not add up to 100%.
Ranks and color classes use unrounded values. Two municipalities that show the same rounded number can have different ranks or colors.
Per-1,000 values are calculated to three decimals and shown with one.
The legend limits are rounded labels. A value shown as 41.3 may sit on either side of a limit labeled 41.3.
methods.rounding_display.source_detail: Applies to every dataset in the observatory.

layers.economy_tab.plain: The Analysis tab puts yearly datasets on the map: jobs, pay, unemployment, income, poverty, commuting, federal money, housing and reported crime. Shade a rate, size a count, move the year, and click the map to see every layer at that place.
layers.economy_tab.plain_es: La pestaña Análisis pone en el mapa conjuntos de datos anuales: empleos, paga, desempleo, ingreso, pobreza, viaje al trabajo, fondos federales, vivienda y delitos informados. Sombree una tasa, muestre un conteo con símbolos, cambie el año y haga clic en el mapa para ver todas las capas en ese lugar.
layers.economy_tab.definition: In Snapshot 2026-10 the tab lists 562 datasets: 286 yearly series for the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico, and 276 counts and shares for a single year (tourism places, places in a flood hazard area or a protected area, the tourism places near transit, transit stops and the residents near them, whether Uber lists the municipality, the change in median gross rent since 2008-2012, land by plan class, and the residents and housing units inside a hazard, inside protected land or near a stop, the health center sites and shortage areas of each municipality, its hospitals and other care facilities, the distance from where residents live to the nearest health center, its drinking water systems (and those outside PRASA, with the residents they serve) and power plants, its expected yearly loss from natural hazards, the landslides mapped after Hurricane María, its wetlands and mangroves, its public housing developments and units, its tax credit housing projects and units, fire, EMS and police stations and public libraries, its tax-exempt organizations by field, its places on the National Register of Historic Places, its substance use and mental health treatment facilities by type, and its EPA-regulated sites, impaired waters and air quality non-attainment areas, households with severe housing problems, street intersections and drive time to a general hospital, which also have barrio values; and the WCRP vulnerability indices, which have values for barrios only). Of the 286 series, 104 are listed in the economy file (some take their values from the Housing page's series, such as poverty and median income) and 182 more come from the Housing page's series (33), from the Population series of the survey (30), from the daytime population series (3), from the survey's series of labor force participation by sex (7), from the education series of public schools and colleges (7), from the Medicare series (3), from the bridges series (3), from the series of community resilience and earthquakes (5), from the airport and ferry series (4), from the night-time lights series (2), from the satellite fire detections series (3), from the fixed broadband series (6), from the road traffic series (6), from the road deaths series (6), from the bank offices and home loans series (6), from the drought series (3), from the storm recovery series (2), from the essentials series (7), from the degrees series (11), from the school conditions series (4), from the test results series (2), from the health providers series (7) from the cut-off series (5) from the jobs within reach series (4) and from the net migration by age series (7). Any dataset can be added to the map as a shaded layer or as sized symbols. Up to two shaded layers and any number of symbol layers can be on at once. The tab holds a year control, six ready-made views and the list of layers on the map with their settings. It also has buttons for the workbench, for clearing the layers and for copying a link, switches for other map layers, the dataset list with a search box, four reading notes and a list of sources with their licenses. The tab loads its data the first time you open it. While the tab is open and a layer is visible, a click on the map opens the economy popup, not the municipality profile.
layers.economy_tab.method: economy.js reads data/economy_series.json (built by economy_series.py) and data/housing_series.json (built by housing_series.py). A housing series that the economy file does not list is added under a 'Housing ·' group. The five tourism counts are built in the browser from municipalities.json.
layers.economy_tab.how_to_read: Start from a ready-made view, then change one thing at a time. Each layer says which year it shows.
caveats: Jobs, pay and establishments count the workplace (Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, QCEW). Income, poverty and commuting describe residents (American Community Survey, ACS). In the 2024 data of Snapshot 2026-10, 9 of the 78 municipalities have more jobs than employed residents; San Juan (1.9 jobs per employed resident) and Mayagüez (1.5) have the most. This fits commuting into job centers, but the ratio does not measure commuting.

Survey figures (ACS, Local Area Unemployment Statistics, LAUS) are noisy for small municipalities. Margins of error are shown where the source publishes them. The jobs data hide cells that would identify one employer, so some sectors are blank in small municipalities.
The informal economy is not in the jobs data. The share of self-employed residents points to some work the jobs data miss, but it is not a measure of the informal economy.

Federal awards are placed where the work is done, as the awarding agency reports it. The awarding agency often records awards for statewide programs under the capital, so San Juan's total can include money that serves other places. See the entry on federal awards, all types.

In Snapshot 2026-10 the latest year (2025) of the jobs and unemployment series is preliminary and can be revised. The unemployment rate has no 2020 value. Some series are not yearly: four census series hold only 2010 and 2020, and the recovery series of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) are by declaration year (12 years from 2001 to 2024 for Public Assistance).
Federal award and recovery amounts (federal awards, FEMA Public Assistance and FEMA Individual Assistance) are amounts obligated (committed) or approved. They are not money spent, damage or need.
Values per resident step in 2020, because the Census Bureau's population estimates change base that year (see the entry on the 2020 break in the population series).

layers.economy_context.plain: 'Also show on the map' repeats eight switches of the Map layers tab, in the order of that tab and with its names, so you can add context to an economy view without leaving the tab.
layers.economy_context.plain_es: "Mostrar también en el mapa" repite ocho interruptores de la pestaña Capas del mapa, en el orden de esa pestaña y con sus nombres, para agregar contexto a una vista económica sin salir de la pestaña.
layers.economy_context.definition: The eight switches are Tourism places, Transit routes, Transit stops, Barrios, Flood hazard zones, Protected areas, Land use (PUT 2015, the Plan de Uso de Terrenos) and Municipality boundaries. Each one is the same switch as on the Map layers tab. A change in one place shows in the other.
layers.economy_context.method: economy.js (ecRenderContext, ecContextSync) sets the Layers-tab checkbox and sends it a change event.
layers.economy_context.how_to_read: Add one context layer at a time. Several overlays together make the economy colors hard to read.
caveats: The sea level and transit planning layers are not in this list. Use the Layers and Transit tabs for them.

layers.economy_inspector.plain: Click a municipality while the Analysis tab is open. A card shows the value of each visible layer for that place and its rank among the 78. It also shows the margin of error where the source publishes one.
layers.economy_inspector.plain_es: Haga clic en un municipio con la pestaña Análisis abierta. Una tarjeta muestra el valor de cada capa visible en ese lugar y su posición entre los 78. También muestra el margen de error cuando la fuente lo publica.
layers.economy_inspector.definition: A click outlines the municipality in black and opens a card. The card has a table with one row for each visible layer. A row gives the name (press it to open the dataset's information), how the layer is shown and for which year, and the value. It adds the margin of error (±) when the source publishes one and the layer is shown 'as published'. For a rate the margin is in percentage points (for example ±1.2 pts). For other datasets it is in the dataset's own unit. It ends with the rank ('#n of N', where 1 is the highest value). A link opens the workbench. On a computer, pointing at the map also shows a small box at the bottom right with each layer's value for the municipality under the pointer. That box is not shown on phones. In the workbench's Inspector tab the same table adds a column for Puerto Rico and a column headed 'Trend' with a trend line for each layer. A caption under each line gives its length, for example '12 yrs · 2014–25' (see the entry on trend lines). The map popup has no trend column. When the jobs data are available, a line names the industry sector, or government, that has the most jobs in the municipality, with its share of the municipality's jobs, for the year the jobs dataset shows.
layers.economy_inspector.how_to_read: Use the rank to place the municipality, and the margin of error to judge whether a small difference means anything.
caveats: Margins of error are 90% confidence margins from the Census Bureau's survey. Many datasets are counts or administrative figures with no margin.
The rank counts the municipalities that have a value. Tied values share the first of their places.
The 'largest sector' line counts private industry sectors and government. Hidden cells can change it in small municipalities.
Rank 1 is the highest value, which for unemployment or poverty is the worst result. Compare ranks only within the same layer and year.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab, jobs as symbols (click a municipality)

layers.economy_dataset_dialog.plain: The info button beside a dataset opens a window with its definition, years, sources and licenses. It also links to the dataset's dictionary entry and lets you download all its years as a comma-separated values (CSV) file.
layers.economy_dataset_dialog.plain_es: El botón de información junto a un conjunto de datos abre una ventana con su definición, años, fuentes y licencias. También enlaza a su ficha en el diccionario y permite descargar todos sus años como archivo CSV (valores separados por comas).
layers.economy_dataset_dialog.definition: The window shows the dataset's group and type (count, dollar total, dollar level, rate or ratio) and a definition. Jobs (qcew_jobs) and the unemployment rate (laus_unemp_rate) have an extra note. Next come the source reference and the years the dataset covers (for example '2014–2025 (12 years)', with 'margins of error at 90% confidence are published' when they are). Then come the geography, the build date and a note on dollars where they apply. A line 'Full entry' links to the dataset's entry in the data dictionary, where you find its meaning, method, cautions and how to cite it. For Public Assistance of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) the window also gives the share of money recorded as statewide for each declaration year. For the federal award datasets it gives the share of awards that name no municipality, by fiscal year. Below are the sources with their license text and links. Buttons add the dataset to the map as a shaded layer or as symbols. 'Download all years (CSV)' saves pr_economy_<dataset>.csv with the columns GEOID (the geographic identifier code), Municipality and one column for each year, plus a margin-of-error column for each year when the source publishes one. Values are as published. Nothing is normalized or inflation-adjusted.
layers.economy_dataset_dialog.method: economy.js (ecInfo), which fills an HTML dialog element. The dictionary link opens dictionary.html#economy.<dataset>, or #housing.<dataset> for series that come from the Housing page.
layers.economy_dataset_dialog.how_to_read: Read the definition and the source before you cite a number. The dictionary entry gives the full method and a citation.
caveats: The license text is what the source states. Check the source's own terms before you reuse the data.
The CSV can start earlier than 2010 because it holds every year of the dataset.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab, dataset list

layers.economy_datasets.plain: The dataset list on the Analysis tab shows every dataset in groups. Type in the search box to find one, then press 'Shade' or 'Symbols' to put it on the map, or the info button to read its definition and sources.
layers.economy_datasets.plain_es: La lista de conjuntos de datos de la pestaña Análisis muestra todos los conjuntos por grupos. Escriba en el buscador para encontrar uno y oprima "Sombrear" o "Símbolos" para ponerlo en el mapa, o el botón de información para leer su definición y sus fuentes.
layers.economy_datasets.definition: In Snapshot 2026-10 the list has 104 groups, shown below with the number of datasets in each. The search box looks for the text you type, as one phrase (not word by word), ignoring accents and capitals, in each dataset's name, group, source reference and definition. A search opens every group that has a match. Without a search only the first group is open. The count beside 'Datasets' shows how many are listed. Each row gives the name and the years it covers (for example 2014–2025, or 'snapshot 2026'), with '± margins' when the source publishes margins of error. 'Shade' adds the dataset as a shaded layer. For a count it is shown per 1,000 residents, and for a dollar total per resident, because a shaded map of a raw count mostly shows how big the municipality is. 'Symbols' adds it as sized circles with the value as published. The info button opens the dataset dialog.
layers.economy_datasets.method: economy.js (ecLoad, ecRenderBrowse). Groups appear in the order of sortGroups in core/datasets.js, the themes of the layer menu (docs/layers.md): population, the economy, hazards and environment, land and housing, infrastructure and mobility, community services, communities, and the visitor economy (Tourism supply) last.
layers.economy_datasets.how_to_read: The group is the tab's own grouping. It is not the dictionary's grouping.
caveats: A dataset can appear under a different group here than in the dictionary. For example, poverty, median income and population are listed under groups of the economy file, and housing series appear under 'Housing ·' groups.

values.Population · People and age: 20 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from the American Community Survey (5-year windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024): the survey's estimate of the population, the share of women and girls, and the count and share of eight age groups (under 3, 3 and 4, 5 to 17, under 18, 18 to 24, 25 to 44, 45 to 64 and 65 and older) and of the broader group 18 to 44.
values.Population · Household types: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from the American Community Survey (5-year windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024): the shares of family households and of one-person households.
values.Population · Disability and veterans: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from the American Community Survey (5-year windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024): the share of veterans among civilians 18 and older, and the share of people with a disability among people outside institutions.
values.Population · Health insurance: 1 dataset in Snapshot 2026-10, from the American Community Survey (5-year windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024): the share of people outside institutions without health insurance.
values.Population · Education level: 1 dataset in Snapshot 2026-10, from the American Community Survey (5-year windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024): the share of adults 25 and older without a high school diploma.
values.Population · Language: 1 dataset in Snapshot 2026-10, from the American Community Survey (5-year windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024): the share of people 5 and older who speak English less than "very well".
values.Population · Poverty and assistance: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from the American Community Survey (5-year windows 2017-2021 to 2020-2024): the share of households that received nutrition assistance (PAN), and the shares of children under 18 and of people 65 and older below the poverty level.
values.Population · Daytime population: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, calculated from the Census Bureau's commuting flows of 2016-2020 and the 2020 Census: the daytime population, the daytime change as a percent of residents, and the share of resident workers who work in another municipio.
values.Vulnerability (CDC/ATSDR SVI): 4 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2022): CDC's Social Vulnerability Index rank among the 78 municipios, overall and for three themes (socioeconomic status, household characteristics, housing type and transportation).
values.Hazards · Facilities and roads in hazard: 17 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): the public facilities, the public schools and their students, and the kilometers of main road inside FEMA's 1% flood area, NOAA's 3 ft sea level rise area and the USGS high landslide susceptibility classes, as counts and as shares.
values.Hazards · Drought (US Drought Monitor): 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, yearly 2000-2026, from the weekly US Drought Monitor: the average share of the area in drought, and the weeks with drought, and with severe drought, over half the area.
values.Hazards · Storm recovery (night-time lig: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, for Hurricanes María (2017) and Fiona (2022), calculated from the monthly night-time light: the months until light came back and the darkest month after each storm.
values.Hazards · Cut off from hospitals (estima: 5 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, estimates for the current year: the share of residents with no open road to a hospital when the roads in FEMA's 1% flood area close (and of them, those on a dry street), when the bridges in poor condition close, and both, and the residents cut off by floods.
values.Economy · Jobs within reach (estimate): 4 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, estimates for the current year: the jobs residents can reach within 30 and 45 minutes by car, and their share of Puerto Rico's jobs.
values.Population · Net migration by age, 2010-: 7 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, estimates for the window 2010-2020: net migration of the people aged 10 to 19, 20 to 29, 30 to 44, 45 to 64, 65 and over, and 10 and over in 2020, per 100 expected, and the number of people aged 10 and over.
values.Communities · Road distance to essential: 7 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, estimates for the current year: road distance from where residents live to a supermarket, any food store, a pharmacy, a bank or cooperativa, a library and a fire or EMS station, and the share of residents more than 5 km from a supermarket.
values.Education · Degrees awarded (IPEDS): 11 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, academic years ending 2015 to 2024: degrees and certificates awarded by colleges, by level (associate, bachelor's, master's and doctor's) and by broad field, counted where the campus is.
values.Education · School conditions (Civil Rig: 4 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, school years 2017-18 and 2021-22: chronic absence, students per counselor, schools with a nurse and schools with no counselor in public schools.
values.Education · Test results (META-PR, 2014-: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, school years 2014-15 to 2018-19: public school students proficient in reading (Spanish) and math on Puerto Rico's test (META-PR).
values.Health · Health care providers (NPPES re: 7 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, for the current year: health care providers registered with a practice address in each municipio, by type (NPPES registry; a municipio with 1 to 9 is empty).
values.Labor force by sex: 7 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from the American Community Survey (three 5-year windows that share no year: 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024), with margins: the labor force participation rate of women 16 and over, of men 16 and over and of women 25 to 54, the gap between men and women in percentage points, the unemployment rate of women, the women 16 and over and the women in the labor force.
values.Economy · Nonprofit organizations: 12 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one snapshot (the IRS file of 2026-10-13): tax-exempt organizations, 501(c)(3) charities and the ten NTEE major groups (IRS Exempt Organizations Business Master File).
values.Economy · Night-time lights (NASA Black: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, yearly 2012-2025, from NASA Black Marble VNP46A3: the mean night-time radiance and the share of pixels of poor quality or gap-filled, with barrio values.
values.Economy · Banks and deposits (FDIC): 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, yearly 2000-2026 (June 30), from the FDIC Summary of Deposits: the offices of FDIC-insured banks and the deposits booked at them. Cooperativas are not in it.
values.Housing · Home loans (HMDA): 4 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, yearly 2018-2025, from the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act data: home loans made, home purchase loans, their amount and the share of decided applications denied.
values.Residents · Flood hazard · FEMA: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): residents inside a Special Flood Hazard Area (1% annual chance) and inside any flood hazard area (1% or 0.2% annual chance).
values.Housing units · Flood hazard · FEMA: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): housing units inside a Special Flood Hazard Area (1% annual chance) and inside any flood hazard area (1% or 0.2% annual chance).
values.Residents · Sea level rise · NOAA (conne: 10 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): residents on land inundated by 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise, one dataset for each height.
values.Residents · Sea level rise · NOAA (low-l: 10 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): residents in low-lying areas that may flood at 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise but are not connected to the ocean, one dataset for each height.
values.Residents · Storm surge · NOAA NHC (near: 10 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): residents where NOAA's storm surge maps show water in a category 1 to 5 hurricane, at any depth and under 3 feet or more, one dataset for each category and depth.
values.Housing units · Sea level rise · NOAA (c: 10 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): housing units on land inundated by 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise, one dataset for each height.
values.Housing units · Sea level rise · NOAA (l: 10 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): housing units in low-lying areas that may flood at 1 to 10 feet of sea level rise but are not connected to the ocean, one dataset for each height.
values.Housing units · Storm surge · NOAA NHC (: 10 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): housing units where NOAA's storm surge maps show water in a category 1 to 5 hurricane, at any depth and under 3 feet or more, one dataset for each category and depth.
values.Residents · Protected areas · USGS PAD-U: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): residents inside a protected area and inside a strictly protected area (GAP status 1 or 2).
values.Housing units · Protected areas · USGS P: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): housing units inside a protected area and inside a strictly protected area (GAP status 1 or 2).
values.Environment · Natural hazard risk: 7 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year: FEMA's expected annual loss from natural hazards in all and from hurricane wind, earthquake, inland flooding, landslide, coastal flooding and tsunami (National Risk Index, December 2025).
values.Environment · Landslides: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, for 2017: landslides mapped after Hurricane María, in all and per km² of land (USGS).
values.Environment · Landslide susceptibility (: 9 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from the USGS map of susceptibility to landslides triggered by intense rainfall (2020): the share of the land in the high-or-above and very-high-or-above classes and in each of the five classes, and the 2020 residents living in the high-or-above classes (an estimate), with barrio values.
values.Environment · Surface heat (Landsat): 5 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from Landsat 8 and 9 land surface temperature on clear summer mornings (June to September 2024-2026): the median and the hottest tenth of the land's temperature, the share of land among Puerto Rico's hottest tenth and the 2020 residents living there (an estimate), with barrio values.
values.Environment · Vegetation (Sentinel-2): 5 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from Sentinel-2 vegetation greenness (NDVI) on clear summer days (June to September 2024-2026, the window of surface heat): the median NDVI, the share of land with dense vegetation and with little or none, and the 2020 residents living on land with little or none (an estimate), with barrio values.
values.Environment · Night surface heat (ECOSTR: 5 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from NASA ECOSTRESS land surface temperature on clear summer nights (21:00 to 06:00, June to September 2024-2026): the median and the warmest tenth of the land's night temperature, the share of land among Puerto Rico's warmest tenth at night and the 2020 residents living there (an estimate), with barrio values.
values.Environment · Slope of the land (USGS 3D: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10: the share of the land steeper than 15% and than 30%, and the mean slope, from the slope of every 10 m cell of the USGS 3DEP elevation model (Horn's method), with barrio values.
values.Infrastructure · Climb on the walk to a: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, for the residents within a 400 m walk of a stop with a current timetable: the median round-trip climb of their walk, and the residents (share and count) whose walk has a stretch steeper than a ramp may be under the 2010 ADA Standards, from USGS 3DEP heights, with barrio values.
values.Environment · Wetlands: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year: wetland area, wetland share of land and mangrove area (National Wetlands Inventory, almost all mapped from photographs of 1983).
values.Environment · Community resilience: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one value a year from 2019 (no 2020): residents with no, one or two, and three or more disaster risk factors, with margins (Census Community Resilience Estimates).
values.Environment · Earthquakes: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one value a year from 2000: earthquakes of magnitude 2.5 or more and 4.0 or more in or just off each municipio (USGS ComCat).
values.Environment · Regulated sites (EPA): 5 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one snapshot each in its source's vintage: Toxics Release Inventory facilities (reporting year 2024), active Risk Management Plan facilities and Superfund National Priorities List sites (EPA Facility Registry Service), and municipal solid waste landfills, all and still open (EPA LMOP, data of 2024). Also by barrio.
values.Environment · Water and air quality (EPA: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10: the share of the area draining to or in a 303(d)-listed impaired water (EPA ATTAINS, 2024 cycle) and inside a sulfur dioxide or a lead non-attainment area (EPA Green Book). Also by barrio.
values.Land use (PUT 2015): 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): the share of each municipality's land that the 2015 land use plan classifies as urban land and as specially protected rural land.
values.Housing · Prices and incomes: 5 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10: four yearly series and the change in median gross rent since 2008-2012, for a single year.
values.Housing · Public housing: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one snapshot (HUD's layer of 2026-06): public housing developments and their units (HUD).
values.Housing · Tax credit housing: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one snapshot (HUD's LIHTC database, release of 2026-04-30): Low-Income Housing Tax Credit projects, their housing units and their low-income units (HUD).
values.Environment · Fires (NASA FIRMS): 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from NASA FIRMS active fire detections (VIIRS 375 m on NOAA-20): vegetation fire detections each year since 2019 and per 100 km² of land, and in the last 12 months, by municipio.
values.Housing · Buildings (Overture): 7 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from Overture's buildings theme (release 2026-10-21.0; OpenStreetMap, Google and Microsoft footprints): the number of buildings, buildings per km², land under roofs, the median footprint, buildings in a FEMA Special Flood Hazard Area (count and share) and the share traced by machine learning, with barrio values.
values.Housing · Severe housing problems: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10 (HUD CHAS 2016-2020): households with one or more severe housing problems and their share. Also by barrio, as estimates spread from census tracts.
values.Transit access: 6 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): the number of transit stops and stations, and the shares of residents within 400 m in a straight line, and within a 400 m walk along mapped roads, of a stop with a timetable on file and of a stop with a current timetable, and whether Uber lists the municipality (1 or 0).
values.Residents · Transit stops within 400 m: 8 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): residents within 400 m of any mapped stop, of a stop with a timetable on file, of a stop with a current timetable, of a frequent stop (20 or more weekday departures) and of a stop with Saturday or Sunday service, and within a 400 m walk along mapped roads of a stop with a current timetable and of a frequent stop.
values.Housing units · Transit stops within 400: 8 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): housing units within 400 m of any mapped stop, of a stop with a timetable on file, of a stop with a current timetable, of a frequent stop (20 or more weekday departures) and of a stop with Saturday or Sunday service, and within a 400 m walk along mapped roads of a stop with a current timetable and of a frequent stop.
values.Infrastructure · Wastewater: 4 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year: the facilities with their own federal permit to discharge wastewater in each municipality, the public sewage treatment plants and the major dischargers among them, and those with a violation on record (EPA ECHO).
values.Infrastructure · Air pollution sources: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year: the facilities the Clean Air Act regulates for air pollution in each municipality, and the major sources among them (EPA ECHO).
values.Infrastructure · Hazardous waste: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year: the handlers of hazardous waste in each municipality, and the large quantity generators among them (EPA ECHO).
values.Infrastructure · Environmental enforceme: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year: the regulated facilities of each municipality that were inspected, and those that received a formal enforcement action, in the last five years (EPA ECHO).
values.Infrastructure · Toxic chemical releases: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year: the pounds of listed toxic chemicals released by the facilities of each municipality that report to the Toxics Release Inventory, in total and to the air (EPA).
values.Infrastructure · Drinking water: 5 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year: community water systems serving each municipality, those with a health-based violation, those that are an enforcement priority, those outside PRASA (non-PRASA) and the residents those serve (EPA ECHO).
values.Infrastructure · Power plants: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year: operating power plants, generating capacity and renewable generating capacity of each municipality (EIA-860M).
values.Infrastructure · Bridges: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one value a year from 2016: highway bridges, bridges in poor condition and their share (FHWA National Bridge Inventory).
values.Infrastructure · Airports and ferries: 4 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one value a year: air passengers boarding and commercial flights departing from 2014 (BTS T-100), air passengers boarding by FAA's count from 2023, and ferry passengers boarding in 2019, 2022 and 2024 (BTS ferry census).
values.Infrastructure · Street connectivity: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10 (Census TIGER/Line 2026): street intersections and intersections per square mile of land. Also by barrio.
values.Public safety: 4 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10: Type I crimes reported to the Police, violent crimes, property crimes and murders, by calendar year from 2017.
values.Infrastructure · Emergency services: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one snapshot each: fire and EMS stations (USGS National Structures Dataset) and police stations (OpenStreetMap).
values.Infrastructure · Broadband (FCC): 6 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from the FCC Broadband Data Collection (the release as of June 30 of each year 2023-2026): broadband serviceable locations, the shares served at 100/20 Mbps or more, underserved and unserved in NTIA's BEAD terms, the locations below 100/20, and the share where fiber is available; also by barrio.
values.Health care · Health centers: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): the permanent sites and the mobile vans of the health centers that hold a federal grant or a look-alike status, as HRSA lists them.
values.Health care · Primary care shortage area: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): the primary care physicians still needed (full-time equivalents), the share of that need met and HRSA's priority score, for each municipality with an area shortage designation.
values.Health care · Dental shortage areas: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): the dentists still needed (full-time equivalents), the share of that need met and HRSA's priority score, for each municipality with an area shortage designation.
values.Health care · Mental health shortage are: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): the psychiatrists still needed (full-time equivalents), the share of that need met and HRSA's priority score, for each municipality with an area shortage designation.
values.Health care · Hospitals and care facilit: 6 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): Medicare-certified hospitals, hospitals with an emergency department, dialysis facilities, nursing homes, home health agencies and hospice providers in each municipality (CMS Provider Data Catalog).
values.Health care · Distance to a health cente: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026), estimated by the observatory: the average road distance and drive time from where residents live to the nearest health center site, and the share of residents within 10 km by road.
values.Health care · Medicare: 3 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one value a year from 2013 (CMS Medicare Monthly Enrollment): people enrolled in Medicare, the share in Medicare Advantage and the share entitled by disability.
values.Health · Treatment facilities (SAMHSA): 4 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, for 2024 (SAMHSA's 2025 National Directories): substance use and mental health treatment facilities in all and by type of care, counts only.
values.Health care · Distance to a general hosp: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10: the observatory's estimate of the drive time and road distance from where people live to the nearest general hospital with an emergency department (CMS list, OpenStreetMap roads). Also by barrio.
values.Education · Public schools: 5 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one value for each school year from 2010-11 (NCES Common Core of Data, through the Urban Institute's Education Data Portal): public schools open, their students, their teachers (full-time equivalents), students per teacher and schools closed since the year before.
values.Education · Colleges and universities: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one value for each year from 2010 (NCES IPEDS, through the Urban Institute's Education Data Portal): colleges, universities and other postsecondary institutions, and their students in the fall.
values.Education · Libraries: 1 dataset in Snapshot 2026-10, one snapshot: public libraries registered in the E-Rate program (USAC).
values.Communities · Comunidades Especiales: 2 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, one delimitation (2006): how many Comunidades Especiales each municipio has and the housing units the 2006 inventory counted in them (Junta de Planificación).
values.Education · Historic places: 1 dataset in Snapshot 2026-10, one snapshot (NPS edits up to 2026-08-07): places on the National Register of Historic Places (National Park Service).
values.Vulnerability (WCRP) · Original 2022 (AC: 7 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single period and for barrios only (no municipio has a value): the overall index and the six area indices of the WCRP Risk and Vulnerability Indicators as published in 2022 by Hunter College for FPR. In review.
values.Vulnerability (WCRP) · Updated 2020–2024: 7 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single period and for barrios only (no municipio has a value): the same indices updated by the observatory with the WCRP method on ACS 2020–2024 and current local conditions (Updated 2020–2024). In review.
values.Tourism supply: 18 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, each for a single year (2026): five counts of tourism places by kind, then the places in a flood hazard area (as a count and as a share), the places inside a protected area, the places with a website, and nine shares of the places near transit: within 400 m of any mapped stop, of a stop with a current timetable, of a frequent stop and of a stop with Saturday or Sunday service, within a 400 m or 800 m walk, and near only an expired or unscheduled stop.
values.Infrastructure · Traffic (FHWA HPMS): 6 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, data year 2025 of FHWA's Highway Performance Monitoring System: daily vehicle-kilometers, per resident, km of arterials and major collectors, the busiest count, trucks and main roads with rough pavement.
values.Infrastructure · Road safety (NHTSA FARS: 6 datasets in Snapshot 2026-10, from NHTSA's Fatality Analysis Reporting System: people killed, fatal crashes, pedestrians and bicyclists killed and motorcyclists killed each year from 2020, and deaths per 100,000 residents and per 100 million vehicle-km over five years. Counts only.
values.Infrastructure · Energy (LUMA): 4 datasets: home and business batteries, their storage in MWh, electricity sales and the share of customers with smart meters, by municipio (LUMA's monthly metrics filed with the Energy Bureau).
values.Infrastructure · Energy (ACS): 2 datasets: the households paying $250 or more a month for electricity, as a share and a count, by municipio and barrio (ACS 5-year B25132, with margins of error).

layers.economy_inflation.plain: The 'Inflation-adjusted' box on a dollar layer restates every year's dollars in the dollars of the latest index year (2025 in Snapshot 2026-10), so years can be compared. It uses the US consumer price index, because the observatory holds no price index for Puerto Rico.
layers.economy_inflation.plain_es: La casilla "Ajustado por inflación" de una capa en dólares expresa los dólares de cada año en dólares del año índice más reciente (2025 en el corte de datos de 2026-10), para poder comparar los años. Usa el índice de precios al consumidor de Estados Unidos, porque el observatorio no tiene un índice de precios para Puerto Rico.
layers.economy_inflation.definition: The box appears on layers whose unit is dollars. It multiplies each year's value by the index of the latest index year (2025) divided by the index of that year. The index is the annual average of the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U), US city average (1982-84 = 100), which runs from 172.2 in 2000 to 321.943 in 2025 in Snapshot 2026-10. Years before 2010, such as the 2001 to 2009 declaration years of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) datasets, use the index of their own year. For a year outside 2000–2025 the nearest year is used. The legend and the layer title then say '2025 dollars'. The margin of error shown in the inspector is multiplied the same way. With 'Change since the base year', both ends are adjusted. 'Show as' options that divide dollars, such as per resident, work on the adjusted numbers.
layers.economy_inflation.method: economy.js (cpiFactor, ecCalc). The index values come from the deflator list in the economy file.
layers.economy_inflation.how_to_read: Use it to compare a dollar amount across years. It does not change a single year's map. Example: $1,000 in 2015 becomes about $1,358 in 2025 dollars, because 321.943 divided by 237.017 is 1.358. For another worked example see the entry on the inflation adjustment.
caveats: The US index only approximates the prices Puerto Rico residents pay. The page says so.
The tab's note says American Community Survey (ACS) dollars are already in the final year of each five-year window. The adjustment treats that final year as the year of the value.
Dollar amounts as published (not adjusted) are in the dollars of their own year.
layers.economy_inflation.source_detail: economy_series.json, deflator list (CPI-U annual averages 2000 to 2025). The map draws no credit line for this layer.

view.label: 2D map: average pay, 2015, in 2025 dollars

layers.economy_presets.plain: 'Start from a view' offers six ready-made combinations of layers. One click replaces the layers on the map with that set and shows a short message.
layers.economy_presets.plain_es: "Empezar con una vista" ofrece seis combinaciones de capas ya preparadas. Un clic reemplaza las capas del mapa por ese conjunto y muestra un mensaje breve.
layers.economy_presets.definition: The six views are listed below with the layers each sets. A view replaces all economy layers with its own, each at its start settings (classes of equal counts, 'Same classes in every year' on). It also sets the other map layers, so that the view is not buried under pins. It keeps on only the layer it names (tourism places or transit routes). It turns off tourism places, transit routes, transit stops, barrios, flood zones, protected areas and land use otherwise. The municipality outlines stay as they are. The year and the base year do not change.
layers.economy_presets.how_to_read: Use a view as a starting point, then open each layer's settings to adjust it.
caveats: A view is a combination of layers. It is not a finding.
The Public money view shows federal amounts obligated (committed). They are not money paid, damage or need. See the codes below.

values.Jobs and pay: Shaded: average pay (qcew_avg_pay). Symbols: jobs (qcew_jobs). No extra layers.
values.Poverty and unemployment: Two shaded layers, so a bivariate map: poverty rate (poverty_pct) and unemployment rate (laus_unemp_rate). Symbols: unemployed residents (laus_unemployed).
values.Job centers and commuting: Two shaded layers, so a bivariate map: jobs per employed resident (jobs_per_employed_resident) and commuters with 45 minutes or more (commute_45plus_pct). Symbols: jobs (qcew_jobs). Also shows transit routes.
values.Public money: Shaded: federal awards per resident (fed_awards_total, 'perCapita'). Symbols: Public Assistance of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), amounts obligated (fema_pa_obligated). These are federal amounts obligated (committed). They are not money paid, not damage and not need. In the 2026-10 snapshot, over all years combined, 77.9% of FEMA Public Assistance money is recorded as statewide and is not in the municipality values (80.9% for the 2017 declarations, 13.1% for 2024, the year this view shows on Latest). Awards that serve the whole island are often booked to the capital.
values.Government and self-employment: Two shaded layers, so a bivariate map: government jobs as a share of all jobs (gov_job_share_pct) and self-employed workers (self_employed_pct).
values.Tourism economy: Shaded: tourism jobs as a share of the municipality's jobs (tourism_jobs, 'shareJobs'). Symbols: accommodation jobs (accommodation_jobs). Also shows the tourism places pins.

view.label: 2D map: Analysis tab, 'Poverty and unemployment' set by hand

layers.economy_shaded.plain: A shaded layer colors each municipality by one dataset. The Analysis tab allows two shaded layers at a time. Colors run from light to dark in five groups.
layers.economy_shaded.plain_es: Una capa sombreada colorea cada municipio según un conjunto de datos. La pestaña Análisis permite dos capas sombreadas a la vez. Los colores van de claro a oscuro en cinco grupos.
layers.economy_shaded.definition: A third shaded layer is refused with a message that says to remove one or to show the new dataset as symbols. Open 'Settings' on a layer's card to change its options. The class limits are set from the values of the 78 municipalities, not from the Puerto Rico figure. With 'Same classes in every year' on, which is the start setting, the limits use the values of all years together, so one color means the same number in every year. Turn it off to use only the year on screen. The legend lists the range of each class and how many municipalities fall in it. A municipality with no value is gray (#EDEDED), and the legend counts it as 'No data'. The settings are listed below.
layers.economy_shaded.method: economy.js (ecAdd, ecBreaks, ecClass, ecRenderMap, ecRenderLegend). Natural breaks use the Jenks method, which groups values to keep each class as uniform as possible. When more than 1,500 values are pooled, every n-th value is used. The sheet is a copy of the municipality outlines in its own map pane.
layers.economy_shaded.how_to_read: With 'Same classes in every year' on (the start setting) a color is a class among all municipalities in all years pooled, so one year can have uneven group sizes. Read the legend counts for the numbers. On the diverging scale red means below the center (below Puerto Rico, or below zero change) and blue means above. Neither means better or worse: a red unemployment rate is a lower rate.
caveats: With 'Same classes in every year' on, some colors may not appear in a year whose values cover a narrower range.
Equal intervals can put most municipalities in one class when one or two are very large.
Shading rates and levels suits comparison between places. Shading a raw count mostly shows how big the municipality is.

values.Show as: Described in the entry on the 'Show as' options.
values.Classes: Quantiles with equal counts, Equal intervals or Natural breaks.
values.Colours: Blue, Green, Gold, Red or Gray. Each ramp has five colors.
values.Opacity: From 20% to 100%. It starts at 85%. The opacity of the first shaded layer sets the opacity of the sheet.
values.Same classes in every year: A checkbox, on at the start.
values.Diverging scale: Options that compare with a center (index, difference, location quotient and change) use a diverging scale of five classes: dark red, light red, pale gray, light blue and dark blue. The limits are set as shares of the largest distance from the center: below −50%, −50% to −10%, within ±10%, +10% to +50% and above +50%. Red means below the center and blue means above. Neither means worse or better.
values.Layer card buttons: Hide, move up or down, open information and remove the layer.

layers.economy_shaded.source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json. Each dataset's source reference is in its information window. The map draws no credit line for this layer.

view.label: 2D map: shaded poverty rate, 2022

layers.economy_symbols.plain: A symbol layer draws a circle on each municipality. The circle's area shows the value, so big circles are big amounts. Symbols suit counts and totals such as jobs or dollars.
layers.economy_symbols.plain_es: Una capa de símbolos dibuja un círculo en cada municipio. El área del círculo muestra el valor, así que los círculos grandes son cantidades grandes. Los símbolos sirven para conteos y totales, como empleos o dólares.
layers.economy_symbols.definition: Each circle is centered on the municipality's center. The circle for the largest value has a radius of 30 pixels (20 on a phone). Other radii shrink with the square root of the value, so the area is proportional to the value, down to a minimum of 2.5 pixels. Larger circles are drawn first so small ones stay visible. The largest value is taken over all years when 'Same classes in every year' is on, and over the year on screen otherwise. Colors: Red, Blue, Gold, Green or Charcoal. If a dataset can be negative, for example a change since the base year, increases are blue and decreases red. The legend shows three circles at the largest value, at half of it and at a tenth of it. No circle is drawn for Puerto Rico as a whole or for a municipality with no value. The center is the area-weighted center of the municipality's largest part, so islands do not pull the point into the sea.
layers.economy_symbols.method: economy.js (ecRenderMap, ecRenderLegend). Circles are Leaflet circle markers in their own map pane. They do not take clicks.
layers.economy_symbols.how_to_read: Compare circle sizes between municipalities in the same layer. Do not compare sizes between two different layers.
caveats: The center of a long or crescent-shaped municipality can fall away from its towns.
Circles overlap in the San Juan area and may hide each other.
layers.economy_symbols.source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json. Each dataset's source reference is in its information window. The map draws no credit line for this layer.

view.label: 2D map: jobs as symbols, 2024

layers.economy_normalisation.plain: Each layer has a 'Show as' menu. It changes the number behind the color or circle. Choices include as published, per resident, per km², share, index, change and percentile.
layers.economy_normalisation.plain_es: Cada capa tiene un menú "Mostrar como". Cambia el número que hay detrás del color o del círculo. Las opciones incluyen tal como se publicó, por residente, por km², proporción, índice, cambio y percentil.
layers.economy_normalisation.definition: The options depend on the kind of dataset. Counts (people, jobs, places) can be shown as published, per 1,000 residents, per km² and as a share of the Puerto Rico total. The jobs datasets (25 in Snapshot 2026-10) can also be shown as a share of the municipality's jobs and as a location quotient. Dollar totals (wages, federal money, recovery money of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, FEMA) can be shown as published, per resident, per km² and, except for federal loans, as a share of the Puerto Rico total. Everything else (rates, ratios and dollar levels such as median income) can be shown as published, as an index or as a difference from Puerto Rico. Every dataset with more than one year also offers 'change since the base year', and every dataset offers 'percentile among municipalities'. The codes below are the ones written in a shared link.
layers.economy_normalisation.method: economy.js (ecNormOptions, ecOut, ecCalc). Land area is the land_km2 field of municipalities.json. Population is the population series. Jobs are the jobs series of the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages (QCEW).
layers.economy_normalisation.how_to_read: Choose the option that answers your question. 'Per 1,000 residents' compares places of different size. 'Index' and 'difference' compare with the island.
caveats: 'Per 1,000 residents' divides by residents, not by workers. Jobs are counted at the workplace, so places that draw commuters show high values.
A location quotient above 1 says an industry is concentrated. It does not say the industry is large.

For the five tourism-place counts the Analysis tab divides by the latest population estimate (2025 in Snapshot 2026-10), but the Map layers tab, the Rankings tab and the municipality table divide by the 2020 Census count. The two views can differ (San Juan: 10.4 and 10.0 places per 1,000 residents in Snapshot 2026-10).

values.value: As published. The dataset's own number in its own unit. Offered for every dataset. The start choice for symbols and for rates, ratios and dollar levels.
values.per1000: Per 1,000 residents. The count divided by the municipality's population, times 1,000, rounded to three decimals. Counts only. The start choice when a count is shaded. Population is the value of the population series for the year shown, or for the latest earlier year, or for its first year when the year shown is earlier. The population series changes basis in 2020 (the 2011-2019 estimates were not revised to the 2020 Census), so in Snapshot 2026-10 the island's population steps up 2.9% from 2019 to 2020 (3.1% for the median municipality), and per-resident values drop by about 3% for that reason alone. Changes that cross 2019 to 2020 include the same jump.
values.perkm2: Per km². The value divided by the municipality's land area in square kilometers. Counts and dollar totals.
values.sharePR: % of the Puerto Rico total. The value divided by the dataset's Puerto Rico figure, times 100. Counts and dollar totals. It is not offered for federal loans. Shares can add up to less than 100% when the island figure holds amounts that belong to no municipality, for example FEMA Public Assistance recorded as statewide, federal awards that name no municipality, or jobs hidden in withheld cells.
values.shareJobs: % of the municipality's jobs. Jobs in an industry divided by all jobs in the same municipality (QCEW), times 100. Only the jobs datasets (25 in Snapshot 2026-10), from 2014.
values.lq: Location quotient (Puerto Rico = 1). The industry's share of the municipality's jobs divided by its share of Puerto Rico's jobs. Above 1 means the industry is more concentrated here than on the island as a whole. Only the jobs datasets. Diverging scale centered on 1.
values.perCapita: $ per resident. The dollar total divided by the municipality's population. Dollar totals only. The start choice when a dollar total is shaded. The same break in the population series in 2020 applies. For FEMA Public Assistance and for federal awards the Puerto Rico per-resident value includes money recorded as statewide or naming no municipality, so it is not comparable with a municipality's value.
values.index: Index (Puerto Rico = 100). The value divided by the Puerto Rico value, times 100. Rates, ratios and dollar levels. Diverging scale centered on 100.
values.diff: Difference from Puerto Rico. The value minus the Puerto Rico value, in the dataset's unit (percentage points for percentages). Rates, ratios and dollar levels. Diverging scale centered on 0.
values.change: Change since the base year. For rates and ratios, the value minus the value in the base year (points for percentages). For counts and dollars, the percent change from the base year, blank where the base value is 0. The base year is chosen in 'Change measured from' (2014 at the start). The dataset's latest year at or before it is used. Blank for years up to the base year. Not offered for the five tourism snapshots. Diverging scale centered on 0. Windows of the American Community Survey (ACS) that overlap share most of their sample, so choose a base year at least five years before the year shown.
values.pctile: Percentile among municipalities. The place of the municipality among the 78 when they are sorted from the lowest value (0) to the highest (100). Municipalities with equal values share the lowest of their places. Puerto Rico as a whole has none.

layers.economy_normalisation.source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json for the datasets, with land area and the tourism counts from municipalities.json. The map draws no credit line for this layer.

view.label: 2D map: tourism jobs as a share of all jobs, 2024

layers.economy_bivariate.plain: When two shaded layers are on, the map shows both at once with nine colors. Each layer is cut into three classes: low, middle and high.
layers.economy_bivariate.plain_es: Cuando hay dos capas sombreadas activadas, el mapa muestra ambas a la vez con nueve colores. Cada capa se divide en tres clases: baja, media y alta.
layers.economy_bivariate.definition: The first visible shaded layer in the list is the horizontal axis of the legend, which increases to the right. The second is the vertical axis, which increases upward. Each layer is cut into three classes, using the class method set on its card: equal counts (terciles), equal intervals or natural breaks. The nine colors run from light gray (low on both), through teal (high on the first only) and magenta (high on the second only), to dark blue (high on both). The legend shows the three-by-three grid and, for each axis, the layer, its year, and the limits of 'low' and 'high'. The legend title says 'terciles of each' only when both layers use equal-count classes. Otherwise it says 'three classes of each'. A municipality with no value in either layer is gray (#EDEDED). In this mode the diverging scale is not used: every layer is cut into three classes.
layers.economy_bivariate.method: economy.js (ecRenderMap, ecRenderLegend, EC_BIV). The color table is indexed by the class of the second layer and then by the class of the first.
layers.economy_bivariate.how_to_read: Find the dark cells (both high) and the pale ones (both low). Colors that mix show where the two layers disagree.
caveats: The map shows where two things are high or low together. It does not show that one causes the other.
The three classes are relative to the 78 municipalities (all years pooled when 'Same classes in every year' is on). They are not thresholds of any standard.
The two layers may show different years. The legend names each layer's year, so read it before you compare.
layers.economy_bivariate.source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json. Each dataset's source reference is in its information window. The map draws no credit line for this layer.

view.label: 2D map: poverty rate and unemployment rate together, 2022

layers.economy_year_control.plain: One year control moves every layer on the Analysis tab. Choose 'Latest' or a year (2010 to 2025 in Snapshot 2026-10), step with the arrows, drag the slider or press Play to watch the years go by.
layers.economy_year_control.plain_es: Un solo control de año mueve todas las capas de la pestaña Análisis. Elija "Último" o un año (de 2010 a 2025 en el corte de datos de 2026-10), avance con las flechas, arrastre el control deslizante u oprima "Reproducir" para ver pasar los años.
