Stops without the note are unknown or not stated, not inaccessible. In Snapshot 2026-10, none of the 1,400 ATI scheduled stops carries the note. In the feed standard, value 1 means that some vehicles can be boarded, not all. The note is not an accessibility audit.
The card compares the timetable end date with the date on your device. For a stop of an operator whose timetable has ended, it still shows the departures that the old timetable lists.

The weekend line shows what the published timetable lists. Many feeds list no weekend departures at all (in the 2026-10 snapshot only 3 of the 18 current feeds list Saturday departures and 1 lists Sunday departures), so 'none listed' often means that the feed does not cover weekends, not that there is no service.
layers.transit_stops_control.source_detail: transport.json (kinds transit_stop and bus_stop). Credit line on the map: 'Stops: ATI GTFS · © OpenStreetMap contributors'.

view.label: 2D map, Map layers tab: Transit stops (zoom in to see points)
3D view, Layers tab: switch on Transit stops (Santurce, San Juan)

municipalities.profile_ranking_download.plain: The Municipality tab, the Rankings tab and the comma-separated values (CSV) download show the municipality statistics in different ways. Some Municipality tab numbers follow your map filters; the Rankings tab and the CSV do not.
municipalities.profile_ranking_download.plain_es: La pestaña "Municipio", la pestaña "Posiciones" y la descarga en CSV (valores separados por comas) muestran las estadísticas de los municipios de formas distintas. Algunas cifras de la pestaña "Municipio" siguen los filtros del mapa; la pestaña "Posiciones" y el CSV no.
municipalities.profile_ranking_download.definition: Municipality tab: the header shows the region, 'residents (Census 2020)' and land area rounded to whole km². The tiles 'tourism places (current filters)', 'in flood hazard area', 'inside protected areas' and 'with a website' are counted live from the places the map is showing, so they follow the category chips, the confidence slider and the worship toggle. The tiles 'places per 1,000 residents' and 'places per km²' show the stored values, which use the default filters. The 'By category' bars and the 'Top types' chips are also live and do not read by_category. The rank note ('#n of 78 by tourism places', '#n by share in flood hazard area') uses the stored assets and sfha_pct and states that ranks use the default filters. Rankings tab: the table lists the stored value of the chosen statistic for every municipality that has one, highest first, with a second column holding assets (except when ranking by tourism places itself); a click on the column heading reverses the order. CSV (comma-separated values): the button 'Download municipality table (CSV)' on the Rankings tab writes one row per municipality with every field of municipalities.json.
municipalities.profile_ranking_download.method: Functions renderMuni, renderRank and downloadCsv in site/js/app.js. In the CSV the object by_category is split into four columns named by_category_ATTRACTIONS, by_category_GASTRONOMY, by_category_ACCOMMODATIONS and by_category_VISITOR_SERVICES (landuse_km2 is split the same way). The file is UTF-8 with a byte-order mark, so Excel shows the accents, and it is named pr_digital_twin_municipalities_ followed by the snapshot label, for example pr_digital_twin_municipalities_Snapshot_2026-10.csv. Rankings options for the fields in this file: Tourism places, % of places in flood hazard area, Places in flood hazard area, Places per 1,000 residents, Places per km², Places inside protected areas, Places with a website and Population 2020.
municipalities.profile_ranking_download.how_to_read: To cite or analyze numbers, use the stored values in the CSV download or in municipalities.json. Numbers read from the Municipality tab tiles can differ from them when you have changed a filter.
caveats: A separate button on the Municipality tab, 'Download <municipality> places (CSV)', exports the places the map is showing, not these statistics.
The CSV holds every field of municipalities.json, including fields documented in other entries.

The Rankings tab rounds the numbers it shows (see the entry 'Rankings tab' for the decimals of each measure). The order uses the unrounded value, so two rows can show the same number. Use the CSV for exact values.
municipalities.profile_ranking_download.source_detail: Inputs are the fields of municipalities.json documented in the municipalities.* entries.

view.label: Map, Municipality tab
Map, Rankings tab

layers.municipality_profile.plain: The Municipality tab is a one-page profile of one municipality: tourism places, flood and protected-area exposure, transit access, housing and land use. Click a municipality on the map, or pick one in the search box or the Rankings tab.
layers.municipality_profile.plain_es: La pestaña Municipio es un perfil de una página sobre un municipio: lugares turísticos, exposición a inundaciones y a áreas protegidas, acceso al transporte colectivo, vivienda y uso de terrenos. Haga clic en un municipio en el mapa, o elíjalo en el buscador o en la pestaña Posiciones.
layers.municipality_profile.definition: The tab opens when you click a municipality on the map, pick one in the search box or the Rankings tab, or follow a link such as index.html#San%20Juan. The first block is headed 'Visitor economy'. Once the tourism place listings are loaded, its tiles are counted from the places the map is showing, so they follow the category buttons, the confidence slider and the worship switch. Before that (the listings are not part of the first load) the tiles show the figures stored for the default filters, a line says so and offers a button 'Load the place listings', and the top types and the list of places in a flood hazard area wait for the listings. Places per 1,000 residents and per square kilometer are the stored values, which use the default filters. The rank line uses the stored values too. The housing section is headed 'ACS 2024', the 2020-2024 window of the American Community Survey (ACS). The parts of the tab are listed below.
layers.municipality_profile.method: app.js (selectMuni, renderMuni). The rank line uses the stored assets and sfha_pct fields.
layers.municipality_profile.how_to_read: Compare a tile with the same tile for other municipalities, not with a target. Read the housing figures as survey estimates.
caveats: Tiles that follow the filters can differ from the stored statistics when you change a filter. The rank line ignores your filters and says so.
The housing tiles are survey estimates. Their margins of error are large in small municipalities, and this tab does not show them. The Housing page does.
The Uber chip is a yes or no from Uber's own cities page. It does not show that a driver is nearby.

In Snapshot 2026-10, the airport chip counts as public only the 10 airports of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) that are marked public use. The card on the stations layer says 'Public use' for 21 airports: those 10 and 11 airports from OpenStreetMap that carry no flag. See the entry on the stations layer.

Without the place listings the tiles show the stored figures for the default filters (confidence 0.50 or higher, no places of worship). In Snapshot 2026-10 they agree with the tiles counted from the listings for every municipality.

values.Header: The municipality's name, its tourism region, its residents (2020 Census) and its land area in square kilometers.
values.Tourism tiles: Tourism places, the share in a flood hazard area, places per 1,000 residents, places per square kilometer, places inside protected areas and places with a website.
values.Mobility tiles: There are up to five mobility tiles. The first two are shares of the places shown and appear when the access file has loaded: places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable, and places with frequent service (20+ weekday departures). The third is the share of the places shown within 400 m of any mapped stop. The first three tiles show a dash when the municipality has no stop counted. The fourth is the number of stops and stations. The fifth is the share of residents within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable (the share for any scheduled stop, expired timetables included, if the field is missing). A line under the tiles gives the stops by state: 'Stops: N with a current timetable · N with an expired timetable · N mapped by volunteers (no timetable)'.
values.Tile colors: Three tiles change color. The flood tile warns when more than 25% of the places shown are in a flood hazard area. The residents-served tile warns when fewer than 25% of residents live within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable. The affordability tile warns when the ratio, rounded to two decimals, is above 1, and is green otherwise. These are the observatory's own signals, not standards. The tile for places inside protected areas is always green.
values.Chips: Tren Urbano stations, bus stations, ferry terminals, airports (with the number open to the public), scheduled stops, taxi stands, electric vehicle (EV) charging points, the state of the municipal bus schedule, and whether Uber lists the municipality.
values.Rank line: The rank among the 78 by tourism places and by share in a flood hazard area, with the default filters. It ignores your filters and says so.
values.Housing section: Headed 'ACS 2024'. It shows the affordability ratio, the median home value and rent, the share of renters who are cost-burdened and the share of seasonal or recreational units.
values.Land use line: The shares of land that are urban, urbanizable and especially protected (Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015), with a link to the full profile on the Housing page.
values.Lists and buttons: Bars by category, the eight most common place types, and a list of up to 60 places inside a flood hazard area (click a row to fly to the place). Two buttons download the shown places as a comma-separated values (CSV) file and zoom to the municipality.

view.label: 2D map: Municipality tab for Ponce

layers.rankings_tab.plain: The Rankings tab lists the 78 municipalities in order of one measure, highest first. Pick the measure from the menu, reverse the order with a click, and download the whole municipality table as a comma-separated values (CSV) file.
layers.rankings_tab.plain_es: La pestaña Posiciones ordena los 78 municipios según una medida, de mayor a menor. Elija la medida en el menú, invierta el orden con un clic y descargue la tabla completa de municipios como archivo CSV (valores separados por comas).
layers.rankings_tab.definition: The menu 'Rank municipalities by' has 26 options, listed below with the field they read. It starts on 'Tourism places'. The table has the rank, the municipality and the value, and a second column with the number of tourism places (not shown when you rank by tourism places). Only municipalities with a value are listed. A click on the column title reverses the order, and the arrow shows the direction. A click on a row selects the municipality and opens the Municipality tab. Numbers are rounded: whole numbers for counts and most percentages, one decimal for places per 1,000 residents, places per square kilometer and the seasonal share, and two decimals for the affordability ratio. The button 'Download municipality table (CSV)' saves one row per municipality.
layers.rankings_tab.method: app.js (renderRank, downloadCsv). The table is built from the stored statistics, so it does not follow the category buttons, the confidence slider or the worship switch.
layers.rankings_tab.how_to_read: Rank 1 is the highest value, not the best result. Compare ranks only within one measure.
caveats: Tied values get consecutive ranks. Their order follows the order of the municipalities in the data file.

In Snapshot 2026-10, 14 municipalities have no stop counted inside their border. They are left out of the ranking by the share of places within 400 m of any mapped stop and by the five access shares (a stop with a current timetable, a frequent stop, Saturday service, Sunday service and only an expired or unscheduled stop).
The table rounds. For citation, use the stored values in the download.
A percentage of places can swing widely where a municipality has few places. In Snapshot 2026-10 the smallest has 36, so one place is 2.8 points. Check the count of places before you compare shares.

Transit stops and stations counts every mapped stop, station and terminal, including OpenStreetMap stops and stops of expired timetables. It reflects mapping and stop density, not how often vehicles run.

The rent change is not adjusted for inflation. In Snapshot 2026-10, 76 municipalities have a rise, and 52 of them rose by less than US consumer prices (36.6% from 2012 to 2024), so by that measure they had a fall in real terms.

values.assets: Tourism places. Count of places in Snapshot 2026-10 (confidence 0.50 or more, no places of worship).
values.sfha_pct: % of places in flood hazard area.
values.in_protected: Places inside protected areas. Count of places.
values.with_website: Places with a website. Count of places.
values.acc_cur400_pct: % of places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable. The nearest stop with a published timetable (ATI, the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, or a municipal system, in a feed that has not ended) is 400 m or less away in a straight line. Municipalities with no stop counted are not ranked.
values.acc_freq400_pct: % of places within 400 m of a frequent stop (20+ weekday departures). A stop with a current timetable and 20 or more departures on a typical weekday is 400 m or less away. Municipalities with no stop counted are not ranked.
values.acc_sat400_pct: % of places within 400 m of a stop with Saturday service. A stop with a current timetable and at least one Saturday departure in the published timetable is 400 m or less away. Municipalities with no stop counted are not ranked.
values.acc_sun400_pct: % of places within 400 m of a stop with Sunday service. A stop with a current timetable and at least one Sunday departure in the published timetable is 400 m or less away. Municipalities with no stop counted are not ranked.
values.acc_paper_pct: % of places near only an expired or unscheduled stop. A mapped stop is 400 m or less away but none with a current timetable: its timetable has ended, or volunteers mapped it and there is none. Municipalities with no stop counted are not ranked.
values.transit_pct: % of places within 400 m of any mapped stop. Municipalities with no stop counted are not ranked.
values.transit_stops: Transit stops and stations. Count of scheduled stops, OpenStreetMap bus stops, bus stations, Tren Urbano stations and ferry terminals inside the municipality. Airports, taxi stands and electric vehicle chargers are not counted.
values.affordability_ratio: Housing: affordability ratio. Median home value divided by the largest 30-year loan a household with the median income can carry (30% of income for housing, 78% of that for principal and interest, 5% rate). American Community Survey (ACS) 2020-2024. Above 1 means out of reach.
values.median_home_value: Housing: median home value, in dollars, ACS 2020-2024.
values.median_gross_rent: Housing: median gross rent, in dollars a month, ACS 2020-2024.
values.renter_cost_burden_pct: Housing: share of renter households that pay 30% or more of income on rent, ACS 2020-2024.
values.vacancy_pct: Housing: share of housing units that are vacant, ACS 2020-2024.
values.seasonal_pct: Housing: share of housing units that are vacant seasonal, recreational or occasional-use units, ACS 2020-2024.
values.gross_rent_change_pct: Housing: change in median gross rent from the 2008-2012 window to the 2020-2024 window, in percent. It is not adjusted for inflation: US consumer prices rose 36.6% from 2012 to 2024. In Snapshot 2026-10, 54 of the 78 municipalities changed by less than that (2 of them fell).
values.urban_pct: Land use: % Suelo Urbano, Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015.
values.protected_land_pct: Land use: % Suelo Rústico Especialmente Protegido, Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015.
values.pop_served_active_pct: Transit: share of residents (2020 Census blocks) within 400 m of a scheduled stop with a current timetable, in Snapshot 2026-10.
values.pop_served_pct: Transit: share of residents (2020 Census blocks) within 400 m of a scheduled stop, expired timetables included, in Snapshot 2026-10.

view.label: 2D map: Rankings tab (open the tab after the page loads)

layers.catalog_tab.plain: The Catalog tab searches everything the dictionary documents and puts it on the map with one button. You can filter by field, geography, year covered, license of the sources and source.
layers.catalog_tab.plain_es: La pestaña Catálogo busca todo lo que documenta el diccionario y lo pone en el mapa con un botón. Se puede filtrar por área, geografía, años cubiertos, licencia de las fuentes y fuente.
layers.catalog_tab.definition: The tab lists the dictionary's entries, 40 at a time. At first it lists only what can go on the map: a yearly series (it joins the Analysis tab), a measure held for each municipality (it shades the municipalities) or a layer (it is switched on). Clear 'Only what can go on the map' to list every entry, methods and categories included. The search box matches the name, the identifier and the field of an entry; on a Spanish page it also matches the Spanish name, where the entry has one, and the words of the entry's Spanish summary. The filters are Domain (the fields and sub-fields of the registry), Geography (the level of the published file an entry describes), Covers year, License of the sources (strictest) and Source. Each row shows the name, the field, the years, the geography and the license class, an 'Add to map' button when the entry can go on the map, and a link to its dictionary entry. 'Open these in the data dictionary' opens the dictionary with the same search and field.
layers.catalog_tab.method: catalog.js (rows, results, rowHtml, apply) reads the index of the dictionary in catalog_index.json, which it fetches the first time the tab opens, with the Spanish names of the entries (site/i18n/es.map.catalog.js) and, on a Spanish page, the words of the Spanish summaries (catalog_es.json). How an entry goes on the map is worked out when the catalog is built (catalog.py map_action): from where the entry says its data live (a yearly series, a field of municipalities.json) or, for a layer, from the list in dictionary_src/map_layers.json. It is checked again in the page: the button appears only when the page knows the target and the menu offers it.
layers.catalog_tab.how_to_read: Use it to find a dataset by topic, then open its dictionary entry before you rely on it. The geography, the years and the license class are there to help you choose, not to replace the entry.
caveats: In Spanish most names of the data stay in English for now; the search also finds an entry by the words of its Spanish summary.

The license is the strictest class among the entry's sources, as recorded in the sources list. It is not a legal review, and it can be strict for an entry that only cites a study. Open the entry to see which source sets it.
An entry with no file or layer link has no 'Add to map' button, although it may be documented.
Adding a layer to the map does not remove the layers already on it. Switch layers off in the Map layers tab or the Analysis tab.

view.label: 2D map, Catalog tab

layers.overview_tab.plain: The Topics tab is what the 2D map shows first. It has one card for each field of the observatory, with a headline figure for the whole island, a small trend line when the figure has a history, and a button that puts its data on the map. Only the municipal boundaries are on the map at the start.
layers.overview_tab.plain_es: La pestaña Temas es lo primero que muestra el mapa 2D. Tiene una tarjeta por cada área del observatorio, con una cifra principal para toda la isla, una pequeña línea de tendencia cuando la cifra tiene historial y un botón que pone sus datos en el mapa. Al inicio, el mapa solo muestra los límites municipales.
layers.overview_tab.definition: The cards come from the domain registry through catalog.json, so a new field appears with no change to the page. A card has the field's name and description in the page language, a status ('Some data' or 'No data yet') when the field is not fully covered, and one block for the field's headline figure and one for each sub-field that has its own. A block has the name of the figure, its value, the period it covers ('Puerto Rico · 2020–2024, five-year estimate') and, for a yearly series, a trend line of the Puerto Rico value for every year. 'Show on map' puts the figure's data on the map: a yearly series is added to the Analysis tab, and a measure held for each municipality joins it too, as a dataset; both are listed in the On the map panel. 'What it means' opens the dictionary entry of the figure. 'Browse N documented items' opens the Catalog tab for the field. A field with no data yet says so. A field with datasets on the wish list gives their number and a button 'What is planned', which lists them: title, status (candidate, checked, building or blocked) and source, read from wanted.json when the button is pressed (about 21 KB compressed). The titles are in English for now. The tab ends with buttons for the Catalog tab and the chat, and a note on what the figures are.
layers.overview_tab.method: catalog.js (renderOverview, cardHtml, metricHtml, spark, apply) reads S.catalog, which app.js fetches at the start from data/catalog.json (the index of the dictionary is in catalog_index.json, which loads when the Catalog tab first opens), and data/wanted.json for the planned datasets. How each figure is worked out: methods.headline_figures.
layers.overview_tab.how_to_read: Read each figure as the number for the whole of Puerto Rico over the period shown. It is not a score, and the fields are not ranked against one another. Press 'What it means' before you quote a figure: tourism figures count listings, and an estimate has a margin of error.
caveats: The names of the figures are in Spanish and English; the long text of the dictionary entries behind 'What it means' is English for now.
The trend line shows the Puerto Rico value for each year the series has. It starts at the lowest value of its own range, so two lines should not be compared by height.
'Show on map' for a yearly series opens the Analysis tab, which loads its data the first time (about 0.4 MB compressed).

view.label: 2D map, Topics tab

layers.integration_points_control.plain: 'Integration points' marks the places where a stop of one transit system lies within 250 meters of a stop of another system. These are natural places to line up timetables, fares and signs.
layers.integration_points_control.plain_es: "Puntos de integración" marca los lugares donde una parada de un sistema de transporte colectivo queda a 250 metros o menos de una parada de otro sistema. Son lugares naturales para coordinar horarios, tarifas y rótulos.
layers.integration_points_control.definition: The switch is off when the page opens. Each point is a white circle with a blue outline, placed midway between the two stops. There are 366 in Snapshot 2026-10, and all are drawn. Pointing at a point names the two operators, the two stops and the distance between them. A note under the switch gives the number found and, when some are left out, says how many are drawn. The 3D view has the same switch in its Route tab, under Planning layers; there a click on a point gives what pointing at it gives on the 2D map.
layers.integration_points_control.method: network.js (setXfer) and twin3d.js (setXfer) draw the transfers list of operators.json.
layers.integration_points_control.how_to_read: A short distance means two systems have stops at almost the same place.
caveats: A pair shows that stops are close. It does not show that riders can transfer: the observatory does not compare timetables, walking routes or fares.
Stops of expired timetables are included.
layers.integration_points_control.source_detail: operators.json, list transfers (366 pairs in Snapshot 2026-10). The points carry no credit line of their own.

view.label: 2D map: Integration points
3D view, Route tab: switch on Integration points

layers.service_gaps_control.plain: 'Residents far from service' draws a circle for each census block with at least 40 residents whose nearest scheduled stop is more than 800 meters away. Bigger circles mean more residents.
layers.service_gaps_control.plain_es: "Residentes lejos del servicio" dibuja un círculo por cada bloque censal con al menos 40 residentes cuya parada con horario más cercana queda a más de 800 metros. Los círculos más grandes indican más residentes.
layers.service_gaps_control.definition: The switch is off when the page opens. The layer has 14,405 circles in Snapshot 2026-10 (distances walked along mapped roads). Circle radius grows with the square root of the residents, from about 5 pixels at 40 residents to at most 14 pixels. Pointing at a circle gives its residents and its distance to the nearest scheduled stop. A note under the switch says how many residents live more than an 800 m walk from any scheduled stop (2,251,110 in Snapshot 2026-10, about 69%) and that circles show blocks with 40 or more residents. The note counts blocks of every size. The circles show only the larger ones. The 3D view has the same switch in its Route tab, under Planning layers, with the same circles and note; there a click on a circle gives what pointing at it gives on the 2D map.
layers.service_gaps_control.method: network.js (setGaps) and twin3d.js (setGaps). Both filter the rows of population_blocks.json in your browser: distance above 800 and residents of 40 or more.
layers.service_gaps_control.how_to_read: Large circles in low-service areas mean many residents far from a scheduled stop.
caveats: Stops from expired timetables still count as stops, so a gap can be larger than shown. Públicos, systems with no published timetable and stops mapped only in OpenStreetMap are not counted, so a gap can also be smaller.
Distances are straight lines and counts are from 2020. It is a planning aid, not a demand forecast.
layers.service_gaps_control.source_detail: population_blocks.json, Snapshot 2026-10: 36,570 rows of 2020 Census blocks, each with longitude, latitude, residents and meters to the nearest scheduled stop. The circles carry no credit line of their own.

view.label: 2D map: Residents far from service
3D view, Route tab: switch on Residents far from service

layers.route_planner.plain: The route planner draws a route between places you name or click, along roads, and then counts the residents and places it would reach. It is on the Transit tab of the 2D map and on the Route tab of the 3D view.
layers.route_planner.plain_es: El planificador de rutas traza una ruta por las carreteras entre lugares que se escriben o se marcan con un clic, y luego cuenta las personas residentes y los lugares a los que llegaría. Está en la pestaña Transporte del mapa 2D y en la pestaña "Ruta" de la vista 3D.
layers.route_planner.definition: The planner draws a route between up to eight points and scores it against the open data. Drag a lettered marker to move a point. The route follows roads unless you switch 'Follow roads' off. The card shows the length and an indicative running time, then what the route would reach. The parts are listed below. The chosen points are kept in the page address as r=lat,lng;lat,lng, to 4 decimals (about 11 meters).
layers.route_planner.method: plan.js is shared by both pages. It matches names against the place-name index (gazetteer.json), routes along the roads with roads.js on roads.bin, and scores the route against the open data. The 2D map draws the route with network.js. The 3D view draws it with twin3d.js. Everything runs in the browser.
layers.route_planner.how_to_read: Use it to compare options. Read each number on the card with its own entry.
caveats: It is a planning aid. It is not an engineering study or a demand forecast.

The running time uses planning speeds without stops or traffic. When some legs cannot follow roads (for example between islands), the length and the time still include them, as straight lines timed at 8 m/s (28.8 km/h).
The place boxes can offer an online address lookup. That sends the text you typed to OpenStreetMap Nominatim. See the search entry.
The GeoJSON file carries the licenses of its inputs. Check each before you publish it.

The address holds the exact coordinates of every point, to about 11 meters. If a start, end or stop is your home or workplace, anyone with the link can see it. Remove the r= part before you share a link, or use points that are not private.

Tourism places within 400 m of the route are counted only when the tourism place listings are loaded (switch on 'Tourism places' in the Map layers tab, then plan again). Otherwise that tile shows a dash and says so; it is never a zero.
Tourism places are offered as start, stop or end points only once the tourism place listings are loaded; until then the place boxes search the town, street, landmark, stop and route index only.

values.Boxes: From, To and up to six added stops, eight points in all. Type a town, street, landmark, stop or Puerto Rico (PR) route number, or press the pin button to click the map. 'Add points by clicking the map' fills the next empty box and then extends the route.
values.Buttons: 'Reverse' swaps the order. The arrows move an added stop, and the cross removes it. 'Follow roads' is on by default. With it off the route is drawn as straight lines. 'Plan route' matches boxes that hold text to the best result and then routes. 'Clear' empties the planner. 'GeoJSON' saves the route. Press Escape to stop choosing points.
values.Route card: The length and an indicative running time. Once the data have loaded it also shows the residents and tourism places within 400 m, the share of the route that runs beside existing routes, the shares in flood and protected areas, the municipalities crossed and the connections at its ends.
values.Red dotted line: A leg that cannot follow roads.
values.3D page: A button flies the camera along the route.

view.label: 2D map: example route
3D view: the same route

layers.operators_list.plain: The Operators list names every transit operator in the observatory and the state of its public timetable: current, expiring, expired or none. Press 'Show' to highlight an operator's routes on the map.
layers.operators_list.plain_es: La lista "Operadores" nombra cada operador de transporte colectivo del observatorio y el estado de su horario público: vigente, por vencer, vencido o ninguno. Oprima "Mostrar" para resaltar en el mapa las rutas de un operador.
layers.operators_list.definition: In Snapshot 2026-10 the list has 44 operators. The menu 'Show' filters it (see the codes below). Each row has a colored dot for the type of operator, a short name with a status pill, and the full name. A line of details gives the routes, stops, weekday trips and the last date of the timetable. It adds flags such as 'no route shapes (drawn along roads)' and 'N routes list stops out of order'. An operator with no timetable feed (a General Transit Feed Specification, or GTFS, file) shows 'No GTFS feed found' (or 'Públicos run without a published schedule') and, when it has one, its number in the federal National Transit Database. 'Show' switches the routes layer on, dims every other operator's lines and zooms to that operator. Press it again to clear. An operator without routes but with a municipality has an 'Open <municipality>' button. The codes below give the filter menu, the status pills and the operator types, with their counts on 4 October 2026.
layers.operators_list.method: network.js (opStatus, renderOpList, highlightOperator). The state is recalculated from the feed's end date every time the page opens. Expired means the end date has passed. Expiring means 60 days or fewer remain. States other than these three come from the stored file.
layers.operators_list.how_to_read: A current state means the timetable's dates cover today. It does not mean service runs as planned.
caveats: The state is judged from one date in the feed. A feed can be out of date in practice while its end date is still ahead.
Operators in none of the sources the observatory reads are not listed.

values.Filter menu 'Show': All operators; Operators with route data (current, expiring, expired and community-mapped); Expired, expiring or no data; and No public data.
values.current: Pill 'Current'. The timetable's end date is more than 60 days ahead. On 4 October 2026: 17 operators.
values.expiring: Pill 'Expires soon'. The end date is 60 days or fewer ahead. On 4 October 2026: 1 operator (Canóvanas, timetable ends 2026-10-31).
values.expired: Pill 'Expired'. The end date has passed. On 4 October 2026: 7 operators.
values.none: Pill 'No public feed'. No timetable data were found. On 4 October 2026: 16 operators.
values.in_ati: Pill 'In the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) feed'. The operator runs inside the ATI network. On 4 October 2026: 2 operators.
values.community: Pill 'Community-mapped'. Routes mapped by volunteers in OpenStreetMap, with no timetable. On 4 October 2026: 1 operator.
values.broken: Pill 'Feed error'. The feed could not be read. Not used on 4 October 2026.
values.unknown: Pill 'Dates unknown'. The feed has no end date. Not used on 4 October 2026.
values.regional (type): Blue dot. The ATI itself. In Snapshot 2026-10: 1 operator.
values.ama (type): Blue dot. The Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses (AMA, the Metropolitan Bus Authority). In Snapshot 2026-10: 1 operator.
values.municipal (type): Green dot. A municipal bus or trolley system. In Snapshot 2026-10: 39 operators.
values.community (type): Gold dot. Routes mapped in OpenStreetMap. In Snapshot 2026-10: 1 operator.
values.publico (type): Gold dot. Públicos. In Snapshot 2026-10: 1 operator.
values.ferry (type): Teal dot. The ferry authority. In Snapshot 2026-10: 1 operator.

view.label: 2D map: routes on, then open the Transit tab

layers.transit_tab_summary.plain: The top of the Transit tab shows four figures. Two count operators: those that publish a schedule and those that publish none. One counts the routes on the map. One gives the share of residents who live within 400 meters of a scheduled stop.
layers.transit_tab_summary.plain_es: La parte superior de la pestaña Transporte muestra cuatro cifras. Dos cuentan operadores: los que publican un horario y los que no publican ninguno. Una cuenta las rutas del mapa. Otra da la proporción de residentes que viven a 400 metros o menos de una parada con horario.
layers.transit_tab_summary.definition: The first figure counts operators whose timetable is current, expiring or expired, with the three counts in brackets. The second counts operators with no public schedule data. The third is the number of routes on the map (165 in Snapshot 2026-10). The fourth divides the residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop, summed over the municipalities, by all residents, and adds the same share counting only operators whose timetable has not expired. The state of each operator is worked out in your browser from the end date of its timetable and today's date in Puerto Rico, so the counts can differ from those on the build date. The button 'Show transit only on the map' switches tourism places off and transit routes on. Other layers stay as they are.
layers.transit_tab_summary.method: network.js (renderNetSummary). Residents come from the coverage records of operators.json, which use 2020 Census blocks.
layers.transit_tab_summary.how_to_read: Read the last figure as a share of residents near a stop in a straight line. It does not say how often vehicles come.
caveats: An operator with no feed may still run service. 'No public schedule' means no timetable data were found.
Stops of expired timetables count in the first residents figure. The second figure leaves them out.

view.label: 2D map: transit routes on, then open the Transit tab

layers.live_status_box.plain: The 'What is live' box says that real-time bus positions are not available to the public and lists what exists, with a status for each source and a link.
layers.live_status_box.plain_es: El recuadro "Qué está en vivo" indica que las posiciones de las guaguas en tiempo real no están disponibles al público, y enumera lo que existe, con el estado de cada fuente y un enlace.
layers.live_status_box.definition: The box opens with 'Real-time bus positions are not available to the public' and the date of the check. Below it each source has a colored status and a one-line detail. There are six sources in Snapshot 2026-10: the real-time feed of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI), the Autoridad Metropolitana de Autobuses (AMA) Móvil app, ATI express buses, municipal systems, the AcuaExpreso ferries and aircraft near Puerto Rico.
layers.live_status_box.method: network.js (renderLiveStatus) reads the live list of operators.json. Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) enters the statuses by hand after each check. The observatory does not test the sources automatically.
layers.live_status_box.how_to_read: Where the observatory shows vehicles moving, it replays a timetable. See 'Vehicles on their timetable now'.
caveats: The check is a snapshot. A feed published after the check date is not shown until the list is updated.

values.not published: The operator has announced a feed but no address exists yet.
values.app only: Positions show in a mobile app, and no public data feed sits behind it.
values.private feed: A third-party app says the operator publishes positions, but no public feed address exists. Access is said to require a request to the operator.
values.none found: No real-time feed exists in the public registries.
values.available, needs a relay: Free live data exist, but their servers do not accept calls from a web page, so a small relay service is needed.

view.label: 2D map: Transit tab, What is live

layers.vehicles_now_control.plain: 'Vehicles on their timetable now' draws a dot for each scheduled vehicle that should be in service at this moment, in Puerto Rico time. It replays timetables. It is not tracking by Global Positioning System (GPS).
layers.vehicles_now_control.plain_es: "Vehículos según su horario ahora" dibuja un punto por cada vehículo con horario que debería estar en servicio en este momento, en la hora de Puerto Rico. Reproduce los horarios. No es un rastreo por GPS (sistema de posicionamiento global).
layers.vehicles_now_control.definition: The switch is off when the page opens. When it is on, the dots update every 5 seconds. The map picks the Sunday, Saturday or weekday file for today in Puerto Rico. A dot is red for the Tren Urbano, teal for ferries, blue for buses of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and green for municipal buses. Pointing at a dot names the route and the operator and repeats that the position is not GPS. A note under the switch gives the number of vehicles, the day type, the time, and the six operators with the most vehicles. Trips of operators whose timetable has expired are left out. Holidays are not modeled. The first time you switch it on, the page downloads the timetable file for the day type (the weekday file is about 2.2 MB in Snapshot 2026-10).
layers.vehicles_now_control.method: network.js (updateNow, setNow). A trip is in service when the time lies between its first and last stop time. Its position is worked out between the two stops around the current time, in proportion to the time elapsed.
layers.vehicles_now_control.how_to_read: Read a dot as where the schedule says a vehicle is, not where it is.
caveats: No public real-time bus feed exists, so a late or canceled vehicle is shown as on time.

The position follows the route line between stops at an even speed. A trip whose stops fit no line of its route (106 of 3,297 weekday trips in Snapshot 2026-10) moves in a straight line, so its dot can sit off the road.
Operators with no published timetable, públicos and OpenStreetMap routes are absent.

In Snapshot 2026-10, on Saturday only 4 operators have a timetable file (ATI, Guaynabo, Juncos and Vega Alta). On Sunday only ATI does, so municipal buses are absent on those days even where they run.

A dot moves between the stops that have a scheduled time. In Snapshot 2026-10, 532 of the 3,297 weekday trips list only their first and last stop; 523 of them still follow their route line, so their dots keep to the road, but the time in between is spread evenly.
layers.vehicles_now_control.source_detail: Snapshot 2026-10: trips.json (weekday, 3,297 trips), trips_sa.json (Saturday, 1,648 trips) and trips_su.json (Sunday, 381 trips). The vehicle dots carry no credit line of their own. Name ATI and the municipal operators when you cite.

view.label: 2D map: Vehicles on their timetable now

layers.map_page.plain: The 2D map shows Puerto Rico on an OpenStreetMap base map. A side panel has eight tabs: Overview, Layers, Catalog, Municipality, Rankings, Transit, Economy and About. A top bar links to the 3D view, the Housing page and the data dictionary.
layers.map_page.plain_es: El mapa 2D muestra a Puerto Rico sobre un mapa base de OpenStreetMap. Un panel lateral tiene ocho pestañas: Resumen, Capas, Catálogo, Municipio, Posiciones, Transporte, Economía e Info. Una barra superior lleva a la vista 3D, a la página de Vivienda y al diccionario de datos.
layers.map_page.definition: The base map is OpenFreeMap vector tiles in the OpenMapTiles schema, made from OpenStreetMap data and drawn by MapLibre GL JS under every other layer. It opens on the 'Positron' style, a light map for data; the 'Base map' choice, first in the Territory group of the Map layers tab, switches to another OpenFreeMap style ('Liberty', detailed, with streets, places and buildings; 'Bright', colorful; 'Dark'; 'Fiord', dark blue), to a map of the USGS National Map (aerial imagery, topographic or shaded relief: picture tiles of its own, with no OpenStreetMap data, which the map inspector cannot read) or to no base map (the data alone, on a plain background, with 'Base map off' in the credit line). The choice changes only the base map, is kept in the page address (bm=positron, liberty, bright, dark, fiord, imagery, topo, relief or none) and in the link to the 3D view, and is remembered in this browser as the default for the next visit. It is added once the map is ready, so the data come first; a short 'Loading the base map…' note shows in the credit line until it appears. The map opens on all of Puerto Rico. Zoom buttons and a scale bar with a metric and an imperial scale sit at the bottom right, with the credit lines of the base map ('© OpenStreetMap contributors · © OpenMapTiles · OpenFreeMap', or on a USGS map 'Base map: U.S. Geological Survey, National Geospatial Program') and of the layers that are switched on. The top bar holds the search box, the 'Ask' chat button, links to the 3D + Time view, the Housing page and the data dictionary, and a label such as 'Snapshot 2026-10' that names the build of the data files the page shows. Hover over the label to see the build date. Transit timetables, routes and stops are refreshed every night and are not tied to that label. The codes below list the other details of the page.
layers.map_page.method: app.js builds the map with Leaflet 1.9.4, up to zoom 19. Once the map is ready it loads site/js/core/basemap.js, the one configuration of every base map, which loads MapLibre GL JS 4.7.1 (the same file as the 3D view) and MapLibre GL Leaflet 0.1.4 and draws the OpenFreeMap style in Leaflet's tile pane, under every overlay pane. The base map does not answer clicks: every click goes to the observatory's layers, as before. If the browser has no WebGL, the style does not load within 30 seconds or eight tile requests in a row fail, the base map is removed, the map keeps its layers over a plain light background and a message says 'Base map unavailable'; the map never falls back to the OpenStreetMap Foundation's own tile servers. The opening view fits the box from 17.86 N, 67.30 W to 18.52 N, 65.20 W. Each overlay has its own stacking level, so flood zones and routes draw above land use and protected areas. common.js runs the panel, the tabs (following the accessible tab pattern of the Web Accessibility Initiative, WAI-ARIA) and the help boxes. docs/basemap.md describes the base map.
layers.map_page.how_to_read: Use the credit lines in the attribution box when you share a picture of the map. Every dictionary entry has a Cite button. On an entry for a layer or tool it cites that control and names its sources. To cite the data themselves, use the Cite button on the dataset entries listed under Related.
caveats: The base map is made from OpenStreetMap, mapped by volunteers. It shows roads and place names, not official boundaries.

The page needs JavaScript and an internet connection. The map code, the fonts and the base map tiles come from other servers. If the map code does not load, the page says so and offers 'try again'. If the base map cannot be drawn (no WebGL, or OpenFreeMap does not answer), the data still show, over a plain background.
The snapshot label covers the files built together. It does not say when each source last changed.

values.Panel and keyboard: The panel's tabs change with a click or with the left and right arrow keys. Press / to jump to the search box.
values.Phone: On a phone the panel stays hidden until you press the menu button. It closes with its close button, a tap on the gray backdrop or the Escape key.
values.Top bar links: Map (this page), 3D + Time, Housing and Data dictionary. The Data dictionary link opens dictionary.html, the page for definitions, sources, licenses and citations.
values.Files and loading: The page opens with only the municipal boundaries. Its first load is the build information, the municipality statistics, the boundaries and the catalog (about 0.16 MB compressed in Snapshot 2026-10). Every layer, the tourism places included, loads its data file the first time you switch it on (1 MB is 1 million bytes). In Snapshot 2026-10 the largest are land use (about 17.7 MB), the tourism place listings (about 16.7 MB, plus a 0.3 MB file of transit access), flood zones (about 8.0 MB) and protected areas (about 1.5 MB). If a file cannot be loaded, the layer's switch turns itself off and a message appears.
values.Inside another page: When the map sits inside another web page, the mouse wheel scrolls that page until you click the map.

layers.map_page.source_detail: Credit lines are drawn by each layer, so they depend on which layers are on. Base map credit line: '© OpenStreetMap contributors · © OpenMapTiles · OpenFreeMap'; on a USGS map, 'Base map: U.S. Geological Survey, National Geospatial Program', with 'Orthoimagery: USDA, USGS' on the aerial imagery. Page code: app.js, network.js, economy.js, chat.js and common.js. The entry of each layer names its data file.

view.label: 2D map

layers.about_tab.plain: The About tab explains what the PR Data Observatory is, who it is for, how to start and how to cite it. It says that Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) developed the observatory as a tool for public use and benefit. It also shows seven headline counts.
layers.about_tab.plain_es: La pestaña Info explica qué es el Observatorio de Datos de PR, para quién es, cómo empezar y cómo citarlo. Indica que Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) desarrolló el observatorio como una herramienta para uso y beneficio público. También muestra siete cifras principales.
layers.about_tab.definition: The 2D map's About tab has these parts, in order. An introduction says what the observatory is and that it is free, needs no account and is built from open and public data. Seven counts follow. Then come a list of the fields the observatory covers (written from the registry, so it grows with the observatory); a list of four groups the observatory is for; six 'Start here' steps, with buttons for the chat and the data dictionary; five example questions for the chat; a guide to the eight tabs and to the top bar; a note on where the data come from; six 'Keep in mind' points; and a privacy note. The tab ends with a closing section that gives the citation line and the current snapshot, and says where to send a correction or a dataset to add. Five of the seven counts come from meta.json when the page loads. The other two come from dictionary_summary.json when the tab is first opened. The 3D + Time view has its own About tab. It has a short description, a 'How to use it' list of five items (move around, pick a clock, turn layers on and off, plan a route, see it in 2D) and a 'Sources, licenses and how to cite' section with a button that opens the data dictionary. The codes below list the counts and summarize each part.
layers.about_tab.method: app.js (renderAbout, loadAboutNumbers). The five counts are read from data/meta.json. The two dictionary counts are fetched from data/dictionary_summary.json the first time the tab is opened, and they are left out if the file does not load. The texts are in index.html and 3d.html. The tab's cite line reads 'Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory' followed by the snapshot label. The last line of the tab gives the same label and the build date.
layers.about_tab.how_to_read: Quote a count with the snapshot label. The tourism place count follows the default counting rules (see Related), not the filters you set on the Map layers tab.
caveats: The counts are the observatory's own counts of listings and mapped points. They are not counts of businesses, visitors or services in operation.
The stops-and-stations count includes stops of operators whose timetable has expired and stops that volunteers mapped in OpenStreetMap.

The tab calls the observatory free, with no account, and built from open and public data. It also says that not every source has an open license: some, such as the municipal transit feeds and the Junta de Planificación's maps, state no license.
The tab also says that hazards are mapped zones, that timetables are not live and that survey numbers are estimates. The entries on those layers give the details.

The tab suggests setting disaster and federal money beside housing and the economy. Federal and recovery amounts in the observatory are amounts obligated (committed) or approved. They are not money spent, damage or need.

The Privacy section says that what you type in the search box or the chat stays in your browser, except the online address lookup. The chat also has a button that opens a GitHub request form with your unanswered questions in the web address. See the entry on what the chat keeps on your device.

values.Residents (2020 Census): 3,285,874. The 2020 Census count of residents (counts.population_2020). It is not a current estimate.
values.Tourism places: 24,209 in Snapshot 2026-10 (built 2026-10-02). Overture listings with confidence 0.50 or more, with places of worship left out (counts.tourism_places).
values.Transit routes, all operators: 165 in Snapshot 2026-10. It includes 16 routes mapped in OpenStreetMap that have no timetable (network.routes).
values.Stops and stations: 4,360 in Snapshot 2026-10: 3,781 scheduled stops, 459 OpenStreetMap bus stops, 91 bus stations, 16 Tren Urbano stations and 13 ferry terminals. In Snapshot 2026-10 the airports (25), taxi stands (9) and electric vehicle charging points (11) are not counted.
values.Documented datasets, variables and measu: The number of items in the data dictionary. It is read from dictionary_summary.json, so it grows as entries are added.
values.Data sources, each with its license: The number of data sources in the dictionary, not counting software and base-map sources. It is read from dictionary_summary.json.
values.What the observatory covers: A list of the fields (domains) of the registry with their descriptions, written when the page loads, so a new field appears with no change to the page. A field with no data yet is marked. A line under the list says that the observatory keeps growing.
values.Who the observatory is for: The tab names four groups: residents and community groups; local and island planners; researchers, students and journalists; and funders, nonprofits and recovery teams.
values.Start here: six steps: 1. Start with the overview (the Topics tab gives one headline figure for each field; the Catalog tab finds any dataset and adds it to the map). 2. Turn on layers (Map layers tab). 3. Click a municipality or a place (Municipality tab). 4. Put economic data on the map (Analysis tab). 5. Ask a question (the Ask button, in English or Spanish). 6. Check and share: open the Data dictionary, copy a link and download tables as comma-separated values (CSV) files.
values.Questions to try: Where is unemployment highest? Show poverty and unemployment together. Tell me about Ponce. What are the most interesting patterns? What data is missing?
values.The eight tabs, as the About tab describ: Overview (one headline figure for each field, with a trend), Layers (map layers, and shading by any of the measures in the menu), Catalog (search everything the observatory documents, filter it and add it to the map), Municipality (the profile of one municipality), Rankings (rank the 78 municipalities and download the table), Transit (operators and the state of their timetables, vehicles on schedule, residents far from service and a route planner), Economy (the tab says 'more than 100 yearly datasets'; there are 103 in Snapshot 2026-10) and About.
values.The top bar, as the About tab describes: Search (press / to jump to it); Ask (a chat that builds every answer from the data loaded on the page and is not generative artificial intelligence); Map; 3D + Time; Housing; and Data dictionary (what every dataset, variable and measure means, its source and license, the glossary, the published data files and how to cite).
values.Keep in mind: Six points: it is a snapshot; places are listings, not a census of businesses; hazards are mapped zones; timetables are not live; survey numbers are estimates; and patterns are not causes. The last point adds that the observatory is for asking better questions and planning, not a legal, financial or engineering determination.
values.Privacy: No accounts. What you type in the search box or the chat stays in your browser, except the online address lookup, which sends that text to OpenStreetMap's Nominatim service. Like any web page, the observatory loads fonts, code libraries and map tiles from other servers (the tab names Google Fonts, cdnjs, OpenStreetMap and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, NOAA), which can see your Internet Protocol (IP) address.
values.Cite it and tell us what is missing: To cite: Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, followed by the snapshot label. The tab asks you to credit the original sources too, and says the data dictionary writes them out. It also says the database keeps growing, points to the chat question 'What data is missing?' and gives FPR's website for a correction or a dataset to add.
values.3D + Time About tab: A short description (real terrain and building heights, and three clocks), a 'How to use it' list of five items, and 'Sources, licenses and how to cite' with the button 'Open the data dictionary'. It says the view uses public data, that most sources have an open license but some (the municipal transit feeds, the Junta de Planificación's maps) state none, and that the Data management page gives each file's license class.

layers.about_tab.source_detail: meta.json (counts, network and transport fields) and dictionary_summary.json (the number of dictionary items and of data sources). Cite line on the tab: 'Foundation for Puerto Rico, PR Data Observatory, <snapshot label>'. The tab asks you to credit the original sources as well, which the data dictionary writes out.

view.label: 2D map: About tab (open the tab)
3D + Time view: About tab (open the tab)

layers.help_buttons.plain: A round '?' button beside a layer, a tile or a chart opens a small box with a short explanation of what it shows and where it comes from.
layers.help_buttons.plain_es: Un botón redondo "?" junto a una capa, un recuadro o una gráfica abre una cajita con una explicación breve de lo que muestra y de dónde proviene.
layers.help_buttons.definition: On the 2D map the box opens for the items listed below. The 3D view has 20 (2026-10-19): the layers it shares with the 2D map have the same help texts in both views (the six facility layers bring theirs with them, from core/facilities.js), except Municipal boundaries, whose 3D text points to the columns instead of the shading. On the Housing page each of the 28 variable blocks (a map and its ranked chart) has a '?' that shows the dataset's definition and its source reference. The other charts and tables on the Housing page have no '?'. A box closes with its close button, with Escape or with a click elsewhere. The texts are short summaries written into the page code. This dictionary gives the full account of each layer and variable.
layers.help_buttons.method: common.js (initHelp) opens a box for any element that carries a data-help key and looks the key up in a list: help.js (2D, loaded with its Spanish on the first press), core/facilities.js (the facility layers, both views, loaded with them), twin3d.js (3D) or housing.js (Housing page).
layers.help_buttons.how_to_read: Read the box as a reminder. For a figure you plan to cite, use the dictionary entry.
caveats: The Tourism places help boxes (2D and 3D) call the classification 'the VIEWPR taxonomy'. This means the grouping of Overture categories into four tourism categories that Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) made. See the entry on classification.

values.Tourism places (2D Map layers tab): The Tourism places switch. Key in the code: places.
values.Places of worship (2D Map layers tab): The Include places of worship switch. Key: worship.
values.Flood zones (2D Map layers tab): The Flood zones switch. Key: flood.
values.Sea level rise (2D Map layers tab): The sea level rise switch and slider. Key: slr.
values.Protected areas (2D Map layers tab): The Protected areas switch. Key: protected.
values.Municipal boundaries (2D and 3D Layers t: The Municipal boundaries switch. Key: muni. The 3D text says that the view opens with the outlines on and that the columns compare a measure across the municipalities.
values.In flood hazard area (2D Municipality ta: The tile that shows the share of a municipality's places in a flood hazard area. Key: sfha.
values.Transit routes (2D Map layers tab): The Transit routes switch. Key: routes.
values.Transit stops (2D and 3D Layers tabs): The Transit stops switch. Key: stops.
values.Stations, terminals and airports (2D Map: The Stations, terminals & airports switch. Key: hubs.
values.Taxi stands and electric vehicle chargin: The 'Taxi stands & EV charging' switch (EV means electric vehicle). Key: taxi.
values.Within 400 m of a stop with a current ti: The tile that shows the share of a municipality's places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable. Key: access.
values.Within 400 m of any mapped stop (2D Muni: The tile that shows the share of a municipality's places within 400 m of any mapped stop, including stops whose timetable has ended and stops that volunteers mapped. Key: transit.
values.Land use 2015 (2D Map layers tab): The Land use 2015 switch. Key: landuse.
values.Housing indicators (2D Municipality tab,: The heading of the housing section. Key: housing.
values.Uber lists service (2D Municipality tab,: The Uber chip. Key: uber. The list was checked on 2026-10-01.
values.Tourism places (3D Layers tab): The 3D Tourism places switch. Key: places3d.
values.Flood zones (3D Layers tab): The 3D Flood zones switch. Key: flood.
values.Sea level rise (3D Layers tab): The 3D sea level rise switch. Key: slr.
values.Scheduled vehicles (3D Layers tab): The 3D vehicle replay switch. Key: trips.
values.Hurricane tracks (3D Time tab): The storm tracks switch. Key: storms.
values.Public facility layers (2D and 3D Layers: The switches of Public housing developments, Fire and EMS stations, Police stations, City halls, Public libraries and Historic places. Keys: fac_pubhousing, fac_fire, fac_police, fac_townhalls, fac_libraries, fac_historic.
values.Comunidades Especiales and WCRP communit: The two switches of the Communities group. Keys: comunidades, wcrp.

view.label: 2D map: Map layers tab

layers.scene_3d.plain: The 3D + Time view shows Puerto Rico as a tilted 3D scene with terrain and buildings, and three clocks: a day of transit, sea level by year and hurricanes since 1851.
layers.scene_3d.plain_es: La vista "3D + Tiempo" muestra a Puerto Rico como una escena 3D inclinada, con terreno y edificios, y tres relojes: un día de transporte colectivo, el nivel del mar por año y los huracanes desde 1851.
layers.scene_3d.definition: The top bar has the search box and links to the 2D map, the Housing page and the data dictionary. The side panel has four tabs: Layers, Time (the three clocks), Route (the route planner) and About. The About tab describes the view and links to the data dictionary (see the entry on the About tab). A time bar at the bottom switches between the clocks. The base map is the OpenFreeMap 'Liberty' style, which draws OpenStreetMap data; the 'Base map' choice, first in the 3D scene group of the Layers tab, switches to another OpenFreeMap style ('Positron', a light map for data; 'Bright'; 'Dark'; 'Fiord'), to a map of the USGS National Map (aerial imagery, topographic or shaded relief, draped over the terrain) or to no base map. A switch keeps every data layer, the terrain and the animated layers. The 3D buildings need OpenStreetMap's building tiles, so they are off on a USGS map and with no base map, and come back with an OpenFreeMap style; the counts on the clusters of stops need fonts, which every style but 'No base map' has. The choice is kept in the page address (bm=) and in the link to the 2D map, and remembered in this browser. The view needs WebGL, a browser feature for 3D graphics. Without it the page says so and points to the 2D map and the Housing page. The page opens on the whole island, tilted 50 degrees (35 on a phone). The codes below give the contents of the Map layers tab, the camera limits, what loads when and how the page behaves inside another page.
layers.scene_3d.method: twin3d.js. MapLibre GL JS 4.7.1 draws the terrain, the buildings and the data layers, which follow the terrain. deck.gl 9.0.38 draws the animated layers (transit trips and storm tracks) over the map. The data are the same data files as on the 2D map.
layers.scene_3d.how_to_read: Use the 3D view to see how places sit in the land. Use the 2D map for numbers, the Analysis tab and the chat.
caveats: The 3D view needs a recent browser with WebGL and downloads more data than the 2D map.
The 3D view has no confidence slider, no worship switch, no economy layers and no layer links. Its address keeps only the camera and a route.

The credit line names the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) for transit. Municipal feeds also supply routes, stops and trips in the 3D view, so credit them too when you cite. The route card names the right source.

values.Map layers tab: 3D scene (terrain and buildings), then the groups of the 2D map, in the same order and with the same layers where both views can draw them: Territory (municipal boundaries, barrios, columns by municipality), Hazards and environment, Land and housing (with public housing), Infrastructure and mobility (routes, stops, stations, taxi stands and EV charging, the walk rings, the vehicle replay), Community services (fire and EMS stations, police stations, city halls, public libraries, historic places), Communities and Visitor economy (tourism places).
values.Base map fallback: If the base map style cannot be loaded, the data layers appear on a plain background with a message.
values.Camera limits: The camera stays inside the box from 16.8 N to 19.6 N and from 69.5 W to 63.5 W, zooms out no further than level 5.5 and tilts up to 80 degrees.
values.Loading: In Snapshot 2026-10 the first screen loads the municipality statistics and boundaries, the routes, the stops and stations (transport.json), the operators and the service figures. The timetable replay and the storm tracks load after the first screen is drawn. The tourism places and every other layer load when you first switch them on.
values.Inside another page: When the page sits inside another page, the map takes two-finger gestures or Ctrl and scroll, so that the host page can still scroll.

layers.scene_3d.source_detail: Credit line on the map, in the attribution box shared by every 3D layer: 'Places © Overture Maps Foundation · FEMA NFHL · NOAA (SLR, HURDAT2) · USGS PAD-US · US Census · ATI GTFS · © OpenStreetMap contributors · © OpenMapTiles · OpenFreeMap', followed by the terrain's own line (see the 3D terrain entry). In that line, FEMA NFHL is the National Flood Hazard Layer of the Federal Emergency Management Agency, NOAA is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, SLR is sea level rise, HURDAT2 is the Atlantic hurricane database of the NOAA National Hurricane Center, AWS is Amazon Web Services, USGS PAD-US is the Protected Areas Database of the US Geological Survey, and ATI GTFS is the timetable data of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado in General Transit Feed Specification format.

view.label: 3D + Time view

layers.buildings_3d.plain: The '3D buildings' switch raises building footprints to the height stored in the OpenFreeMap map tiles, which draw OpenStreetMap data. A building with no height value is drawn 6 meters tall.
layers.buildings_3d.plain_es: El interruptor "Edificios en 3D" levanta la huella de cada edificio hasta la altura guardada en los mosaicos de mapa de OpenFreeMap, que dibujan datos de OpenStreetMap. Un edificio sin valor de altura se dibuja con 6 metros de alto.
layers.buildings_3d.definition: The switch is on at the start. Buildings appear from zoom level 13. Each is a prism standing on the terrain. Its height is the render_height value in the OpenFreeMap tiles, and 6 meters where the tile has none. A building part raised above the ground starts at its minimum render height. Color runs from light beige at 0 meters through gray-beige at 30 meters to darker brown-gray at 90 meters. Buildings are 85% opaque.
layers.buildings_3d.method: twin3d.js (setupScene): a fill-extrusion layer on the 'building' layer of the base map's vector tiles.
layers.buildings_3d.how_to_read: Use it to see the scale of the built area. A tall prism means a height value in the tile, not a measured height.
caveats: Buildings that nobody mapped are missing. A mapped building with no height value is drawn at the default 6 meters, so a tall building can look low.

The heights come from the OpenFreeMap tiles. The observatory has not checked how OpenFreeMap sets the render_height value, so it cannot say whether a height was recorded by volunteers or estimated. The heights are not surveyed and must not be used for engineering.
layers.buildings_3d.source_detail: Credit line on the map: '© OpenStreetMap contributors · © OpenMapTiles · OpenFreeMap'.

view.label: 3D + Time view: San Juan

layers.terrain_3d.plain: The '3D terrain' switch lifts the map into relief. The 'Terrain exaggeration' slider stretches the heights, from 1 to 3 times, so hills are easier to see.
layers.terrain_3d.plain_es: El interruptor "Terreno en 3D" levanta el mapa en relieve. El control deslizante "Exageración del terreno" estira las alturas de 1 a 3 veces, para que las lomas se vean mejor.
layers.terrain_3d.definition: The switch is on at the start. The slider runs from 1× to 3× in steps of 0.1 and starts at 1.3×. It stretches heights for display. Light and dark relief shading (hillshade) is always on, at a fixed strength. The map also draws a sky and haze at the horizon. Heights come from elevation tiles in the Mapzen 'terrarium' format, served by Amazon Web Services (AWS) Open Data, which hold data up to zoom level 15. Beyond that level the tiles are enlarged. Data layers such as flood zones, routes and land use are draped on the relief.
layers.terrain_3d.method: twin3d.js (setupScene, setTerrain), with the terrain source, its Terrarium encoding and its credit read from site/js/core/basemap.js. The terrain source is https://s3.amazonaws.com/elevation-tiles-prod/terrarium.
layers.terrain_3d.how_to_read: Read the relief as a picture of the land. Do not read heights off the screen.
caveats: Exaggeration changes the picture, not the data. Slopes look steeper than they are above 1×.
The license of the elevation tiles is in the AWS Open Data registry entry. Check it before you reuse the tiles.
layers.terrain_3d.source_detail: Credit line on the map: 'Terrain: Mapzen / AWS Open Data · 3DEP, SRTM and GMTED2010 data courtesy of the U.S. Geological Survey · ETOPO1: NOAA', as the terrain tiles' attribution page asks.

view.label: 3D + Time view: El Yunque

layers.transit_replay_3d.plain: 'A day of transit' replays every scheduled weekday trip of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) and municipal timetables as a colored trail that moves across the map. It is a timetable replay, not tracking by Global Positioning System (GPS).
layers.transit_replay_3d.plain_es: "Un día de transporte colectivo" reproduce cada viaje con horario de un día de semana de la ATI (Autoridad de Transporte Integrado) y de los horarios municipales como una estela de color que avanza por el mapa. Es una reproducción de horarios, no un rastreo por GPS (sistema de posicionamiento global).
layers.transit_replay_3d.definition: The switch 'Scheduled vehicles' is on at the start. The clock runs from 00:00 to 23:59 and starts at 07:00. Speeds are 30×, 60× (one minute of clock each second, the start setting), 180× and 600×. The clock wraps around at midnight. A trail shows the last 7 minutes of each trip, fading behind the head. The colors are red for the Tren Urbano, gold for ATI buses, green for municipal buses and teal for ferries. These are not the route colors of the 3D map, where ATI buses are blue. The label beside the controls says 'N vehicles in service', counted once a minute of the clock as trips whose first stop time is at or before the clock and whose last stop time is at or after it. On a computer the replay starts by itself. On a phone, or when your device asks for reduced motion, it waits for Play.
layers.transit_replay_3d.method: twin3d.js (tripsLayer, tickBody). deck.gl draws the TripsLayer from trips.json, the weekday file of a typical Wednesday (3,297 trips from 25 operators in Snapshot 2026-10). Each trail follows its trip's route line (the operator's shape, or the roads the route is snapped to), timed between the stops that have a scheduled time (tripPoints in common.js). In Snapshot 2026-10, 3,191 of the 3,297 trips follow their route line; 106 whose stops fit no line of their route run in straight lines between stops.
layers.transit_replay_3d.how_to_read: Read the trails as where the timetable says vehicles are at that time. A quiet map at night is a quiet timetable.
caveats: The replay includes trips of operators whose timetable has expired. In Snapshot 2026-10, 372 of the 3,297 weekday trips belong to operators whose feed had ended by the build date. The 2D map leaves them out.
Only the weekday file is used. The Saturday and Sunday files are not replayed in 3D, and holidays are not modeled.
No public real-time bus feed exists, so late or canceled vehicles run on time here.
The credit line on the map names ATI only. In Snapshot 2026-10, 1,168 of the 3,297 weekday trips come from municipal feeds (ATI has 2,129), so credit the municipalities too when you cite.
layers.transit_replay_3d.source_detail: trips.json, Snapshot 2026-10: the weekday file, a typical Wednesday, with 3,297 trips. The shared attribution box on the map names 'ATI GTFS' (the timetable data of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, in General Transit Feed Specification format). The trails carry no credit line of their own.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Time tab, A day of transit

layers.columns_3d.plain: 'Columns by municipality' raises each municipality into a column whose height shows one measure. The menu has 33 measures (the 35 of the 2D map's shading less its three 'shown' measures, plus population change 2010 to 2020) and any dataset of the Analysis tab. The columns start off.
layers.columns_3d.plain_es: "Columnas por municipio" levanta cada municipio como una columna cuya altura muestra una medida. El menú tiene 33 medidas (las 35 del sombreado del mapa 2D menos sus tres medidas de lugares mostrados, más el cambio de población de 2010 a 2020) y cualquier conjunto de datos de la pestaña Análisis. Las columnas empiezan desactivadas.
layers.columns_3d.definition: With a measure chosen, each municipality rises as a column standing on its own area. The column height is proportional to the value, starting at zero. The largest value reaches 14,000 display meters (12,000 for population change). These are map heights, not real heights. Color follows five groups of about equal size, in the same light-to-dark blue as the 2D map. The legend under the menu shows three numbers: the lowest value, the second class limit (the value two fifths of the way along the sorted list) and the highest value. A click on a column, or on the municipality when columns are off, opens a card with a link to the 2D map. The codes below list the 33 measures and the card. A yes/no measure (whether Uber lists the municipality) raises the listed municipalities to one height and leaves the others as a flat gray sheet; rent change, which can fall, uses the red-to-blue scale of population change.
layers.columns_3d.method: twin3d.js (METRIC, setMetric, addMunicipalities). The menu lists the fields below.
layers.columns_3d.how_to_read: Read heights as 'more or less than other municipalities'. The tallest column is the largest value, not a target.
caveats: A value that equals a class limit takes the lower class in both the 3D view and the 2D map. The limits themselves can still differ for the shares of places near stops (see the caveat on municipalities with no stop counted).

In Snapshot 2026-10, 14 municipalities have no stop counted. The 3D view uses the stored shares of places near stops (any mapped stop, a stop with a current timetable, a frequent stop, only an expired or unscheduled stop) for every municipality, in the columns and on the card. For those 14 the stored value is 0% or close to it (0.5% for Toa Alta and 0.9% for Arroyo, for the shares near any mapped stop and near a stop with a current timetable), which means not measured. The 2D map leaves those 14 unshaded for those shares and works out their class limits from the other 64 municipalities, while 3D keeps all 78 in the limits, so the limits and a few colors of these shares can differ between the two views.
Tall columns hide what is behind them. Rotate or tilt the view.

Heights start at zero, so a column twice as tall is not twice as different when the values of all municipalities are close together. In Snapshot 2026-10 the affordability ratio, for example, runs only from 0.97 to 1.92.

When many municipalities share a value, several class limits are equal, and the classes between them stay empty, as in the 2D map. In Snapshot 2026-10 this happens for the measure 'Transit: % of residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop (incl. expired timetables)' (40 of the 78 municipalities have 0%), for residents near a stop with a current timetable (46 at 0%) and for the shares of places near a stop with a current timetable (47), near a frequent stop (59) and near only an expired or unscheduled stop (33). The legend then repeats a number (for the first of these measures it reads 0%, 0% and 81%), but the colors and the heights follow the measure.

values.sfha_pct: % of places in flood hazard area.
values.transit_pct: % of places within 400 m of any mapped stop.
values.acc_cur400_pct: % of places within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable.
values.acc_freq400_pct: % of places within 400 m of a frequent stop (20+ weekday departures).
values.acc_paper_pct: % of places near only an expired or unscheduled stop.
values.pop_change_pct: Population change 2010 to 2020 (%). In Snapshot 2026-10 every municipality lost population (from −29.0% to −0.1%), so the scale is one-sided: column height and red shade show the size of the loss. If a measure had both gains and losses, red would mean loss and blue would mean gain.
values.affordability_ratio: Housing: affordability ratio (value divided by maximum loan).
values.pop_served_active_pct: Transit: % of residents within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable.
values.pop_served_pct: Transit: % of residents within 400 m of a scheduled stop (incl. expired timetables).
values.gross_rent_change_pct: Housing: rent change 2012 to the latest year (%). Column height is the size of the change; red is a fall, blue a rise.
values.pop_walk_active_pct: Transit: % of residents within a 400 m walk of a stop with a current timetable.
values.pop_walk_pct: Transit: % of residents within a 400 m walk of a scheduled stop (incl. expired timetables).
values.uber_listed: Uber lists service (yes/no). Listed municipalities stand at one height; the others stay flat and gray. A listing on Uber's cities page, not measured coverage.
values.acc_walk400_pct: % of places within a 400 m walk of a stop with a current timetable.
values.acc_wfreq400_pct: % of places within a 400 m walk of a frequent stop (20+ weekday departures).
values.acc_walk800_pct: % of places within an 800 m walk of a stop with a current timetable.
values.acc_sat400_pct: % of places within 400 m (straight line) of a stop with Saturday service.
values.acc_sun400_pct: % of places within 400 m (straight line) of a stop with Sunday service.
values.Municipality card: The region, the residents (2020, and the change since 2010), the tourism places, the share in a flood hazard area, the share within 400 m of a stop with a current timetable and of any mapped stop, the stops and stations, the Tren Urbano stations, the airports and whether Uber lists the municipality.

layers.columns_3d.source_detail: municipalities.json (the fields named in the codes below) and municipios.geojson, joined in your browser. The shared attribution box on the map names 'US Census' and 'Places © Overture Maps Foundation', among other sources. See the entry on the 3D scene for the full line.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Layers tab, Territory, Columns by municipality

layers.hazards_3d.plain: In the 3D group Hazards and environment, 'Flood zones' drapes the flood zones of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) on the terrain. 'Sea level rise' draws a sea level layer whose height comes from the Time tab. Both are off when the page opens.
layers.hazards_3d.plain_es: En el grupo "Riesgos y ambiente" de la vista 3D, "Zonas inundables" cubre el terreno con las zonas inundables de FEMA (Agencia Federal para el Manejo de Emergencias). "Aumento del nivel del mar" dibuja una capa de nivel del mar cuya altura viene de la pestaña "Tiempo". Ambos están desactivados al abrir la página.
layers.hazards_3d.definition: Flood zones are filled at 45% opacity with the same four colors as the 2D map. Red is for floodways, darkest blue for V and VE zones, mid blue for other Special Flood Hazard Area zones and light blue for the 0.2% annual chance zone.
