A click opens the 2D map's section for up to two zones under the click: the zone, whether it is a Special Flood Hazard Area (1% annual chance) or a 0.2% annual chance zone, the subtype spelled out and the credit 'FEMA National Flood Hazard Layer'. Where other areas are under the click too (land use, a protected area, a Comunidad Especial, a barrio), the same card has a section for each, as on the 2D map. The flood file (about 8 MB) downloads the first time you switch it on. The 'Sea level rise' switch draws the tile layer of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) at 70% opacity below the flood zones. The label beside it gives the feet and the year, for example '1 ft · 2050' (the start setting: Intermediate scenario, year 2050). The height comes from the year and scenario set in the Time tab. Choosing the Years clock switches this layer on by itself.
layers.hazards_3d.method: twin3d.js (addFlood, setSlr, currentFeet); the card's section is floodPopup in access.js, which both views share. The flood filter keeps polygons in the Special Flood Hazard Area or in the 0.2% zone.
layers.hazards_3d.how_to_read: Read the flood zones as FEMA's mapped hazard. Read the sea level layer as a what-if at the chosen height.
caveats: Flood zones are mapped hazards, not predictions. They say nothing about a building's elevation or insurance.
The sea level layer is a screening tool. It is not a forecast for a year. See the sea level entries.
If NOAA's tiles do not answer, a message appears and the layer stays empty.

The flood zones are a simplified copy of FEMA's data for context. FEMA's printed flood maps and Flood Insurance Study are the official designation. This is not a flood determination for any property. Read the source's terms before you rely on it.

NOAA says the sea level layer shows water at the highest high tides and does not model storm surge, erosion, subsidence or new construction. NOAA calls it a planning reference that should not be used for navigation, permitting or other legal purposes.
layers.hazards_3d.source_detail: flood.geojson. The sea level tiles are streamed live from NOAA, and the year and scenario curves are typed into the page code. Credit lines on the map: 'FEMA NFHL' and 'Sea level rise: NOAA OCM' (the NOAA Office for Coastal Management).

view.label: 3D + Time view: Layers tab, Hazards

layers.storm_controls_3d.plain: The Hurricane controls draw the tracks of storms that came within 250 kilometers of Puerto Rico since 1851. You can filter by years and strength, play them through time and open any storm from a list.
layers.storm_controls_3d.plain_es: Los controles de huracanes dibujan las trayectorias de las tormentas que pasaron a 250 kilómetros o menos de Puerto Rico desde 1851. Se puede filtrar por años y por fuerza, reproducirlas en el tiempo y abrir cualquier tormenta desde una lista.
layers.storm_controls_3d.definition: The switch 'Storm tracks within 250 km' is off at the start and shows the number of storms drawn. Two sliders set a year window from 1851 to 2025 (all years at the start). The menu 'Minimum category near PR' (Puerto Rico) offers All (including tropical storms), Hurricane (Category 1 or more), Major (Category 3 or more, the start setting) and Category 4 or more. In Snapshot 2026-10, at the start (Major), the map shows 29 of the 157 storms. Lines are colored by the category near the island, and line width grows with the category. Dots mark recorded positions, colored and sized by wind. Pointing at a line shows the name, the year, the category near Puerto Rico, the peak wind in knots and the closest approach in kilometers; a click on a line shows the same in a card (on a phone, which has no pointing). 'Strongest in window' lists up to 25 storms by category, then wind, then newest. A click on a row fits the map to that storm's whole track.
layers.storm_controls_3d.method: twin3d.js (stormsLayers, renderStormList, tickBody). deck.gl draws the lines and dots from hurricanes.json.
layers.storm_controls_3d.how_to_read: Thicker, darker lines are stronger near the island. A long line is the whole track, which can reach far from Puerto Rico.
caveats: Old tracks and winds are less certain than recent ones. Counts by decade are not a trend.
Lines join recorded positions with straight segments.
The list and the card label every category 0 storm 'Tropical storm'.
The minimum-category menu has no Category 2 or more choice.

values.0: Category 0, gray: tropical storm or depression strength near the island. 92 storms in Snapshot 2026-10.
values.5: Category 5, dark red. 5 storms in Snapshot 2026-10.
values.Play through the years: Moves a year forward 4 times each second and shows the storms of the chosen year and the 10 years before it (11 calendar years), with older ones fading. Dragging a window slider returns to the whole window.

layers.storm_controls_3d.geography: Atlantic storms within 250 km of Puerto Rico
layers.storm_controls_3d.source_detail: hurricanes.json, Snapshot 2026-10: 157 storms from 1851 to 2025. Credit line on the map: 'NOAA (SLR, HURDAT2)'. NOAA is the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, SLR is sea level rise and HURDAT2 is the Atlantic hurricane database of the NOAA National Hurricane Center.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Time tab, Hurricanes 1851–2025

layers.land_layers_3d.plain: The 3D view can drape the Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 and the protected areas of the US Geological Survey (USGS) on the terrain. Both are off when the page opens.
layers.land_layers_3d.plain_es: La vista 3D puede cubrir el terreno con el Plan de Uso de Terrenos 2015 y con las áreas protegidas del USGS (Servicio Geológico de Estados Unidos). Ambas capas están desactivadas al abrir la página.
layers.land_layers_3d.definition: Land use is drawn from the class colors stored in the file at 45% opacity, with water and road polygons left out. A click opens the 2D map's section: the class name, code and municipio, and the credit. In Snapshot 2026-10 the land-use file is about 17.7 MB and loads the first time you switch the layer on. Protected areas are green at 35% opacity with a dark green outline. A click opens the 2D map's section for up to two records under the click: the name, the designation spelled out (Local Park for LP, for example; a code the card does not know is shown as stored), the manager, the public access, the acres and the Gap Analysis Project (GAP) status. Overlapping areas share one card, with a section for each, as on the 2D map.
layers.land_layers_3d.method: twin3d.js (addLanduse, addProtected); the card's sections are landusePopup and protPopup in access.js, which both views share.
layers.land_layers_3d.how_to_read: Use the drape to see the pattern. For the full meaning of a code, read the dictionary entry.
caveats: The land-use plan is a planning classification, not zoning, and dates from 2015.
'Protected' has a wide meaning. It includes recreation areas and military land.
layers.land_layers_3d.source_detail: landuse.geojson and protected.geojson. Credit lines on the map: 'Junta de Planificación' for land use and 'USGS PAD-US' for protected areas (PAD-US is the Protected Areas Database of the United States).

view.label: 3D + Time view: Layers tab, Land use and Protected areas

layers.navigation_3d.plain: You move the 3D view with the mouse, with touch, with the keyboard or with the buttons at the right. Four quick-view buttons fly to San Juan, El Yunque, Ponce and the whole island.
layers.navigation_3d.plain_es: La vista 3D se mueve con el ratón, con el tacto, con el teclado o con los botones de la derecha. Cuatro botones de vista rápida llevan la cámara en vuelo a San Juan, El Yunque, Ponce y toda la isla.
layers.navigation_3d.definition: The 3D view has four ways to move: the mouse, touch, the keyboard and the buttons at the right. The codes below describe each way and the four quick views. Letter keys steer the map only when nothing else has the focus.
layers.navigation_3d.method: twin3d.js (NavPad, goHome, topDown, the keydown handler) with MapLibre's own controls. The quick views are the VIEWS list.
layers.navigation_3d.how_to_read: Press the keyboard button in the controls to see these keys in the page.
caveats: Keyboard keys need the map or the page to have the focus. A key typed in a box does nothing to the map.

values.Mouse: Drag to pan, right-drag or Ctrl-drag to rotate and tilt, scroll to zoom, double-click to zoom in.
values.Touch: One finger pans, two fingers zoom and rotate, and two fingers dragged up or down together tilt.
values.Keyboard: Click the map first. Arrow keys pan, and Shift with arrow keys rotates and tilts. The + and − keys zoom. N turns north up. T looks straight down or returns to the tilted view. H shows the whole island. Q and E rotate 15 degrees. The / key jumps to the search box. Escape closes the keyboard help and stops a camera flight.
values.Buttons: Buttons at the right zoom in and out, and a compass resets north and shows the tilt. Other buttons rotate left and right (30 degrees each press), tilt up and down (10 degrees), look straight down or return, show the whole island, show keyboard help and 'find my location'.
values.Find my location: Asks your browser for your position when you press it. The observatory does not store or send it.
values.Reduced motion: If your device asks for reduced motion, camera moves are instant and the replay does not start by itself.
values.San Juan: Quick view: center 18.44 N, 66.09 W, zoom 12.6, tilt 62°, rotated −20°.
values.El Yunque: Quick view: center 18.30 N, 65.79 W, zoom 11.5, tilt 68°, rotated 30°.
values.Ponce: Quick view: center 18.00 N, 66.61 W, zoom 12.5, tilt 60°, rotated 10°.
values.Island: Quick view of the whole island: center 18.20 N, 66.45 W, zoom 8.4 (6.6 on a phone), tilt 50° (35° on a phone), rotated −8°.

view.label: 3D + Time view

layers.places_3d.plain: The 3D 'Tourism places' layer shows tourism places as a heat map from far away and as colored points when you zoom in. Four category buttons filter them.
layers.places_3d.plain_es: La capa "Lugares turísticos" de la vista 3D muestra los lugares turísticos como un mapa de calor desde lejos y como puntos de colores al acercar el mapa. Cuatro botones de categoría los filtran.
layers.places_3d.definition: The layer holds the same places as the 2D map with confidence 0.50 or more and no places of worship (23,467 with a pin in Snapshot 2026-10, shown beside the switch once loaded; holiday rentals are counted but not drawn). The layer starts switched off: its file (about 2.8 MB compressed) loads the first time it is switched on, and from then the place search also lists tourism places. The 'Render as' menu offers 'Heat at island scale, points when zoomed' (start), 'Points' and 'Heat'. Points show from zoom level 10.5 (everywhere in 'Points' mode), grow as you zoom and take the category color. A point inside a Special Flood Hazard Area of the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) has a dark blue rim. The heat map adds one unit for each place and fades out between zoom levels 11 and 13. A click on a point opens a card with the name, the type, the municipality, the flood zone when the place is in a hazard area, the access badge and the distance to the nearest stop with a current timetable (the same lines as the 2D pop-up), and the credit 'Overture Maps'.
layers.places_3d.method: twin3d.js (addPlaces, updatePlacesMode, placesFilter). The filter keeps places of the chosen categories, with a confidence of at least 0.50, that are not places of worship.
layers.places_3d.how_to_read: Use the heat to see where visitor places cluster. Use the points to see single places.
caveats: In 'Heat' mode the heat fades out between zoom levels 11 and 13, so a close-up shows no places.
Overture listings can be missing, duplicated or out of date. The 3D view has no confidence slider and no worship switch.
The 3D view does not recalculate flags when you change a button. The rim and the card come from the build and from the stored access columns.
layers.places_3d.source_detail: places.json. Credit line on the map: 'Places © Overture Maps Foundation'.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Places layer, San Juan

layers.route_planner_3d.plain: The Route tab of the 3D view plans a route like the 2D planner, drapes it on the terrain and can fly the camera along it.
layers.route_planner_3d.plain_es: La pestaña "Ruta" de la vista 3D planifica una ruta igual que el planificador 2D, la coloca sobre el terreno y puede llevar la cámara en vuelo a lo largo de ella.
layers.route_planner_3d.definition: The boxes, buttons and results are the same as in the 2D planner. The route is drawn as a dark line with a white edge. A leg that cannot follow roads is a red dotted line. Lettered markers can be dragged. After a route is planned a button 'Fly along the route' appears. The camera then follows the line at tilt 64 degrees and zoom 14.8, turning to face ahead, and covers the route in about 45 seconds, at a speed between 120 and 1,500 meters per second. A mouse press, a touch, the wheel or Escape stops the flight, and the button reads 'Stop flying' while it runs. If your device asks for reduced motion, the flight does not start and a message says why. The chosen points are kept in the page address as r=.
layers.route_planner_3d.method: twin3d.js (planHost, flyAlong) with plan.js. The route is drawn as fresh map layers each time it changes, and the routes layer is refreshed so that the whole route shows on the terrain.
layers.route_planner_3d.how_to_read: Fly along a route to see what it passes. Read the numbers on the card with the 2D planner's entries.
caveats: A flight is a visual aid. It is not a drive time. The running time on the card uses planning speeds.
The planner's other limits apply. See the route planner entry.

The address holds the exact coordinates of every point, to about 11 meters. If a start, end or stop is your home or workplace, anyone with the link can see it. Remove the r= part before you share a link, or use points that are not private.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Route tab with an example route

layers.sea_level_clock_3d.plain: The 'Sea level by year' controls turn a year and a scenario of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) into the sea level layer. Pick a year from 2020 to 2150 and one of four scenarios, and the map shows the matching NOAA layer.
layers.sea_level_clock_3d.plain_es: Los controles de "Nivel del mar por año" convierten un año y un escenario de NOAA (Administración Nacional Oceánica y Atmosférica) en la capa de nivel del mar. Elija un año de 2020 a 2150 y uno de los cuatro escenarios, y el mapa muestra la capa de NOAA correspondiente.
layers.sea_level_clock_3d.definition: The year slider runs from 2020 to 2150 in steps of 5 and starts at 2050. The scenario menu offers Intermediate-Low, Intermediate (start), Intermediate-High and High, the NOAA 2022 scenarios. A note says, for example, '2050 · Intermediate ≈ 1.0 ft (0.30 m) above the 2000 baseline → showing the NOAA 1 ft layer'. The height is rounded to whole feet and held between 1 and 10 feet. Moving either control swaps the layer when the height in whole feet changes. Play moves the year forward 12 years each second until 2150, then stops. Pressing Play again at 2150 restarts at 2020. Playing needs the Years clock, and choosing it switches the layer on.
layers.sea_level_clock_3d.method: twin3d.js (currentFeet, setSlr, the year and scenario handlers). The conversion from year and scenario to feet is described in the entry 'Sea level rise by year and scenario'.
layers.sea_level_clock_3d.how_to_read: Read a year as a position on a scenario curve. Several years show the same layer, because heights are rounded to whole feet.
caveats: The curves are global average sea level above the 2000 level, read approximately from the tables of NOAA's 2022 report and typed into the page. They are not NOAA's published values for Puerto Rico.
The map is a what-if at a height, not a forecast for a year.
The note on the page calls the scenarios 'planning what-ifs'.
The layer never shows less than 1 ft, so the first years show more water than the scenario gives (see the entry 'Sea level rise by year and scenario').
The layer never shows more than 10 ft, so the highest part of the High scenario is capped (see the same entry).

NOAA says the sea level layer shows water at the highest high tides and does not model storm surge, erosion, subsidence or new construction. NOAA calls it a planning reference that should not be used for navigation, permitting or other legal purposes.

values.Scenario curves: The four curves (meters above the 2000 level for 2020, 2050, 2100 and 2150) are listed in the entry 'Sea level rise by year and scenario'.

layers.sea_level_clock_3d.source_detail: twin3d.js, SCENARIOS: the curves, typed into the page from NOAA's 2022 report (no data file). The layer itself is NOAA's tile service. Credit line on the map: 'Sea level rise: NOAA OCM' (the NOAA Office for Coastal Management).

view.label: 3D + Time view: Time tab, Sea level by year

layers.time_bar_3d.plain: A bar at the bottom of the 3D view has a play button, a label, a slider and three buttons that choose the clock: Day, Years or Storms.
layers.time_bar_3d.plain_es: Una barra en la parte inferior de la vista 3D tiene un botón para reproducir, una etiqueta, un control deslizante y tres botones que eligen el reloj: "Día", "Años" o "Tormentas".
layers.time_bar_3d.definition: Day: the slider runs from 00:00 to 23:59 in one-minute steps and the label reads like '07:00 · weekday transit'. Years: the slider runs from 2020 to 2150 in steps of 5 and the label reads like '2050 · Intermediate sea level'. Storms: the slider runs over the storm window and the label reads like '2024 · storms, trailing 10 years'. The window is the chosen year and the 10 years before it (11 calendar years). Choosing Years switches the sea level layer on. Choosing Storms switches the storm tracks on. Leaving Years switches off a sea level layer that Years switched on, but not one you switched on yourself. Play advances the Day clock at the chosen speed, the Years clock by 12 years each second and the Storms clock by 4 years each second. The Years and Storms clocks stop at their end. The Day clock wraps around at midnight. The Time tab in the side panel has the same controls with explanations. The three clocks are independent: each keeps its own value.
layers.time_bar_3d.method: twin3d.js (setMode, tick, togglePlay, syncClock). Animation uses the browser's frame timer. A long pause between frames (for example a background tab) counts as at most a quarter of a second of play.
layers.time_bar_3d.how_to_read: Press Play on a clock, then change the clock with the buttons to compare.
caveats: The clocks do not move together. The Day clock is a time of day, not a date.

values.Day: The transit replay clock. See 'A day of transit'.
values.Years: The sea level clock. See 'Sea level by year'.

view.label: 3D + Time view: time bar

layers.mobility_3d.plain: The 3D Mobility section draws transit routes (on at the start) and, if you switch them on, stops, stations, terminals and airports, taxi stands and EV chargers and the 400 m walk rings, as the 2D map does. Another switch controls the vehicle replay.
layers.mobility_3d.plain_es: La sección "Infraestructura y movilidad" de la vista 3D dibuja las rutas de transporte colectivo (activadas al inicio) y, si se activan, las paradas, las estaciones, terminales y aeropuertos, las paradas de taxis y la carga de vehículos eléctricos y los radios de 400 m a pie, como el mapa 2D. Otro interruptor controla la reproducción de vehículos.
layers.mobility_3d.definition: Routes use the operator colors of the 2D map: Tren Urbano red (4 pixels), buses of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) blue, municipal systems green, públicos gold and ferries teal (2.5 pixels). All other lines are 2 pixels. Dashed lines mean the feed lists stops out of order. Dotted lines mean no road path was found. Width does not change with trips. A click opens a card with the route name, the operator, the route label, weekday trips, how the line was drawn and the credit. Stations show as dots: Tren Urbano red, ferry terminals teal, bus stations and airports charcoal, with airports slightly larger. A click on a station opens the same card as on the 2D map (name, kind, municipality, routes, modes, departures, timetable dates, operator and source). Stops, taxi stands and EV chargers and the walk rings are the 2D map's layers, with the same cards: see the entries of their switches, which both views share.
layers.mobility_3d.method: twin3d.js (addRoutes, addHubs, addStops, addTaxi, addRings). The files are transit_routes.geojson and transport.json; the cards are transportPopup in access.js.
layers.mobility_3d.how_to_read: Compare the line style with the 2D legend to see how a line was drawn.
caveats: Routes of operators whose timetable has expired stay on the map.
A route in a feed is not proof that the service runs today.

The credit line on the map names the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado (ATI) only. In Snapshot 2026-10, municipal feeds supply most routes: 127 of the 165 routes are not ATI routes, and 111 of them are municipal. The route card names the right source (ATI, a municipal feed or OpenStreetMap). The station card names its source, as on the 2D map. Of the 145 stations, terminals and airports in Snapshot 2026-10, 29 bus stations come from municipal feeds, 65 points (47 bus stations, 7 ferry terminals and 11 airports) from OpenStreetMap and 14 airports from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Credit those sources too when you cite.
layers.mobility_3d.source_detail: transit_routes.geojson (routes) and transport.json (kinds bus_station, rail_station, ferry_terminal and airport). The shared attribution box on the map names, for transit, 'ATI GTFS' (the timetable data of the Autoridad de Transporte Integrado, in General Transit Feed Specification format) and 'OpenFreeMap © OpenStreetMap contributors'.

view.label: 3D + Time view: Layers tab, Mobility

layers.profile_page.plain: One page for each municipio with every dataset of the observatory for that place, grouped by field, with its rank among the 78 municipios, Puerto Rico's value and its trend.
layers.profile_page.plain_es: Una página por municipio con todos los conjuntos de datos del observatorio para ese lugar, agrupados por campo, con su posición entre los 78 municipios, el valor de Puerto Rico y su tendencia.
layers.profile_page.definition: Open it from a municipality on the map (the pop-up's 'Area profile' link or the Municipality tab) or as profile.html?area= and the municipio's five-digit code (72127 is San Juan). The page reads the same files as the Analysis tab. Each field of the registry has a table; each row is a dataset with its latest value as published and its margin of error, the value a shaded map compares (per 1,000 residents, per resident or a share), its rank among the municipios that have a value (1 is the highest), Puerto Rico's value on the same measure, and a trend line of up to 15 years. Datasets with no value for the place are left out, unless an empty place has a meaning (a shortage area: 'No area shortage designation'). A small map marks the municipio and its five similar municipios. 'Download CSV' saves the rows.
layers.profile_page.method: profile.js with Core.datasets (the list of files the Analysis tab also reads), Core.engine, Core.stats and Core.minimap. The page draws its first field (Housing) and the similar municipios as soon as their files arrive, then fetches the other files and draws every field; until then it says it is loading the other fields, and 'Download CSV' waits for them.
layers.profile_page.how_to_read: A rank says where the place stands among the municipios, not whether that is good: rank 1 in poverty is the highest poverty.
caveats: Datasets of different years sit side by side: read each row's year.
Survey values have margins of error; read them before comparing two places.

view.label: Area profile of San Juan

layers.chat.plain: 'Ask the observatory' is a chat box that answers questions about the Analysis tab's datasets, in English or Spanish. It is not a language model. Every answer is built from numbers computed in your browser, and nothing you type leaves your browser unless you choose to open the GitHub request form.
layers.chat.plain_es: "Preguntar al observatorio" es un chat que contesta preguntas sobre los conjuntos de datos de la pestaña Análisis, en inglés o en español. No es un modelo de lenguaje. Cada respuesta se arma con números calculados en el navegador, y nada de lo que se escribe sale del navegador, a menos que se decida abrir el formulario de solicitud de GitHub.
layers.chat.definition: 'Ask the observatory' answers questions about the datasets of the Analysis tab (562 in Snapshot 2026-10) and the map layers, in English or Spanish. Type up to 400 characters. Each answer is in the language of the question. A reply can hold text, small tables, links and buttons. It can also change the map: shade datasets, switch on layers, set the year, select a municipality, move the map to a place, shade the barrios of a municipality or open the workbench. When the observatory has no data for what you ask, the answer shows the nearest dataset and says that it is an approximation and what is missing. A question the chat cannot match, or answers only with an approximation, is saved on your device in a wishlist without asking, so do not type personal information. The codes below describe how to open it, what it remembers and what it can and cannot answer.
layers.chat.method: chat.js and ask.js. 1. The question is cleaned: accents and capitals are removed. In a short question, a word one letter from a topic of the observatory is read as that topic (two letters from eight letters on), and the answer says so. 2. Municipality names are found, and some well-known place names (Santurce, Isla Verde, Levittown) with their municipality. 3. chat.js's word list turns words into dataset keys, from specific phrases to general ones. 4. ask.js (loaded with the first question) reads the question again with a lexicon of everyday words in both languages, Puerto Rican ones included (guagua, carro público, la AMA, la AAA, la luz, cuido, chavos, derrumbes, envejecientes), the names of the map layers, the glossary terms and the words of the datasets' own names. It finds the topics that step 3 left, the layers, a time ("después de María" is 2017) and what must not be drawn. 5. Two topics are composed: a topic that a map layer shows (transit) turns that layer on, the other is shaded, and the answer gives the correlation of the two across municipalities. 6. Rules choose the kind of answer (see the entry on answer types). 7. A handler computes the answer from the Analysis tab's dataset values and writes the sentences from templates, with the source, period and geography of what it shows. No server is called. No language model is used.
layers.chat.how_to_read: Ask short questions that name a dataset: 'unemployment', 'rent', 'tourism jobs'. Add a municipality or a year to narrow the answer.
caveats: The chat matches words. An unusual phrasing can still fail, and a word can match a dataset by chance: the word 'bar', for example, selects restaurant and bar jobs.
Answers find patterns across places. They do not show causes.
An approximation is not the measure you asked for: the answer names what is missing (for example, there are no traffic data, so commutes of 45 minutes or more stand in).
Transit layers and vehicles follow scheduled timetables (GTFS), not live positions.

An answer that puts datasets on the map replaces the layers on the Analysis tab. It also switches off tourism places, transit routes, barrios, flood zones, protected areas and land use, unless the question names them. A question that names only layers adds them and leaves the rest as it is.
Sensitive places are counted, never drawn: the chat never shows shelters for victims of violence, a person's home or contact details, or health facilities as points.
When the chat saves a question, its reply says it added the request 'so the team can see what people ask for'. The request stays on your device unless you copy it or open the GitHub form.

values.Opening it: Press the 'Ask' button in the top bar of the 2D map, or a suggested question in the About tab. The window's language follows your browser at first and changes with the 'ES' or 'EN' button. The bin button clears the conversation.
values.Memory: The chat remembers the datasets, year and municipality of the last answer, so a follow-up such as 'Where is it highest?' works.
values.What it can answer: The datasets of the Analysis tab (562 in Snapshot 2026-10), found by their rules, by their own names in English and Spanish, by the words their dictionary entry lists for asking, or by everyday words (vivienda, transporte, guaguas, la luz). Two topics at once ('transporte y vivienda': the routes and stops, with rent shaded). A layer by its name or an everyday name ('rutas de guagua', 'zonas inundables', 'bomberos'), on the 2D map and the 3D view; on the 3D view also the terrain, the 3D buildings, the scheduled vehicles, the storm tracks and the routes by trips in the hour. A place and a topic ('pobreza en Santurce'); the barrios of a municipality ranked ('¿qué barrios de Ponce tienen más pobreza?') for datasets with barrio values; a municipality's own change in a trend. Two places or more side by side, a place's profile, a composite index. The definition of a glossary term ('¿qué es el margen de error?') and the source of a layer. 'What data is missing?' from the wanted-data list and 'How big is the database?' from the data inventory.
values.What it cannot answer: Questions about single tourism places, live transit positions, or topics the observatory has no data for (traffic, outages, diseases): for these it shows the nearest dataset, says it is an approximation and adds the question to the wishlist.

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask' in the top bar

layers.chat_correlation.plain: When you ask how two datasets relate, the chat measures how closely they move together across the municipalities. The number is called r and runs from −1 to 1. If the link is not weak, the chat names the biggest exceptions.
layers.chat_correlation.plain_es: Cuando se pregunta cómo se relacionan dos conjuntos de datos, el chat mide cuánto se mueven juntos entre los municipios. Ese número se llama r y va de −1 a 1. Si la relación no es débil, el chat nombra las excepciones más grandes.
layers.chat_correlation.definition: r is the Pearson correlation of the two datasets across the municipalities that have both values, and it needs at least 8. Each dataset is used in its default form: per 1,000 residents for counts, per resident for dollar totals and as published for the rest, in the latest year or the year you name. If the absolute value of r is below 0.3 the chat says the datasets 'show little relationship'. Above that it says they 'rise together' (r above 0) or 'move in opposite directions' (r below 0). When the absolute value of r is 0.3 or more, the answer also names up to three exceptions: the municipalities farthest from the line of best fit, which is the straight line that runs closest to all the dots. The 'patterns' answer is described below.
layers.chat_correlation.method: chat.js (chPearson, chInsights, Tools.correlate). The scatter chart of the workbench uses the same coefficient.
layers.chat_correlation.how_to_read: r is the Pearson correlation. 0 means no straight-line link between the two. 1 means the places line up perfectly. −1 means they line up in opposite directions. A strong r says the two move together across places.
caveats: A pattern across places is not proof that one thing causes the other. Large places, small samples and survey noise can drive it. The chat says this in its answer.
The rules about which pairs count as expected are a choice made in the code. They are not statistical tests.

The chat screens many pairs and shows the strongest, so some links arise by chance. Federal award and Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) Public Assistance figures per resident are among the 26 datasets, even though part of that money cannot be placed in a municipality and awards for the whole island are often booked to the capital. In the 2026-10 snapshot, the share of federal award dollars that name no municipality runs from 3.4% to 24.7% by fiscal year, and the share of Public Assistance recorded as statewide runs from 11.0% to 88.3% by declaration year. A link that involves them may reflect where money is booked, not need. When you do not name a year, each dataset uses its own latest year. Treat every result as a question to check, not a finding.

values.Patterns (the 'patterns' answer): The chat compares pairs of 26 datasets from different areas of life and lists at most five. The pairs, cut-offs and results are in the entry on the patterns ranking.

layers.chat_correlation.source_detail: economy_series.json and housing_series.json, read in your browser. The chat draws no credit line. Its 'sources' answer gives the source links.

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask' and try 'What are the most interesting patterns?'

layers.chat_answers.plain: The chat gives one of about twenty kinds of answer, chosen by rules from the words in your question. This entry lists them with an example of each.
layers.chat_answers.plain_es: El chat da uno de unos veinte tipos de respuesta, elegido mediante reglas a partir de las palabras de la pregunta. Esta ficha los enumera con un ejemplo de cada uno.
layers.chat_answers.definition: The rules look first for what must not be drawn (a shelter for victims of violence, a person's home, drug points) and for a term to define, then for clear words (clear, missing, patterns, size, help, sources, catalog), unless such a word is part of a topic ('agua limpia', 'ayuda federal'), then for two or more datasets with comparing words, then for trend words, then for ranking words. A municipality name alone gives its profile. One dataset with a municipality gives that municipality's value. Datasets without other words are shown on the map; layers without datasets are switched on. A bare year changes the year. Anything else falls to the last answer, which suggests datasets.
layers.chat_answers.method: chat.js (chIntent, chRefine and the Handlers) and ask.js. The answers use the same functions as the Analysis tab: values, ranks and the correlation.
layers.chat_answers.how_to_read: If an answer is not what you wanted, name the dataset more directly or open the Analysis tab.
caveats: A question can match more than one kind. The rules pick the first that fits, in the order given above.
The 'missing' list names candidate datasets that are not in the observatory. The source, license and terms of a candidate are not yet confirmed.

values.show: Name one to four datasets without comparing words, for example 'Show poverty and rent'. The chat puts them on the map (rates as shading, counts as sized symbols), then says where the first one is highest and lowest and what the Puerto Rico figure is. With two datasets it adds the correlation when it is 0.3 or stronger. A year in the question sets the year.
values.value: A dataset and a municipality, for example 'Unemployment in Ponce': the municipality's value, its place among the 78 (highest first) and the Puerto Rico value. For counts it also gives the per-resident view.
values.rank: Words such as highest, lowest, top, best, worst or 'where is': a table of the top municipalities and the Puerto Rico value. The table has 5 rows at the start. A number in the question ('top 10') sets the length, up to 15. For counts a second table gives the per-resident ranking. Words such as lowest, least, bottom or fewest turn the table around. The words best and worst do not change the order. Both return the highest values, so 'where is unemployment best?' returns the highest unemployment rates. Use lowest or least for the other end. With one municipality named ('¿dónde en Bayamón es más alto el alquiler?'), the table ranks its barrios when the dataset has barrio values, and the map is shaded by barrio; otherwise the answer gives the municipality's place among the 78 first.
values.compare: Two or more datasets with words such as related, versus, together or compare, for example 'Show poverty and unemployment together' or 'poverty vs rent': the correlation of the first two across municipalities, the biggest exceptions and a scatter plot.
values.trend: One dataset with words such as changed, since, trend or over time: Puerto Rico's change between the first and last year (or the years you name) and the three municipalities that rose most and fell most. Municipalities that start with a count below 50 or a dollar total below $100,000 are not ranked in these two lists. The numbers in the text use the dollars of each year, but for dollar datasets the map the chat opens is inflation-adjusted, so its colors and the sentences can disagree. If no municipality fell, the second list is headed 'Rose least'. The map shows the change since the first year and the trend chart opens. With one municipality named, the answer gives that municipality's change first and its place among the 78 by change, and selects it on the map.
values.municipality: A municipality name alone: a table of 12 indicators (population, poverty, median household income, unemployment rate, jobs, average pay, jobs per employed resident, government job share, tourism jobs share, long commutes, median rent and federal awards per resident) with its value, the Puerto Rico value and its place among the 78, and a line naming the ones where it is in the top or bottom five.
values.sources: Words such as sources, license, definition, 'what does X mean' or 'how is X measured' with one to three datasets: the definition, the years, source links with licenses, a button 'Open the full source details' for each dataset and a button 'Entry in the data dictionary' (in Spanish 'Entrada en el diccionario de datos') that opens the dictionary entry of the first dataset.
values.catalog: 'What data do you have?': the dataset groups with their counts, or the datasets on a topic you name (up to 14 listed). Buttons offer 'See everything that is missing' and 'Open the data dictionary'.
values.insights: Words such as patterns, interesting or surprising: where jobs concentrate, and up to five of the strongest links between datasets from different areas of life. Each can be shown on the map. The line about jobs and residents compares workplace jobs with residents. It can reflect employers that report all workers at one site as well as commuting. It is a lead, not a measure of commuting.
values.missing: 'What data is missing?' or 'wish list': the candidate datasets of the wanted-data list (30 in Snapshot 2026-10), grouped by theme, with status, update frequency and license, and the requests kept on your device.
values.size: 'How big is the database?': the size of the published data and the five biggest files.
values.year: A bare year such as '2019' sets the year control.
values.clear: 'Clear' or 'reset' empties the Analysis tab's layers and the selected municipality. Other map layers stay as they are.
values.help: 'Help' or a greeting: a short description and example questions.
values.fallback: Anything else: 'I could not match that to a dataset', the closest datasets by word overlap and any matching entries of the wanted-data list. A question with two or more content words is also added to the wishlist on your device.
values.layers: A layer named alone, for example 'Muestra las rutas de guagua' or 'zonas inundables en Toa Baja': the layer is switched on (it shows in the 'layers on' chip, and 'Turn all off' and Undo treat it like any other), the map moves to the place if one is named, and the answer says where the layer comes from and offers the datasets that go with it.
values.explain: 'What is X?' or 'qué significa X' for a glossary term: its definition and source, with a link to the glossary. For a layer: where it comes from.
values.sensitive: A question about a shelter for victims of violence, a person's home or contact details, or drug points: the answer says that the observatory never shows them, and draws nothing; for drug points it shows the reported crimes of the municipality.
values.nodata: A topic the observatory has nothing on (elections, places of worship, shelters): the answer says so, adds the question to the wishlist and offers the nearest layers as buttons.
values.crisis: A question about suicide, self-harm or overdose deaths: the answer says that the observatory has no data on this and gives the 988 line and, in Puerto Rico, the Línea PAS of ASSMCA (Administración de Servicios de Salud Mental y Contra la Adicción): 1-800-981-0023, 24 hours, free and confidential, or its chat at lineapas.assmca.pr.gov. Nothing is shaded, no place is ranked and the question is not a data wish. The treatment answer to 'near me' gives findtreatment.gov (SAMHSA) and the same two lines. Both answers end with the sources of that sentence, linked: ASSMCA's home page (https://assmca.pr.gov/), which states every fact of it (the number, 24 hours, free, confidential and the chat), and the Línea PAS site (https://lineapas.assmca.pr.gov/), which states the number, 24 hours and the chat; checked 2026-10-21. The glossary term Línea PAS cites ASSMCA's Línea PAS page (https://assmca.pr.gov/linea-pas).

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask' and try 'Where is unemployment highest?'

layers.chat_privacy.plain: The chat runs in your browser. What you type is not sent to Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) or to any other server, unless you press the button that opens the GitHub request form. Two small items are kept on your device: your language choice and a wishlist of questions the chat could not answer.
layers.chat_privacy.plain_es: El chat funciona en el navegador. Lo que se escribe no se envía a Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR) ni a ningún otro servidor, a menos que se oprima el botón que abre el formulario de solicitud de GitHub. Se guardan dos datos pequeños en el dispositivo: el idioma elegido y una lista de preguntas que el chat no pudo contestar.
layers.chat_privacy.definition: The chat reads the observatory's own data files and makes no other call. It keeps one item in your browser's storage: a wishlist (twin.wishlist.v1) of up to 50 questions it could not answer, each with the date. The language you chose is kept by the page, not by the chat (twin.lang, in local storage and, for the current visit, in session storage). You can see the wishlist in the answer to 'What data is missing?'. The conversation itself is not stored. It is gone when you close or reload the page. The one place where text you type leaves the page is the online address lookup of the search box. It is not part of the chat. The codes below describe the two buttons that sit under the wishlist.
layers.chat_privacy.method: chat.js (chAddWish, chCopyWish, chIssueUrl). The issue address is https://github.com/Foundation-for-Puerto-Rico/pr-data-observatory/issues/new with the title and body in the address, so you can read the text before you submit.
layers.chat_privacy.how_to_read: Do not type personal information into the chat. It is not needed, and it would be kept in your wishlist if the chat could not answer.
caveats: Clearing the site data in your browser removes the wishlist.
Page loads still send the usual requests (the page's own files, fonts, libraries and map tiles) to other servers, which can see your IP address.
The GitHub button sends the wishlist text to GitHub when the new tab opens, before you submit the form. See the codes below.

The 'See in 3D' button opens the 3D view with your question in the address after the '#' sign. That part of an address is not sent to any server, but it stays in the browser's history, and in the link if you copy it.

values.Copy button: Copies the wishlist text so that you can paste it where you choose.
values.GitHub button: Opens GitHub in a new tab with your unanswered questions already in the web address, so GitHub receives that text when the tab opens, before you submit anything. No issue exists until you submit the form. An issue you submit on GitHub can be seen by others, depending on the repository's settings. Remove any personal information from the list before you press the button.

view.label: 2D map: press 'Ask'

data.dictionary.plain: The whole data dictionary in one file: every entry, source record and glossary term. The data dictionary page reads smaller files made from it. You can download it and use the dictionary in your own tools.
data.dictionary.plain_es: Todo el diccionario de datos en un archivo: cada entrada, cada registro de fuente y cada término del glosario. La página del diccionario de datos lee archivos más pequeños hechos a partir de él. Se puede descargar para usar el diccionario en herramientas propias.
data.dictionary.definition: dictionary.json is a JSON file (a standard text format for structured data) with 12 parts: built, snapshot, snapshot_built, domains, kinds, entries, sources, aliases, id_alias, glossary, domain_info and coverage. 'entries' has one record for each documented dataset, variable, map layer, boundary, category, measure and method. 'sources' has one record for each source of data or software. 'glossary' has one record for each term or abbreviation. The table of codes describes each part.
data.dictionary.method: dictionary.py reads the dictionary's entry files, source records and glossary, adds the names, units, years and sources that the economy and housing series catalogs already hold, reports any published data field that has no entry, and writes one compact JSON file with no spaces. Entries are sorted by area, group and name. A second, much smaller file, dictionary_summary.json, holds only the counts that the About tab shows. dictionary.py also writes, from the same content, the files the dictionary page reads (docs/performance.md): dictionary_list.json, read first, with the list, the filters, the sources, the glossary and the words the search looks in; and one file for each top-level domain, dictionary_detail_<domain>.json, with the rest of each entry (the whole summaries, definition, method, how to read it, cautions, codes, related entries and where it appears), which the page fetches the first time an entry of that domain is opened, printed or exported.
data.dictionary.how_to_read: Download it to use the dictionary in your own tools. Find an item in 'entries' by its id, which is also the part of the page address after the # sign (for example dictionary.html#roads.network). The ids in an entry's 'sources' list are keys of the 'sources' part. When you cite the file, give its 'snapshot' label and its 'built' date.
caveats: The file describes the data of the snapshot named in 'snapshot'. Its 'built' date can be later than 'snapshot_built', because the dictionary is rebuilt on its own as well as at the end of a full build.
Figures in the entry text (counts, shares, sizes) come from a particular snapshot or file and carry its date. Check the date before you reuse a figure.

Entries describe the observatory's data, not the original sources. Each source keeps its own license and terms. The 'sources' records give the license as the publisher states it, which is not legal advice.
No license is stated for the dictionary text itself. It is FPR work.
dictionary_summary.json is a separate small file with the counts the About tab shows: entries, data sources and glossary terms. It is not a copy of the dictionary.

values.built: Date the file was written, as YYYY-MM-DD.
values.snapshot: Label of the data snapshot the dictionary describes, copied from meta.json (for example 'Snapshot 2026-10').
values.snapshot_built: Date of the full build of that snapshot, as YYYY-MM-DD (the first ten characters of generated_at in meta.json).
values.domains: The ten areas used to group entries, in display order.
values.kinds: The seven kinds of entry: variable, layer, table, boundary, category, measure and method.
values.entries: List of entry records. Each has id, name, domain, group, kind, plain, definition, unit, value_type, geography, coverage, method, sources, where and added, and may have source_detail, how_to_read, caveats, see_also, values, example and status. 'authored' is true when an author wrote the entry and false when a series catalog filled it.
values.sources: One record for each source, keyed by its id: kind (data or software), name, publisher, url, license, licence_url, credit (the credit line), access, cadence, used_for, terms_note, verified (when its link was last checked) and used_by (how many entries cite it).
values.aliases: Older source ids and the canonical id each one stands for, for example 'osm_roads' for 'osm'. Entries and meta.json can use an older id.
values.id_alias: Economy series ids that share one entry with a housing series, so that a link with either id opens the same entry.
values.glossary: List of terms and abbreviations: term, expansion, plain explanation and see_also links.
values.domain_info: Optional descriptions of the areas. Empty in the file written on 2026-10-04.
values.coverage: Two lists the build checks: 'undocumented' (published data fields with no entry) and 'unauthored' (series variables with no hand-written entry). Both were empty in the file written on 2026-10-04.

data.dictionary.source_detail: dictionary.py (build); the entries, sources and glossary written by Foundation for Puerto Rico (FPR); the observatory's own build step, not an external source

view.label: Data dictionary (the page built from this file)
Data dictionary: table of published data files

layers.data_dictionary_page.plain: The data dictionary page explains every dataset, variable, map layer and measure in the observatory: what it means, where it comes from, how it is worked out and what to watch out for. You can search it, filter it, copy a citation, download tables and read the sources, licenses and glossary.
layers.data_dictionary_page.plain_es: La página del diccionario de datos explica cada conjunto de datos, variable, capa del mapa y medida del observatorio: qué significa, de dónde viene, cómo se calcula y qué precauciones tomar. Permite buscar, filtrar, copiar una cita, descargar tablas y leer las fuentes, las licencias y el glosario.
layers.data_dictionary_page.definition: The page opens with a search box and four counts: documented items, data sources, glossary terms and published data files. 'Browse the dictionary' lists the entries by area and group. You can narrow the list with the search box and with these filters: area, source, kind (variable, map layer, published table, boundary, category, measure or method), time (one snapshot, every year, five-year windows, every ten years, by event, live, or not tied to a year), geography (the level of the published files an item describes), year covered, license of the sources (the strictest class among an item's sources) and 'Has margins of error'. A click on an entry opens it. An entry starts with a plain description and a list of facts: unit, type, geography, years, updates, area, kind and the date it was added. It then gives the definition, how it is computed, how to read it, cautions, codes, sources with their licenses, where it appears in the observatory (links to the views and to the data files you can download) and related entries. Three buttons end an entry: Cite, Copy link and, for yearly series, Download all years (CSV), which saves a file in comma-separated values (CSV) form. Four more sections follow the entries: Sources and licenses, Glossary, Published data files (a summary that links to the Data management page) and How to cite. The map, the 3D view and the Housing page each have a 'Data dictionary' link in their top bar.
layers.data_dictionary_page.method: dictionary.js builds the page in your browser. dictionary.py writes data/dictionary.json from the entry files, the source records and the glossary, with the names, units, years and sources that the economy and housing series catalogs already hold, and makes from it the files the page reads: data/dictionary_list.json, read first, with the list, the filters, the sources, the glossary and the words the search looks in, and data/dictionary_detail_<domain>.json, the rest of the entries of one top-level domain, fetched the first time one of them is opened (the entry says it is loading until then). Downloading the dictionary or printing the page fetches the detail files still missing. It also reads data/registry.json for the counts of the published data files and the geography level of each file, and the page works without it if the file does not load. The search removes accents and capitals from your words and keeps the entries that contain all of them. With a search the list is flat, and entries are sorted by how well the words match: a match in the name counts most, then the id, the group and the plain description. An entry's body is built the first time you open it. The filters are written into the page address as q, domain, source, kind, time, moe=1 and file, so you can share a filtered list.
layers.data_dictionary_page.how_to_read: Read the plain description first and then the cautions, which say what a number does not mean. Numbers quoted in entries come from the snapshot named in the top bar and change when the observatory is rebuilt. Definitions and methods do not. To cite a variable, open its entry and press Cite. To send a reader to an entry, press Copy link.
caveats: The page needs JavaScript. Without it the page shows a message and no entries.

Search needs every word to match. It looks in the id, name, area, group, kind, descriptions, method, unit, geography, source details, cautions and source names. It does not look in the codes tables, the related links or the glossary. A misspelt word finds nothing.

A citation names the snapshot and the original sources, and it uses the day you press Cite as the access date. The license text in the sources section is what each source states, not legal advice. Check the source's own terms before you reuse its data.
The page's introduction says the observatory uses public data, most of it under an open license. Not all: some sources state no license (the Data management page names them for each file).

A yearly-series file holds the values as published, with no inflation adjustment and no rescaling. A margin-of-error column appears only when the source publishes margins. A value the source does not give is an empty cell.
Print opens every entry in the current list and hides the top bar, the side panel, the filters and the buttons. A long list makes a long printout, so filter first.
Sizes of the published data files are in kilobytes of 1,024 bytes and megabytes of 1,048,576 bytes. Entries that give a size in megabytes of 1 million bytes read about 5% larger for the same file.

values.Search box: Type words such as poverty or flood. The list updates after a short pause. The x button empties the box.
values.Area: Ten areas, for example Housing, Hazards and environment or Map layers and tools. The same areas are buttons in the left column. Each choice shows how many items it holds.
values.Source: Every source that at least one item uses, with the number of items. The button 'Show the N dictionary items that use it' on a source card sets the same filter.
values.Kind: Variable, Map layer, Published table, Boundary, Category, Measure or Method. Only kinds that have items are listed.
values.Time: One snapshot, Every year, Five-year windows, Every ten years, By event, Live, or Not tied to a year. Only choices that have items are listed.
values.Geography: The level of the published data files that an item describes: whole island, municipality, barrio, census block, points (places and stops), lines (routes), areas or network. An item that describes no file (a method, for example) has none. Only levels that have items are listed, with the number of items.
values.Covers year: Keeps the items whose years include the year you pick. The list runs from 2000 to the snapshot year, with 'Before 2000' (storm tracks start in 1851) and 'Projections' (sea level scenarios run to 2100). A snapshot counts for its own year only.
values.License of the sources (strictest): Keeps the items whose most restrictive source has the class you pick: open, open with conditions, FPR's own, not stated, or licensed and not open. It describes the sources an item uses, as recorded in the sources list, not a legal review. Open the entry to see which source sets the class.
values.Has margins of error: Keeps only the series whose source publishes margins of error. In Snapshot 2026-10 all of them are American Community Survey series.
values.Data-file filter: On the Data management page, the link in the 'Documented by' column lists only the items that describe that file. The address then carries file=<name>. This filter has no menu of its own.
values.Reset filters: Clears the search and every filter, including the data-file filter.
values.Expand all and Collapse all: Expand all opens the first 60 entries of the list and says so when the list is longer. Collapse all closes every entry.
values.Cite: Opens a panel with four formats (Credit line, APA 7, Chicago and BibTeX) and a Copy button. The credit line names the sources and the snapshot. The APA 7, Chicago and BibTeX texts also give the address of the entry, the original sources and the date you pressed Cite. The panel repeats the credit lines of the sources underneath.
values.Copy link: Copies the address of the entry, for example dictionary.html#economy.qcew_jobs. The button then reads 'Link copied'.
values.Download all years (CSV): Only on the entries that describe a yearly series (a field of economy_series.json or housing_series.json). File pr_digital_twin_<id>.csv, with each dot of the id turned into an underscore. Columns: GEOID (the geographic identifier code), Municipality and one column for each year. A margin-of-error column follows each year when the source publishes margins. The file has 79 rows: the 78 municipalities and Puerto Rico (GEOID 72).
values.Download the dictionary (CSV): File pr_digital_twin_data_dictionary.csv, with one row for each entry whatever the filters on the page. See the entry on CSV and GeoJSON downloads for its columns.
values.Links that open an entry: dictionary.html#<id> opens that entry and scrolls to it, for example dictionary.html#economy.qcew_jobs. If a filter hides the entry, the filters are cleared first. An economy id that shares an entry with a housing series (for example economy.poverty_pct) opens the shared entry. Other anchors are #browse, #sources, #glossary, #files, #cite and #src-<source id> for one source card.
values.Sources and licenses: One card for each source: publisher, license or terms, credit line (with a Copy button), how the observatory gets the data, how often it changes, what the observatory uses it for, good to know, and when its link and license were last checked ('Link and license checked', 'Link works; license wording unclear', 'Link did not respond when checked' or 'Not yet checked'). A menu separates data sources from base maps, libraries and tools. 'Find a source' searches names, publishers, licenses, uses and credit lines.
values.Glossary: Terms, abbreviations and Spanish words in A to Z order, with a letter strip. Each term has a plain explanation and, where useful, links to entries.
values.Published data files: A summary of the files in the observatory's data folder: their number, total size and share of the hosting limit (1 gigabyte for a GitHub Pages site), and the records and values of the data files, with a link to the Data management page, which lists each file. A note below explains that the folder only grows.
values.How to cite: A citation of the observatory as a whole in the same four formats, and five points of good practice: name the snapshot, name the year of the data, keep the unit, share the view, and note that some data have extra terms.
values.Print: Prints every entry in the current list, opened, without the top bar, the side panel, the filters and the buttons. Entries avoid breaking across pages.

layers.data_dictionary_page.source_detail: dictionary_list.json and the dictionary_detail files (made from dictionary.json), registry.json, economy_series.json and housing_series.json, read in your browser. Citations use the credit lines and licenses in the source records. The page draws no credit line of its own. Icons: Material Symbols (Google), Apache License 2.0.

Data dictionary: an entry opened by its address (jobs on the Analysis tab)
Data dictionary: sources and licenses
Data dictionary: glossary

Data dictionary: how to cite

layers.data_management_page.plain: The Data management page lists every data file the observatory publishes, with its records, fields, values, size, the dates it was first published and last updated, the dictionary items that document it and its compliance review. It also shows how the data grew over time and counts what is not published.
layers.data_management_page.plain_es: La página de Gestión de datos lista cada archivo de datos que publica el observatorio, con sus registros, campos, valores, tamaño, las fechas de su primera publicación y de su última actualización, los elementos del diccionario que lo documentan y su revisión de cumplimiento. También muestra cómo crecieron los datos con el tiempo y cuenta lo que no se publica.
layers.data_management_page.definition: The page opens with six figures: published files, size (with its share of the 1 GB GitHub Pages limit), records, values, documented items and the last update. The table of published data files has the columns File (a download link), What it holds, Domain, Records, Fields, Values, Size, First published, Last updated, Documented by (a link to the file's entries in the data dictionary) and Compliance review, a totals row for the files shown, a text filter, filters by kind and by review, sorting on every column and a download of what is shown as a comma-separated values (CSV) file. The Growth section draws one total at a time by date, with a table of every date. 'What is not published' gives counts only, each with its rule. The Definitions section defines record, field, value, vertex, size, the two dates, documented by, compliance review and the totals.
layers.data_management_page.method: datamgmt.js builds the page in your browser from data/registry.json (registry.py and ledger.py). It loads no other data file.
layers.data_management_page.how_to_read: Sort by Values to see where the data points are, by Last updated to see what changed recently and by Compliance review to see what still needs a review. The totals row adds the files shown. Records, fields and values are counted for data files only.
caveats: The page needs JavaScript. Without it the page shows a message.
Documentation and index files are listed and sized, not counted.
Sizes use 1 MB = 1,048,576 bytes.

The page is public and open to search engines (since 2026-10-20). It is read-only: it is generated from the observatory's repository at each build, and only the Foundation for Puerto Rico team can change the data, through reviewed changes.
layers.data_management_page.source_detail: registry.json, read in your browser. Icons: Material Symbols (Google), Apache License 2.0.
